en: The Mahāvastu Avadāna, First Section. The Mahāvastu Avadāna. Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Great Buddha, and to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The beginning of the Mahāvastu: There are these four practices of the Bodhisattvas.
Which four?
The practice of the natural state, the practice of aspiration, the practice of conformity, and the practice of non-retrogression. Homage to the Tathāgata Aparājitadhvaja,

the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, in whose presence this very Śākyamuni, while still in the cycle of existence and having become a universal monarch (*cakravartin* king), first planted the roots of merit while engaged in the practice of the natural state.

Homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One of the past, in whose presence this very Blessed One Śākyamuni first made his root-of-merit vow while engaged in the initial course of conduct for the vow as a preeminent merchant, [vowing]:
"O, may I in a future time become a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Awakened One; and just as this Blessed One Śākyamuni is, may my name also be Śākyamuni," and so forth in detail.
"May it even come to pass that Kapilavastu shall become my city as well."

Homage to the Tathāgata Samitāvin, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, in whose presence this very Blessed One Śākyamuni, while he was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) established in the practice of conformity (*anulomacaryā*), made a conforming vow (*anulomapraṇidhāna*). [What is the practice of turning back?]
Homage to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One,
by whom this Blessed One was first prophesied thus:
"Young man, in a future time, after immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite eons, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a Perfectly Awakened One."
I shall set forth in detail the prophecy concerning the young brahmin Megha, within the section on the "Lamp" subject matter.

From this point onward, during his practice of non-retrogression, he was successively prophesied by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and by immeasurable Tathāgatas thereafter, saying: "You shall become a Buddha."
Thereafter, the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū also prophesied:

"O monk Abhijit, in a future time, after a hundred thousand kalpas, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni," and so forth; thus I shall relate in detail the prophecy concerning the monk Abhijit.
Homage to Vipaśyin, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Homage to Krakucchanda, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Homage to Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
By that Blessed One, this very Blessed Śākyamuni was prophesied and consecrated in the position of crown prince:

"Jyotiṣpāla, in a future time immediately after me, you shall become the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni. Thus I shall set forth in detail the prophecy concerning the monk Jyotiṣpāla.
Thus: Homage to the perfectly awakened ones of the past, future, and present.
The introductory salutations are completed.
The beginning of the Mahāvastu from the Vinayapiṭaka, according to the recension of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins of the Middle Country.
There are four kinds of full ordination: full ordination by one's own [nature], full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula, full ordination by a group of ten, and full ordination by a group of five.
There, they were ordained by self-ordination; indeed, they were fully ordained at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the presence of the Blessed Ones.
Those who, having undertaken them, abide by the ten paths of wholesome action, become much closer to awakening.
And even there, he is preeminent.

Thus, for the sake of being disciplined by a Buddha, having practiced these very good deeds and approached Dīpaṃkara in due succession among millions of living beings, he saw him— wonderful to behold, serene in every way, inspiring confidence, and surrounded by a community of disciples— and conceived a longing thought: "It would be well if I, having surpassed the world itself, were to move through the world for the sake of the world and be born for the benefit of this world."

Having understood his attainment of perfect awakening and his firm resolve, the Self-Existent One, in brief, prophesied [his enlightenment] on the basis of equality with himself and equality with all self-arisen ones.
In the future, after an immeasurable time, you will become a Buddha in the Śākya clan as the son of the Śākyas, for the sake of gods and humans.
Thus was he prophesied by the Blessed One, the Supreme among Men, the Lion among Men, as the foremost of men, a true man, who has practiced the conduct of the Supreme Man.
Thus, seeking the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva wanders through cyclic existence for the sake of the world and for his own sake.
Whatever gift, ethical discipline, commitment, or fast he practices, he does so free from stinginess while seeking the benefit of the world.
Through the four means of attraction—generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and sharing in both joy and sorrow—the Victor encompasses all sentient beings.

There was nothing whatsoever that he did not give away, whatever was present at hand. And upon seeing a beggar, his mind becoming even more serene, he repeatedly gave away his eyes and his flesh, his wife and children, his wealth and grain, and even himself and his life— by this means, through many tens of millions of births.

For thousands of aeons the Bodhisattva wandered through saṃsāra, contemplating the welfare of beings; knowing the proper time as it truly is, skilled in the knowledge of the superior and inferior qualities of individuals, and awaiting the right moment, he approached the Tuṣita realm.
In the Tuṣita abode, the Sugata—who brings an end to existence—cultivating the realization that existence is impermanent, entered his final birth.

For the sake of liberation from existence, the Blessed One practiced austerities that were extremely difficult, subsisting on only a single sesame seed or a single jujube fruit until he became exceedingly emaciated.

Realizing that this was not the path to liberation, though his body was suffering extreme pain, at the time of the river’s flow, he bathed in the river Nairañjanā. Then, in the foremost city called Gayā, he sat down like an undaunted lion.
During the first watch of the night, having thoroughly purified his divine eye, the Blessed One directly knew the various destinies and transmigrations of sentient beings.
In the middle watch of the night, you recollect your former dwellings; you have directly known, in many ways, the former dwellings of others and of yourself.
And in the final watch of the night, whatever is to be known by the Charioteer of Men to be Tamed, all that the Self-Existent One fully awakens to in a single moment, in its state of equality.
Thus ends the introductory verses of the glorious Mahāvastu.

The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having realized the purpose for which he had come forth, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery—the teacher of gods and humans; [the account of] the introduction and the occasion is to be told in detail.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys through the hells.
There he sees beings in the eight great hells, each with its sixteen secondary hells, undergoing many thousands of various kinds of hellish sufferings.

And I, the Venerable Elder Kolita, while wandering on a tour of the hells, saw beings experiencing many sufferings in the hells. In the Saṃjīva hell, they were with their feet upward and heads downward, being consumed by axes and hatchets.
Others, with malicious thoughts and intentions toward one another, tore each other apart with iron claws; sharp sword-blades appeared in their hands, with which they cut one another’s limbs.
And they do not die as long as their evil karmas have not been fully exhausted.
In the Kālasūtra great hell, he saw beings whose limbs were marked with black threads, being struck and exhausted, being split apart with axes, and being split apart with saws.
And although their bodies are cut and hacked, they heal again; they experience unpleasant sensations, yet they do not die because they are sustained by karma.

In the Saṃghāta great hell as well, he saw thousands of beings being crushed by mountains that were blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame; rivers of blood flowed forth, and those mountains repeatedly closed upon them, yet they did not die for such a long time because their karma sustained them.
He saw thousands of beings cast into the Raurava hell, amidst dense masses of copper that were blazing, aflame, and glowing with fire, and enveloped in smoke, experiencing thousands of sufferings.

And in the Mahāraurava hell, amidst a fire that was blazing, aflame, and glowing, he heard the sound of those who had been cast therein crying out with great screams; that sound was echoed back by the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, which surround the four great continents.
It comes within the range of hearing of humans in Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru.

In the Tapana hell, he saw many thousands of beings experiencing exclusively painful sensations; from their heels up to the nape of their necks, they were being pounded with iron hammers and undergoing thousands of other sufferings, yet they did not die so long as their karma remained to support them.
In that great hell, which was blazing, aflame, and glowing with light, many thousands of beings were reborn, experiencing painful sensations.

In that great hell, which is a hundred yojanas on all sides, thousands of flames arise from the eastern wall and strike against the western wall; thousands of flames arise from the western wall and strike against the eastern wall; arising from the southern wall, they strike against the northern wall.
Rising up toward the north, they strike back toward the south;
rising up from the ground, they strike down upon the surface; rising up from the surface, they strike back down upon the ground.
Those thousands of beings fall down from all sides, yet they do not die for such a long time because they are propped up by their karma.
In the Pratāpa great hell, mountains are blazing, aflame, and turned into fire;
those mountains are traversed by the hell-beings who are pierced by spikes.
They experience such sufferings and pass away for such a length of time because they are sustained by their karma.
Released from that great hell, they plunge into the Kukkula (Chaff) hell;
and there, being burned in the chaff, those people run about, yet they do not die because they are sustained by their karma.
Released from the *kukkuḷa* hell, they plunge into the *kuṇapa* (corpse) hell;
there they are devoured by black creatures with iron mouths, yet they do not die because they are propped up by their karma.
Released from the heaps of corpses in hell, they see delightful trees and forest glades; seeking happiness, they run toward those forest glades.
There too, hawks, vultures, crows, and owls with iron beaks tear away the flesh from the fresh trees and devour it.
Although their bones remain as mere remnants, the skin, flesh, and blood are produced once again, yet they do not die because they are propped up by their karma.
Terrified by those birds, they perceive what is not a refuge to be a refuge, and enter the Forest of Sword-Leaves and the Hell-Pot.
Furthermore, for those who have entered there, winds blow that cause sharp sword-leaves to fall;

these strike the limbs of those beings so that not even a single part of their body remains unscarred, not even a space the size of the tip of a hair. Yet, they do not die because they are sustained by the power of their karma.
Wounded and lying there, their bodies smeared with blood, those beings plunge into the Vaitaraṇī river—a harsh river of caustic lye—which pierces even their most delicate limbs;
yet they do not die, because they are propped up by their karma.

Then the hell-wardens, having pulled them out from there with iron hooks onto the riverbank— onto ground that was ablaze, set on fire, and become a mass of glowing heat— spoke thus to those who were cast down.
"Aha! O men, what do you desire?"
They spoke thus:
We are hungry; we are thirsty.

Then those hell-guardians force open their mouths with iron pincers that are blazing, glowing, and radiant; they heat iron bars until they are blazing, glowing, and radiant, and having forced open their own mouths, they cast red-hot, blazing, and radiant iron balls into them.
May you enjoy that.
And they cause him to drink molten copper along with salt.
May you drink!

As it blows, it burns the lip; having burned the lip, it burns the tongue; having burned the tongue, it burns the palate; having burned the palate, it burns the throat; having burned the throat, it burns the intestines; having burned the intestines, it takes up the mesentery and passes out through the lower part. Yet they do not die at that time because they are propped up by their karma.

Thus, having seen sentient beings experiencing thousands of sufferings in the eight great hells, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana exclaimed, "Alas, what misery! and returning to the Jeta Grove, he related the matter in detail to the fourfold assembly.
In this way, beings experience thousands of various sufferings in the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary hells.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must perform what is wholesome, one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having thus heard this from the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, many thousands of beings, both gods and humans, were struck with wonder.
(8) Thus, in brief, is the description of the hells.
I shall also describe it in detail.
The Fully Awakened One himself beheld this world and the world beyond, the coming and going of beings, and the cycle of death and rebirth.
Reflecting upon the fruitfulness of actions dependent on living beings and their ripening according to their respective places, the Sage himself realized this.
Having directly known them, Gautama declared the eight hells;
the Blessed One, who has realized the Dharma through direct perception, possesses the eye regarding all phenomena.
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, and the two Rauravas;
then further Mahāvīci, Tapana, and Pratāpana.
Thus these eight hells have been described, difficult to escape;
they are crowded with those of fierce deeds and each has sixteen secondary hells (utsada).
It has four sides and four gates, divided and measured into sections;
it rises a hundred yojanas high and extends for a hundred yojanas all around.
Encircled by iron walls and covered with iron,
their ground is made of iron, blazing and filled with intense heat.
The dwellings were spacious with ploughs made of solid iron, difficult to approach,
hair-raising in appearance, terrifying, formidable, and painful.
All of them are most terrifying, filled with hundreds of flames;
each one shines forth, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Where many beings, fierce and doers of great evil,
are tormented for a long time, even for hundreds of years.
With iron staffs, the thick-walled guardians of hell strike those enemies who have committed evil deeds.
I shall proclaim their names to you in due order;
listen with respect and attention as I speak.
In the Saṃjīva hell, beings are suspended with their feet upward and heads downward,
and are then carved with adzes and axes.
Then, driven by the power of anger and filled with rage, they quarrel with one another using their own sharp, self-arisen iron claws.
And another of them was born with sharp razors in their hands,
by which they cut one another, being possessed of wicked minds.
Their limbs fail them when struck by cold winds;
yet, due to the ripening of their past karma, their entire bodies continue to burn.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared that Saṃjīva is the abode of those who perform evil deeds.
(10) Released from Saṃjīva, they plunge into Kukūla;
having come together, they are struck [there] over a long, vast, and extensive expanse.
They indeed run there for many yojanas,
being burned by the glowing embers and experiencing manifold suffering.
Released from the Kukkula hell, you plunge into the Kuṇapa hell;
there, with your manly strength destroyed, you lie upon a corpse vast and long of limb.
Then those black creatures, harsh with mouths as sharp as fire and feeding on flesh and blood, pierce the skin and devour him.
Having emerged from the corpse-pit, the beautiful trees,
green and covered with foliage, come toward them as they seek happiness.
Then hawks, vultures, and crows with iron beaks,
having torn it from the moist tree, devour it while it is still dripping with blood.
And when they have been devoured until only the bones remain,
their skin, flesh, and blood grow once again.
Terrified, they leapt up, perceiving a refuge where there was no refuge,
and approached the dreadful Forest of Sword-leaves while being struck down.
(11) Then, wounded, distressed, and smeared with much blood, they leave the Forest of Sword-Leaves and go to the Vaitaraṇī River.
Therefore, they plunge into that river of heated alkaline water;
and their limbs are pierced through one by one as they are wounded.
Then the servants of Yama, having pierced them with iron hooks and lifted them up,
force them to eat glowing iron balls on the banks of the river.
They cause copper and bronze to be melted down;
having taken that as their food, it passes out through the lower part of the body.
Having followed the wrong path and failing to perform wholesome deeds, you shall go to the hells as a result of these evil actions.
Those who thoroughly avoid evil deeds and whose conduct is exclusively wholesome do not go to an unfortunate rebirth.
Therefore, since karma has two forms— the auspicious and the evil—
one should avoid evil deeds and practice what is auspicious and pure.
In the Kālasūtra hell, they are stripped like moist trees;
having been marked with lines, their limbs are cut with adzes and axes.
Then iron plates, heated for a long time,
were wrapped around his limbs, burning and afflicting them.
Having been burned and crushed, the iron plates are opened wide;
they tear away the skin and flesh, and spread out the blood.
Then, having split [the body] from the heels up to the nape of the neck,
he is crushed violently even many times in the Kālasūtra hell.
In that terrible darkness where no news can be seen,
they descend into that hell amidst masses of smoke.
And they run there for many yojanas,
trampling one another at the boundaries through the power of supreme mantras.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
shall describe this Kālasūtra, the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
And in the Saṃghāta hell, great mountains descend from above;
into the space between them, beings are driven like deer.
Those mountains also, coming together through the causal condition of the karma of sentient beings,
afflict many living beings like masses of fire.
From their tormented limbs, much blood flowed forth;
and amidst the upheaval of their bodies, rivers of pus began to surge.
And in iron troughs with iron pestles,
enemies are crushed for even many hundreds of years.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared this hidden abode of those who perform evil deeds.
In the Raurava hell, a great multitude of people are confined;
as the fire blazes forth, they utter a terrifying cry.
And when the fire goes out, they then become silent;
but when the fire has flared up again, they roar with a great sound.
And the second is declared to be Raurava, which causes the hair to stand on end; it is a hell with boundless shores, profound and impossible to cross.
There, seizing their staffs, the stout wardens of hell torment their enemies for many hundreds of years.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
declared Raurava to be the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
In the Tapanīya hell, heated iron is raised up;
and those who cry out are tormented by sufferings equal to a mass of fire.
There, a great multitude of people of evil conduct,
who have committed sinful deeds and performed wicked acts, are confined and cooked.
As soon as it is cooked and thoroughly boiled, many dogs—
large-bodied, powerful, and feeders on flesh and blood— devour it.
And when they have been devoured until only the bones remain,
then their skin, flesh, and blood are produced once more.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
declared this place of torment to be the abode of those who perform evil deeds.
In the Pratāpana hell, there are iron-tipped spears with iron points;
there is a mountain, terrifying and fearsome, consisting of a great mass of fire.
There, the multitude of people, shrouded in evil conduct,
wander about with their sinful deeds, like cats moving among gravel.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared Pratāpana to be the dwelling place of those who perform evil deeds.
Then there is Avīci, a place of suffering that is exclusively and intensely bitter;
it is vast, scorched by heat, and enveloped by a multitude of flames.
Just as iron balls are heated in a fire,
so too is the Avīci hell below, above, and on all sides.
The bodies of those dwelling in hell are equal to fire;
they perceive the firmness of their own karma, and therefore they do not experience fear.
And seeing the door opened, they rush toward it,
for even there is an exit for those who seek liberation.
And those for whom evil karma committed in the past has not yet ripened do not obtain release from hell, due to the condition of that karma.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared Avīci to be the abode of those who commit evil deeds.
The one named Saṃjīva.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who in this world have been rivals, or those who harbor enmity, or enemies—whether enemies over fields, enemies over property, or enemies over embankments—or rival kings, or thieves, who, having gone into battle, die after having harbored hostile thoughts toward one another; it is as the ripening of that karma that beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil, unwholesome karmas.
As the ripening of what karma do they diminish?
Those living beings who, while alive here, are carved with adzes, axes, and hatchets, are cut down as the ripening of that karma.
As the ripening of what karma does a cold wind blow upon them?

(16) Those who here gave fodder and food to jackals, buffaloes, pigs, and chickens, thinking, "I shall kill them for their meat," as the ripening of that karma, nails grow on the hands of those [beings], or iron clubs [appear]. Just as weapons and vehicles were given here, so you [shall be commanded]: "With these weapons, slay such-and-such a village, city, or town, or men, or animals."
Or, as the ripening of that karma, staves or swords grow from their hands like crows.
By whom was this Saṃjīva [created]?
There, those denizens of hell think to themselves: "This is Saṃjīva (Reviving) and Kālasūtra (Black Line); therefore, this is the Saṃjīva hell."
The one named Kālasūtra.
That hell extends as far as those with weapons in hand, even unto where it is filled with light.
There, the hell-guardians, having placed those denizens of hell against a moist tree, carve them according to the black cord into eight parts, six parts, or four parts.

Now, some go cutting [the bodies] like stalks of sugarcane, starting from the heels up to the nape of the neck; others, however, go cutting like stalks of sugarcane, starting from the nape of the neck down to the heels.
Being in such a state, they experience excessively painful sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
(17) By the ripening of what desire are beings reborn there?

Those who here are bound by means of elephant-irons and such, or are made to perform labor, [being commanded]: "Cut off so many hands! Cut off so many feet! Cut off the noses of so many! Tear out the sinews and flesh of so many! Tear out the arms of so many! Tear out the flesh of the backs of so many!"—whether five times or ten times—by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil, unwholesome karmas.
There, those denizens of hell, being beaten and reviled by the guardians of hell, cried out, "We are burning! (sabhussū).
Terrified, many thousands of living beings remain there as if they were no longer alive.
Then, many thousands of strips of cloth belonging to the guardians of Yama—burning, blazing, and emitting flames—travel through the air before them.
As they were approaching, they made a noise,
saying, "They are coming!"
Having arrived, they each wrap around their bodies.
There they burn their skin; they burn even the hide, the flesh, and the sinews, until everything has been completely consumed by fire.
Then their flesh and blood, having been torn away, are consumed by fire.
Being in such a state, they experience intense painful sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?

Those by whom many living beings have been caused to be killed here while they were still alive, or those who, as beggars, eunuchs, all types of criminals, or those of immoral conduct who have gone forth, have made use of robes or waist-bands— by the ripening of that karma, sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the maturation of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
Now others tore her apart from the heels up to the nape of the neck.
Now, others tear open [the body] from the nape of the neck down to the heels.
Now others, starting from the nape of the neck down to the hips, made garments of rags.
Being thus situated, they experience intense sensations.
As the ripening of what karma do sentient beings take birth here?
Those who here have had *eraka* grass mats made, or *vārṣika* grass mats made, or *cīraka* grass mats made, by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
That mass of smoke and darkness in hell—which is all around—is sharp, pungent, and terrifying;

having pierced the outer skin, pierced the inner skin, pierced the flesh, pierced the tendons, and pierced the bones, it emerges from the marrow of the bone and penetrates even further into the flesh.
All the bodies there become faint and are utterly consumed by it.
Wandering there for many hundreds of yojanas, they trample one another and fall back.
Being thus situated, they experience intense sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who, in this world, having placed incense in holes, burrows, prisons, or cages— whether belonging to *sāhikas*, *kiṃpuruṣas*, rats, cats, or pythons— thereby guard the exits, or those who disturb bees with smoke, are reborn there as a result of that karma.
Furthermore, it is indeed due to the ripening of various kinds of evil and unwholesome karmas that sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those reborn there [experience] the full details of other [conditions] as well.
By what means is this Kālasūtra [hell] produced?

There, the hell-guardians take the denizens of hell and, having placed them against a moist tree, carve them according to the *kālasūtra* (black-thread) system; for this reason, it is called the *Kālasūtra* hell, as they are to be treated accordingly.
(20) [The hell] named Saṃghāta.
That hell is situated between mountains, made of iron, blazing and fiercely aflame, radiant with light, and extending for many hundreds of yojanas.
There, the hell-guardians, with weapons in their hands, point them out to those denizens of hell.
Then, being afraid, they entered that mountain cleft.
Then a fire appeared before them;
they were terrified and turned back,
and then the fire appeared behind them.
Then those rocks came together with one another; as they were coming together, they made a sound, saying, "They are coming! They are coming!"
When they have gathered together, they crush them just like sugarcane.
Then those rocks rose up into the air.
They enter beneath them;
when they have entered, many thousands of living beings are then crushed by those rocks as if they were stalks of sugarcane, and rivers of blood flow forth.
The skeletons, devoid of flesh and joined together by sinews, are cast aside.
They experience such feelings and yet do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those who here have caused insects to be crushed, or have had floors trampled, or [have caused suffering] in the Sword-Leaf Hell, there living beings are likewise tormented while still alive;
or lice, or nits, or bugs are squeezed with nails—by the ripening of that karma, sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those reborn there also experience the ripening of other evil, unwholesome karmas.
Those skeletons were placed in iron vats that were burning, blazing, and aflame, and with iron pestles that were burning, blazing, and aflame,
they were pounded for five hundred years.
Being in such a state, they experience such painful and intense sensations.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?

Those living beings who, while still alive here, are pierced by spears or afflicted by clubs and swords, or by whom living beings are slain with blazing [weapons] and crushed with mortars and pestles— due to the ripening of that karma, sentient beings are reborn there.
By what is this called a "compound"?
There, the beings in hell undergo compression; therefore, this hell is called Saṃghāta (the Crushing).
There, those hell-beings, many thousands in number, are each individually confined within small cells; with their modes of movement cut off, they move about.
Fire blazes from their hands;
as the fire blazes, so they make a sound;
as the fire goes out, so they become silent.
Being thus situated, they experience intense feelings.
As the ripening of what karma do sentient beings take birth there?
Those who here in this world have caused others to be made to perform labor while being without protection or without allies; or who have set fires to houses, or set fires to forests;

or who, having placed fire in holes, in burrows, in prisons, or in cages—whether belonging to *sāhikas*, *kiṃpuruṣas*, rats, cats, or pythons—and have guarded the exits; or who have caused honey or betel to be scorched by fire—the ripening of that karma occurs there for them.
Beings are reborn.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
... [the hell] named Mahāraurava.
That hell is vast, made of iron, blazing, fiercely flaming, and glowing with light, extending for many hundreds of yojanas in length.
There, the hell-wardens of those hells, with mallets in their hands, point them out.
Then, being terrified, some ran, some fled, some did not flee, some retreated to various places, some did not retreat, and some, trying as best they could to persuade him, went out to meet him.
Then those hell-wardens strike them, saying, "Whom are you addressing here as you come forward? and they are shattered and destroyed just like pots of curd.
Both those who run and those who do not run, being in such a state, experience painful, harsh, and bitter sensations.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

By these [beings], having covered the sun and moon here, bonds were made; having caused them to enter, they release them. "In this place, you must not look upon the sun and moon"—by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
As the ripening of what karma do the heads of those beings fall off?

By whomsoever the heads of living creatures were crushed here—whether snakes, scorpions, or *śataghnīs*—as the ripening of that karma, their heads are crushed; by what means is that Raurava [attained]?
There, those denizens of hell, weeping, are unable to call out to their kinsmen, saying "O mother! or "O father!"
Therefore, this is designated as Raurava.
The Tāpana hell.
There, those hell-beings—many thousands of living beings—remain confined.
Now they eat, having avoided [trees] that are still moist.
When they have become fleshless skeletons, held together by sinews, then, having fainted, they fall down with a single convulsive sensation.
Then, as a result of the ripening of their karma, a cold wind blows upon them.
By that, their skin, flesh, and blood are produced.
Then they lead those who have become such as this before him.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who have prepared houses here that are without doors, their walls become covered with living creatures; or else, they are perforated there by knives. As the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn therein.
In that regard, as the ripening of what karma are they devoured?
Those living beings who here were made to be eaten by lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas while still alive, are devoured as the ripening of that karma.
As the ripening of what karma does a cold wind blow upon them?
Because they gave fodder and food here for deer, buffalo, pigs, and chickens, thinking, "I shall slaughter them for the sake of their thick meat," as the ripening of that karma,
a cold wind blows upon them.
By whom was this sun created?
The denizens of hell are burned; therefore this hell is named Tapana, for it is surrounded on all sides by glowing iron spikes that have been driven in from every direction.
There, some of those hell-beings are roasted impaled on a single stake; some are roasted impaled on two, and some even up to ten stakes.
When one side has become cooked and broad, then [he should proceed] with the second side.
Moreover, some hell-beings, due to the ripening of their excessive evil and unwholesome karmas, undergo transformation by themselves.
Being thus, they experience intense sensations.
From the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those who have caused living beings to be impaled on stakes here in this world—those beings, as the ripening of that karma, are reborn there in the body of sheep.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the sovereign influence regarding rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
... ... by what means is this called "Avīci"?

From its eastern wall, rays of light strike the western wall; from its western wall, rays of light strike the eastern wall; from its southern wall, rays of light strike the northern wall; and from its northern wall, rays of light strike the southern wall.
The flames arising from the ground strike against the surface; the flames falling upon the surface strike against the ground; that entire hell is pervaded by flames.
There, those hell-beings—many thousands of living beings—are cooked in various ways, just like pieces of wood.

Being thus situated, they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet they do not pass away for as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted; such is the karma previously performed and undertaken by them while in human form, which must necessarily be experienced.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
By the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who here are killers of their mothers, or killers of their fathers, or killers of Arhats, or those with malicious intent who shed the blood of a Tathāgata— all such beings are reborn there as the ripening of all these unwholesome courses of action.
In this way, moreover, beings are reborn there as the result of various kinds of evil and unwholesome karmas.
Therefore, this place is called Avīci.

There, those denizens of hell experience bitter, intense, and harsh sensations in Avīci, such as they do not in other hells; there, the hell-wardens, being terrified, compel them to perform tasks, and a cold wind blows there as it does nowhere else.
Indeed, here in the great hell Avīci, they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations; for that reason, this great hell is named Avīci.
(26) Thus ends the sutra titled "The Chapter on Hell" in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a tour among the animals.
There he saw beings reborn in the animal realm experiencing various kinds of suffering.

While the Venerable Kolita, the Elder, was wandering on his travels among the border regions, he saw beings in the animal realm who were extremely miserable, subsisting by uprooting and eating both dry and fresh grasses, and drinking both cold and warm water; yet they have no mother known, no father, no brother, no sister, no teacher, no one in the position of a teacher, nor any friend, relative, or kinsman.
They devour one another, they drink each other's blood, they kill one another, and they tear one another apart.

They go from darkness to darkness; they go from the states of woe to the states of woe; they go from miserable rebirths to miserable rebirths; they go from calamities to calamities; they experience various thousands of sufferings and with difficulty emerge from the animal realms.
Having seen that great danger in the animal realm, go to Jeta’s Grove and proclaim it in detail to the fourfold assembly.
In this way, those beings who have been reborn among the animal wombs experience various sufferings and thousands of miseries, and they emerge from the animal wombs only with great difficulty.

Therefore, I say that there is something to be known, something to be attained, something to be understood, something to be fully awakened to, and the holy life to be lived; and nothing sinful whatsoever should be done in the world.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys among the hungry ghosts.
He sees beings reborn in the world of hungry ghosts, experiencing various thousands of sufferings.

While wandering on his journey among the hungry ghosts, the Venerable Elder Kolita saw in the world of the pretas certain pretas who were extremely miserable; they had massive bodies with needle-like mouths and constricted throats, and though they were constantly consuming food, they found no satisfaction.

How much more so for those who have not performed meritorious deeds, by whom nothing at all is obtained—those who are ill-colored, unsightly, foul-smelling, poorly endowed, of little renown, and repulsive to behold;
naked and uncovered, tormented by hunger and thirst, they long for excrement, urine, spittle, snot, phlegm, pus, and blood.

Due to the ripening of their karma, a wind blows for them, crying out, "There is water! There is water! There is rice! There is gruel! Hearing that sound, they cross over rivers and mountains, thinking, "Here we shall eat; here we shall consume; here we shall drink."
In that way, having previously formed their hopes, they become hopeless.
A wind blows for them saying, "It does not exist, it does not exist"; hearing that sound, they become despondent and fall headlong right there.
The female ghost recites this verse:
For five hundred years, I have heard this cry:
"Behold how extremely difficult it is to obtain even water in the world of the pretas!"
(28) Another female preta recites this verse:
For five hundred years I have heard this cry from a hungry ghost in the world: "Alas! Look how exceedingly difficult it is to find!"
Another female preta spoke this verse:
For five hundred years, this cry has been heard by me:
"Look how exceedingly difficult it is to obtain even a spoonful of gruel in the world of the hungry ghosts!"
Another female preta spoke this verse:
The thirsty approach the river, yet the sand shifts away; those scorched by heat seek shade, yet the sunlight shifts away.
Another female preta recites this verse:
Fie on this life of those who lived when we were here;
though wealth was present, you did not provide a lamp.
Having seen that great peril in the world of hungry ghosts, he returned to the Jeta Grove and, in many ways, announced it in detail to the fourfold assembly.
Thus, beings born in the realm of hungry ghosts experience thousands of various sufferings.

Therefore, I say that one must know, attain, understand, fully awaken to, and practice what is wholesome; one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of living beings, both gods and humans, attained the deathless.
(29) The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys among the asuras.

He sees that in the city of the asuras, the asuras have massive bodies, are fierce in appearance, and are full of malice; having passed away from among the asuras, they cause others to fall into states of ruin.
The Venerable Elder Kolita, while wandering on a journey among the asuras, saw five hosts of asuras who were deeply afflicted by malice toward the gods.
It occurs to them:
"We are below; the gods are above."
Then they become agitated, become malevolent, and overflow with resentment; they manifest anger, wrath, and hostility.
Having arrayed their fourfold army— having arrayed the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry— they break through the divine outposts, namely the yakṣas called Karoṭapāṇis,
the yakṣas called Mālādhāras, and the yakṣas called Sadāmattas.
Having broken through these divine outposts, they engage in battle with the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Having harbored malicious thoughts toward those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who have performed meritorious deeds and possess great majesty, they—upon the dissolution of the body after death—are reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in perdition, and in the hells.
Having seen this great danger for the asuras, he came to the Jeta Grove and related it in detail to the fourfold assembly.
Thus, beings in the great ocean, in the city of the asuras, experience various sufferings.

Therefore, it must be known, it must be understood, it must be attained, it must be fully realized, and the holy life must be lived; I declare that no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having heard [the teaching] from the Elder, many thousands of living beings, both gods and humans, attain the deathless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently goes on a tour among the gods of the Four Great Kings.

There he sees the gods of the Four Great Kings, who have performed meritorious deeds, who are of great renown, long-lived, beautiful, and possessed of abundant happiness; they possess divine life-span, beauty, happiness, sovereignty, and retinues; they possess divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, divine garments, and divine ornaments.
Ornaments fastened in front are seen behind, and those fastened behind are seen in front; even their shadows are not seen. They are self-luminous, moving through the air, going wherever they desire.
Abounding in food and drink, they dwell in celestial palaces made of jewels, endowed and possessed of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, playing, delighting, and enjoying themselves.
Yet the Elder perceives that such prosperity ends in misfortune.

Then, those who are self-luminous, passing away from among the Cāturmahārājika gods, are reborn in the hells, they are reborn among animals, or they are reborn among the hungry ghosts and the bodies of asuras.

Then the Elder, having seen that suffering of change among the gods of the Four Great Kings, exclaimed, "Alas, what misery! and returning to the Jetavana, he announced in detail to the four assemblies:
"In this way, through the ripening of wholesome karma, sentient beings are reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
Having experienced divine prosperities there, when they pass away from that state, they are reborn in the bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras.
Even the gods are impermanent, unstable, and subject to the nature of change.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must perform what is wholesome and practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be done in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of beings, both gods and humans, attain the deathless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently goes on tour among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
There he sees the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, who have performed meritorious deeds, who are of great renown, long-lived, powerful, and full of happiness;
(31) who possess divine longevity, strength, bliss, sovereignty, retinues, and divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, garments, ornaments, and objects of sensual pleasure;

who are self-luminous, moving through the air, dwelling in ease, going wherever they wish, having abundant food and plentiful drink, and [residing] in divine palaces made of jewels and in the eight great pleasure groves.

In the Vaijayanta palace, at the edge of the Nandā lotus pond, in the Kovidāra grove, in the Mahāvana forest, in the Pāruṣyaka and Citraratha parks, in the Nandana and Miśraka groves, and in other celestial palaces made of jewels, they sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves,
endowed and possessed of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure.

Śakra, the lord of the gods, likewise, surrounded by eighty thousand apsarases in the Vaijayanta palace, endowed and possessed of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, sports and enjoys himself.

The Elder, having seen such prosperity of those Trāyastriṃśa gods, having seen their divine wealth, having seen the celestial city Sudarśana, having seen the arrangement of that celestial city Sudarśana made of the seven precious gems,
and having seen the celestial assembly hall Sudharmā— entirely made of beryl and one thousand yojanas in extent— wherein dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods and Śakra, the lord of the gods.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are seen seated and assembled in the Sudharmā assembly hall outside the city of the gods for divine affairs; seated there, they behold the entire celestial city of Sudarśana.
Thus, having seen the entire prosperity of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Elder returned to the Jeta Grove and related it in detail to the four assemblies.
Thus, through the ripening of wholesome karma, beings are reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and experience divine prosperities.
That too is impermanent, unstable, and subject to change.
Falling away from there, they are reborn among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must perform what is wholesome, one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a tour of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika gods, up to the Śuddhāvāsa gods.

He sees the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, who have performed meritorious deeds, are of great renown, long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness; they are self-luminous, move through the atmosphere, feed on joy, abide in bliss, go wherever they desire, are free from passion, are gods who are arhats, attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, are of a nature not to return to this world, and are unmixed with all foolish ordinary people.
Having seen such splendor of the gods, the Elder returned to the Jeta Grove and related it in detail to the fourfold assembly.
In this way, through the ripening of wholesome karma, sentient beings experience the prosperities of the gods among the deities;
yet even that is impermanent and subject to the nature of suffering and transformation.
The entire world is a source of peril; the entire world is ablaze.
The entire world is set on fire; the entire world is trembling.
The Buddhas teach the Dharma— unwavering and unshakable, yet cultivated by ordinary beings— for the attainment of the supreme goal.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must awaken, one must do what is wholesome, and one must practice the holy life; nor should any evil deed whatsoever be performed in the world.
Having heard [the teaching] from the Elder, many thousands of living beings, both gods and humans, attained the deathless state.
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having realized the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain as the teacher of gods and humans;

he was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, having attained the highest gain and fame, and receiving the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick. There...

Unstained like a lotus in water, establishing beings who possess merit in their merits, settling beings who possess the fruits in the fruits, and placing beings who possess latent tendencies in those very tendencies; distributing the rain of the Deathless among gods and humans, leading thousands of living beings to the Deathless, [he rescues them] from the wilderness of the beginningless cycle of birth, old age, and death, and from the treacherous wilderness of cyclic existence such as the hells.

Having rescued them from the terrible great precipice and established them in safety, on firm ground, in peace, in auspiciousness, and in fearlessness—namely, in Nirvāṇa—he won over Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Ceti, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Kuru, Pañcāla, Śibi, Daśārṇa, Aśvaka, and Avantī; and having exerted himself in wisdom, he dwelt in the self-existent, divine, imperturbable, and continuous abidings.

The Buddha dwells by means of the dwellings of a Buddha; the Conqueror dwells by means of the dwellings of a Conqueror; the Knower dwells by means of the dwellings of a Knower; the All-Knowing One dwells by means of the dwellings of an All-Knowing One. Furthermore, the Blessed Buddha, having attained mastery over the mind, dwells by whichever dwellings he desires to dwell in.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed early in the morning, set out for the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Then, not long after the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had departed, this thought occurred to him:
It is indeed still too early to wander for alms in the city of Rājagṛha; what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods?
It has been a long time since I last approached the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods.
Then indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his supernatural power, proceeded step by step toward the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods.
A great many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host saw the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar; having seen him, they went out to meet the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Here, here is the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Welcome to the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana; a warm welcome to the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It has been a long time since the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana made an occasion to come here."
Then those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and stood to one side.
Thereupon, a certain son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa host addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as follows:

"It is wonderful, noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana! It is marvelous, noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana! That unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is so difficult to attain—that it takes as many as a hundred thousand eons!
Then, O Blessed One, that son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
For a hundred thousand eons, there was a monk named Abhiya who possessed lust, hatred, and delusion.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, at that time there was a city named Vasumatī, which was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, inhabited by happy people, populous, free from violence and civil unrest, with thieves well-restrained, and perfected in its legal administration.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, in the great city of Vasumatī there was a guild-leader named Uttiya, who had performed meritorious deeds; he was of great renown, wealthy, possessing vast riches and great enjoyments, with abundant property, an abundance of wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses, an abundance of gold, silver, assets, and means of livelihood, an abundance of elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and an abundance of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants. He was filled with faith and serene confidence in the teaching of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū; he took the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as his auspicious refuge, and was deeply devoted to the monks headed by Nanda.
Then indeed, Maudgalyāyana, the monk Nanda and the monk Abhiya approached the house of the merchant Uttiya.
Monk Nanda Maudgalyāyana was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected in that merchant’s family, whereas monk Abhiya was not so treated.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, the daughter of the merchant Uttiya was the wife of a certain wealthy householder in the great city of Vasumata.
She, Maudgalyāyana, was exceedingly devoted to the monk Nanda.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya, being by nature envious, slandered the monk Nanda with a false accusation of unchaste conduct.
The monk Nanda was unchaste, of evil character, unrestrained, and one whose sinful deeds were concealed;
he had committed a grave offense with the daughter of the merchant Uttiya.
In the great city of Vasumati, that [teaching] was practiced such that the great multitude of people considered it worthy of being heard and believed.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the brahmins and householders in the great city of Vasumata, as well as the merchant Uttiya, no longer thought that the monk Nanda should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped as they had done before. For it is possible that when noble persons return [to their former ways], they become remorseful because of unwholesome karma.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this thought occurred to the monk Abhiya:
The monk Nanda was free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion; he was an Arhat of great merit, yet I, being by nature envious, falsely accused him with a charge of unchastity.
I have produced much demerit.
"What if I were now to ask the monk Nanda for forgiveness and confess my transgression in the presence of the Blessed One, the All-Conqueror?"
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya asked the monk Nanda for forgiveness and confessed his transgression in the presence of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya approached the merchant Uttiya and, having approached him, said this to the merchant Uttiya:
"Householder, I wish to perform a service for the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with his community of disciples; grant me the necessary means."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the merchant Uttiya gave abundant gold and bullion to the monk Abhiya, as did other great householders.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in the great city of Vasumata, there were two chief perfume merchants who were devoted to the monk Abhiya.
Then, indeed, the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyanābhaya, with a hundred thousand pieces of gold in his hand, approached those two chief perfumers and said this to them:
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, I desire the filaments from these hundred thousand [pieces].
I shall offer them as a service to the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū, together with his community of disciples."
O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those two chief perfumers avoided the *śatasahasrakeśara* [flower].

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya, having satisfied and served the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with the community of disciples with abundant solid food, soft food, and delicacies, and knowing that they had eaten, washed their hands, and put away their bowls, scattered, strewed, and showered the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with the community of disciples with that hundred-thousand-petaled *kesara* flower; and having scattered, strewn, and showered it, he gave rise to this thought:
"O, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Sarvābhibhū is now."
May I likewise be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, my body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
strong with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident with the four grounds of self-confidence—
just as this Blessed One, Sarvābhibhū, is now.

And thus may I set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world together with its Dharma; and may I maintain a harmonious community of disciples, just as this Blessed One Sarvābhibhū does now.
And thus gods and humans would consider that what is to be heard and believed should be regarded as the Veda of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū even now.

"Having thus crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvana, may I lead others to final nirvana. May that be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū, having understood this very aspiration of the monk Abhiya, spoke as follows.

"Abhiya, in a future time, in the kalpa called Śatasahasra, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,

an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans— just as I am now, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and a body resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics."

Endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and perfectly confident with the four grounds of self-confidence, just as I am at this present time.

And thus you shall set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, god, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma; and thus you shall lead a harmonious community of disciples,
just as I do now.
And those gods and humans will think that what you say is to be heard and believed, just as they now think of me;

thus, having crossed over, you will help others cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvana, you will lead others to final nirvana, just as I do now.
Thus you will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.

And immediately after the monk Abhiya had been predicted by the Perfectly Enlightened One Sarvābhibhū for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this trichiliocosm world-system shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways.

The eastern direction rose up and the western direction sank down; the eastern direction sank down and the western direction rose up; the southern direction rose up and the northern direction sank down; the southern direction [sank down and the northern direction rose up].
The northern direction sinks down while the southern direction rises; it sinks down in the center while rising at the edges, and it rises in the center while sinking at the edges.
And the gods of the earth raised a cry and caused their voices to be heard.

This monk Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One, the All-Conqueror, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; this will be for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods who roam the atmosphere, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods,
the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, and so on up to the gods of the Brahma-realm, raised their voices and made the sound resound.

(40) "Thus, friends, the monk Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings—both gods and humans. It was the appearance in the world of an immeasurable, sublime, and great radiance."

And those intermediate spaces between worlds in the world— which are regions of darkness, shrouded in darkness, gloom, shrouded in gloom, desolate, unknown, and never before perceived, where even these suns and moons, so possessed of great supernatural power and majesty, cannot reach with their radiance nor illuminate with their light— even those places were suddenly filled with that illumination, though it was not the proper time for such light.
And those beings who were reborn there also conversed with one another.
"Indeed, friends, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings too have been reborn here."

And furthermore, at that very moment, at that very instant, all sentient beings became endowed with absolute happiness— even those reborn in the great Avīci hell— surpassing indeed the splendor of the gods,
the splendor of the nāgas, and the splendor of the yakṣas.
And the palaces of Māra became darkened, devoid of splendor, and joyless.
Fragments measuring one *krośa* fell down; fragments measuring two *krośas* and three *krośas* also fell down; fragments measuring one *yojana* fell down;
and fragments measuring two and five *yojanas* also fell down.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of regret, and consumed by the burning pain of an internal thorn.
The verses sung in response.
Having given that gift, he made this aspiration:
"May I become a leader of the world, a teacher of gods and humans, and may I proclaim the noble Dharma."
I shall wander with the torch of Dharma; I shall beat the drum of Dharma with its banner;
I shall raise the noble banner of Dharma; I shall blow the conch shell.
And thus may there be for me this revelation and teaching of the Dharma;
and thus may I establish many beings in the noble Dharma.
And thus may gods and humans hear my well-spoken words;
and thus may I set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many beings.

May I establish the aggregate of wisdom for those beings who have fallen into hardship, who are oppressed by birth and old age, whose nature is subject to death, and who have eyes only for worldly existence, so that they may avoid the lower realms.
May I liberate from the cycle of existence those scattered throughout the six realms of rebirth— in the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci hells.

May I liberate from the cycle of existence those who have been cooked or not yet cooked in hell, who are tormented by the states of woe, whose nature is subject to death, and who experience little pleasure and much suffering.
I shall act for the welfare of the world, teaching the Dharma to gods and humans;
thus may I discipline sentient beings, just as this Light of the World does.
Thus may I wander through this world with a mind free from attachment, just as he wanders;
and may I turn the wheel, peerless and incomparable, highly honored and worshipped by gods and men.

And having known the aspiration, the Victorious One Susamudgata— the wise seer of the goal— made a prediction that was unbroken, flawless, and without blemish, as all the necessary causes were present.
"In a future time, after hundreds of thousands of eons, you shall become a Buddha, a leader of the world.
Then, in the city called Kapila at the Deer Park, this vow of yours as a Śākyan will bear its fruit."
Then the earth, with its oceanic boundaries, trembled, and among the hosts of gods in heaven,
a proclamation arose for that radiant one, rising up as a resounding voice.
(43) This Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One— the Sage who has overcome all, whose banner is the song of the most excellent well-spoken [Dharma]— "You shall become a Victor."
You will bring about the welfare and happiness of the world, including its Brahmās, gods, and asuras;
the host of asuras will diminish, while the assembly of humans and gods will increase.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those two chief perfumers, having heard the prophecy regarding Abhiya’s unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, were thrilled, satisfied, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness; they conceived this thought:
"When the monk Abhiya has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, may we then become his foremost disciples— the pair of the foremost, the pair of the auspicious—
just as this pair of disciples of Sarvābhibhū was, with one foremost in wisdom and one foremost in supernatural power."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Uttiya the merchant’s daughter heard that the monk Abhiya had been prophesied by the Blessed One, Sarvābhibhū, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the daughter of the merchant Uttiya, having honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, made this aspiration:
By the monk Abhiya, who was of an envious nature, a false accusation was made against me.
Whatever merit I have acquired by performing services for the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with his community of disciples— by this root of merit, wherever the monk Abhiya may be reborn,
may I there falsely accuse him with an unfounded charge,
until he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
"It might be," Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that he might think thus:
"At that time, on that occasion, there was another disciple of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū named Abhiya."
This should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I was a disciple named Abhiya of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū.
"It may be," Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that it might occur to you thus:
"Those two who were the chief perfume merchants in the great city of Vasumata at that time and on that occasion were others. [But they were not.]
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at that time and on that occasion, you two were the two chief perfumers.
That is your original vow.
"It might be," said Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "that it might occur to him thus: 'Was she not someone else at that time, on that occasion, who was the daughter of the merchant Uttiya? [End of section]
Therefore, by virtue of that vow, this female heretic shall give me false accusations wherever I am reborn, until I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
"It may be, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that it might occur to you thus: 'Was that merchant named Uttiya in the great city of Vasumata at that time and on that occasion someone else? [It was not.]”
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
This very son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, was at that time and on that occasion the merchant named Uttiya in the great city of Vasumata.
He remembers a hundred thousand of these eons and recollects the Dharma.
Thus ends the chapter on Abhijñā, together with its verses, in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
(45) "O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, from this point back through immeasurable and incalculable eons, this is how I have made my vow for enlightenment."
I have made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, yet I have not received a prophecy.
"Maudgalyāyana, three hundred Buddhas named Puṣpa were honored by me, yet I was not prophesied by them."
For immeasurable and incalculable eons I have wandered and transmigrated, and I have honored immeasurable perfectly awakened Buddhas, yet I was not prophesied by them.
In this regard, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there are four practices of a bodhisattva.
Which are the four?
Namely: the practice of natural disposition, the practice of aspiration, the practice of conformity, and the practice of non-retrogression.
And what, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of natural disposition?
In this regard, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, such is the very nature of a bodhisattva.

They become respectful toward their mothers and fathers, honoring the ascetics and brahmins, and showing deference to the elders of the family; they abide having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action and teach them to others, saying, "Give gifts!
Perform meritorious deeds! They honor the Buddhas who remain in the world as well as their disciples; yet, even so, they do not yet resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Those of great renown first worship the Tathāgatas with great reverence;
yet even then, those supreme among men do not yet direct their minds toward the Foremost Person.
Tens of millions of those who have attained mastery worship them, for they have long ago reached the perfection of mastery;
yet these Leaders do not even give rise to a thought for crossing the ocean of knowledge.
And those millions of Pratyekabuddhas, persons of ultimate reality, honor them;
yet those wise ones do not at all give rise to a mind [of pride] regarding their own knowledge of all phenomena.
This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of natural disposition.
And what, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of the vow?

From this point, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, there arose in the world a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the city of Śākyamuni was named Kapilavastu; its extent was as follows.
At that time, I was the guild-president.
Having drunk the rice gruel, he made a resolution for awakening.
When they have accumulated a vast store of merit and have cultivated both body and mind,
those who possess excellent forms approach and direct their minds toward awakening.
By whatever wholesome merit I have previously acquired, may I attain omniscience;
and may my vow not fail, but rather may this very vow be fulfilled.
May whatever accumulation of roots of merit I have become great for all living beings;
and whatever unwholesome karma I have committed, may its bitter fruit fall upon me alone.
Thus may I wander through this world with a mind free from attachment, just as he wanders;
may I set in motion the wheel that is peerless, well-honored, and worshipped by gods and humans.
He was the one who first gave a drink of rice-gruel to the supramundane Buddha, the Blessed Śākyamuni, in an incalculable eon ago from this time.
That was my first aspiration at that time.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon from now, a Tathāgata named Samitāvin arose in the world— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.

Now at that time, the Bodhisattva was a universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four continents, endowed with the seven treasures, righteous, a king of dharma, who lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action.

He possessed these seven treasures, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Furthermore, he had a full thousand sons, all of them brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Thus, having conquered this earth— these four continents, namely Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru, bounded by the oceans and mountains— entirely, without thorns, without weapons, without oppression, without punishment, and by means of righteousness (dharma), he dwells there as its sovereign.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Cakravartin attended upon the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin and his community of disciples with all requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick—and he had a palace constructed out of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby, consisting of eighty-four thousand pillars.
And each pillar was fashioned from ten million pieces of gold;
you had eighty-four thousand gabled chambers constructed, variegated and beautiful, made of the seven precious substances— namely, gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having had a palace built with such characteristics, the wheel-turning monarch presented it to the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin and made this aspiration:

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans—

just as this Blessed One, the Samitāvin, is now; may I be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, my body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, and possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

May I be endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata and be strong, and with the four grounds of self-confidence be perfectly confident—just as this Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One, is now; and having crossed over myself, may I help others cross over; being comforted myself, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvana myself, may I lead others to final nirvana.

May that be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Thus, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is this vow of the Tathāgata.
Thus may I wander through this world as he wanders with a mind free from attachment;
may I set the wheel in motion, peerless and incomparable, honored by gods and humans.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin:

Now, after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, and these disciples have also passed into parinirvāṇa, and this proclamation of the Dharma has disappeared— after how much time, indeed, will a Buddha, a Blessed One, appear in the world?
In one eon he did not see [a Buddha];
in two eons he did not see [one].
Only after a thousand eons does he behold a Buddha in the world.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, great compassion for sentient beings arose within the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin, who was endowed with great mercy.
And the five activities of a Buddha must necessarily be performed.
Which five?

The wheel of Dharma must be set in motion; the mother must be converted, the father must be converted, and those beings who are to be converted by a Buddha must be converted; the crown prince must be consecrated.

"This one shall become a Buddha in the world after my passing, just as I am now; even so, this Bodhisattva Ajita shall become a Buddha in the world after my passing—Ajita by name, Maitreya by lineage—in the royal capital of Bandhumatī."
"What if I were now to remain here for a hundred thousand eons?"
Then indeed, the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin addressed the monks.
While I was here, alone and secluded, dwelling in retreat, this very reflection arose in my mind:

"Indeed, after I have entered parinirvāṇa, and these assemblies of disciples have also entered parinirvāṇa, and this proclamation of the Dharma has disappeared—after how much time from now will a Buddha appear in the world?
For one eon he did not see one; for two eons he did not see one.
For three eons he did not see one;
for a hundred thousand eons I behold a Buddha in the world.
I must certainly perform five deeds of a Buddha; furthermore, that being who is to be consecrated as the crown prince has been reborn among the long-lived gods.
"What if I were to wish to remain for a hundred thousand eons? Do you, monks, wish to remain for a hundred thousand eons? Who will remain with me?
Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that world was taken up by eight million four hundred thousand monks, all of whom had attained mastery over their powers.
We, O Blessed One, shall remain; we, O Sugata, shall remain.
Then indeed, the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin and those disciples remained for a long time, throughout a vast expanse of time.

At the time of the world's dissolution, when humans pass away, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods; likewise, when the king passes away, he too is reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods, and the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, goes to the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods.

When the time for the process of evolution has arrived and the world-system has been established, sentient beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, pass away from the Ābhāsvara deva realm and come to this state of existence.

A Bodhisattva, having passed away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come to this human state, becomes a Cakravartin king who has conquered the four continents; having completely subdued these four great continents by means of the Dharma alone, he dwells therein.
When human beings become limited in lifespan and old age, sickness, and death become manifest, then the Blessed One Samitāvin, together with the community of disciples, comes to Jambudvīpa.
Having arrived, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
In the same way, King Cakravartin attended upon the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin with all requisites— robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick—
and having had a palace made of the seven precious gems constructed exactly like that, he offered it to the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One.
