By this means, for a hundred thousand eons, the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin remained together with his community of disciples; for a hundred thousand eons, he was attended by the Bodhisattva, who in every single eon,
having caused a palace made of the seven precious gems to be built exactly like that, presented it to the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin.
Desiring unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, while being a wheel-turning monarch, I gave hundreds of thousands of palaces made of jewels to those who were self-controlled and tranquil.
In an incalculable eon from now, having given that gift, he made this aspiration: "May I become a leader of the world;
as a teacher of gods and humans, may I proclaim the noble Dhamma."
And thus, through this revelation and teaching of the Dharma to me, may I establish many beings in the noble Dharma.
And thus may gods and humans hear these well-spoken words of mine;
and thus may I set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many beings.
I shall wander with the torch of Dharma; I shall beat the drum of Dharma with its banner;
I shall raise the noble banner of Dharma; I shall blow the conch shell.
When the world has fallen into hardship, oppressed by birth and old age, and subject to death;
when the eye of existence is obscured and the lower realms prevail, may I establish the aggregate of wisdom.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci—
may I liberate those scattered throughout the six realms of existence from the cycle of becoming.
May I liberate from the cycle of existence those who are cooked and uncooked in hell, tormented by the lower realms, subject to death,
and possessing little happiness and much suffering.
(53) May I act for the welfare of the world, teaching the Dharma to gods and humans;
thus may I discipline sentient beings, just as this Light of the World does.
Then the second vow was made.
He gave eighty sandalwood palaces to the world-transcending Buddha, his teacher.
I, O Blessed One, [was present] in this [eon] incalculable from here.
That was his third vow.
King Arka gave eighty thousand caves made of the seven precious gems to the one named Parvata.
At that time, there was a fourth vow.
For six years he practiced the perception of impermanence, being instructed by Ratnendra regarding the signs of desire.
At that time, there was a fifth aspiration.
Thus ends the Bahubuddhasūtra in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on the Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, set out for the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Then, not long after the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had departed, this thought occurred to him:
It is still too early to wander for alms in the city of Rājagṛha;
what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods?
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,

just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, in a single moment and with a single stride, rose up into the air from Rājagṛha and stationed himself in the realm of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
The sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those many sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in verses:
Having coursed for a hundred thousand eons toward the ripening of enlightenment, after a very long time, the Buddha Anantaratana has appeared in the world.

Having spoken thus, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and stood to one side. Standing to one side, they vanished.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Thus, enlightenment is indeed difficult to attain, for it takes a hundred thousand eons.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana— just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— in that very moment,
having vanished from the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods, reappeared in the city of Rājagṛha.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having walked for alms in the city of Rājagṛha, returned from his alms-round after his meal; having set aside his bowl and robe and washed his feet, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One as follows.
"In this regard, Blessed One, having dressed early in the morning and taken my bowl and robes, I set out for the great city of Rājagṛha for alms."
"Venerable Sir, not long after I had departed, this thought occurred to me:"
It is still too early to wander for alms in the great city of Rājagṛha.
What if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods?
It has been a long time since I last approached the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods.
Then, as quickly as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, in that very instant I rose up from Rājagṛha into the air and arrived at the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods.

"Lord, many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host saw me approaching from afar; having seen me, they approached where I was, bowed their heads at my feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host addressed me in verse:"
Having coursed through hundreds of thousands of eons for the ripening of enlightenment, after a very long time, the Buddha Anantaratana has appeared in the world.
Having spoken thus, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host bowed their heads at my feet and departed.
Then, O Blessed One, this thought occurred to me:
"Since unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is to be achieved through such hardship— indeed, by means of a hundred thousand eons—
what if I were now to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter?
I shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to me."
In this regard, what did the Blessed One say?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, even a hundred thousand of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host is indeed small in number.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, for immeasurable and incalculable eons, roots of merit have been planted by immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who were aspiring for perfect enlightenment in the future.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I truly recall thirty crores of Buddhas named Śākyamuni whom I—while having been a universal monarch (cakravartin) and aspiring for future enlightenment—honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated together with their assemblies of disciples; and those Blessed Buddhas granted me prophecies.

In a future time, you will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, and a teacher of gods and humans.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I recall eight hundred thousand Buddhas named Dīpaṃkara whom I—while having been a wheel-turning monarch and aspiring for perfect enlightenment in the future—honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated together with their assemblies of disciples; and those Blessed Buddhas gave me prophecies. As it was done in the first chapter, so it should be understood everywhere.
In a future time, you will become...
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, five hundred Buddhas named Padmottara.
This must be performed everywhere:
"In a future time, you shall become..."
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eight thousand Buddhas named Pradyota.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, three crores of Buddhas named Puṣpa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighteen thousand Buddhas named Māradhvaja, under whom I practiced the holy life while aspiring for future enlightenment;
and those Blessed Buddhas gave me their prophecies.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, five hundred Buddhas named Padmottara whom I honored together with their assemblies of disciples.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, ninety thousand Buddhas named Kāśyapa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, fifteen thousand Buddhas named Pratāpa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, two thousand Buddhas named Kauṇḍinya.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighty-four thousand pratyekabuddhas.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Samantagupta.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a thousand Buddhas named Jambudhvaja.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighty-four thousand Buddhas named Indradhvaja.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, fifteen thousand Buddhas named Āditya.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, sixty-two hundred Buddhas who had different names.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, sixty-four Buddhas named Samitāvin.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it was under the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suprabhāsa that the Bodhisattva Maitreya first planted the roots of merit, while King Vairocana,
in his capacity as a universal monarch (cakravartin), was aspiring for future perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when Suprabhāsa was a Tathāgata, the lifespan of human beings was eighty-four thousand koṭis of years, though there were occasional fluctuations in that lifespan.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there were three assemblies of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Suprabhāsa.

The first assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-six koṭis, all of whom were arhats who had exhausted their outflows, lived the holy life, were liberated through perfect knowledge, had completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and had attained their own goal.

The second assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-four koṭis, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had lived their vows, who were liberated through perfect knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed, and who had attained their own goal. The third assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-two koṭis, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had lived their vows, who were liberated through perfect knowledge, and whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed.
of those who have attained their own goal.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, upon seeing that Blessed One Suprabhāsa, King Vairocana experienced noble joy, noble intensity, and sublime gladness and delight.
For ten thousand years, he honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated that Blessed One together with his community of disciples.
Honoring and respecting that assembly, favoring that community of disciples, and favoring that lifespan, he generated this thought:

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Suprabhāsa is now! May I teach the Dharma, endowed with all excellent aspects and complete in all its aspects, just as the Blessed One Suprabhāsa does here now!"
"May I maintain a harmonious community of disciples just as the Blessed One Suprabhāsa does now;
and may gods and humans consider me worthy of being heard and worthy of being trusted, just as they do now for the Blessed One Suprabhāsa.
May that be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
And thus he spoke, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and even more than this.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it was only after Maitreya Bodhisattva had been engaged for forty-four kalpas that he subsequently resolved his mind upon awakening.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Aparājitadhvaja, whom I, together with the community of disciples, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated for a thousand years.
While seeking future perfect enlightenment, I— having been a universal monarch named Rājā Dṛḍhadhanuḥ— covered him with five hundred great pairs of fine cloth garments.
And after he had attained final nirvana, a stupa was constructed, one yojana in height and one yojana in its base.
And this vow, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, was constant and uninterrupted.

At whatever time beings might be without shelter, without protection, without refuge, and without resort; at a time when they are characterized by excessive greed, excessive hatred, and excessive delusion; at a time when they live having undertaken unwholesome dharmas and for the most part fill the states of woe—at that time, at that moment, may I awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
May that be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas perform what is difficult to do; they carry out their conduct for the sake of the world.
The Blessed One said this, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, being uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thirty billion Victors named Śākyamuni were present before him,
as were eight hundred thousand named Dīpaṃkara.
And sixty thousand named Pradyota...
likewise three koṭis of those named Puṣpa, lions among speakers.
There were eighteen thousand Sugatas named Māradhvaja,
under whom he practiced the holy life out of a desire for omniscience.
I made offerings to five hundred Sugatas named Padmottara,
and to another two thousand named Kauṇḍinya.
He honored immeasurable and incalculable millions of billions of Pratyekabuddhas,
as well as thousands of Buddhas named Jambudhvaja.
There were eighty-four thousand Sugatas named Indradhvaja,
and ninety thousand named Kāśyapa.
Fifteen thousand Buddhas named Pratāpa, Sugatas,
and fifteen thousand named Āditya.
And six thousand two hundred Sugatas with various names,
and sixty-four thousand named Samitāvin.
These, Kolitaśiri and others, as well as immeasurable possessors of the ten powers—
all these illuminators of the world have been overtaken by impermanence.
And as for those powers of yours, Kolita, and those excellent marks of a Great Man—none of them escape the reckoning of impermanence; they do not endure beyond it.
Having understood the extremely terrible power of impermanence immediately following his being honored,
he applied the exertion of vigor for the sake of overcoming that power of impermanence.

Maudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon from now, there was a Perfectly Enlightened One named Ratna, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
At that time, I was a universal monarch (cakravartin).

Then, for this Blessed One Ratnavat, eighty-four thousand gabled pavilions were constructed by me—variegated, beautiful to behold, and made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby.
Having offered those to that Blessed One, I made a vow for enlightenment.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not pass into final nirvana as long as the crown prince has not been consecrated.
He shall become a Buddha in the world immediately after me, just as Maitreya was prophesied by me thus: "He shall become a Buddha immediately after me."

Thus the Blessed One, together with eighty-four thousand disciples, remaining throughout eighty-four cycles of world-dissolution and evolution—when the world was dissolving, the Blessed One, together with eighty-four thousand disciples, went to the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods; when the world was evolving, he returned here and taught the Dharma here.
"I shall become once again a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
Having caused eighty-four thousand gabled pavilions to be constructed, I present them to the Blessed One Ratnavat.
This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of the vow.
And what is conformable practice?
In this regard, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a bodhisattva mahāsattva stands established in accordance with awakening.
This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, ... is the irreversible practice.
They revolve and transmigrate; this is the conduct of transmigration.
They become irreversible from enlightenment through their irreversible conduct.
Herein, the *Daśabhūmika* and the *Dīpaṃkaravastu* are to be performed.
Homage be to the Buddhas; homage to the Arhats.
The peerless vision of the Dharma occurs at the beginning of the practice of the ten stages for those whose selves have been cultivated over many hundreds of eons;
it is through these that the wise always exercise their miraculous powers upon the glorious ten stages of the Victors.
Freed from pride, arrogance, intoxication, and delusion in every respect, endowed with equanimity and gentleness,
and having conceived reverence for all the All-Seeing Ones, listen to the teaching of the Supreme Jina.
When the Tathāgata— the source of joy for the Śākyas, resembling a heap of gold— had entered nirvāṇa, the earth,
together with its mountains and forests, its oceans as its garment, and its peaks, trembled.
Beholding the earth trembling with a terrible and most hair-raising quake,
Kāśyapa, who had reached the further shore of the excellence of the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), then resolved his mind [upon enlightenment].

Why indeed does the earth, together with its mountains, wearing the ocean as its garment—the bearer of wealth—tremble with such an exceedingly dreadful sound? Surely the Tathāgata has passed into final nirvāṇa.
And he, possessing the divine eye, beheld the Tathāgata— who is worshipped by the best of gods and kinnaras,
and who has brought an end to all bonds of existence— attained to final nirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
"It is certainly not fitting for me to follow the Tathāgata Gautama by means of supernatural power;
rather, I shall go forth [into homelessness] to see with my own feet that peerless Sage, the best among speakers."
Knowing this, the venerable Kāśyapa, that monk of refined mind, being the most excellent among many monks, hurried with an agitated heart and gradually proceeded toward the place of final nirvana.
And he had made this supreme aspiration at the feet of the Jina Kāśyapa:
"May I worship those two feet of the Great Sage by pressing them to my head."
Then four powerful Mallas approached, carrying large torches;
they directed their breath toward the burning torch that had been fanned by the most skilled wrestlers.
Led toward the funeral pyre by those heroes of chariots, possessed of prowess and strength,
she was simultaneously extinguished— like a torch drenched with a stream of water.
Having approached the doubt and perplexity of the Mallas, [Aniruddha], who possesses divine vision, with a head bowed in reverence and well-disciplined, he asked this question: "I ask this."
What indeed is the cause here, and what is the condition, by which these sons of the Conqueror have been brought to this state?
They have entered into extinction like sudden torches; tell me the reason for this, O Noble One, exactly as it is.
The deities are indeed pleased with Kāśyapa; this is surely his cultivation of supernatural power.
The fire will not burn at all until he who has reached the further shore of the supreme has arrived.
And this vow of that Kāśyapa, who maintains the dhuta-precepts, is being fulfilled:
that he may indeed worship with his head those two feet of the glorious Great Sage, the possessor of the ten powers.
And that Kāśyapa, the son of the Conqueror, whose dust was shaken off, preceded by a multitude of monks,
approached the funeral pyre of the Conqueror with palms joined, his head and mind bowed in reverence.

(66) Seeing the Tathāgata, who possessed a most excellent form, situated upon that heap of wood, he uttered these words: "Fie on existence!"—words which revealed the characteristics of the true nature of reality.
What living being indeed, having approached existence, will not fall under the power of death—
that one who is like a blazing fire or gold, extinguished like a flame without fuel?
Having joined his palms in reverence, the highly renowned Kāśyapa fell with his head at the feet of the Jina’s son; bowing thus, the great seer pays this final homage to the Sage.
And those two feet, marked with the excellent wheel and worshipped by the best of gods and dānavas,
likewise emerged after rending that funeral pyre, empowered as they were by gods, yakṣas, and nāgas.
Then Kāśyapa, standing nearby, placed those two feet upon his head, supported them with his hands, and spoke to the great ṛṣi, the upholder of the Vedas, O Sage.
(67) But why, O Sage who retains what you have heard, have these two feet lost their luster and no longer shine? Tell me the cause in its entirety; for what reason do they no longer delight the eyes?
Having heard this collection of what has been heard, the wise Śrutasaṃcayadhara said this to Kāśyapa:
"The feet of those who grieve are as if scorched by the force of tears; they weep, their limbs shattered by lamentation."
"O sage of excellent vows, behold this: because of the weeping that afflicts the people, these two excellent feet of the Great Sage do not shine as they did before."
Bowing his head again and again, he pressed those two feet marked with the signs of the excellent wheel with the palms of his hands, O Sage, his mind intent on reverence for the Teacher.
And those two feet of the Teacher were saluted by Guṇadhara, who upholds the dhuta-precepts;
they blazed with the splendor of the funeral wood of the Lord of the World, fanned by the force of the wind.

(68) While the body of the Moon-like Victor was being cremated, those five hundred self-controlled ones gathered together at the time of the Nirvāṇa ceremony and, having approached, held a council for the purpose of the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*).
The Teacher, who possesses the most excellent marks and is the leader of gods and asuras, has entered into final nirvāṇa.
What benefit is there in dwelling here for long? Let us too cast off this body this very day.
Having attained the imperishable, sorrowless, and infinite state, our tasks are in every way perfectly accomplished;
having transcended all states of existence and becoming, we attain final liberation right here.
When this had been said, Kāśyapa, purified by the ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa) and having attained mastery, then spoke to those who were self-controlled:
"Surely you have not yet fully realized here and now that unconditioned liberation which is Nirvāṇa."
The heretics and those who follow external paths may bring about a blemish upon the peerless teaching;
this alone is what must be guarded by the ascetic, as it is like a fleeting smoke.
O Protector of the World, many lions among men (69), as well as those future ones of great intelligence and heroism—
may they indeed arise for us with vigor, if the teaching of the Teacher is not compiled.
Therefore, being unimpeded and perfectly united, sing the supreme teaching of the Sugata;
so that this well-chanted truth may shine for a very long time among men and gods.
"So be it," they replied, honoring the words of Kāśyapa who had attained mastery; yet their minds were troubled, wondering, "Where now will the assembly of those who uphold the Dharma gather?"
In the most prosperous forest grove of Ramyaka,
in the excellent city of Rājagṛha belonging to the Magadhan king, may it be in the cave named Saptaparṇa.
On the northern shore of Mount Vaihāyasa, on its excellent flank,
amidst various trees and upon a portion of ground with stone surfaces, may there be an assembly for the Dharma.
And those sons of the Conqueror, established in the power of mastery over supernatural faculties, rose into the path of the sky;
in that very instant, they departed like a flock of swans toward Lake Mānasa.
Established at the side of that most excellent mountain peak, they approached that forest and sat down;
and as they were well-established in the Sugata’s well-proclaimed teaching, multitudes of divine drums resounded.
And having heard the drum sounding its roar, those executors of the Sugata’s teaching,
beholding the terrible trembling of the earth, spoke these words to Kāśyapa, who had shaken off all dust:
But, O wearers of the dhuta-qualities, the earth with its rivers and oceans trembled,
and there arose the delightful sounds of celestial drums along with the scattering of divine garlands.
Kāśyapa, who was endowed with the practice of the dhutas, spoke to those sons of the Conqueror who had attained self-mastery:
"These hosts of gods have assembled here, having heard the most excellent and supreme teaching."
Those hosts of gods, possessing all the excellent marks and filled with joy through their reverence,
perform worship for the Peerless One so that they may hear his teaching, which is supreme among all things.

For indeed, throughout many hundreds of existences and eons, for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the multitudes of men and gods, he has thus long since undertaken this vow: "Once I am myself liberated, I shall liberate all living beings."
Having attained the supreme truth, which is free from sorrow and the cessation of the suffering of existence within all states of being,
I shall turn the wonderful, excellent wheel in the city of Kāśī for the benefit of gods and men.
Together with those five sages, the Leader, the best among those who teach discipline,
delivered millions of billions of beings from birth, old age, and death.
Thus the Lion among Men, having gladdened gods and humans who were attached to existence,
has now attained parinirvāṇa— the Blessed One, having crushed all opposing disputants and being free from all worldly concern.
Having heard these delightful words of Kāśyapa, who maintains the dhuta-precepts,
the hosts of gods standing in the sky joyfully uttered these charming words:

Excellent, excellent, O you who are skilled in the dhuta-precepts! You act according to the Teacher’s instruction and are not otherwise. You speak of the virtues of the one of infinite wisdom; gods and humans are well-pleased in Jeta’s Grove.
For he is the supreme among gods and men; for he is the foremost person, the Great Sage. He is the supreme refuge, the Lord who has seen what is to be seen, for the welfare of living beings.

Therefore, the Knower, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, has taught that the aggregates are like lightning and bubbles, and like a mass of foam— luminous and insubstantial— for whom this discourse on qualities proceeds.
O Kāma, this discourse on whose virtues is being propagated is taught by the Supreme Person; it is like the head of a black cobra, and resembles a weapon, a disease, or a jar of poison.
By means of his supreme and most virtuous views, he beheld that immovable, ultimate bliss;
that wonder which was revealed by one free from envy and delighting in sharing it with others.
Just as when the sun has risen, a firefly becomes lusterless and no longer shines,
so too when the Sun-like Jina has arisen, the unrestrained followers of other schools become lusterless.

Having reached the perfection of the power of the bases of psychic mastery, the Lord, possessing the eye of the Conqueror’s strength, is now extinguished; behold the Blessed One, resembling a golden image.
Fie upon this existence, which resembles an autumn cloud or the city of the sand-dwellers (Vālīkā),
wherein that ocean of supreme wisdom, the accumulation of all virtues, has indeed passed away into extinction!
Through hundreds of reasons and causes, the Leader roars the lion’s roar of a man;
having beheld existence as nothing other than death, no interval for it can be found.
Adorned with the finest celestial flowers, the sky shone as the Sugata spoke his praises;
perfumed by the essence of divine sandalwood, the sky shone with the fragrance of nectar.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O Son of the Conqueror, establish [the teaching] so that those who have attained mastery may discern the minds of the assembly that have fallen into doubt.
Then Kāśyapa spoke to Aniruddha, Upāli, the Elder, Alakuṇḍala-Bhaṭṭiya, and Sundarananda.
O sons of the Conqueror, look upon the minds of those in this assembly;
ask whatever doubts you may have, wherever they may arise.
Having promised "So be it," those experts in the teachings of the Jina perceive the minds of others as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of their hand.
To him who had long arms and was self-mastered, Kāśyapa spoke these words:
"Upon the peak of Gṛdhrakūṭa, you have lightly fashioned the earth."
Eighteen thousand have assembled in this assembly;
may I thus generate such supernatural power that everyone may recognize it.
Having reflected thus, Kāśyapa, who had attained mastery, spoke this:
"I shall lightly create clouds in the sky consisting of the waters of the Gaṅgā."
Let various fragrant flowers blow from all sides;
and quickly cause the raw stench of human beings to disappear.
Kāśyapa spoke thus to the one named Haryakṣa, who had attained self-mastery:
"O son of the Sugata, quickly produce such a concentration that the possessions of householders do not pass away to another state."
Kāśyapa spoke thus to the self-controlled one named Varuṇa:
"May [this practice] turn back the gadflies, mosquitoes, and humans that cause distress."
(75) Kāśyapa spoke thus to Ajakarna, who had attained self-mastery:
"Avert hunger, thirst, and disease for human beings."
Having promised "So be it" to Kāśyapa, those sons of the Conqueror attended to the places as they were commanded and remained vigilant as instructed.
Then the Elder Kāśyapa said to Kātyāyana:
"Proclaim the life-story of those great-souled kings of Dharma."
When this had been said, the one of great wisdom born of the Kātyāyana clan spoke of the conduct of the Buddhas to Kāśyapa, who was questioning him.
Listen, O sons of the Conquerors, to the conduct of the all-seeing Buddhas,
whose practice and conduct are pure, as it truly and sequentially unfolds.
Indeed, O sons of the Conqueror, there are ten stages of the bodhisattvas.
What are these ten?
The first stage is taught as "Difficult to Conquer" (Durārohā);
the second is named "Fixed in Mind" (Baddhamānā), and the third is "Adorned with Flowers" (Puṣpamaṇḍitā).
The fourth is named Rucirā, the fifth is Cittavistarā;
the sixth is named Rūpavatī, and the seventh is known as Durjayā.
The eighth is the designation of birth, the ninth is from the status of crown prince, and the tenth is from the consecration;
these are the ten stages.
When this had been spoken in verses, the wise Kāśyapa addressed these words, which were exceedingly meaningful and peerless, to Kātyāyana: (76)
Describe accurately the transformations of the stages,
and how those of great renown revolve as they wander through saṃsāra.
Speak also of how those who are the essence of beings come together;
declare that according to what their resolute intentions truly are.
And how beings endowed with sentient nature conceptualize,
and how they give gifts— all that I shall fully proclaim.
"Having seen thus, and speaking what is pleasing to the mind, the Fully Awakened Ones likewise describe the arising of perception. Thus spoke Kāśyapa.
Having heard these words of yours, those self-controlled Great Beings have stood ready with reverence toward the Great-souled Perfect Buddhas.
When this had been said, Kātyāyana spoke to Kāśyapa.
Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, it is not possible to measure the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattvas as being "only this many eons" or "infinite.
For Bodhisattvas, the entirety of *saṃsāra* is conceptualized as a stage through the perception of it as a single unit; therefore, they are designated as "stages."
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke to the venerable Kātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, if one stage is immeasurable,
how then will there be the inclusion of the remaining stages?"
When this had been said, the Venerable Kātyāyana addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verses:
Just as an immeasurable eon has been revealed by the Knower himself, who speaks without falsehood,
and as there is teaching throughout many such eons— this indeed, O sirs, is the instruction of the Best of Men.
Thus, the immeasurable stages have been revealed by the one who knows them, whose own intellect is unimpeded;
likewise, the definition of general conventions proceeds throughout the remaining stages.

O Son of the Conqueror, Bodhisattvas dwelling on the first stage are indeed ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), yet they have attained the fruit [of their practice]; they shine as objects of veneration for the world. And regarding this, it is said: "Through renunciation, these Bodhisattvas of great renown are perfected in giving;
they illuminate the worlds like the sun and moon with their radiant beams."
For bodhisattvas dwelling on the first stage, there are eight modes of conduct.
Which eight?
Namely: generosity, compassion, indefatigability, absence of pride, study of all treatises, valor, approval by the world, and fortitude.

And here there are verses (78): Those wise ones, feeling compassion for the masses of suffering beings, find complete satisfaction through the words and qualities of the Blessed Ones who possess sweet voices; thus do beings conduct themselves on the first stage of the earth.
Having reflected upon those treatises that spread forth— which are devoid of essence and consist of mere worldly attachment—
and having gone forth, considering this world to be like a blade of grass, they experience intense sensations and accumulate wholesome merit.
For one reason, bodhisattvas regress from the second stage.
By which one?
They perceive a relish in the realms of existence.
Bodhisattvas regress from the second stage for two reasons.
By which two?
And they become desirous of the qualities of sensual pleasure and indolent.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas regress from the second stage for three reasons.
By which three?
They become covetous, full of fear, and weak in their resolute intention.
By six modes, bodhisattvas established on the first stage regress from the second stage.
By which six?
Furthermore, they do not dwell frequently with the perception of impermanence; rather,
they abound in resentment and possess stubborn enmity.
They become full of sloth and torpor,
and they become devoted to worldly affairs.

O sons of the Conqueror, those bodhisattvas who have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back—all of them have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back because of these twelve aspects; there is nothing beyond this.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Conqueror, how much merit do these Bodhisattvas— who are both those liable to regression and those not liable to regression— generate when they first produce the thought, 'May we become perfectly enlightened Buddhas'?"
When this had been said, the venerable Kātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Behold, O Son of the Conqueror! One who would give Jambudvīpa, filled with a collection of the seven jewels, to those who possess the ten powers, generates far more merit for the sake of awakening while making a vow for enlightenment.

And one who, O Son of the Conqueror, would give the four continents, heaped with jewels, to those who possess the ten powers, generates far more merit for the sake of awakening while making a vow for enlightenment.

And one who, O Son of the Conqueror, would give a triple-thousandfold world system containing many jewels to those who possess great qualities, generates far more merit for the sake of awakening while making a vow for enlightenment.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, if someone were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with many kinds of jewels and offer them as worship to the Protectors of the World, he would generate far more merit than that if he were to make a vow for enlightenment. Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, if someone were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the ocean with many kinds of jewels and give them as worship to the Supreme Persons, he would generate far more merit than that if he were to make a vow for enlightenment.
What is the reason? For these are not the intentions of ordinary men; rather, it is for the welfare of many people that those heroes conceive such aspirations.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Kātyāyana.

"Furthermore, O son of the Jina, as for those bodhisattvas who dedicate [their merit] toward non-retrogression, does their first vow arise when they have accumulated wholesome merit (*kuśala-puṇya*), or rather when they have accumulated roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*)?
When this was said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Those of great renown first worship the Tathāgatas with great reverence; yet even then, these best of men do not yet direct their minds toward the Supreme Person.

And those millions of Pratyekabuddhas worship those individuals who have realized the ultimate truth; yet even so, those wise ones do not give rise to a conceited mind regarding their own knowledge of all phenomena.
Tens of millions of those who have attained mastery worship them, for they have long since reached the perfection of mastery;
yet these Leaders do not even give rise to a thought directed toward crossing the ocean of knowledge.
When they have accumulated a vast store of merit and have cultivated their bodies and minds,
they come together and direct their thoughts toward enlightenment for those who possess excellent forms.
By whatever root of merit has been acquired by me, may I possess all-seeing vision;
and may this vow of mine not be long delayed—may this very vow be fulfilled!
"May this accumulation of my roots of merit become great for the sake of all living beings;
and whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by me, may I pass through its bitter fruit."
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
And how, O son of the Conqueror, do bodhisattvas become firm in their valor, such that they become irreversible?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Kāśyapa in verses:
If, in the interval until I become a knower of the ultimate truth, I should dwell even in the Avīci hell, I accept that;
I do not withdraw my vow for omniscience—this is my firm resolve.
He is capable of abandoning birth, old age, death, sorrow, and calamities; he will not turn back his mind from his purpose.
He is the benefactor of the world’s people who brings about the end of the mass of suffering—this is the power of the stride of those bulls among men.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, when an irreversible Bodhisattva first generates the thought of enlightenment, what marvelous qualities then manifest?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
The earth, abounding in jewels, resounds with its cities, towns,
and rivers when the foremost beings of the world first manifest their original vows.
When the first vow for the state of a Lion among Men arises, a radiance like the splendor of the sun blossoms throughout all directions.
And the hosts of the best of gods, exultant, raised their voices in succession, saying:
"This one, infinitely exalted, makes his vow for the state of a Lion among Men."
For he is exceedingly radiant and must be protected by us for the sake of the world;
performing auspicious deeds, he accumulates merit—this is indeed a marvel.
When this had been said, the venerable Kāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Victor, how many difficult deeds have been performed by these irreversible bodhisattvas while they were established in the first stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verse:
Having given away their beloved wives, their heart’s delights, their sons, their heads, their eyes, and their abundance of ornaments and vehicles,
those bulls among men do not seek rest nor fall into dejection, but remain intent upon omniscience. (83)
Though they are subjected to threats of execution, imprisonment, and flogging by fierce men who are intensely inclined toward unwholesome deeds,
those faultless ones, seeing them, respond with supreme gentleness and a mind of loving-kindness, addressing them with smooth words.
Upon seeing a supplicant endowed with pride and negligence, great men attain supreme joy;
having given, they become delighted as their virtues increase, and they do not undergo remorse, for they are free from the despair of asceticism.
Thus ends the first stage in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Then the Elder Kāśyapa said to Mahākātyāyana:
"The first stage, O Great Being, which is so delightful, has been pointed out."
As the sons of the best of men transition to the second stage,
what state of mind arises in the bodhisattvas immediately thereafter?
And what are the resolute intentions that exist on the second stage, O Son of the Conqueror? One should explain these for the Bodhisattvas exactly as they are.
Then the elder Kātyāyana said this to Kāśyapa:
"I shall proclaim the delightful instruction concerning the bodhisattvas."
(84) For those who are transitioning to the second [dhyāna], dissatisfaction first arises toward existences; there is no doubt that this belongs to the Bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Conqueror, for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the second stage, these resolute intentions arise:

namely, they possess a virtuous resolute intention; they possess a gentle resolute intention; they possess a sweet resolute intention; they possess a sharp resolute intention; they possess a vast resolute intention;

they possess a diverse resolute intention; they possess a profound resolute intention; they possess an inexhaustible resolute intention; they possess an unimpaired resolute intention; and they possess a unique resolute intention.
They possess lofty aspirations; they possess uncringing aspirations; they possess indefatigable aspirations; they possess unartificial aspirations;

they possess pure aspirations; they possess firm aspirations; they possess natural aspirations; they possess satisfied aspirations; they possess aspirations directed toward individuals; and they possess infinite aspirations.
O Dhātudharmadhara, how do bodhisattvas come to possess auspicious aspirations?
It is said:
They do not have any doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
thus is their noble resolute intention taught.
How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do Bodhisattvas come to possess a gentle and affectionate disposition?
It is said:
Even while their limbs are being severed, their minds do not become angry;
thus, their resolute intention (adhyāśaya) is described as affectionate and gentle.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a sweet disposition?
It is said:
(85) Supreme among men practice wholesome deeds within;
thus, through their purified intellects, their higher aspirations become sweet.
How, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, do Bodhisattvas come to possess sharp resolve?
It is said:
Those endowed with pure intention awaken thus in the world as well as in the supramundane;
in this way, those of pure karma possess sharp higher intentions.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess vast resolve?
It is said:
"For the sake of the welfare of all beings, they accumulate abundant merit;
thus, the noble intentions of the supreme sages become vast."
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess diverse resolute intentions?"
It is said:
Free from stinginess, they give various and pleasing gifts;
thus do the high resolves of those who perceive the Supreme become manifold.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, do bodhisattvas become those whose resolute intention is inexhaustible?
It is said:
Their minds are undaunted, and they possess the prowess of penetration;
thus, their resolute intention is said to be undaunted.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess unimpaired resolute intentions?
It is said:
They cannot be led astray by anyone with a malicious mind;
thus, their resolute intention is never impaired.
(86) And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess uncommon resolute intentions?
It is said that when no other aspiration whatsoever arises in a being except for the sake of the happiness of all beings, they know that to be uncommon.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess an exalted resolve?
It is said:
Having heard the doctrines of other non-Buddhist teachers, contempt arises;
because of that, they become lions among men with exalted intentions.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, do bodhisattvas come to possess a noble and ungrudging resolve?
It is said:
The wise do not accumulate merit for the sake of enjoying the qualities of sensual pleasure;
therefore, their higher aspirations remain forever free from miserliness.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess an irreversible resolute intention?
It is said:
Those who have made a firm resolve for Buddhahood are not overwhelmed by sensual desires;
therefore, their resolute intentions are known as "irreversible."
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess an uncontrived resolute intention?
It is said:
They do not desire the state of a *vaśin* or a *pratyekabuddha* in any way whatsoever;
thus, their resolute intention remains forever uncontrived.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas become pure in their resolute intention?
It is said:
Having renounced gain and honor, those who long for the ultimate truth possess pure higher resolve; thus it is taught.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, do bodhisattvas become firm in their resolute intention?
It is said:
"Though assailed by the worlds, they do not withdraw their vigor from the Dharma;
such is the firmness of the high resolve of those great seers."
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a resolute intention that accords with their true nature?
It is said:
Overwhelmed, they do not eat the food of others, being intent on their own [practice]. O Noble One, such is their natural disposition and high resolve, which is thus praised.
And how, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, do bodhisattvas become possessed of a satisfied resolute intention?
It is said:
They do not flow toward sensual pleasures here, but always delight in renunciation;
such a resolute intention, being satisfied, is praised in a bodhisattva.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, do bodhisattvas come to possess resolute intentions toward individuals?
It is said:
The wise long for the state of self-arisen omniscience;
thus they possess an incomparable and constant resolve directed toward the person (pudgala).
(88) And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess infinite resolute intention?
It is said:
Through the perfection of the quality of non-giving, they do not crave great enjoyments;
thus, these supreme persons possess infinite noble intention.
Endowed with all these twenty qualities, those excellent persons are skilled in all dharmas and possess sublime, virtuous intentions.
"Indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, it is by being endowed with these twenty resolute intentions that Bodhisattvas come to be.
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, in how many ways do bodhisattvas abiding on the second stage regress from the third stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O upholder of the ascetic virtues, by twenty-eight causes, bodhisattvas abiding on the second stage fall back from the third stage.
By which twenty-eight aspects?
That is to say, they become those who value gain; they become those who value honor; and they become those who are intent upon fame and renown.
They are deceitful, they pursue gain through dishonest means,
and they are intent on harsh speech and provocation.
They do not bestow gifts with abundant reverence toward the Three Jewels; they do not seek out the conduct of a bodhisattva among those worthy of offerings;
and when they do reach the stage of a bodhisattva’s conduct, they do not honor it.

They do not take up a burden that is obtainable through excessive honor; nor, having taken up a burden that is unobtainable, do they cast it off. They do not feel distressed by living in a crowded place.
They wear garlands, garments, ornaments, jewelry, and ointments;
yet they are content with even a few virtues.
They are constantly delighted by things that please the world,
yet they do not conceive of all elements as impermanent;
rather, they take supreme pride in their own complexion and form.
They do not abandon their distorted views,
nor do they fulfill the words and phrases as they were taught; furthermore,
they become stingy regarding the teaching.
They regard those who are unworthy recipients,
yet they do not bestow gifts upon those who are worthy;
and they possess harsh continuums of being.
And they act without due consideration.
O upholder of the ascetic practices (dhutadharmadhara), whatever bodhisattvas dwelling on the second stage regress from the third stage, they all regress by means of these twenty-eight modes;
regarding this, it is said as follows:
Thus, this is called the second stage of the Bodhisattvas,
who possess various treasuries of wholesome qualities and act for the welfare and happiness of the world.
For those who are joined with faults turn back in such a manner;
but the wise, though they may likewise turn back [from worldly things], do not turn back [from their goal].
Those who are steadfast in their burden undertake a heroism that is difficult to ascend;
and for the sake of compassion for the world, they practice it amidst manifold sufferings.
All those Tathāgatas are worthy of worship by both gods and humans;
for it is precisely because they have preceded their actions with wisdom that they encounter various forms of suffering.
The wise conform to this world of diverse elements;
therefore, their fame has spread throughout the world, including the realms of gods and humans.
Thus ends the second bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O Son of the Best of Men, what kind of mind arises in Bodhisattvas who are transitioning from the second stage to the third stage?
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke thus to Kāśyapa:
"Listen to the unsurpassed mind of transition belonging to the Bodhisattvas."
The mind of the Bodhisattvas, O friend, is inclined toward renunciation as they pass from the second stage to the third, O Son of the Conqueror.
These lords of men bring happiness to all sentient beings as they abide;
yet they do not do so for the sake of their own pleasure, nor for the sake of awakening in any way whatsoever.

They barter even their children and wives for a single well-spoken verse. In former times, while acting as a virtuous Bodhisattva king, he abandoned his kingdom, his dense forests, his armies, and his mountain retreats— all things held dear— [in exchange for] such acquisitions.
But the human thickets are forests where uneven ground is not found.

Thickets of grass, shrubs, thorns, and creepers, as well as dense forests where trees are difficult to grasp, are but minor obstacles; however, the thickets of deceit, malice, and slander are the true thickets of humanity.
"Speak, O Brahmin, to Bhaṇḍin."
(91) ...a single well-spoken verse was uttered by the Bodhisattva;
desiring the ultimate truth, that [verse] was purchased by the Bodhisattva.
This well-spoken verse was acquired with great effort from the hand of a snake-charmer:
"As long as one lives, whatever evil deed has been committed remains within this very basket."
Having approached the royal sage Ṛṣideva, the brahmin, with a joyful heart, spoke these well-spoken words: "This [woman] exists."
"Your head shall be its price," he said.
"Speak quickly to me, O Brahmin, this well-spoken verse."
Even if they should perform some unwholesome deed while longing for the conduct of a bodhisattva,
it does not shine forth when overwhelmed by the power of vast merit, like an oil lamp shrouded by the rays of the sun.
The rākṣasa said this to the king named Surūpa:
"There is a well-spoken verse for sale; if you will buy it, I shall give it to you."
Its price would be that it would devour the prince, the queen, and you yourself.
If you have need of it, let it be taken; for this verse is indeed consistent with the Dharma.
Thus spoke King Surūpa, free from attachment and out of reverence for the Dharma:
"Let it be taken; let the verse be given; let it be fitting; do not delay."
(92) Thereupon, the rākṣasa spoke this well-spoken verse:
It is better to dwell in hells amidst lamentations, tremblings, encounters with the undesired, and separations from the beloved, than to make one's home in the company of base men.
A piśāca spoke these words to the minister named Sañjaya:
"Give me your own heart; listen to this well-spoken verse."
"I give you my heart; speak a well-spoken verse," said the hero Sañjaya, free from suffering, to the piśāca.
Thereupon, the piśāca recited this well-spoken verse:
A blazing fire is never extinguished by grass and wood;
likewise, craving for sensual pleasures is never quenched by the enjoyment of those very objects.
A poor man spoke these words to the merchant named Vasundhara:
"This well-spoken verse shall be given in exchange for my entire wealth."
The Bodhisattva said:
I give you all my possessions; recite for me a well-spoken verse, for the virtuous praise that which is well-spoken among all things.
Thereupon, the poor man recited this well-spoken verse:
Where foolish beings dwell, even crowded places are empty;
yet even a single person who possesses true knowledge makes a place full, though it be empty. (93)
A man said this to King Surūpa:
"It is possible to hear well-spoken words at the price of Jambudvīpa."
The Bodhisattva said:
I give you all of Jambudvīpa, whatever you desire;
speak quickly, speak well-spoken words; speak the truth, if you so wish.
Thereupon, a man recited this well-spoken verse:
Where various forms of "I-making" and "mine-making" arise,
and where pride is produced for the sake of its cessation, there the Tathāgatas appear.
The hunter spoke thus to the deer named Satvaram:
"This is a well-spoken verse; give me your flesh and listen to it."
"If I may hear a well-spoken word in exchange for this flesh subject to decay, I shall give you my flesh; speak quickly that well-spoken word."
Then the hunter spoke this well-composed verse:
The dust from the feet of the virtuous is better than a mountain made of gold;
that dust removes sorrow, while that mountain increases it.
(94) A servant spoke thus to the king named Nāgabhuja:
"It is possible to obtain well-spoken words even through a kingdom consisting of the four continents."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I give you sovereignty over the four continents; speak quickly!
Do not delay; tell me this well-spoken word."
There, his servant recited this well-spoken verse:

The wise say that the agitation of a person of wisdom is like the tearing out of a cataract; therefore, having attained the power of knowledge, one should lead away the defilements along with their roots.
Having severed them with a mind free from defilement, the pure Saṅgha shines forth. The Teacher of the World, followed by the virtuous, shines as one who has not laid down his burden and is pure.
Thus, for the sake of a well-spoken word, he fell once more into a precipice;
and again, for the sake of a well-spoken word, he abandoned his ship in the great ocean.
Having heard a well-spoken verse, his eyes were surrendered once more;
having heard a well-spoken verse, he fell again into a mass of fire.
For the sake of the meaning of well-spoken words, the highly renowned bulls among Jinas undertake many such difficult practices.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, how do those bodhisattvas who abide on the third stage regress from the fourth stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O Dhutadharmanidhi, by means of fourteen aspects, bodhisattvas dwelling on the third stage transition to the fourth stage.
By which fourteen?
They are devoted to the practice of gambling with dice and crooked games;
they resort to solitude too frequently;
and while exercising their sovereignty, being overcome by greed, they seize all the property of those living within their own realm.
Without investigating the offense, they order executions; they do not protect those deserving of death;
and they subject men to torture.
They fall into error;

and even while possessing wealth, they do not share it for the sake of their livelihood. Having gone forth, they do not master the great learning as it is being taught by the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
Having previously made a vow, they do not teach extensive learning;
they associate with those bound by material gain rather than those bound by the Dharma;
and they do not frequently speak in praise of the Buddha.
They teach that the perfectly awakened ones are equal to the world,
and they do not lead one to perceive the perfectly awakened ones as being supramundane.
O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, by these fourteen ways, bodhisattvas abiding on the third stage regress from the fourth stage.
For whatever Bodhisattvas, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), who abide on the third stage might have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back from the fourth stage,
all of them do so for no more than these fourteen reasons.
(96) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, when irreversible Bodhisattvas first produce the thought of awakening, with what kind of happiness are they endowed, and how many beings become possessed of the essence of happiness?
When this was said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
That which is inconceivable and marvelous arises, wherein all sentient beings come to possess the essence of happiness;
and that which is born as the mind of the great sages, consisting of the cultivation of the path to enlightenment.
Those who were certain that [their stay] would last for seven nights, even those who had reached the terrible abodes of hell,
and the living beings in the realms of the hungry ghosts— they all became truly happy.
For seven nights, living beings do not pass away through the Bodhisattva’s skillful compassion;
the earth, together with the oceans, trembles,
and the summit of Mount Meru revolves with its radiance.
This [wind] operates at the junctures of the earth; it moves in the firmament, of this there is no doubt.
By the power of the entire mass of all virtuous deeds, it revolves continuously throughout everything.

(97) Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva who had become a Trāyastriṃśa deity named Nāmatideva, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was seen, praised the Blessed One to his face,
before the assembly of those who have attained mastery, with these verses:

I bow to you, the peaceful one, the self-controlled one... who is skilled in mindfulness and discipline, honored by gods and asuras; whose form has the luster of gold, whose body is unassailable like the rising sun, and who shines with splendor; who is filled with the thirty-two perfect marks described by those of virtuous conduct; who is supreme in virtue, full of radiance, possessing strength greater than that of the earth, mountains, and elephants, and bearing the highest power.

For a long time, the Sage—whose conduct was manifold, who was skilled in bestowing exceedingly vast fruits out of a desire for the exhaustion of existence, and who was inclined toward tranquility through various praiseworthy virtues and manifold roots of merit born of loving-kindness—renounced his eternal abode honored by asuras and gods, and descended to the surface of the earth; he was born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, established in glory, and possessed of unshakable fortitude, intent upon awakening sentient beings.

That supreme one, resembling a white lotus and possessing the form of an elephant, entered the womb of Queen Māyā; thus did the Lord of the World, having left his abode in the excellent Tuṣita heaven, come here to uplift all beings who were intoxicated, blind, and fallen upon the treacherous path of doubt.

At that time, the earth—strewn with jewels and filled with heaps of various treasures—trembled; and they paid homage to that Great Sage, the Lord of the Śākyas, who was rich in conduct, steadfast in mindfulness, and endowed with supreme virtues. (98)

The queen Māyā was enjoying herself in happiness upon the roof of the palace, as if in the most excellent abode of the Lord of the Gods, with dances, songs, graceful movements, and instrumental music that were pleasing to the ear, heart, and eye—just like a goddess among the immortals.

That queen spoke to the king who was feeling dejected: "O Lord of the Earth, choose a boon; if you wish, let me go to the Lumbinī grove, which is strewn with flowers, filled with the sweet warbling of cuckoos, and gladdening to the mind and heart."

Having gone there, he wandered with his women in the forest, joyful and happy, out of a desire for the woods. As she was wandering through the garden, she saw the Lumbinī tree, bearing young creepers and tender shoots;

grasping its branch, she stood there gracefully, filled with supreme delight and pleasure, and while guarding that branch, she gave birth to the Conqueror, the one of unconquered mind, the Great Sage, the Supreme One.

Where the gods bathed the Jina with two streams of water, one cold and one warm, filled with the finest flowers— him who was being born, him who had just been born as a king honored in the realm of the gods, the great lord of the three worlds, compassionate, transcendent of the world, a refuge here in heaven and on earth, the ender of old age and death, the steadfast one who had not yet touched the ground, whose eyes resembled lotus petals, and the delight of both gods and asuras.
All the gods, joyful and satisfied, descended from their abodes beginning with the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, intending to enter the forest.
Born of the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, he has descended to the surface of the earth; established in glory, his fortitude is as unshakable as a mountain.

With seven strides, like the king of bulls or the moon, he has measured out the world; the eldest, the most excellent, the foremost in the world, I am here, and for me there is no more old age, death, or the afflictions of existence.

A divine parasol, strewn with jewels, variegated with flowers as radiant as crystal, and possessing the white luster of a pale cloud, was released from his hand and remained poised in the air, covering the prince; it was fashioned by the gods, peerless, with a high staff white as pearl, adorned with gems and gold, and fanned by incomparable whisks made of soft, fierce hair resembling conch shells.

The drums resounded like the roar of clouds, and the hosts of winds and birds cried out with great voices; divine showers of flowers, mixed with sandalwood powder, were released by the gods into the mouth of the Victor, the supreme in power.

With an excess of joy, the gods and demigods—stirred by hundreds of musical sounds—proclaimed "Victory! to the one who brings happiness. By the splendor of the Tathāgata, the various jewels on the surface of the earth and in the waters of the ocean were likewise agitated.
Thus ends the third bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
(100) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, as for those bodhisattvas who are established in the state of non-retrogression, how many kinds of actions do they perform that are not based on improper grounds?
Then the Elder Kātyāyana, who was learned in the teachings of the Jina,
addressed Kāśyapa, the observer of the dhuta-precepts, with these verses:
Understand those actions which Bodhisattvas practice;
understand those which they do not practice because they are improper occasions.
Bodhisattvas of great renown do not deprive even their mother, their father, or likewise an Arhat, of life.
They do not cause a schism in the Saṅgha, nor are they destroyers of stūpas;
they do not, in any way whatsoever, harbor malice toward the Tathāgata.
They do not indulge in evil deeds on their perverted backs;
they do not let even a small thing go to waste—how much less so that which is abundant?
And as they wander through saṃsāra, they never become attached to anything previously seen,
whether it be for the sake of the Dharma, for wealth, or for merit preceded by knowledge.
Those who sit and lie down in the shade of a tree neither harm its leaves nor destroy them when provoked to anger.
The supreme among men practice the ten wholesome paths of action;
they do not employ mantras that destroy the bodies of others. (101)
Relying upon their karma and relying upon curiosity,
they do not despair in times of adversity, nor do they rejoice in times of prosperity.
Physical action, verbal action, and likewise mental action,
as well as purified higher intentions and the perfection of generosity;
Having reached the eighth stage and beyond, they are irreversible;
honored by the world, they practice wholesome deeds with single-minded devotion.
Starting from the first stage up to the seventh,
these best of people practice mixed karma upon these stages.
Great beings who practice such deeds as these fulfill the ten stages for the sake of compassion toward the worlds.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, do those irreversible Bodhisattvas go to the states of woe among ordinary worldlings, or not?
Do they go to the lower and lower destinies among ordinary worldlings, or not?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, those bodhisattvas who possess the nature of non-retrogression do not, in any way, for anything, or at any time, by chance, go to hell,

or go to the animal realm, or become poor, or become weak. Rather, O Brahmins, they become Pratyekabrahmins, Indras, Upendras, lords of yakṣas, yakṣas, nāgas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and lords of gandharvas."

Universal monarchs and regional kings, chief ministers and guild masters, leaders of the countryside, princes, sons of guild masters, sons of the chief queen, and commanders—all become endowed with every form of heroism and valor; they are possessed of great strength, worthy of being looked up to and gazed upon, worthy of salutation, their words are accepted, and they are beloved and dear to many people.
They become pleasing to many people, worthy of praise, and refreshing; they possess great wealth, great prosperity, and large retinues; they are full of great energy and great splendor.
If some, for whatever reason, disparage the noble ones while abiding on the seven stages, they will go to the great hell of Avīci; indeed, they will go to the individual hells.
They are not reborn among the pretas with their extremely emaciated bodies, nor are they reborn among the asuras.
They do not go to the lowly animal realms;
they are not reborn among the people of Uttarakuru;
and they do not undergo female birth.
They do not become impotent.
Furthermore, in all ten stages, men possess all major and minor limbs and have unimpaired faculties.

Yet, if a bodhisattva deprives another bodhisattva of life, or a disciple of a perfectly enlightened one (samyaksaṃbuddha), or a stream-enterer (śrotāpanna), or those beings who are destined for the state of a pratyekabuddha— having deprived such a person of life, he goes to hell.

Whatever killing Bodhisattvas may commit on the seven stages, or whatever they take that is not given, or whatever fully complete unwholesome karma they perform, it is not capable of leading the Bodhisattva to hell.

Furthermore, those unwholesome actions that were accumulated by Bodhisattvas prior to their initial vow remain obstructed by the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), like a herd of deer blocked by a great mountain.
Yet, until that vow-mind is attained, they ripen in the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh births—even if only as a headache.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, those irreversible Bodhisattvas who, having propitiated the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, go forth from the home life into homelessness—by what kind of instruction do those Tathāgatas [guide them]?
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke thus to Kāśyapa:
"By means of parables, through discourses that are secluded, and in gradual succession."

The lords, skilled in the Jātakas and other supreme teachings, proclaim the conduct of Bodhisattvas which brings great benefit— the discipline of self-control, generosity, and restraint— to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata, the supreme among men, who performs incomparable deeds for the benefit of the great multitude— of him the wise one speaks thus in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Such a lord is called a Blessed One; he undertakes what is difficult with prior knowledge.
In the teaching of the Victor, a bodhisattva like him is extremely rare in the world. (104)
"O bearer of the ascetic virtues, such is the Dharma that the perfectly awakened ones teach in the assembly of bodhisattvas."
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, from what point onward are these Jātaka stories spoken by the Conqueror to be understood?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
O bearer of the ascetic virtues, these Jātaka stories spoken by the Victor pertain to this eighth stage.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Mahākātyāyana:
From what point onward, O Son of the Conqueror, do Bodhisattvas relinquish all their possessions and perform difficult acts of renunciation?
When this had been said, Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the dhuta qualities, from the eighth stage onwards, Bodhisattvas relinquish all their possessions and perform difficult acts of renunciation."
"O upholder of the ascetic qualities, from the eighth stage onwards, Bodhisattvas are to be honored by means of worshiping a perfectly awakened Buddha."
In this regard, the following is said:
From the eighth stage onwards, O sons of the Conquerors, Bodhisattvas are to be regarded as perfectly awakened Buddhas; from this point forward, they are irreversible.
From this point on, they attain profound meditations;
from this point on, their refined knowledge proceeds.
From this time forth, they speak words preceded by knowledge;
from this time forth, the wise abandon a censurable life.
From this point forward, they follow whatever pure birth they attain;
from this point forward, they experience whatever pure form they assume.
From this point forward, whatever characteristic they desire, they become accordingly.
From this time forward, whatever deity they desire, they shall become that very one.
From this point on, they become either worldlings or destroyers of existence;
from this point on, they loathe sensual desires and praise liberation.
From this time forward, there will be many preeminent speakers who are disciples of the illustrious, perfectly awakened Buddhas, the gods beyond gods.
Then, having passed away, they will be exhorted by the Buddhas who reveal the Dharma:
"O wise ones, teach the Dharma; accept the banner of the sages!"
From this time forth, they discipline many people in arhatship;
from this time forth, they discipline many people on the stage of training.
From this time forth, the gods, yakṣas, and guhyakas followed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva until he attained self-becoming (buddhahood).
From this time forth, that form shall be supreme in the world including the gods;
from this time forth, even the complexion, as well as brilliance, renown, fame, and strength, shall be unequaled by the world for these most excellent Bodhisattvas. (106)
And because the Buddhas have not arisen, they possess the five supernormal powers;
seeing the faults in sensual desires, they praise renunciation.
From this time forth, the gods and the asuras, together with Brahmā,
being delighted by their qualities, approached with palms joined in reverence.
Whatever activity belongs to those who have attained mastery is such that it is the same as the activity of Bodhisattvas on the eighth stage.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Conqueror, what kind of Dharma do these irreversible Bodhisattvas teach to sentient beings while exercising the sovereignty of universal monarchs? And in the absence of Buddhas, by what kind of means of integration do they integrate sentient beings, and what kind of people do they treat with equanimity?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O bearer of the ascetic qualities, those irreversible bodhisattvas who exercise the sovereignty of universal monarchs teach the Dharma to sentient beings in this way.
They demonstrate to sentient beings that which is conjoined with the ten paths of wholesome action.

They teach: "May there be no killing of living beings; stealing must not be committed; the wives of others must be protected; and falsehood, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong views must be abandoned."
Having set out heaps of bullion, gold, and wealth before the dwellings, they spoke thus in salutation: "Let whoever needs anything from this take the wealth!
My enjoyments were acquired through the Dharma; may you not be despondent."
"I offer garlands, perfumes, incense, and delightful powders; may you not be despondent, but take your pleasure."
When this had been said, Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
By what kinds of actions do bodhisattvas, while exercising the sovereignty of universal monarchs, come to possess the seven jewels?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Just as the bull among men, the king of the four continents, possessing abundant wealth and treasuries,
obtains the seven jewels— so shall I proclaim this.

The supreme among men obtains the precious wheel, which resembles the orb of the rising sun and is beautiful with its collection of a thousand excellent spokes, arising from his former roots of merit.
When one gives a gift accompanied by the proper mode of service with a faultless intention,
that best of men obtains the wheel of invincible victory, which is unassailable.

He obtains a marvelous jewel of an elephant, the color of a white water-lily amidst a mass of snow, with seven limbs firmly planted on the ground, and possessing a speed equal to the force of the wind.
Having established a bridge over difficult and uneven terrain,
that destroyer of enemies obtains the supreme jewel of an elephant that travels through the sky.

Then the king, through his accumulation of merit and skillful deeds, obtains that jewel of a horse, dark as a bumblebee, golden-hued, swift as the wind, with a lion-like gait, and with its hooves raised high.
(108) Carrying his mother, father, elders, and likewise his teacher on excellent vehicles— by that merit, the king obtains the marvelous jewel of the horse.
A woman obtains a jewel-gem of incomparable color, endowed with the brilliance of lapis lazuli, a delightful and excellent treasure through infinite strength and vigor.
For in a previous existence, while dwelling there, he was devoted to the restraint of contentment with his own wife;
as a lord of men, he therefore obtained that jewel of a woman.
The king, possessing great mastery, obtains the noble jewel of a householder— one who is wealthy, endowed with various excellent riches, and possessed of vast accumulations of hoarded treasures.
A donor of various accumulations of wealth, endowed with profound respect for his teachers,
thereby obtains the treasure of a householder, possessing abundant riches and merit.

The king who has desisted from unwholesome conduct obtains the supreme jewel of a counselor— one who is skilled in the sacrifice of sight, wise, discerning, a banner for his leader, and master of the four continents.
For those who have gone astray on the path, whose eyes are struck down and destroyed, he shows the way;
thereby one obtains the jewel of the supreme leader, the excellent guide.
By these deeds, the holders of the ascetic virtues have produced the jewels;
and by that very dharma, the lord of men rules the earth.
(109) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O Son of the Conqueror, by how many modes do these bodhisattvas who have first produced the thought of awakening, while abiding on the fourth stage, regress from the fifth stage?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
O Dhātudharmadhara, those bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon awakening and who, while abiding on the fourth stage, regress from it to the fifth stage due to seven factors.
By which seven?
They become corrupters of bhikṣuṇīs;
they become corrupters of men;
and they become corrupters of paṇḍakas.
Furthermore, by the power of mantras, they cause unreal diseases to arise in others;
they cause those who possess good conduct to fall away from their virtue;
and they become shameless.
And they become free from trepidation.
O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, whatever bodhisattvas first produce the thought of awakening, if they abide in these seven ways while on the fourth stage, they regress from the fifth stage.
Thus, O son of the Sugata, this fourth stage has been taught,
which is delightful for those bodhisattvas who are intent upon awakening.
Thus ends the fourth bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O Son of the Conqueror, for those irreversible Bodhisattvas who pass from the fourth stage to the fifth stage, what is their state of consciousness at the transition?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
