They perceive all states of existence as ablaze due to passion, hatred, and delusion;
the transitional consciousness, which occurs immediately after the fourth or fifth [moment of consciousness], is without refuge and devoid of joy.
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, regarding those Perfectly Enlightened Ones whom the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, honored on the fifth stage—what were the names and lineages of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones? How large were their assemblies of disciples? What was the extent of their radiance? And what was the measure of their lifespan?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
There was a supreme Victor named Śākyamuni, surrounded by a retinue of ten million self-controlled ones;
he possessed a fathom-wide radiance, was as solid as a mountain, resembled a mountain of gold, and had conquered all enemies.
The lifespan of that Supreme among Men was six thousand years at that time;
his name was Yaśavrata, and he was an exceedingly beautiful Buddha.
By virtue of his lineage he was Gautama, and this Blessed One was then the son of a merchant;
having given an offering of rice gruel to the Buddha and his retinue, he made a solemn aspiration.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through giving to the Saṅgha of Arhats with full devotion—by that may I become a seer of the ultimate truth; may my merit be entirely [for that purpose].
The final incarnation will be a lion among men named Sundara Sudarśana;
he will belong to the Bhāradvāja gotra, and his radiance will extend for ten yojanas.
The retinue of that essence of beings consisted of ten million who had attained mastery;
the lifespan of that subduer of Māra was ten thousand years.
(111) And there was a universal monarch named Dharaṇīdhara;
he spoke thus to that Jina Sudarśana and his community of disciples:
"A wise man said, 'I give everything as an offering for the benefit [of others]';
and thus, O King, you made this supreme vow."
May I ferry across the people who have not despaired, though they are caught in the ocean of old age and death... The Blessed One was named Nareśvara;
his clan was Vāsiṣṭha, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas.
He had a retinue of twelve million who had attained mastery;
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was nine thousand years.
And there was a universal monarch named Aparājita;
with a mind full of faith, he spoke these words to the Lord of Men, the One Possessing the Ten Powers:
I give these eighty-four monasteries to you as your magnificent endowment, variegated with the limbs of the seven precious gems and possessing many kinds of jewels.
Having given that gift to that lord of men, he made this aspiration:
"May I become thus; may I attain the powers of a Jina."
Formerly, there was a Jina named Suprabha, who had a minister named Vijaya;
he belonged to the Kāśyapa clan, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas.
And his community of disciples consisted of eighteen koṭis of those who had shaken off the dust [of defilements];
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years.
Having paid homage to that supreme Jina, Vijaya invited him who destroys existence;
the Daśabala consented, and then Vijaya was filled with joy.
Having satisfied him with excellent, refined food and delicacies of such exquisite flavor as he had never tasted before,
you then made this subsequent vow.
May I too become thus, honored by the best of men, a benefactor to humans and gods;
may I also become a supreme leader, one endowed with the ten powers, a tiger among speakers.
Formerly there was a Buddha, a Tathāgata named Ratanaparvata;
he belonged to the Gautama clan, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas.
There was an entourage of thirty million humans whose minds were disciplined;
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years.
And at that time, there was a universal monarch named Acyuta;
pressing his feet, which were like those of a Jina, he spoke this to the best of men and gods:
O Nara-nāga, I give eighty-four thousand palaces,
beautifully adorned, to me and my community of disciples.
Having understood the acceptance [of his request], the king, with a joyful mind,
made a vow in the presence of the one who bears the excellent marks.
By this merit, may I become a protector for those without a protector, through conduct that has accumulated the most excellent virtues and through deeds of tireless vigor.
The Perfectly Awakened One, whose mind was as pure as the expanse of the sky, was named Kanakaparvata;
he was honored by the best of men and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan.
The radiance of his body, born of his auspicious karma, extended for six yojanas,
and he had a retinue of five koṭis of those who had attained mastery.
At that time, the lifespan of human beings was ten thousand six hundred years; and for fourteen thousand years, it was thirty-seven thousand years, indeed.
At that time there was a universal monarch named Priyadarśana,
radiant with the seven treasures, ruler of the four continents, and protector of the earth.
Having prostrated at the excellent feet of the Fully Awakened One, Kanakavarṇa-parvata, he,
together with his assembly of ministers and preceded by a necklace of pearls, made this request.
O Hero, I give to you, along with your assembly of disciples, my kingdom filled with cities and towns, as well as the four great wealthy islands, without any attachment.
Whatever food belongs to the seers, whatever clothing, and whatever medicinal preparations;
and whatever couches and seats there are, even those found in the most excellent palaces.
Everything that has been offered is for your enjoyment in its twelvefold form;
O you who possess the most excellent form, out of compassion, please show mercy.
Having given this gift, that protector of the earth,
with a joyful mind, made an aspiration in the presence of Saṃpūrṇakuśala.
Perceiving the ultimate truth, having attained the supreme perfection of fearlessness,
may I thereby become an excellent leader who brings about the destruction of all substrates of existence.
The Blessed One, bearing the thirty-two marks, was named Puṣpadanta;
he was a perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha) of the Vatsa lineage who perceived the ultimate truth.
The bodily radiance of that most excellent Jina extended for nine yojanas,
and thirty-four crores of those who had attained mastery followed that One Endowed with Ten Powers.
And the measure of the lifespan of human beings was fifty thousand years;
thus, one should not entertain doubt regarding that instruction.
And at that time, there was a king, a lord of men named Durjaya;
having approached Puṣpadanta, he paid homage at his feet together with his retinue.
(115) With palms joined in reverence and full of faith, he said this to Puṣpadanta, O Lord of Men:
"May the Daśabala accept my provision of food for seven days."
Knowing his acceptance, King Durjaya, whose strength was superior,
covered the surface of the earth with long strips of gold.
There he places variegated seats made of jewels;
and he sets out a diverse array of food, fragrant and freshly prepared.
Eight hundred parasols made of the seven precious gems are held by men and gods;
they wear ornaments, bearing various beautiful decorations and flowers.
Thus, for each one who has attained mastery, they hold in their hearts and minds a variegated jewel-parasol, stainless like the surface of the moon or a conch shell.
Having fully satisfied the Sugata named Puṣpa along with his retinue, the king then made a mental aspiration,
and that very aspiration was subsequently fulfilled.
"May I, like you, become a perfectly awakened Buddha and proclaim the Dharma to humans and gods.

... [Omitted] ... There was a Blessed One, a perfectly awakened Buddha named Lalitavikrama, who possessed the thirty-two marks; he was of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, a destroyer of existence, and one whose afflictions were shaken off.
And from his own body there issued forth a radiance extending for thirty-two yojanas;
and the retinue of that best of men consisted of thirty million self-mastered ones.
At that time, the lifespan of humans was eighty-four thousand years;
and there was then a king who possessed the fourfold army and was beloved and pleasing.
The protector of the earth had forty million palaces made of many jewels constructed,
as well as one preeminent palace.
The king causes vast and blameless lodgings to be constructed,
and he provides for the sages food and medicinal requisites suitable for their needs.
Having offered [this] to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples,
the king, with a joyful heart, made this aspiration in the presence of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
May I become one like the rare and peerless One of Ten Powers, who crushes old age, death, and delusion;
may I become the supreme among men and gods, crushing the words of the hosts of evil factions.
The Blessed One, possessing the thirty-two marks, was named Mahāyaśas;
by lineage he was Kāśyapa, of widespread fame and immeasurable renown.
The body of that merit-filled one was fifty yojanas in height,
and he had fifty-five million self-mastered bhūtas as his followers.
At that time, the measure of lifespan was eighty-four thousand years;
for human beings then, this [measure] was fourfold, namely eighty-four [thousand].
At that time, there was a king named Mṛgapatisvara,
the sovereign of the four continents, possessed of vast and excellent power, whose wheel was unconquered.
That lord of the earth caused a forest grove, sixty-nine yojanas in extent, to be constructed with branches of jewel-masses, most excellent and covered with choice cloths.
Having made the earth have a surface of lapis lazuli gems, adorned with various ornaments,
scented with the fragrance of the finest aloe-wood incense, and its surface strewn with fragrant flowers;
There, the protector of the earth, with a serene mind, gratified that lion among speakers, that bull among men, with exquisite food for seven days.
That daytime dwelling of the One Possessing Ten Powers, which resembles the grove of the best of gods.
Having given [this] to the one of great fame together with his community of disciples,
the king, with a joyful heart, then made this further vow:
May I be honored by many people, self-become, not led by others, and omniscient;
indeed, through that merit of mine, may I become a powerful Tathāgata.

The Victorious One Ratnacūḍa, a treasury of vast strength and merit, skilled in what is right and wrong, possessed deep-blue eyes; he was a steadfast one, an accumulation of incomparable virtues. (118)
And his radiance extended for a hundred yojanas all around his body;
at that time, he was Sarvadarśin, of the Bhāradvāja clan.
His Saṅgha consisted of ninety-nine koṭis of those who had shaken off the dust;
at that time, the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, there was a universal monarch, the great and powerful ruler of the four continents,
named Maṇiviṣāṇa, who governed the people according to the Dharma.
The protector of the earth had ninety-two billion palaces of manifold forms constructed, dedicated to that Jina Ratana.
He fed Ratnacūḍa— who resembled excellent gold and was honored by hosts of men and gods—
along with his retinue, for ten years without ceasing.
And on the first day, having fed the Sugata together with the community of disciples,
the best of men presented excellent palaces to the Holder of Virtues.
Having given that gift to that Great Being, the excellent king,
with a devout mind, makes a vow in the presence of the Victor.
With the net of delusion severed, with a serene mind and unhindered eloquence,
may he ferry across all people fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra.
In the same way, on the fifth stage, there are immeasurable lions among men—
both Pratyekabuddhas as well as the sons of the Conquerors who are still in training and those beyond training.
These and all other Tathāgatas have been fully honored by the Blessed One;
thus has the root of merit been accumulated for the sake of the entire world.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O sons of the Conqueror, by how many factors do those bodhisattvas who have made the vow for enlightenment, while abiding in the fifth stage, fall back from the sixth stage?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

O son of the Conqueror, bearer of the dhuta-qualities, there are four ways in which Bodhisattvas who have made aspirations for enlightenment, while abiding on the fifth stage, fall back from the sixth stage.
By which four?
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, they associate with practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*).
While being greedy for the divine and nāga deities of the eighth stage, they tremble at meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
yet, they frequently dwell in abundance in the cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
They conceptually construct the mind that takes an object as its object according to its causes.

For whatever Bodhisattvas, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), having made the vow for enlightenment, while abiding on the fifth stage, turn back from the sixth stage— all of them have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back by means of these four modes.
Thus, O worthy one, this fifth stage has been explained and demonstrated for those Bodhisattvas who possess manifold merits.
Thus ends the fifth bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
(120) Thereupon, the Elder Kāśyapa spoke to Kātyāyana: "Tell me of the mind of the wise Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage."
Then the Elder Kātyāyana addressed the sage Kāśyapa, who maintained the dhuta-precepts, with a verse:
Bound by a mere slight taste, this worldly cycle is exceedingly terrible;
[from this] one is born again.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"The field" means:
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke to Mahākāśyapa:
"Listen to the field of the Lords of the World, which is based upon the true meaning."
And I shall describe the secondary field (*upakṣetra*) of those supreme speakers;
having heard those words and the teaching, O best of men.
One sixty-first [part] of a trichiliocosm is examined as a buddha-field;
four times that should be known as an upakṣetra (sub-field) of the same kind.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, do the Perfectly Awakened Ones arise in all Buddha-fields, or do they arise only in some?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Only a very small portion of the field remains non-empty, being occupied by those who bear incomparable forms;
many millions of billions of fields are empty of the most excellent of men.
For rare indeed is one who bears the excellent marks, whose awakening has been fully realized over a long period of time,
who is skilled in all dharmas, possessed of supreme splendor, and a being who is the foundation of happiness for all sentient beings.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Indeed, O son of the Conqueror, what is the cause, what is the reason, that two perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously in a single field?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Whatever task is most difficult to accomplish—the Buddha-activity—this Naga among men fulfills it all; this is the natural law of the Buddhas.
If one who possesses the eye [of wisdom] should be incapable regarding the qualities of a Buddha,
then two Great Beings, Tathāgatas, will arise.
And because the great seers avoid that which is the presence of what is incapable [of coexistence],
therefore two bulls among men are not born in the same field.

It is never heard that the Buddhas, those supreme among men and sons of the Conquerors, have entered parinirvāṇa while the Buddha-qualities still remained incomplete; they have all passed away only after having transcended the path.
(122) "The Perfectly Awakened Ones who have passed away, those yet to come, and those in the present—
all these supreme among men attain Nirvana through the Dharma of the Buddha."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Victor, which other Buddha-fields are there at present where the Perfectly Awakened Ones are currently teaching the Dharma?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa with verses:
In the eastern direction lies the Buddha-field called Sunirmita;
there dwells the preeminent Victor named Mṛgapatiskandha.
In the eastern direction lies the Buddha-field named Kṛtāgada;
there dwells the Victor named Siṃhahanu, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
In the eastern direction, there is a Buddha-field named Vibhūṣita;
there dwells the Great Sage Sarvadarśin, the Teacher of the World.
In the eastern direction lies the Buddha-field Akkanthaka;
there the Teacher named Jñānadhvaja instructs living beings.
In the eastern direction, a Buddha-field was beheld;
there dwells a Jina named Sundara, who has the luster of a golden image.
In the southern direction lies the buddha-field named Drumadhvaja;
there dwells the perfectly enlightened one named Anihata, who brings joy to the gods.
In the southern direction lies a delightful buddha-field;
there dwells the Great Sage, the Perfectly Awakened One named Cārunetra.
In the southern direction lies the Buddha-field Akardama;
there dwells the perfectly awakened one, the guide named Mālādhārī.
In the western direction lies the Buddha-field called Avigraha;
there dwells the perfectly enlightened one named Ambara, the destroyer of existence.
In the northern quarter lies a delightful Buddha-field;
there dwells the Perfectly Awakened One named Pūrṇacandra, who has heard the ritual injunctions.
In the downward direction there is a well-established Buddha-field;
there dwells the Perfectly Awakened One, the Tathāgata named Dṛḍhabāhu.
In the region above, in the direction of the zenith, is the Buddha-field named Anuddhṛta;
there dwells the illustrious Buddha known by the name Ari-sūdana.
Beyond this, there are many thousands of Buddha-fields;
beyond those thousands of Buddha-fields, no further ten million fields can be discerned.
No end is perceived to the millions of empty buddha-fields;
no end is perceived to the millions of thousands of world-systems.
Just as the prior limit of the wheel of saṃsāra is not known,
even so the prior limit of world-systems is not known.
The prior limit of the Buddhas who have passed away is not known;
the prior limit of those making vows for enlightenment is not known.
The prior limit of those possessing the qualities of non-retrogression is not known;
the prior limit of those who have attained the stage of consecration is not known.
(124) For those dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, no prior limit is known;
for those passing away from the Tuṣita heaven, no prior limit is known.
For those lying within the mother’s womb, no prior limit is known;
indeed, for those remaining in the mother’s womb, no prior limit is known.
The prior limit of the heroes who are being born is not known;
the prior limit of the World-Protectors who have been born is not known.
For those being held in the crooks of their arms, the prior limit is not known;
for those taking steps forward, the prior limit is not known.
For those laughing with great laughter, the prior limit is not known;
for those surveying the directions, the prior limit is not known.
No prior limit is known for those being carried on one's lap;
no prior limit is known for those being led away by the Gandharvas.
For those going forth from the cities, no prior limit is known;
for those approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree, no prior limit is known.
For those who are attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata, no prior limit is known;
for those who are setting in motion the wheel of Dharma, no prior limit is known.
For those who discipline millions of beings, the prior limit is not known;
for those who roar the lion's roar, the prior limit is not known.
For those relinquishing the formations of life, the prior limit is not known;
for those heroes attaining nirvana, the prior limit is not known.
(125) For those who have attained nirvāṇa and are lying at rest, the prior limit is not known;
for those heroes who are still meditating, the prior limit is not known.
Understand this as it truly is: the assembly of teachers is thus;
here and there, a perfectly awakened Buddha is seen within the Buddha-fields.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O sons of the Conqueror, if there are this many perfectly enlightened Buddhas, and each single perfectly enlightened Buddha brings immeasurable sentient beings to final nirvana, will they not, in a short time, bring all sentient beings to final nirvana?
Thus, this world would become entirely empty in every respect, devoid of all sentient beings."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
May it be perpetually empty, perfectly fulfilled in its immediate continuity;
may it be perpetually non-abiding and without objective support, yet firmly established.
The element of earth is small, whereas sentient beings are far more numerous;
thus have the ordinary worldlings been described by that Seer of the Ultimate.
"How could there be an end for the many beings who hear the teaching of the Best of Men?"— thus it was said by the Great Seer.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, by how many modes do these beings who have made the vow for perfect enlightenment, while abiding on the sixth stage, turn back from the seventh stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), there are two ways in which bodhisattvas, while making the vow for awakening and abiding on the sixth stage, fall back from the seventh stage.
By which two?

They long for the meditative attainments of the cessation of perception and feeling, and at the time when the perfectly awakened Buddhas, through their thorough knowledge of beings, declare "I am the Great-Souled One who brings peace," they listen with attentive ears, honoring the deity.

"O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), whatever bodhisattvas there may be who, while abiding on the sixth stage, have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back from the seventh stage— all of them do so, have done so, or will do so by means of these two modes."
Thus is this sixth stage of those supreme in virtue,
of the lords of deer, of the benefactors, the great seers, the bodhisattvas.
Thus ends the sixth bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, what kind of transitional consciousness arises for those irreversible bodhisattvas who are passing from the sixth stage to the seventh stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
The mind of the supreme great person proceeds toward self-restraint for the benefit of others;
that which causes them to transition from the seventh stage to the [subsequent] stages is called the "connecting mind" (*sandhicitta*).
(127) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O Son of the Conqueror, as for these irreversible bodhisattvas, from the first stage onwards, with what kind of bodily action are they endowed? With what kind of verbal action are they endowed?
With what kind of mental action are they endowed? And with what kind of nature are they endowed?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, for those bodhisattvas who are irreversible, these deeds occur starting from the first bhūmi.

They abstain from taking life and speak in praise of abstaining from taking life; they commend those beings on the stages who, through their resolute intention, do not deprive another of life even by association with evil friends.

After they had developed compassion for those beings who were crying out across seven successive worlds, and having undertaken the precepts— whether by renouncing their kingdoms or abandoning whatever power they held—
they went forth from the home life into homelessness and extensively taught the Dharma of abstaining from taking life.
Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, in the past, while dwelling on the seventh stage, this Supreme Person became a king named Kuśa.
His queen was named Apratimā, who was this Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhulaśiri.
And this Devadatta, who is now a man of the Kali age, was at that time a regional king named Jaṭhara.
Having heard of that peerless goddess, lust for desire completely overwhelmed his mind.
He dispatched a messenger to King Kuśa.
"Give me the peerless goddess; she shall be my wife.
If you do not give her, then prepare for battle and ready your mount."
O King, send to me that which you have resolved;
(128) otherwise, if you do not send it to me, you shall dwell with your kingdom in my power.
Having heard this, King Kuśa said this to his wife:
"Listen, O Queen, to the words of the womb; speak your decision."
Then the queen, shedding a torrent of tears, spoke to King Kuśa.
"O Bhadra, indeed I could have been cut or split by you, O lord of men, even with weapons that were not superior; yet I have reached the perfection [of patience]."
O King, behold the head of Jaṭhara, severed by me with its crown intact; drenched in blood, let it wrap itself around your feet.
But by me, a living being, that arrow was released and made to serve as food;
having devoured my own body for the sake of its belly, it shall once again pierce the earth.
On the back of a horse, in a chariot, on the shoulder of an elephant,
and at the forefront of the best of warriors, I have brought about the end of the belly.
I am the mantra, I am the twilight ritual, and I am the speaker of words;
likewise, by means of reasons and causes, I cause even that which is not to be killed to be slain.
I alone am peerless; by these two means I shall bring about liberation.
For my illusions are indeed incalculable, and the world is as straw to me.
(129) "And how might the king— who wears perfumes and garlands, who moves about on the terraces of his palace, and who is attended by thousands of women— become free from longing?"
Then, O Son of the Conqueror, Queen Apratimā employed such a stratagem that, by means of it, King Jaṭhara became confident and entered the inner apartments of King Kuśa,
falling under the power of Queen Apratimā.
Then that incomparable goddess, having placed her right foot upon the heart of King Jaṭhara and resting her left foot upon his ankle, sang these verses:
The bees, their wings variegated with the pollen of flowers, drink from that flowering forest creeper when the season of blossoms arrives.
O base man, you have never before heard its form; nor do other bees here offer their affection to it.
O base man, that lotus pond which the wild elephant once climbed— its mud stirred up by water and its own limbs afflicted by passion—
neither has its former beauty been heard of by you, nor do other wild elephants ever show affection for it again.

She who, like a cluster of pearls bestowed upon the chest of a king honored by the earth, sports throughout the night— you, O lady of faultless limbs, are determined to obtain her, just as one standing upon the earth seeks to reach the full moon.
(130) Then indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, King Jaṭhara cried out at that time.
"Be gracious, O Goddess; grant us refuge," they said.
King Kuśa spoke to that peerless queen.
"O Goddess, grant fearlessness to this base man who has come to you for refuge;
for to one with palms joined in supplication, it is indeed the duty of the virtuous to do so."

Once upon a time, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, this Blessed One was a nāga king named Ugra; he was brought under control by a snake-charmer through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs and fell into great distress.
And due to negligence, that snake-charmer became one whose spells had failed.
Then this thought occurred to that Naga king Ugra:
"Indeed, this base man is within my reach to be reduced to ashes;
however, this is not befitting us who are devoted to the protection of Dharma."
The verses were recited in response.
"Even though you were capable of reducing me to ashes by your own splendor, since your mantra has been lost, I grant you safety: live with me for a long time."
Long ago, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, this very Blessed One was Siṃha, the king of beasts, and this wicked man Devadatta was that hunter.

Then, while he was dwelling in a grove suitable for a lion, wandering in the forest alone, sitting in confidence, motionless, at ease, and not looking around, a hunter— whose enmity had been nurtured by former intentions— pierced him with a poisoned arrow.
Though pierced, he remained steadfast, endowed with profound fortitude, and established in his own strength;
undaunted, with his neck slightly raised, he then perceived that wicked man, terrified and having sought refuge, and fell into reflection.
"Indeed, this base man is within my power to slay, even if he were to flee to a mountain peak, a cave, a tree, or the depths of the earth;
nevertheless, considering that 'enmities are not stilled by enmity,' he spoke this verse:"
"I have been pierced today by a poison-smeared arrow that strikes the vital organs;
for one who is thus terrified, there is no fear of you."
Long ago, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, this very Blessed One was a highly esteemed caravan leader.
And this caravan, with that very wicked man Devadatta acting as its guide—having been instigated by bandits—set out upon the path through the wilderness.
With his mind bound by the persistence of former enmity, he approached in order to have that caravan leader killed by bandits.

Those merchants, led by the caravan leader, captured the bandits; and as they were being led toward execution with the guide at their head, crying out in distress and without refuge, they sought protection from the caravan leader alone.
And the guide, having committed an offense against others, joined his palms in supplication and begged the caravan leader for safety.

In him, who dwells in compassion and has cultivated it through hundreds of thousands of existences, compassion arose; and having granted fearlessness even to those who were life-threatening, he spoke to the guide.
"Smoke released by me with the wind would destroy the region;
therefore, I grant life to the guide along with the thieves."

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (*dhutadharma*), when this very Blessed One was a king, he granted inconceivable safety to his chief queen, who had committed a great offense and had been brought to the place of execution.
Endowed with the gentleness and uprightness cultivated in former lives, he consoled the chief queen and spoke this verse:
"Alas! Let him cause the weapon to fall from his body onto an unbaked clay vessel;
I grant you safety, and that place shall remain as it was before."

O bearer of the ascetic virtues, hundreds of thousands of such difficult deeds have been performed by Bodhisattvas who are irreversible, through such actions of body, such actions of speech, and such actions of mind.

Bodhisattvas, while wandering through cyclic existence, possess manifold virtues; nevertheless, having come under the influence of karma, those bodhisattvas perform actions that are characterized by a summary of their qualities. They are firm in their prowess, endowed with fortitude, true to their vows, upright, and free from deceit.
They are not miserly;
they are not fickle;
and they are gentle.

They are compassionate, capable of enduring hardship, possessed of inexhaustible minds, and unmoved in spirit; they are invincible, difficult to conquer, endowed with courage, perfected in generosity, and perfected in their vows.
They are eloquent, possessed of manifold eloquence, endowed with insight, and free from craving.
They become attached to the ultimate truth; they become graspers of what has been grasped;
and they become pure in their conduct.
Their minds become unshakable;
they become endowed with extreme reverence;
and they become perfected in the proper conduct toward elders and virtuous persons.
They are skilled in means;
they are capable of joining together the composition of all undertakings;
and they are experts in the grammatical junctions of words regarding royal affairs.
They possess speech that does not falter in assemblies and are patient with harsh words. Having wisdom as their banner, they are skilled in gathering a great multitude of people.
Possessing an even mind, they have doors of livelihood that are untainted.
They are accomplished in their professional activities and skilled in providing assistance;
they are also skilled in alleviating the sufferings of others.

They are firm and sweet in their appreciation of the perils [of sensory pleasures] and are skilled in uprooting faults regarding what is loathsome to behold. They are untiring in concealing the private failings of others. And they possess roots of virtue that are skilled in discerning passion, hatred, and delusion, without desiring the attainment of fruits.
They become skilled in the exhaustion of afflictions, in tranquility, and in benefiting others;
they remain free from doubt regarding all who provide assistance;
and they possess intentions that are untiring with respect to all dharmas.
They become endowed with aspiration for the profound dharmas of the Buddha; they become those whose bodily, vocal, and mental actions are unsullied in the realization of the ultimate truth;
and they become those whose virtuous actions are untainted by the reality of attachment to existence.
They possess supreme knowledge and unafflicted eloquence; they aspire to the domain of the Buddhas and are intent on never turning back;
they have wisdom as their banner, their speech is untiring, and they are skilled in exhortation.
They come to possess a nature free from corruption, they become devoid of defeat,
they become free from fault,
and they become entirely rid of the three kinds of mental agitation.
They remain steadfast in speech and are free from lustful desires.
They refrain from sexual intercourse and are skilled in gathering all sentient beings; having entered into the world, they possess the strength of firm resolve.
They are expert in discerning the various proper and improper courses of action in all undertakings and are well-disposed toward sentient beings. Thus, they are endowed with such virtuous qualities.
These preeminent ones, steadfast in their countless virtues, possess an even-mindedness toward all sentient beings.
To this, it is said:
It is not possible for all birds to reach the end of the sky;
likewise, it is not possible for all sentient beings to know the qualities of the Self-Arisen Ones.
And whatever mantras or medicines, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, are fashioned for the benefit and happiness of the world to assist sentient beings,
all of them were brought forth by Bodhisattvas.
And whatever medicines circulate in the world for the sake of the welfare and happiness of sentient beings—all of those have been taught by the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, all those treatises that circulate in the world and are endowed with the determination of reality have been composed by Bodhisattvas.
Whatever enumeration, calculation, seals, and numerical positions exist here in this world—all these are the method of the bodhisattvas.

Whatever scripts exist in the world— namely, Brāhmī, Puṣkarasārī, Kharoṣṭhī, Yāvanī, Brahmavāṇī, Puṣpalipi, Kutalipi, Śaktinālīpi, Vyatsastalipi, Lekhalipi, Mudrālipi, Ukara, Madhura, Darada, Cīna, Hūṇa, Apīra, Vaṅga, Sīphala, Tramida, Dardura, Ramaṭha, Bhayavaicchetuka, Gulmala, Hastadā, Kasūla, Ketuka, Kusuva, Talika, and Jajarideṣu, as well as Akṣabaddha— all these are the methods of the Bodhisattvas.
Gold, silver, tin, copper, lead, and the fields of gems and jewels—all these are the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
Whatever means there may be that are devised for the benefit of the world, all of these have been brought forth by the Bodhisattvas.
In this regard, the following is said:
Those foremost among men, who understand the welfare of the world, move through existence as unequaled beings;
they practice what is most beneficial for gods, humans, and guhyakas, for the ultimate attainment belongs to the lords.
(135) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O Son of the Conqueror, what thought arises in those who are irreversible?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

"O upholder of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), those bodhisattvas who are irreversible—when they pass from the seventh stage to the eighth stage—a mind conjoined with great compassion arises;
thus is this called the seventh stage of the bodhisattvas."
Thus ends the seventh bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Conqueror, by the Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, while abiding in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, in which Samyaksaṃbuddhas was merit planted? What are the names of those Samyaksaṃbuddhas?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), hear first the names of those Perfectly Awakened Ones, the Blessed Ones born of the Śākya royal lineage, by whom roots of merit were accumulated—those of vast power, excellence, and renown: Satyadharmavipulakīrti, then Sukīrti, Lokābharaṇa, Vidyutprabha, Indratejas, Brahmakīrti, Vasundhara, Supārśva, Anupavadya, and Sujyeṣṭha.

Sṛṣṭarūpa, Praśastaguṇarāśi, Meghasvara, Hemavarṇa, Sundaravarṇa, Mṛgarājaghoṣa, Āśukārī, Dhṛtarāṣṭragati, Lokābhilāṣita, Jitaśatru, Supūjita, Yaśarāśi, Amitatejas, Sūryagupta, Candrabhānu, Niścitārtha, Kusumagupta, Padmābha, Prabhāṅkara, Dīptatejas, Satva... (136)
King Gajadeva, Kuñjaragati, Sughoṣa, Samabuddhi, Hemavarṇalambadāma, Kusumadāma, Ratnadāma, Alaṃkṛta, Vimukta, Ṛṣabhagāmī, Ṛṣabha, Devasiddhayātra,
Supātra, Sarvabandha, Ratnamukuṭa, Citramukuṭa, Sumukuṭa, Varamukuṭa, Calamakuṭa, Vimalamukuṭa, Lokadhara, Vipulojas, Aparibhinna, and Puṇḍarīkanetra.
Sarvasaha, Brahmagupta, Subrahma, Amaradeva, Arimardana, Candrapadma, Candrābha, Candratejas, Susoma, Sumudrabuddhi, Ratanaśṛṅga, Sucandradṛṣṭi, Hemakroḍa,
Abhinnarāṣṭra, Avikṣiptāṃśa, Puraṃdara, Puṇyadatta, Haladhara, Ṛṣabhanetra, Varabāhu, Yaśodatta, Kalamākṣa, Dṛṣṭaśakti, and Naraṃpravāha.

Pranaṣṭaduḥkha, Samadṛṣṭi, Dṛḍhadeva, Yaśaketu, Citracchada, Cārucchada, Lokaparitrātā, Duḥkhamukta, Rāṣṭradeva, Rudradeva, Bhadragupta, Udāgata, Askhalitapravarāgra, Dhanunāśa, Dharmagupta, Devagupta, and Śucigātra; these are the first hundred [names] of the noble faction.

The Blessed One is the Dharmadhātu, Guṇaketu, Jñānaketu, Satyaketu, Puṣpaketu, Vajrasaṃghāta, Dṛḍhahanu, Dṛḍhasandhi, Atyuccagāmī, Vigataśatru, Citramāla, Ūrdhvasandhi, Guṇagupta, Ṛṣigupta, Pralambabāhu, Ṛṣideva, Sunetra, Sāgaradharapuruṣa, Sulocana, Ajitacakra, Unnata, Ajitapuṣyala, Purāṣa, and Maṅgalya.
Mubhuja, Siṃhatejas, Tṛptavasantagandha, Avadhyaparamabuddhi, Nakṣatrarāja, Bahurāṣṭra, Āryākṣa, Sugupti, Prakāśavarṇa, Samṛddharāṣṭra, Kīrtanīya, Dṛḍhaśakti,

Harṣadatta, Yaśadatta, Nāgabāhu, Vigatareṇu, Śāntareṇu, Dānapraguru, Udāttavarṇa, Balabāhu, Amitaujas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Devalokābhilāṣita, Pratyagrarūpa, Devarājagupta, Dāmodara, Dharmarāja, Caturasravadana, Yojanābha, and Padmoṣṇīṣa.

Of manifest prowess, walking with the gait of a royal swan, adorned with his own auspicious marks, white-crested, wearing a jeweled crown, of praiseworthy complexion, adorned with divine ornaments, clothed in garments from the wish-fulfilling tree, of noble form, possessing unimpaired intellect, a lotus among men, profound in wisdom, Śakrabhānu, Indradhvaja, Dānavakula, Manuṣyadeva, Manusyadatta, Somacchatra, Ādityadatta, Yāmagupta, and Nakṣatragupta.
Sumitrarūpa, Satyabhānu, Puṣyagupta, Vṛhaspatigupta, Gaganagāmī, Śubhanātha, Suvarṇa, Kanakākṣa, Prasannabuddhi, Avipranaṣṭarāṣṭra,
Udagragāmi, Śubhadanta, Suvimaladanta, Suvadana, Kulanandana, Janakṣatriya, Lokakṣatriya, Anantagupta, Dharmagupta, and Sūkṣmavastra— these constitute the second hundred of the noble faction.
Pratyāsannabuddhi, Satvasaha, Manuṣyanāga, Upasena, Suvarṇacārin, Prabhūtavarṇa, Subhikṣākānta, Bhikṣudeva, Prabuddhaśīla, Nahīnagarbha, Anālambha, Ratnamudra,
Hārabhūṣita, Prasiddhavedana, Sugandhivastra, Suvijṛmbhita, Amitalocana, Udāttakīrti, Sāgararāja, Mṛgadeva, Kusumahastha, and Ratna...

Śṛṅga, Citravarṇa, Padmarajavarṇa, Samantagandha, Udāragupta, Praśāntaroga, Pradakṣiṇārtha, Saṃkṣiptabuddhi, Anantacchatra, Yojanasahasradarśin, Utpalapadmanetra, Atipuruṣa, Anivartikabala, Svaguṇaśākha, Saṃcitoraḥ, Mahārāja, Cārucaraṇa, Prasiddharaṅga, and Trimaṅgala. (138)
Suvarṇasena, Vartitārtha, Asaṃkīrṇa, Devagarbha, Suprītyarati, Vimānarāja, Parimaṇḍanārtha, Devasattva, Vipulatarāṃśa, Salīlagajagāmī, and Virūḍhabhūmi—
thus ends the eighth stage in the *Śrīmahāvastu-avadāna*.

Then, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (*dhutadharma*), after that, there were further [lords]: the Blessed One Citrabhānu, Cārubhānu, Dīptabhānu, Rucitabhānu, Asitabhānu, Hemaratha, Cāmīkaragaura, Rajakaratha, Suyakṣa, Akṣobhya, Apariśrotavāhana, Devālaṃkṛta, Subhūṣitakhaṇḍa, Śithilakuṇḍala, Maṇikarṇa, Sulakṣaṇa, Suviśuddha, Vimalajendra, and Devacūḍa.
Mandāravagandha, Pataṅgacara, Cārugandha, Indracūrṇa, Śailarājaketu, Arimardana, Maṇicakra, Vimalottarīya, Satyābharaṇa, Dṛḍhavīrya, Nandigupta, Ānandamāla, Cakravālagupta,
Dṛḍhamūla, Ānandacandra, Brahmadhvaṃsadeva, Saumbhavatsabāhu, Samīkṣitavadana, Satyāvatāra, and Supratiṣṭhitabuddhi.
Hāraśītalāṅga, Sukhaprabha, Bhūrisattva, Bhadragupta, Candraśubha, Bhadratejas, Iṣṭarūpa, Cakravartidatta, Suvicakṣaṇagātra, Vaiśrāvaṇarāja, Samṛddhayajña,
Saṃmataraśmi, Darśanakṣama, Srajamālādhārī, Suvarṇaviṣāṇa, Bhūtārthaketu, Ratnarudhiraketu, Mahārṣacūḍa, Tejagupta, Varuṇarāja, and Udāttavastra.
Vajragupta, Dhanyabhānu, Uttaptarāṣṭra, Viśālaprabha, Lokasundara, Abhirūpa, Hiraṇyadhanyaśirika, Prabhūtadehakarṇa,
Prāgjita, Vicitramukuṭa, Dānavagupta, Rāhuvamī, Puṇyarāśi, Salilagupta, Śamitaśatru, Ratnayūpa, Suvikalpāṅga, Ajitabala, Satyanāma, and Aviraktarāṣṭra.

Vaiśvānaragupta, Madhuravadana, Kusumotpala, Uttarakururāja, Añjalimālādhārī, Dhanapatigupta, Taruṇārkabhānu, Anurūpagātra, Ratnakaraṇḍaketu, Mahākośa, Bahulakeśa, Puṣpamañjarimaṇḍita, Anapaviddhakarṇa, Anāviddhavarṇa, Sitāsitalocana, Araktapravāḍa, Siṃhoraska, Ariṣṭanemi, and Bahurāja—
these constitute the first hundred on the side of the Noble Ones in the ninth stage.
Bhūmideva, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Sādhuprabha, Jyotigupta, Bahuprabha, Satyavacas, Bhavadevagupta, Saṃvṛttatejas, Nirupaghāta, Jānutrasta, Ratnaśayana, Kusumaśayana,
Citraśayana, Dantaśayana, Supratiṣṭhitacaraṇa, Sarvadevagupta, Arajottarīya, Svāyaṃbhavendra, Prasannavarṇa, Bhavaketu, and Kṣīrapūrṇāmbhas.
Anantabuddhi, Kanakanāgarājatejas, Bandhanāntakara, Anugravarṇakṣemagupta, Jinakāntāra, Vimala, Marīcijāla, Ajitasenarāja, Kanakarāśi,
Gaura, Padmamāla, Rājakṣetragupta, Samapakṣa, Cāturdeva, Devagupta, Puṣkalāṅga, Dvijātirāja, Bahusena, Kumudagandha, Śavalāśva, Ṣaḍviṣāṇapāta, and Surabhicandana.
King Sahasradātā, Abhayadeva, Arinidhan, Vimalaśikhara, Durārohābuddhi, Yajñakoṭigupta, Ratnacaṅkrama, Jālāntara,
Pariśuddhakarmā, Kāmadeva, Gururatna, Śatasahasramātṛ, Śucipraroha, Stimitarāja, Vṛddhadeva, Gurujanapūjita, Jayantadeva, Sujātabuddhi, Samīkṣitārtha, Ujjitapara, Devābhika, and Asuradeva.
Gandharvagīta, Vīṇāravaghoṣa, Śuddhadanta, Sudanta, Cārudanta, Amṛtaphala, Mārgodyotayitā, Maṇikuṇḍaladhara, Hemajālprabha, Nāgabhogabāhu,
Kamaladhara, Aśokasattva, Lakṣmīputra, Sunirmitarūpa, Īśvaragupta, Lokapālarāja, Sunidhyāna, Agrapuruṣa, Anihatavarṇa, Kundapuṣpagandha, and Aṅkuśa.

Resembling a fresh creeper, he is the deliberation on what ought to be done; he is self-luminous, possessing the nature of light; he is the banner of the noble lineages, radiant as the king of gods, a god manifest before one's eyes; he is the passion of the sun upon the serpent, with flowers for his upper garment;
he is the one without bitterness, the first king, the king of the white lotus, and the king of abundance.
The second noble category is on the ninth stage.

He of supple limbs, the ultimate being, whose limbs are unmoistened, the hero of Dharma, the excellent ford, who has struck down the Mallas of the world’s darkness, who possesses the fragrance of the *kunda* flower, the unrestrained one, whose limbs are not scorched, the king of preceptors, of most excellent and foremost intelligence,

whose fame is unsurpassed, whose grasp is never severed, the teacher of the gods, the jewel-flower, the pure being, the peak of lapis lazuli, the wearer of variegated garlands, the fragrant-bodied one, and the one of infinite treasury.

He who is perfectly composed, whose splendor is truth, who moves without dejection, who is valiantly courageous, whose speech is unconfused, the god of gods, the god of men, the one borne by men, whose hand holds jewels, beloved of the world, the one who has entrusted his purpose [to others],

whose roots are never withered, who is free from thirst, the king of all arts, the treasury of the planets, whose kingdom is devoted to him, who wears the garland given by Śiva, who was given by Śikhara, who wears variegated garlands, who possesses a great celestial palace, whose limbs are not heated by affliction, and who is adorned with a net of variegated gold.

King Tejagupta was one whose passion was stilled, who had gathered his faction, who was not drawn away [by distractions], whose scent was like red sandalwood, whose mind was unshakable, whose jaw was well-formed, whose fame blazed forth, who wore a fashioned garland, and who possessed a crown upon his head.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.

(141) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, those bodhisattvas who have fully gathered roots of merit, who have accomplished their deeds, who have transcended the ninth stage and perfected the tenth stage, and who, having approached the Tuṣita heaven, desire human existence and enter the mother’s womb— proclaiming such things as 'not returning again' and so forth— these are the most excellent persons whose marvelous and wonderful qualities are not shared even with the Pratyekabuddhas and others."
And by the hosts of those who have attained mastery, as well as by those in training and ordinary worldlings.
When this had been said, Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
The perfectly awakened ones are endowed with excellence in their descent into the womb;
they are endowed with excellence in their stay in the womb and excellence in their birth;
and the perfectly awakened ones are also endowed with excellence in their mother.
The perfectly awakened ones are endowed with the perfection of renunciation; the perfectly awakened ones are endowed with the perfection of vigor;
and the perfectly awakened ones are endowed with the perfection of the attainment of knowledge.
"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, how do the perfectly awakened Buddhas come to possess the perfection of the descent into the womb?"

The Hero, Śrīghana, who has accumulated a store of former roots of merit, gazes with preeminent vision from the Tuṣita abode at those who have been looked upon [for rebirth] at the time of his passing.
Thus does the Benefactor contemplate that thought which brings benefit to men and gods;
the Great Being, the teacher of the hosts of deities, is surrounded by the foremost of the immortals.
The time for my passing has now truly come; beings have fallen into great darkness.
Having eyes destroyed and turbid eyes, they shall be liberated upon reaching me.
(142) What woman now is thus devoted to the restraint of virtue and to tranquility— she who is of noble birth, easy to speak with, fond of generosity, and possessed of gentleness?
And she is radiant... who indeed is she, whose darkness of passion and hatred has been destroyed;
who has reached the perfection of beauty and virtue, whose conduct is unimpaired, and who is possessed of vast merit?
Who is capable of bearing me for ten months, and who can endure the secret joys?
Who shall be my mother, and into whose womb shall I enter today?
While gazing about, he saw among the harem of King Śuddhodana a woman resembling a celestial nymph, like a flash of lightning— Māyā.
Having observed her, he addressed his mother: "I shall descend from the immortals, entering my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the welfare of gods and men."
To him the host of gods, wearing excellent ornaments and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O Supreme Person, may your vow, endowed with undiminished virtue and merit, be fulfilled!"
We too, for the benefit of the world, having renounced many delightful sensual pleasures,
shall dwell in the human realm for the sake of honoring the Blameless One.
Furthermore, O Teacher of the multitude of beings, although we do not desire separation from you,
nevertheless, O lotus-eyed one, you will become the refuge for humans and gods.
(143) Thus indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, the perfectly awakened ones are endowed with the excellence of the descent into the womb.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do the perfectly awakened ones become endowed with the perfection of dwelling in the womb?
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, Bodhisattvas while in their mother’s womb remain supported by the mother’s birth canal;
they remain supported by the mother’s back;
they remain supported by the mother’s belly.
They remain leaning against their mother's side.

"O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, when [the womb] is obstructed, one cannot find any location whatsoever by relying on a false sūtra or upon corals and lapis lazuli gems; yet there is a place where, in every respect, Bodhisattvas do not remain in their mother’s womb, and yet they do remain.

Furthermore, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, when a Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, hosts of gods approach him and, with palms joined in reverence, ask: ‘What is an auspicious moment? What is a fortunate day?’"
With joyful minds, the Bodhisattvas greet those hosts of gods who thus inquire of them; raising their right hands, they do not cause any pain to their mother.
Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), Bodhisattvas who have entered their mother’s womb do not remain in any manner whatsoever—crouching, on their side, or otherwise.
Rather, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, Bodhisattvas sit cross-legged and do not cause any distress to their mother.
Furthermore, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, it is said that Bodhisattvas, while still within their mother’s womb, speak of the discourse on existence by virtue of their roots of merit.

Furthermore, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb, divine musical instruments were played constantly and continuously; they never ceased, whether by day or by night.

And, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (*dhutadharma*), for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva while he is in his mother’s womb, hundreds of thousands of celestial nymphs manifest themselves, and divine rains of flowers and divine rains of powders never cease at any time.
Starting from the time they were first in their mother’s womb until their final parinirvāṇa, the divine incense of agallochum never ceased for the Bodhisattvas and those endowed with the ten powers.
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, Bodhisattvas are not produced from a mother and father;
rather, they are spontaneously born through the perfection of their own qualities.
In this regard, the following is said:
Then, O lotus-petal-eyed one, that dark-complexioned Māyā, pursued by the many arms of the Gandharvas, spoke these very sweet words to Śuddhodana: "Even though he is with me..."
By means of this concentration, I shall practice non-violence and the holy life with my vital breaths;
I shall also abstain from taking what is not given, from intoxicants, and from idle chatter.
O best of men, I shall likewise desist from harsh speech and from slander;
O lord of men, I shall desist from false speech—this is my resolve.
I shall not give rise to envy toward the desires of others, nor shall I harbor malice;
with a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, I abandon wrong view.
"O Protector of the Earth, I practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night;
thus does my desire arise."
Moreover, O protector of the earth, let there be no thought of sensual desire for me;
look upon me so that no unrighteousness may arise in me, who am a practitioner of the holy life.
The king, having fulfilled his resolve, spoke these words to Bhāriyā:
(145) "Take your pleasure here in this excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your disposal."
Taking that foremost thousand of devoted women,
she ascended that excellent celestial palace and sat down, surrounded by a retinue full of pleasing qualities.
For some time, she spent that period in silence upon her bed— which resembled a snow-white lotus— delighting in tranquility and self-restraint.
Then, their minds filled with curiosity, many celestial maidens wearing exquisite garlands approached the Mother of the Jina, desiring to see her; they stood upon the beautiful summit of the palace.
Having approached and beheld Māyā reclining upon her bed, radiant like excellent lightning,
he conceived vast joy and bliss, and then rained down celestial flowers.
"Even among humans, such a form as this is indeed well-born; it is a marvel!
Were she to remain for some time within, she would not be equal even to the wives of the gods."
O friends, behold the playful charm of this woman, such as it is and appropriate to her;
she shines upon her couch, captivates the mind, and glitters like the very essence of gold.
This [garland] shall bear that Great Man, who delights in ultimate generosity, self-restraint, and virtue, who brings an end to all outflows, and is free from dust; O Queen, what is lost for you?

The Blessed One, the Giver of Boons, has taken up residence here in this belly, which is curved like a bow, resembles the palm of a hand, possesses a row of excellent hair, and is adorned with beautiful lines; yet he remains unsullied by impurity.
"You are a woman worthy of him, a most excellent mother; and he is indeed a preeminent man, a Blessed One who brings an end to existence. O Queen of the King of Men, what is lacking for you?"

Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, in whatever birth the mothers of Bodhisattvas bear a Bodhisattva in his final existence, in that birth the supreme women possess a celibacy that is perfectly pure, complete, and unbroken.
Not even in their minds did passion arise for any men among those most excellent women, beginning with their own husbands.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the mother of the Bodhisattva becomes possessed of a body clothed in celestial garments and adorned with celestial ornaments; and hosts of Apsarases attend to the Bodhisattva’s mother, providing her with bathing, anointing, massaging, and sprinkling.
When the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother experiences laughter together with hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.
Likewise, celestial maidens who have reached the full bloom of their prime were fanning the sleeping Bodhisattva’s mother with garlands of mandārava flowers.
And when the Bodhisattva descends into the womb of that supreme lady, the mother of the Bodhisattva does not experience any sufferings as other women do.
Beginning from the Tuṣita heaven, all Bodhisattvas have the five hindrances suppressed even before they have attained the sovereignty of Dharma.
And when ten months are complete, all bodhisattvas manifest from the mother’s womb through her right side, yet that side is not pierced;
nor does any delay occur therein, for as soon as they are born, it is as if they have already been born.
In this regard, the following is said:
Then, when the tenth month was complete, the mother of the one of abundant merit,
her purpose fulfilled, approached Śuddhodana and spoke these words.
"O Lord of Men, the thought of going to the garden has arisen in me; quickly prepare my vehicle and likewise provide appropriate protection."
Having heard these words, King Śuddhodana, with a joyful mind,
the protector of the earth, spoke with longing to his excellent retinue.
Quickly prepare and report to me the vast army, abounding in elephants and horses, crowded with foot soldiers, and variegated with spears, arrows, and javelins.
Let ten hundred thousand excellent horse-chariots be harnessed,
adorned with the sweet, resonant sounds of golden bells.
Quickly prepare ten million superior, well-equipped elephants, resembling dark clouds and clad in armor.
Let the brave warriors, clad in armor and mail, become ready and irreversible;
let twenty thousand of them quickly prepare themselves.

(148) Let the women, wearing excellent garlands and garments, carry the noble horse-chariot for the Queen— a chariot with a vast network of golden mesh, resounding with the tinkling of many small bells.
And quickly make the Lumbinī grove free from grass, dust, leaves, and refuse; well-swept and pleasing, like a celestial realm for the Queen.
And fashion each excellent tree from *dukūla* cloth, silk, wool,
and *kośikāra* fibers, like the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of the preeminent god in heaven.
Having assented with "So be it" at the word of that son of a king,
[the attendants] reported to the king that what was commanded had been accomplished without delay.
That mother of the one who crushes the host of Māra, her face charming with grace,
ascended those delightful vehicles together with her retinue.
Adorned with various ornaments, crowded with foot-soldiers, elephants, and throngs of chariots, that well-ordered army of the preeminent among men shines resplendent as it marches forth.
Having entered that excellent forest, the Mother of the Jina, accompanied by her friend Māyā,
wanders about like the wife of a chief of the immortals in the Citraratha grove, knowing the ways of pleasure.
Having approached for the sake of sport, she playfully yawned while grasping a branch of a *plakṣa* tree with her arms at the time of the birth of that illustrious one.
Then twenty thousand incomparable, excellent apsarases,
with their ten fingers joined in the añjali gesture, greeted Māyā and said:
Today you shall give birth to one who crushes the cycle of old age and rebirth, as delicate as the offspring of the immortals—
a queen who brings welfare to gods and men, honored in heaven and on earth, and a benefactor to both humans and deities.
Do not give way to despondency; we shall perform the necessary preparations for you. Tell us what must be done; see it as already accomplished, and do not worry.
Without causing distress to his mother,
the Sage, the supreme speaker, appeared from her right side, mindful and fully conscious.
Then, as soon as that best of men appeared, thousands upon thousands of cities filled with heaps of various jewels blazed forth, and a stainless radiance manifested.

Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, there is no being among the host of beings who is able to prophesy a Bodhisattva immediately upon his birth in his final existence, except for the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm.
In this regard, the following is said:
With his head finely wrapped in a cloth, accompanied by eight thousand excellent Maheshvaras dressed in the garb of Brahmins, he approached the city of Kapilavastu.
Wearing excellent garments and adorned with choice ornaments, those best of beings approached the gate of the royal palace with joyful minds and spoke to the doorkeeper.
"Go to Śuddhodana and say: 'These [sages] are experts in the rules for the qualities of the marks.'"
"If you grant permission, they shall remain for eight thousand [years] and then enter."
Having heard these words, the doorkeeper approached the excellent king;
with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, he spoke thus to the lord of men:
O you of incomparable strength and radiant splendor, rule the kingdom for a long time with happiness, having slain your enemies!
At your gate stand those who resemble the immortals, desiring to enter.
With perfectly full and stainless eyes, moving with the sweet voice of an elephant in rut—of them I have no suspicion, for they are not humans; they are the sons of the gods.
As they walk back and forth, the dust of the earth does not cling to their excellent feet;
nor is the sound of their joints ever heard as they walk.
With profound and sweet gestures, noble appearance, and a tranquil gaze,
they generate vast joy in people who behold them.
Without doubt, O best of men, these excellent women have come to see you—
the god among gods, the lion among men— in order to pay homage and rejoice.
Having heard these words, the lord of men said to the doorkeeper: "O sir, having received my permission, let them enter the magnificent palace."
Those foremost hosts of immortals, equal to the sky and pure in their conduct,
entered the royal palace of the chief of the noble Ikṣvāku lineage.
King Śuddhodana, too, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose from his seat along with his retinue through the power of his reverence.
The king saluted them all with a welcome full of affection;
"We are delighted by the sight of you, and by your power of tranquility and self-restraint."
These excellent seats, fashioned in exquisite forms, are here;
please, sirs, be seated for our sake out of favor toward us.
Then, upon those excellent seats with variegated legs of gold and silver color,
they sat down comfortably, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance.
Having sat down for only a short while, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty hear the purpose for which we have come here."
Your son has been born with all limbs faultless...
having attained the perfection of the marks...
We too are skilled in marks; we discern faults and virtues by means of marks.
If it were not a burden to you, we would behold the form of your son, that Great Man.
He says: "Come, behold my son, who is secure in his noble reputation, renowned among gods and men, and who has reached the perfection of the marks and qualities."
Then the excellent king brought forth the Sugata— who is honored by humans and gods, who possesses a golden complexion, and who rests upon a soft bed of Kācalindika wool.
Having beheld from afar the excellent feet of the Best of Men, the Great Lords,
with their crowns slipping from their heads, prostrated themselves upon the surface of the earth.
Having established the moon, pure as cow’s milk, upon the summit of the earth,
they stood for a very long time, rejoicing in the One Possessed of Ten Powers, who was longed for.
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, as soon as Bodhisattvas are born, they practice all human arts and crafts without a teacher.
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures from the time they depart for the Tuṣita heaven onwards.

"O Son of the Conqueror, what is the cause, what is the condition, that although their afflictions have not been abandoned, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures, and how did Rāhula come to be born?
When this was said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Because they have accumulated virtue, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures; because of their noble resolve, supreme resolve, and sublime resolve, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures;

because they have no desire for desires, because they possess the banner of wisdom, because they do not take those as their ultimate refuge, and because longing does not arise within them, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures.

Because they are noble, because they are not base, and because they are thoroughly cultivated by virtue, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures; and because they are esteemed by the world as persons of the highest caliber, [the thought arises]: "He will become a perfectly awakened Buddha."

"Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), it is thus heard that Rāhula, having passed away from the Tuṣita realm, descended into the womb of his mother Yaśodharā, the Kṣatriya maiden."
The universal monarchs were of spontaneous birth.

They were as follows: Kusumacūḍa, Hemavarṇa, Gāndharva, Sumāla, Ratnadaṇḍa, Suvimāna, Ārjava, Māndhātā, Sunaya, Suvastra, Bahupakṣa, Toragrīva, Maṇiviraja, Pavana, Marudeva, Supriya, Tyāgavān, Śuddhavaṁśa, and Durāroha; these and others such as these were the hosts of universal monarchs who were of miraculous birth, just like Rāhulabhadra.
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do Bodhisattvas become perfected in their Great Renunciation?"
Long ago, O son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva went forth from home.
Having entered the royal palace, he addressed Chandaka with a verse:
"Chandaka, bring Kaṇṭhaka quickly; do not delay long!
Today I shall conquer the difficult-to-vanquish battle; be alert!"

With his face filled with tears and sighing deeply, Chandaka uttered these sorrowful cries and shed these tears in order to awaken the sleeping royal folk: [He spoke thus: "O King, awake! Arise, O Lord of the Earth! Your son has gone away; he has departed for the sake of asceticism."
Why now have you fallen away, your excellent burden of a sheath slipped off, lying upon a bed of floods of tears, overcome by passion?
You were asleep at the very time for longing, grief, and lamentation; now is the time and place for waking.
Even the Queen herself, having remained awake for a very long time, now lies asleep with a form resembling a flash of lightning;
at the moment of departure for the excellent city of the gods, she is like a celestial nymph moving with grace for the sake of the support of men.

(154) Now his queen, the mother of that lord of men, whose eyes were large, beautiful, and full of affection, was overcome by sleep; though she was being addressed with piteous words concerning the separation from her beloved, she did not perceive him speaking.

Where does that army dwell— composed of excellent elephants, horses, and infantry, equipped with various armors and weapons such as iron arrows, spears, shafts, and javelins— and what benefit does it provide, since it did not perceive the Bull of the Śākyas as he was departing?
Whom shall I awaken? Who indeed could be my companion? Or what shall I do, O gods, now that I am utterly lost?
Alas! Deprived of one who resembles molten gold, the king will surely cast off his body along with his kinsmen.
The host of gods spoke to him in sweet tones: "O Chandaka, why do you lament? Why are you distressed?
Even if all the sons of Māra were to rise up together, they would not be able to create an obstacle for him; how much less so you?"

Even if someone were to sound thousands of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs for the sake of awakening Kapilavastu, the Lord of the Immortals and the others would not wake; for that excellent city is indeed filled with prosperity and sleep.

Behold now in the sky the gods with crest-jewels of precious gems, who, following the will of him who is honored in heaven, bow down with palms joined in reverence, prostrating with their heads and paying homage, saying: "You are our kinsman; you are our refuge."
Therefore, bring forth Kaṇṭhaka, the horse born with the Nāyaka, whose body is like gold refined by cow’s milk.
For there is no one on earth or in heaven who can create an obstacle for the Lord of Men; bring forth that best of horses!

Then, moved by the words of that possessor of great virtues, the obedient groom, weeping, presented him with his own horse— white as a bed of blooming night-lotuses or jasmine, with a body like the full moon.
This is the Protector, his limbs adorned with excellent marks, ready, with feet that shine brightly, moving with graceful gait.
O you who possess a noble form, may that which you have now resolved upon be fulfilled for you, O lady of broad shoulders and chest!
And let your enemy, O Graba, broken by his own weakness and his sharpness shattered, be swiftly tormented, overwhelmed by the excellence of your splendor.
And let your hope, O Naralambaka, which is joined with great purpose, be fulfilled like a mountain of gold.
May those who create obstacles for you depart;
may they instead bring about your welfare and obtain great strength.
And as for the vow you undertake, may you reach its fulfillment, O you who move with the playful gait of a noble elephant in rut.
And the jeweled pavement of the royal palace, struck by Kaṇṭhaka’s hooves,
resounded sweetly through the night, emitting a wondrous sound.
And the four world-protectors, with their crowns loosened and their excellent garlands hanging down,
placed their hands— resembling red lotuses— at the neck and feet [of the horse].
In front, the bearer of the excellent vajra, the teacher of the thirty-three gods, with a jeweled crest bound upon his head,
Indra, the thousand-eyed one, goes before the best of men.
"O tiger among speakers, this horse Kaṇṭhaka carries what is merely a matter of name;
the gods carry the rain of excellent rays that has been taken up by the most eminent hand."
Having departed from this excellent city, the lion among men gazed back at that preeminent city and said:
"I shall not enter it again until I have reached the further shore of old age and death."
"Thus indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-qualities, were the Perfectly Awakened Ones endowed with the Great Renunciation.
Truly, O bearer of the dhuta-qualities, I am not capable of describing in detail the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb up to his Great Renunciation for an eon or even the remainder of an eon;
nor is it possible to fully comprehend his virtues."
Thus, the perfectly awakened ones are endowed with many such qualities.
(157) Having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, even before attaining the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they become endowed with the five eyes.
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, explain in detail the five eyes; the assembly, crowded with gods and humans, as well as the hosts of all beings, are listening with attentive ears."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, these five are the eyes of the perfectly enlightened ones."
Which five?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
"O bearer of the dhuta-qualities, these five eyes belong to the perfectly awakened ones; they are not shared by pratyekabuddhas, arhats, those in training, or any ordinary worldlings.
In this regard, O bearer of the dhuta-qualities, the fleshly eye belongs to the Tathāgatas.
The fleshly eye of another being does not possess that radiance, nor that subtle vision, nor that vision of reality which [the Bodhisattva] possesses;
yet, having attained all-seeingness, whatever extent of space the Bodhisattvas wish to survey, their vision proceeds there unimpeded.
For what reason?
Because of having accumulated vast wholesome roots.

Just as, for example, by the power of supernatural faculties, a universal monarch together with his fourfold army travels through the air from continent to continent, so too should this be understood.

The fleshly eye of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is described by such mere characteristics as follows: "By the power of their supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*), even when they do not desire it, while walking upon the earth, the ground remains motionless; where it is elevated, it sinks, and where it is depressed, it rises; this is to be seen in such a manner. And so forth.
And even in an eon, it is not possible to reach the limit of the qualities of the perfectly awakened Buddhas by means of the fleshly eye.
What is the reason?
For indeed, there is nothing whatsoever of the perfectly awakened ones that is equal to the world.
Indeed, everything belonging to the great seers is truly supramundane.
For in this way, the realization of the perfectly awakened ones is likewise supramundane.
And that color and location of the flesh-eye of the perfectly enlightened ones have arisen in the same way as they do in the bodies of other sentient beings.

The divine eye of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones is superior to, more extensive than, and clearer than that eye by which the terrestrial gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and the gods of the desire realm and the form realm [perceive].
That [consciousness] proceeds among forms consisting of mind.

By means of this eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) which is possessed here through the examination of the state of being an eye, individuals beginning with those of the eighth stage up to the person who is an Arhat are distinguished; therefore, the eye of wisdom of the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is even more clearly manifest than that.
In this regard, what is the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) of the Perfectly Awakened Ones?
That is the mental mastery of the ten powers.
In that regard, what are the ten powers?
Namely: first is the power of those of immeasurable intelligence who know what is possible and what is impossible;
and second is the power that knows the path leading everywhere.
They know the world to consist of various elements; this is proclaimed as the third power.
They know the diversity of inclinations; this constitutes the fourth power.
He knows the skillful actions of other men; that is his fifth power.
They recognize the power of karma, both auspicious and inauspicious; that is his sixth power.
He knows the purification from afflictions; this is the seventh power. He knows the meditative absorptions and attainments; this is the eighth power. He knows former abodes in their many varieties.
The ninth power is that they possess the completely purified divine eye;
the tenth power is that they attain the destruction of all afflictions.
These are the powers of mental mastery by which the All-Seer, whose fame has spread throughout heaven and earth, is designated as "the One Possessing the Ten Powers."
That mental discernment-knowledge which exists within these ten powers is called the Dharma-eye.
In that regard, what is the Buddha-eye?
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
That is to say: the Tathāgata’s unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past;
his unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future;
and his unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present.
All bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all vocal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;
all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
There is no loss of zeal; there is no loss of vigor;
there is no loss of mindfulness.
There is no decline in concentration;
there is no decline in wisdom;
there is no decline in liberation.
There is no stumbling; there is no shouting;
there is no loss of mindfulness.
There is no unconcentrated mind;
there is no equanimity without discernment;
there is no perception of diversity.
The knowledge regarding these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is called the Buddha-eye.
(160) When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, does this designation "prophecy" refer to such stages as these, or rather does it refer to the perfectly awakened Buddhas?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
At one time, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, attended by twenty-eight hundred self-controlled ones.

In that regard, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha were analyzed by the Blessed One; since the perfectly enlightened ones possess unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, he proclaimed the ten stages.
Beginning with Śākyamuni, the perfectly enlightened one, the ten stages were taught.
In this regard, the following is said:
The Visionary One, wandering through existence with a mind long purified, gives away beloved things;
thereafter, having descended upon the circle of the earth, he himself realizes the supreme, beloved knowledge as a Tathāgata.
With a well-pleased mind, he gives women adorned with various garments and ornaments;
for him, a wondrous and diverse reward is proclaimed as the fruit of that deed.

As he wandered through various states of existence among sentient beings, he did not hurl spears, iron arrows, javelins, or *tomaras*. Likewise, his path as he wandered through villages and cities was free of grass, clumps of earth, and thorns, and caused no injury.
Even when his own servant speaks according to the Dharma, he listens with respect and does not interrupt him;
therefore, when he speaks the Dharma in the great assembly, no one finds it unpleasing nor fails to be satisfied.
He gives excellent gifts... he thus removes longing as well as doubt;
then from his body there arises a cool radiance, like a flame of blazing fire.
No supplication made by any beggar is ever in vain when addressed to the God among Men; therefore, his teaching shall not be fruitless. This is the marvel in the crushing of Māra’s forces.
With minds full of joy, they offer beautiful golden palm leaves to the Jinas;
therefore, those kinsmen of the world always possess incomparable splendor throughout the worlds—this is a marvel.
With a mind always well-pleased, he constantly gives sandals made of jewels and wooden shoes;
thereafter, that best of men always walks four finger-breadths above the earth, without touching it.
When addressed with harsh words again and again by others, the Lord, remaining composed, endures them and does not retaliate;
because of this, as he walks, the earth—with its mountains and its high and low places—sinks down and rises up.
By his policy, he gathers the wretched under his protection and uplifts the great multitude who were falling;
consequently, the earth, filled with heaps of jewels, sinks down for him and rises up again.
And by means of proclaiming his own qualities, the Perfectly Awakened One taught the Dharma discourse named "The Recollection of the Buddha."
At the conclusion of that, the Venerable Vāgīśa praised the Perfectly Awakened One to his face.
