Homage be to you, O Buddha of infinite vision, whose eye is all-pervading, who bears the marks of a hundred merits;
compassionate for our welfare and skilled in the ultimate truth, I bow to you, Gautama, with words that are beautiful.
Having crossed over yourself, O Great Sage, you ferry others across; you have no fear, O Supreme Person who brings security.
Revealing the state exactly as it is, you lead many people to the truth of the Deathless.
The morality of the Great Seer, who possesses infinite vision, is profound, noble, vast, and well-spoken.
You, O crusher of enemies, are distinguished in this morality; you are firm in your vows in this world and in the world beyond.
O Great Sage, your conduct is unbroken, flawless, stainless, and without blemish; it is free from outflows.
Having attained purity and supreme purification, you always shine like a fire upon a mountain peak.

O person, you have reached the further shore in the stability of mind; likewise, you are a master in meditative concentration. Having attained supreme mastery over the mind, you shine forth, free from all crookedness and flaws.
Homage be to you, Gautama, whose valor is truth! You who dwell at will in the peaceful concentration free from conflict, honored among gods and men, and who possess the radiance of a golden garland.
Just as Virocana shines in the sky, or like the moon on the fifteenth day in a pure sky, so do you shine while established in meditative concentration, O person, like refined gold. (164)
Desiring [the goal] yet lacking wisdom, beings do not understand the universal exertion of one who dwells in the bliss of concentration free from conflict. Homage to you, honored by gods and humans!
When you look out like one who goes among the Nāgas, and when you have come to the further shore beyond death—
endowed with wisdom and mindfulness, with a stainless mind— then this earth, the bearer of beings, trembles.

Having realized the truth through direct vision, and having personally attained supernormal knowledge just as it was heard of old, speak these words, O Supreme Person; you shine like Maghavā, the thousand-eyed one.
This great calamity and terrible fear is now ended; henceforth there shall be no further arising of it.
Its suppression proceeds downward; it is extinguished like the sound of the wind or the fading of a flame.
The vision of liberation for one whose mind is liberated is inconceivable, not dependent on the path of ratiocination.
That speech of the Hero, which is beyond doubt, shines forth; it is well-timed, gentle, and born of truth.
Proclaim those words of yours, free from agitation, in the presence of the people;
for having heard your sweet and well-spoken speech, they drink it like those afflicted by thirst drinking water from the ocean.

Cultivate loving-kindness toward sentient beings who harbor hatred; [attain] sovereign power, supernatural success, and supreme eloquence, so that you may reach the further shore of the most excellent dharmas, such as no one else in this world-system has done.
And you possess unsurpassed wisdom, O Sage, incomparable and peerless in all the world;
you alone are the most excellent among all living beings, just as Mount Meru is among the peaks of mountains.

There is no one equal to you, no one similar or like you; how could there be anyone superior to you, O bearer of virtues, in terms of qualities? You alone are the most excellent person in the ultimate sense, as immovable and blissful as the nirvāṇa of all phenomena.
Having abandoned passion, delusion, hatred, pride, and the ensnaring thirst,
you shine with a mind freed from blemish, like the full moon in a clear sky.
Since you, being upright, seek here that which is true—a great bridge traversed by noble beings—speak these words, O foremost of persons; like Maghavan with his thousand eyes, you shine resplendent.

Cultivating this concentration— which is liberated from afflictions, stainless, and perfectly peaceful— you shine forth for the welfare of beings as their refuge, like the sun, O Conqueror honored by gods and humans.
Unattached both here and in the world beyond, you delight in meditation while established in contemplation;
many gods have gathered together and pay homage with palms joined to the Great Sage who is worthy of veneration.
The eye becomes manifold and of many kinds for those of purified vision—
the Buddhas, who crush old age and death, and who are the tamers of the untamed.
The Blessed One’s conduct is supramundane; his wholesome roots are supramundane.
The walking, standing, sitting, and lying down of the Sage are supramundane.
That body of the Sugata which brings about the destruction of the bonds of existence—even that, O friend, is supramundane; herein no doubt should be made.
The wearing of robes by the Sage is supramundane; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, the taking of food by the Sugata is likewise supramundane.
The teaching of the Nara-nāgas is considered to be entirely transcendent of the world;
I shall explain, according to reality, the majesty of those possessed of supreme intelligence.
Having taken account of the influence of place and time, as well as the ripening of karma,
the Leaders teach the Dharma that is true or has been manifested.
The Buddhas conform to worldly conventions in order to follow the ways of the world; they conform to designations just as they conform to that which transcends the world.
The four Supreme Persons display their modes of conduct,
yet no exhaustion arises for those who perform auspicious deeds.
They indeed wash their feet, yet no dust clings to them;
their feet have the luster of lotus petals—this is their conformity with the world.
The Fully Awakened Ones indeed bathe, yet no impurity exists in them.
Her limbs possess the luster of a golden image; this is her conformity with the world.
They use tooth-sticks and their mouths possess the fragrance of a blue lotus;
they put on their undergarments and wear the upper robe and the triple set of robes.
Having blown upon their garments with the wind, they do not disturb the body;
this is the conformity with the world of these lions among men.
They sit in shade and are not oppressed by the heat;
this is the conformity with the world of the Buddhas, who are the outflow of merit.
They partake of medicine, yet no disease exists for them;
this great fruit of leaders is their conformity with the world.
The Lords are able to prevent karma, yet the Jinas demonstrate karma;
they conceal their sovereignty—this is their conformity with the world.
They indeed take food, yet hunger does not afflict them;
for the sake of providing for people, this is their conformity with the world.
They indeed drink water, yet thirst does not afflict them;
this is the wonder of the great seers—this conformity with the ways of the world.
They put on robes, and the Victor is always clothed;
such is his form as a god—this is his conformity with the world.
They cause the afflictions to grow, yet the razor does not cut them; these hair-like afflictions, resembling dark collyrium, are merely a conformity with the ways of the world.
They demonstrate old age, yet for them no old age exists;
these Victors, endowed with the qualities of a Victor, thus conform to the ways of the world.
Having reached the perfection of merits over incalculable millions of eons, they demonstrate their exertion; this is their conformity with the world.
The exalted body of the Sugata was not produced through sexual union;
yet they teach that he had a mother and father—this is conformity with the world.

Since the time of Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata has been free from passion; yet he shows Rāhula as his son—this is his conformity with the world. Having traversed the perfection of wisdom for incalculable millions of eons, he acts thus.
And they manifest the state of childhood; this is their conformity with the world.
Having uttered improper mantras in this world together with its gods, they seek them again at sacred fords; this is merely following the ways of the world.
Having awakened to incomparable enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, they demonstrate a lack of zeal; this is their conformity with the world.
All perfectly awakened ones are endowed with supreme qualities and are perfected in speech.
The speech of the perfectly awakened Buddhas is endowed with sixty qualities.
By which sixty?
The speech that issues from the mouth of the Best of Men is sweet as the sound of song;
the voice of the Sugata is like the resonance of the lute and the flute, and like the cry of the noble swan.

The speech of those of supreme intelligence is as sweet as the roar of clouds, its resonance equal to the song of the cuckoo or the sound of a chariot, and it possesses the power of the ocean’s thundering and the cry of the crane.

The speech of those who bear the excellent marks is like the song of the *kinnara* and the *kalaviṅka*, like the sound of the voice of the best of clouds, like the trumpeting of a noble elephant, like the roar of a bull or the king of beasts, and it emits laughter.
The sound of the drum was deep and resonant, its vibration stirred by the forest deities and the wind;
it was a voice that shook the earth, belonging to the foremost among men and gods.

From the mouth of the Jina, which possesses a voice equal to that of a fivefold musical ensemble and is free from the agitation of wild geese and peacocks, there issues forth speech with lips like the *bimba* fruit and a beautiful, slender tongue.
The speech of those preeminent in excellent qualities is as sweet as the song of the Gandharvas, its resonance like the falling of raindrops— neither too diffuse nor too condensed.
The tinkling of excellent *kiṅkiṇī* ornaments, beautifully gathered and sounding like golden nets,
produced by the clashing of jewelry on earth and in heaven, belongs to those preeminent in speech.
Neither too rapid, not faltering, uninterrupted, and sweet, their speech proceeds with a flow of well-articulated phrases; such is the speech of those who bear the marks of excellence.
He attends to every assembly, even if it consists of millions of world-systems;
with most sweet speech, he makes himself understood by the entire assembly of those who possess the ten powers.
Among the Śakas, Yavanas, Cīnas, Ramaṭhas, Palhavas, and Daradas, as well as among the assemblies of bandits,
she moves through all regions, being described in a single way.
The speech emerging from the best of men does not overstep the assembly;
the voice of the Ten-Powered Ones, steady in its rhythm, neither increases nor diminishes.
It is not broken, it is not pushed back, and it is not distressed;
it does not falter or produce harsh, clattering sounds—the voice of the Sugata resounds with sublime tones.
Nor is she possessed of corrupt words, nor is she deficient in speech; she employs every word with complete application.
Skilled in all words, whether auspicious or inauspicious, she gladdens the entire multitude of people.
When the speech of those who possess virtue issues forth from their mouths, with their teeth so pure,
the flocks of birds dwelling in the sky and those in the forest rejoice.
Whatever sound is pleasing to anyone, that voice, produced from the words of the Sugata, fulfills his intention as it moves through the assembly.
Accompanied by excellent fragrance, resembling the resonance of mountain rivers, pure,
and echoing with the cries of ospreys and cranes, this voice arises as the most excellent sound among all sounds.

The cries of the *śakunta* and *jīvañjīvaka* birds resound like the voice of the Victor, resembling the sound of golden palm leaves and possessing a resonance equal to the charming tones of sharp-sounding drums and mṛdaṅga drums.
The speech of those who have reached the supreme perfection is always to be known and understood; it is profound and awe-inspiring in form, yet pleasant to the ear and heart-stirring.
And their speech, worthy of being heard from the lute and full of endearment,
belongs to those who possess all virtues, who have accumulated a vast store of merit, and whose fame is infinite.
Speech has been taught in accordance with reality.
The perfectly awakened ones teach the Dharma in this way.
“Monks, I do not teach that those phenomena which are impermanent are permanent;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are permanent are impermanent;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are suffering are happiness.”
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are pleasant are suffering;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are not self are the self;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are self are not-self.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are impure are pure; nor do I teach that those phenomena which are pure are impure;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are material are immaterial.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are wholesome are unwholesome; nor do I teach that those phenomena which are unwholesome are wholesome;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are untainted are tainted.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are with outflows are without outflows;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are determinate are indeterminate;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are indeterminate are determinate.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are inferior are superior;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are superior are inferior;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are based on the household life are based on renunciation.
Nor do I teach that those dharmas which rely on renunciation are based on the household life.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, the Perfectly Awakened Ones are speakers of truth, speakers at the proper time, speakers of reality, speakers of meaning, speakers of suchness, speakers of what is not otherwise, speakers of what is not false, speakers of the Dharma, and speakers of the Vinaya.
Long ago, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), a son of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita heaven, a Bodhisattva named Śikharadhara,

spoke directly to the Blessed One with reverence, respect, and humility, his hands joined in añjali, on the day the Wheel of the Dharma was set in motion by the Perfectly Awakened One at Ṛṣivadana in the excellent Vānārasi forest.
Excellent! Your speech, O one of virtuous form, is not obstructed;
excellent indeed is your delightful speech, which is meaningful and purposeful.
Excellent! O Great Sage, you speak well with a harmonious voice, endowed with the qualities of phonetic euphony; excellent indeed that you proclaim the four truths.
Excellent, O Deva and Gandharva, as they drink in your sweet words!
Excellent indeed that you have set in motion here this peerless, irreversible wheel.
In this world, there is no one equal to you in physical form, complexion, lineage, or strength;
nor in deportment, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, tranquility, or self-control.
Today, O Hero, ten billion beings have become joyful in this first fruit;
they are disciplined in the teaching of the Son of the Gods, under the first Sage.
O Lord, O Hero, you have led thirty koṭis to the first fruit;
in the second teaching, you have likewise led men and sons of gods.
Furthermore, fifty koṭis of sons of gods were disciplined in the third teaching of the Sage and liberated from the states of woe.
Furthermore, eighty koṭis were established in the fruit of stream-entry;
having been tamed within the fourth teaching, they were liberated from the miserable destinies.
Therefore, O Supreme among Men, there is no one equal to you in loving-kindness;
O Bull among Men, you have become even more compassionate in your compassion.
Delighted, O Great Sage, these tigers among men, born as the most beautiful in the world, wander for the benefit of all sentient beings.
After a very long time, O bull among men, you have been born as a prince,
a leader for those who have gone astray and a delight to the eyes of the afflicted.
May the true Guru and Protector never disappear;
O Kinsman of the World, may your state be infinite.
The states of woe have been thinned by your splendor, O Self-Existent One;
the heavens have been made spacious, having attained you, O Supreme Person.
This person, who belongs to the group fixed in falsehood,
will fulfill [his potential] upon reaching you, who belong to the indeterminate group.
O you who are praised by the gods, even that person whose destiny was uncertain will, having encountered you,
fulfill their destiny as one born of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened One.
And the purification of marvelous qualities is attained by reaching you,
O Sun among Men, who are called the destroyer of darkness.
O Bull among Conquerors, O Great Sage, as you speak these true teachings,
the worlds, including Indra, rejoice in your words.
Thus do the hosts of gods, their minds filled with joy, praise the giver of boons,
the supreme among men, who is endowed with infinite virtues and worthy of all praise.

O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, the Perfectly Awakened Ones are perfected in the rules of conduct; they are capable of knowing the right time, possess pure vision, and see things without partiality. They are endowed with the methods of the past, have raised the banner of the Dharma—the peerless banner—and are skilled in the teachings, possessing inexhaustible knowledge. They bring others to maturity at the proper time, set in motion those who lack guidance, and revile the wrong paths.
In this regard, the following is said:
Endowed with all excellent qualities, all of them are certain regarding all matters;
they are the leaders and guides, the Buddhas honored by the wise.
With unconfused knowledge and a purified mind,
they shine throughout the three worlds like the full moon in the sky.
With their beautiful and virtuous feet, beloved by the good, these leaders,
having perfectly produced merit, let out a great roar.
The heroes, firm in their conduct, instruct the people;
seeing reality as it is, they crush the disputes of other beings.
Born in the world, O best of men, yet you are not defiled by the world;
having transcended all designations, you are masters whose domain is profound.
Having taken up the heavy burden, the wise do not despair;
acting exactly as they speak, their conduct is beyond reproach.
Having burned that terrible poison of false views with the fire of knowledge,
the Lord bestows supreme fearlessness upon living beings who are neither terrified nor trembling.
Having crossed the wilderness and reached safety, O bulls among men, those wise people call out: "Right here is this place free from fear!"
The arising of old age, death, and disease does not exist here;
the occurrence of weariness and sorrow is not found here.
Having heard his sweet words, those gods and humans,
acting in accordance with his instruction, attain that happiness.
Therefore, they possess widespread and supreme fame throughout the three worlds;
honored by the virtuous, they continue their practice and do not cease.
Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, the Perfectly Awakened Ones offer gifts to sentient beings for the sake of their welfare.
For example, the Blessed One spoke of the supreme offering made by Queen Kusumā to the King of Kaliṅga; likewise, the Blessed One spoke of the offering of words made by the merchant Dhruva.
And likewise, in that most excellent city of Rājagṛha, the Blessed One engaged in a supreme offering;
skilled in his own methods, he elevated Upāli’s offering of words.

Likewise, that lion among debaters, the self-controlled master of those who have attained mastery, the Blessed One, the Great Sage, having received that supreme offering from another who had arrived at the slopes of Mount Meru, spoke thus to the community of monks: [He said: "This [is the case]..."
I shall proclaim all these delightful offerings;
listen now to the auspicious play of that one who is preeminent among beings.
When that best of men had appeared and the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion,
the King of Kaliṅga ruled over a prosperous kingdom free from thorns.
There was one named Abhaya; this was his view:
"There is no fruit for wholesome or unwholesome actions"—this was his certainty.
There is no world beyond, nor is there anywhere the fruit of giving;
one who is free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion does not exist.
Having attained that vision, he would assemble the people;
he proclaims his own view and thereafter does not turn back from it.
If my father were to speak thus to me in person,
having approached me himself, then I would believe it as such.
At all times he was then possessed of virtue and a mind of loving-kindness.
If there is fruit for that, his destination shall be the city of the gods.
Having become a god, he will recognize me and liberate me from this view.
Thus there is a world beyond; abandon this evil view.
Since the occurrence of that other world is not perceived, may my father come and gladden my heart.
Then, out of compassion for the world, the Sage, the Great Compassionate One, being exceedingly confident,
himself assumed the form of the King of Kaliṅga.
Having ascended the excellent palace and entered the inner apartments,
he likewise showed the inhabitants of the inner apartments that display of his natural state.
Then that emanated king, standing poised in the sky,
the wise and supreme among men, spoke to King Abhaya.
Having abandoned one's own duties and being occupied with the affairs of others,
that which is joined with false views is called "kingdom" though it is no kingdom at all.
Today your destiny in this world will be the great and terrible hell;
and the same destiny shall also befall those who show it to you.
For one who has been struck down strikes others; one who is ruined causes others to perish;
and one who is himself blinded by his own shamelessness blinds others as well.
Having plundered others, you yourself are plundered; having killed others, you yourself are killed. O evil-minded one, you cause even those beings who are happy to suffer.
Immersed in the mire of sensual desire, greedy for pleasures and infatuated with them,
the king— desiring to see the world beyond— [sought] the guiding principle of all phenomena.
It is impossible, O Lord of the Earth, that you, being devoted to sensual pleasures,
would be unable to go from this world to the next, O Master.
Having understood both the gratification in sensual pleasures as well as their defects,
and knowing the escape from sensual pleasures, I indeed recognize your successive lineage.
Having heard this, Abhaya, the best of men, trembled with fear;
bowing low, he spoke thus to Sudarśana in the sky.
I have faith in you, O Lord; it is even so and not otherwise. Be gracious to me, O Protector; deliver me from fear.
Therefore, having entered the inner apartments, the minister said: "The Teacher, the peerless person, has come;
I am yours to be disciplined, as are many other people."
This offering was performed by that one of supreme intelligence, the one of excellent wisdom, for the sake of favoring sentient beings.
The queen of King Kusumbha, renowned as Kusumā,
was beloved by King Kusumbha and was the most excellent among thousands of women.
His mother and father, both aged and dependent on staffs, spoke thus to their daughter: "O Kusumā, my child, listen!"
We are old, while you are young and agitated by desire;
we wish to release you, and we wish for our own death.
Having heard these words, Kusumā attained the realization:
"If my father-in-law were to put this man to death, it would be a disgrace to me."
"I shall give them most dreadful food mixed with poison,
by eating which both of these will undoubtedly die."
When her mind had become fixed upon her parents with such cruelty,
the Teacher then gave rise to compassion for Kusumā.
Then the Teacher, the Fully Awakened One, causes Kusumāyā’s mother and father to disappear and establishes two other emanations in their place.
Kusumā brought that food mixed with poison;
she said to the created beings, "Mother and father, please eat this food."
Those created by the Jina eat their food without wavering;
nothing at all afflicts their bodies, for they are indeed mere emanations.
On the second day, and likewise on the third, fourth, and fifth,
having eaten food mixed with poison, they sustained themselves as if it were nectar, being transformed by magic.
Then, having joined her palms in reverence, Kusumā said to Nirmitā:
"Introduce yourself to me, if I am worthy of your favor."
To Kusumā, who was thus entreating him with palms joined in reverence, the emanated being said:
"Whosoever among you knows your transgression and likewise acts accordingly [should speak]."
The Buddha, a tiger among men, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
has arisen from a noble lineage and is possessed of all branches of knowledge and virtues.
All qualities—past, future, and present—have become known to that lion among speakers; abandon your doubt in this matter.
Having ascended the excellent palace together with his womenfolk, that king requested:
"We wish to see him who perceives all things."
Having paid homage to him who is endowed with all virtues, go for refuge;
then the Jina will speak to you regarding that very matter about which you ask us.
Having promised "So be it" to the emanation,
the king then quickly ascended the palace together with his harem.
Immediately, that king, together with his women's quarters, bowed low with palms joined in reverence;
accompanied by Kusumā, the king spoke these words:
To those who are endowed with all noble qualities, who are compassionate toward the worlds,
and who have been fully embraced [by the Dharma], I offer this salutation with joined palms and a joyful heart.
Then the Teacher addressed his disciples who delight in the teaching—
Cāruvarṇa, Siṃhahanu, Dṛḍhabāhu, and Anindita.
Kīrtimant, Mahānāga, Cāturanta, Mahābala, Nīlakeśa, Vṛddha, Śānta, and Śāstraviśārada.
Likewise, she who is equal to a female crane, whose desire is secret and blameless,
who is Siṃhanandinī, large-eyed, and possesses this unsurpassed mark.
"O monks, I am going; follow after the Teacher!
Making Kusumā my leader, I shall guide many people."
Having promised "So be it" to the Self-Existent One who had attained mastery,
they surrounded the Perfectly Awakened One and spoke these words:
O Hero, our feet shall follow the same stride as that of the birds;
we shall follow the Fully Awakened One wherever the Visionary One goes.
In the twinkling of an eye, the Blessed One, surrounded by his disciples, arrived at the city of Kusumapura out of compassion for living beings.
The Leader, skilled in meditation, mentally emanated the form of Vajrapāṇi and meditated upon the host of deities with his mind.
He emitted a halo of light extending for fourteen yojanas,
and the deities paid homage to the journey of the one of supreme intelligence.
Then Queen Kusumā, bowing low, spoke to the Sugata:
"O Lord, with palms joined in reverence, I desire to worship your feet."
Then the Teacher, the maker of light, having surpassed all directions with his radiance, took his stand upon the summit of that excellent palace.
Then Queen Kusumā, together with the king,
paid homage at the feet of the Jina, and the queen’s retinue also paid homage to the Bull among Men.
O best of men, honored by the gods, we go to you for refuge.
What kind of fruit does one obtain after killing both mother and father?
Listen, Kusuma, to the truth regarding the fruit of killing one's mother and father:
immediately thereafter, one is reborn in the Mahāvīci hell.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, the Teacher, the Leader, skilled in speech,
revealed the Great Avīci hell to Kusumā.
Then Queen Kusumā, terrified of the dreadful hell and shedding a torrent of tears, spoke these words:
O compassionate one, what kind of fruit arises in the next world for one with a wicked mind toward his mother and father? Speak that which is true.
For one with a wicked mind, that very thought regarding a flower would not be abandoned; indeed, that same [state of mind] results in both immediate and future-world fruit through such violence.
Then, filled with joy and bliss, she relinquished her cruel mind before the King of Dharma.
Then the All-Knowing One speaks of the gratification of sensual pleasures;
the Supreme among Men speaks also of the danger inherent in sensual pleasures.
Then, he of inconceivable prowess speaks of the escape from sensual desires;
possessing the vision of reality, he proclaims the marvelous qualities of nirvana.
Placing Kusumā at their head, the Sage disciplines twelve koṭis of humans, thinking, "This is an offering."
In the city of Kāśivardhana, there was a preeminent merchant named Dhruva;
this sinful vision of his occurred during a meeting with his mother and father.
He who, having gathered together his mother, his father, and his circle of kinsmen who have grown old and lost their youth, should satisfy them with various kinds of food and drink.
And when the mass of fire is blazing, one should cause both ancestors to be cremated;
an offering should be made to him, for his merit shall be infinite.
He manifested thousands of rākṣasīs,
who stood before Dhruva as he lay upon his excellent palace bed.
With staffs in hand, with whips in hand, and likewise with spears in hand;
with axes in hand, with swords in hand, and likewise with flaming torches in hand.
Then, with tomara-spears in their hands and hundreds of iron arrows in their grasp,
and with spears and mallets in their hands, they stood before the merchant.
O lowest of men, you have attained a view that is repeatedly censured;
having embraced this censured falsehood, you ought not to place your faith in it.

Those who have performed difficult deeds for you, those who have been your benefactors in the past, and those who possess a mind of loving-kindness toward you in times of distress— to them you desire to do harm.
To those whom it is impossible to repay in any way by means of offspring,
even by giving them all manner of jewels— you desire their death.
Death is better for you than life, and certainly not such a sight as this,
you who obstruct the vision practiced by the truly great men.
Today, life no longer exists for you, along with your wife, your kinsmen, your servants, and your sons; and after death, your destination shall be hell.
Indeed, O worthy ones, may it be well with you,
regarding this person who is possessed of false views and whose mind is deluded by the conceit of being a scholar.
Let us surely destroy that merchant, who possesses evil views and disparages the noble vision, as he leads other people toward the same ruin.
Having heard these words, Dhruva became agitated in mind;
with his limbs perspiring and bowing low, he was filled with trepidation.
With a bewildered mind, looking about in all directions, his heart became terrified;
joining his palms in reverence, he spoke these words.
May the hosts of Rākṣasas be gracious toward my retinue and me;
you are my goal, my refuge, and indeed my sanctuary.
Command me: what must I do today so that fearlessness may come to me and my circle of kinsmen, and so that we may not fall into an evil rebirth?
And those hosts of spirits, stationed in the sky, said to Dhruva, the merchant:
"Do not go to us for refuge; go instead to him alone for refuge."
To the one who desires the welfare of all beings, the Buddha honored by those of purified conduct,
the speaker transcending all worlds, the Lion of the Śākyas, the delightful one.
Where indeed is that Blessed One, honored by all beings?
We too would go for refuge to that Sage, the best of men.
Endowed with all virtues, he was in the city of Ratnakholaka,
in the Gandhamādana garden, which was covered with various flowers.
Honored by ninety thousand who have attained mastery,
the wise Sage, skilled in the monasteries, dwells there.
Go for refuge to him together with all your kinsmen;
behold that Sun among Men and abandon that [wrong] view.
And whatever auspicious Dharma he teaches, established through parables, behold that with wisdom; in this way your life shall become meaningful.
And if you do not go, O merchant, you will certainly not attain [the goal];
this death of yours is immediate, so practice with faith in that.
Then the merchant, together with his kinsmen, having become deeply dejected in mind,
prostrated himself upon the ground with his head where that Supreme Person was.
Endowed with all excellent qualities, the Sage of great compassion,
together with your circle of kinsmen— I, who possess great fame, go to you for refuge.
O you who bring an end to the fear of the fearful, you are capable of granting fearlessness. O Great Being, I am one who has taken refuge in fear; please be my protector.
I wish to worship the feet of the Teacher, the best among debaters;
I wish to see that True Person, if we are worthy of his grace.
Then the Teacher arose, preceded by those who have attained mastery;
in the blink of an eye, the Leader arrived out of compassion for sentient beings.
Seeing him standing in the sky— tamed, patient, and honored—
joy arose in the merchant along with his kinsmen.
The merchant has come for refuge to that tiger among speakers; may you, O merchant, attain the state of one whose appearance is truly well-born.
Having accepted his transgression, the Tathāgata, the best of men,
the truth-speaking sage, proclaimed the four truths.
The All-pervading One, the Sun among men, reveals in detail the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karmas, just as a lion roars in the forest.
Having heard this lion’s roar, the merchant, together with his attendants,
attains the sweet and true fruit in the very first moment.
That preparation which was performed for him by the Great Seer,
those who are skilled in all dharmas call it the "offering" (upahāra).
There was once a king named Taru on a certain island in the ocean;
in him arose a wicked vision, beloved by the foolish.
One who, having invited a brahmin, a śramaṇa, or even another beggar,
does not feed them— they say that he possesses the mark of excellence.
Having invited a great multitude of people, including many Śūdras and Brāhmaṇas,
he who brings them to hunger by subjecting them to imprisonment;
Upon his rebirth in the northern direction, he will be born there as one of great power and vast renown, possessing abundant clothing and ornaments.
The king causes the people to accept this through his sinful mind;
having heard his words, the great multitude believes them.
Having understood this vision, the Sage, who is worshipped by gods and gandharvas,
instantly manifested five thousand monks.
Having reached that island where the lord of men was ruling his kingdom, those groups of self-controlled ones walked about there.
But the king, having seen those created [beings] described by the monk,
descended from his vehicle and, having paid homage at his feet, spoke:
I invite you, O sages, with sincere devotion;
may the sages grant me their favor, if we are worthy of it.
Knowing that he had accepted [the invitation], he then rushed out;
having prostrated at the feet of the sages, he went to his own royal palace.
Perceiving that the night had turned to dawn, he said to the king's man:
"Go, approach the sages, and invite them on my behalf."
And they were ushered by the king into the most wonderful hermitage of the ṛṣi,
which was a refuge endowed with all virtues and secured by firm bolts and excellent mechanisms.
When the seven days had passed, the king inspected them;
their facial complexions were not dejected, and they sat in meditation as described by the monks.
Having further avoided that, the lord of men,
having transcended the second [level], examines the second.
On the third, fourth, fifth, sixth,
seventh, ninth, and tenth week, he spoke these words.
The gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, guhyakas,
and asuras have come in the form of sages for the purpose of inspiring me with a sense of spiritual urgency.
Declare yourselves if we are to be favored;
or, if you are to be favored by us, declare yourself.
"You are worthy of favor, O lord of the earth," he said these words to you:
"Act in accordance with whatever word we shall speak."
This Teacher dwells in the city of Kāśī, in the auspicious grove at Vārāṇasī;
he has reached the further shore of all dharmas and is the destroyer of all doubts.
Having ascended the excellent palace, the multitude together with their kinsmen entreated him:
"O Best of Men, we wish to see the Peerless Person."
Having heard these words, he replied, "So be it.
Then the Teacher ascended into the air and approached that island.
The four who had attained mastery— Kuñjara, Karabhogaja, Vāraṇa, and the great meditator Manāpa— all came together.
Having seen the Fully Awakened One, shining with the luster of the moon,
they praised him— the Teacher of the true nature of reality— with palms joined in reverence.
With a serene mind and joyful heart, endowed with all forms of virtue,
O Protector of gods and humans, homage to you, the one who supports humanity!
Who indeed are you, O Great Being, of great majesty and great splendor, of great intelligence and great arms? Speak according to the truth.
Born into a royal lineage and established in the kingdom of Dharma, I am the refuge of all beings; thus do they know me as the Buddha.
I am the protector, the leader, and the seeker of the gods and humans;
I am the one who brings an end to doubt, the perfectly awakened one, honored by the gods.
Having heard this, King Tara spoke thus to the Fully Awakened One:
"Homage to you, O tiger among speakers, destroyer of all doubts!"
Having ascended the excellent palace together with our kinsmen, our followers, and the entire kingdom, O virtuous one, we go to you for refuge;
be our refuge.
And the king explained his own view to the great seer;
having heard that, the tiger among men spoke thus to the king.
O Lord of the Earth, it is no gain for you that you place your faith in this evil path leading to miserable rebirths; abandon this pernicious view!
Having abandoned that view, the king spoke these words:
"O wise one, teach me the Dharma wherein suffering is brought to an end."
And for him, the Supreme Person,
who is confident in the Buddha-dharma, cultivated that which is endowed with Dharma for the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having understood that Dharma, the king, together with his retinue,
abandoned the three fetters and attained the first fruit.
And an incalculable multitude has attained the first fruit;
behold, O King, the supreme power of loving-kindness, O virtuous man!
Those monks who are manifested there are not considered to be actual monks;
the Jinas, who are experts in the teachings, declare this to be a mere offering.
It is impossible, O Son of the Victor, that the Tathāgatas could attain omniscience while still remaining within those coarse stages.
These tigers among speakers, these supreme among men, have shown that they do not let time pass in vain, for they have fulfilled all the stages.
Having gone to the forest at Vārāṇasī, the Leader, preceded by the Buddha-dharma,
extensively proclaimed the ten stages.
The Fully Awakened Ones, who know what is right and wrong, understand the supreme intention of all;
they examine the resolute intentions of all living beings through their birth stories.
By means of sweet song and right method,
the Fully Awakened One, who perceives qualities and understands all beings, has well-disciplined a great multitude of people.
Having encountered the supreme friend, one who is disciplined by excellent wisdom, they are not born, they do not age, and they do not die in any way whatsoever.
The wise understand one another’s profound conduct;
they all possess infinite eloquence and are beautiful in every limb.
Thus ends the tenth stage, named Abhiṣekavatī, in the glorious Mahāvastu Avadāna.
On the peak of Vulture Mountain, in the assembly of five hundred who had attained mastery, he spoke the introductory discourse on instruction known as "The Ten Stages."
The *Daśabhūmika* is completed.
Those beings who aspire to Buddhahood must study this; it should be taught to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and to those who have seen the truth and possess faith, but not to others.
For these [latter] would have faith in this matter, while others would harbor doubt.
The ten stages from the first stage up to the tenth stage are completed; this is the vicinity of the Mahāvastu.
The *Dīpaṃkaravastu* begins as follows:

"From this point, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon ago, there was a universal monarch named Arcimat. He had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, was endowed with the seven jewels, ruled over the four continents, was a conqueror, was beloved by his citizens and countryfolk, was righteous, a king of Dharma, and lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action."

He possessed the seven treasures, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure—such were his seven treasures.
And he had a full thousand sons, O son, who were heroes, brave, of excellent form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Thus, having completely conquered these four great continents, bounded by the oceans and mountains—entire, free from thorns, and without punishment, without the use of force, and without oppression—by means of righteousness alone, he dwells therein.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, King Arcimat had a royal capital named Dīpavatī. It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north. It was surrounded by seven walls made of gold and covered with gold.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees, variegated and beautiful to behold, made of the seven precious substances:
gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
The trunk of the golden palmyra tree had leaves and fruit made of silver;
the trunk of the silver palmyra tree had leaves and fruit made of pearls;
and the trunk of the pearl palmyra tree had leaves and fruit made of beryl.
The trunk of the palmyra tree made of beryl had leaves and fruit made of crystal;
the trunk of the palmyra tree made of crystal had leaves and fruit made of musāragalva;
the trunk of the palmyra tree made of musāragalva had leaves and fruit made of ruby.
The trunk of that palmyra tree was made of ruby, while its leaves and fruit were made of pearl.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those palm trees are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and pleasant to hear.

Just as, for example, when a five-piece musical ensemble is skillfully played by expert musicians, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, refreshing, and not unpleasant to hear— even so, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at that time and at that season, the people in the royal capital of Dīpavatī were addicted to wine; they sported, enjoyed themselves, and diverted themselves, being fully endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, accompanied by that sound of palm-leaf clapping.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was surrounded by seven networks of railings, variegated and beautiful to behold, made of seven precious substances:
gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
The gold foot had a silver needle, base, and support;
the silver foot had a pearl needle, base, and support;
the pearl foot had a lapis lazuli one; the lapis lazuli foot had a crystal one; the crystal foot had a musāragalva one; and the musāragalva foot had a ruby one.
The base was made of ruby, while the needle and the mounting frame were made of gold.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those railings and lattices were covered with two golden nets: one made of gold and one made of silver.
The golden net had silver bells,
and the silver net had golden bells.
Furthermore, around that royal capital of Dīpavatī, there were three gates on each side—wondrous and beautiful to behold—made of the seven precious substances:
gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those gates had door-sills made of two kinds of precious materials, gold and silver;
they had thresholds made of two kinds of precious materials, gold and silver;
and they had crossbars made of two kinds of precious materials, gold and silver.
The panels were made of two kinds of material: crystal and silver.
The inlays on the panels were of two kinds: gold and silver.
The decorative ornaments were made of four kinds of material: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, of those gates, one half consisted of gold and the other half of silver.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those four gates had threshold bolts of four colors: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
The door-panels were of two colors: gold and silver.
The bolt-fastenings were of two colors: gold and silver.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in front of those gates, shafts were erected—three men’s height in width, three men’s height in depth, and twelve men’s height in elevation;

they were variegated and beautiful to behold, made of seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby. These seven precious substances were gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those gates were covered with two kinds of golden nets each: a golden net made of gold and a golden net made of silver.
On the golden net there were silver bells, and on the silver net there were golden bells.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those golden nets are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, pleasing, enchanting, and not disagreeable to hear. In just this way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those golden nets are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, pleasing, enchanting, and not disagreeable to hear.

Furthermore, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was indeed not empty of such sounds as these: namely, the sounds of elephants, the sounds of chariots, the sounds of infantry; the sounds of kettledrums, the sounds of clay drums, the sounds of small drums, the sounds of conchs, the sounds of flutes, the sounds of lutes, the sounds of singing, and the sounds of musical instruments; and the sounds of "Eat! Consume! Drink! Give gifts! Perform meritorious deeds! Practice the Dharma toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas! May it be well with you! Thus it was.

Furthermore, in the center of that royal capital Dīpavatī, there was a sacrificial pillar named Valguyā, variegated and beautiful to behold, made of seven precious substances— gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāgalva, and ruby—
twelve yojanas in height and four yojanas in its base-width.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Arcimat had a chief queen named Sudīpā; she was gracious, beautiful to behold, noble in appearance, and endowed with the most excellent and abundant beauty.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in twelve years the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara will descend from the Tuṣita abode; the Śuddhāvāsa gods announce this to the Pratyekabuddhas."
The Bodhisattva will descend; leave the Buddha-field!
The one of infinite wisdom and vision will descend from the Tuṣita heaven;
leave the buddha-field of the one who bears the excellent marks.
Having heard the word "Buddha" from the supreme Maheśvaras, those Pratyekabuddhas,
self-arisen ones who have mastery over their own minds, entered parinirvāṇa with liberated hearts.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in twelve years, the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara will descend from the Tuṣita heaven. The Śuddhāvāsa gods, having assumed the guise of brahmins, will teach the mantras, the Vedas, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man to those brahmins, so that when the Bodhisattva arrives here, they may prophesy his destiny."
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at the time of his passing away from the Tuṣita abode, the Bodhisattva performs four great surveys:
namely, the survey of the time, the survey of the region, the survey of the continent, and the survey of the family.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas are born into two types of families: either a kṣatriya family or a brāhmaṇa family.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the family in which Bodhisattvas are born is endowed with sixty qualities.
With which sixty factors is it endowed?
And that family, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is well-known;
and that family is thoroughly understood.
And that family has ample space;
it is endowed with noble birth,
endowed with a distinguished lineage, and endowed with a succession of ancestors.
Endowed with a lineage of former ages well-known [to others], endowed with a lineage of former ages of great renown,
and possessing many wives.
And one who has many followers;
and one who is not fickle;
and one who is not greedy.
Fearless, undaunted, and possessed of wisdom.
And one who is virtuous,
yet does not look after his own property—
that family enjoys its wealth.
And that family becomes firm in friendship,
grateful,
and knowledgeable in proper conduct.
And it proceeds without desire, and it proceeds without hatred, and it proceeds without delusion.
One who goes toward fearlessness;
one who fears reproach;
and one who possesses gross discernment.
And Puruṣakāramati,
and Dṛḍhavikramaṇa,
and Cetiyapūjaka.
One who worships the gods,
one who worships the ancestors of old,
and one who is devoted to ritual action.
One who is devoted to renunciation, one who is devoted to vows,
and one who has previously attained [the fruit] and subsequently [lost it].
Resounding with celestial sounds;
the eldest of the clan;
the most excellent of the clan.
Of noble lineage,
attained mastery over his family,
and of great renown.
And he has a great retinue;
a retinue that is tireless;
and a retinue that is devoted.
An unbreakable retinue, reverence for one's mother, reverence for one's father,
and the state of being a true ascetic.
He possesses Brahminhood;
he honors the elders of his family;
and he has abundant wealth and grain.
And he possessed abundant treasuries and granaries;
abundant elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep;
and abundant female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.
And that family becomes invincible against others who are adversaries or enemies.
In whatever family, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas are born, that family is endowed with these sixty qualities.
Those beings who are endowed with a noble family—beings of such a kind as these—attain great compassion.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at the time of his passing away, the Bodhisattva made a great preparation.
Thousands of sons of gods were addressed by the son of a god.

"Be born in the sixteen great provinces of the Middle Country among families of great kṣatriyas, families of great householders, royal families, and families of royal ministers; when you have been disciplined, the great masses of people will come to discipline."
At the time of his passing away, the Bodhisattva surveys: "Where shall I be reborn?"
"This King Arcimat has performed meritorious deeds and possesses great majesty; he is a universal monarch, lord of the four continents, and he is worthy to be my father."
She searches for one who is graceful, of noble birth, pure of body, possessing little passion, and short-lived— such that only seven nights remaining out of ten months would be left of her lifespan.
Having given birth to all those Bodhisattvas, the supreme among men,
on the final seventh day, the mother gives up her life.
What is the cause here, O all-knowing mothers, that after giving birth to the best of men, you so quickly abandon your lives?
In the Tuṣita realm during the spring season, the Bodhisattva, examining his mother, attained great mindfulness through his auspicious karma.
If there should remain a remnant of life for a woman here,
one should cross over her chest for seven days and ten months.
For what reason? Because it is improper for one such as me to engage in sexual intercourse after having maintained the supreme state in future times.
Moreover, even if they were to indulge in sensual pleasures with the mother of the Sugata,
the father of the hosts of gods would not be said to have broken his conduct.
The Blessed One indeed constantly speaks of the faults of sensual desires;
yet the mother of the Lord of the World indulges in sensual desires.
And those jewel-caskets situated in the palaces of kings—
the jewel that is the Best of Men, the vessel which is the Mother of the Jinas.
While searching, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva saw it.

In the royal capital of Dīpavatī, King Arcimat had a queen named Sudīpā, who was gracious, of noble birth, pure of limb, and of little passion; yet she was short-lived, with only seven nights remaining from ten months of her lifespan.
Then, while surveying the world from the enclosure of Arcimat’s palace,
he saw a woman who resembled the consort of an immortal, like a flash of lightning, and as radiant as a well-kindled lamp.
Having observed his mother, he addressed the immortal one: "I shall descend;
I will enter my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the happiness of gods and men."
To him the host of gods, wearing excellent ornaments and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O Supreme Person of undiminished virtue and beauty, may your vow be fulfilled!"
We too, for the benefit of the world, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures,
shall dwell in the human realm for the sake of making offerings to you, O Supreme God.
With uplifted minds, they rained down a shower of Mandārava flowers of stainless, radiant color from the sky, addressing him with pure and very sweet words.

Dwelling among the gods of Yama, delightful through the pacification [of passions] yet unmixed with sorrow or suffering, you neither rejoice nor indulge in sensual pleasures; this is truly marvelous in you.
That you, having surpassed the host of Maruts, illuminate the ten directions with a radiance like a mountain of gold, O bull among gods— this too is a marvel.
O you of immeasurable intellect, that you surpass the hosts of gods, including Maheśvara and the dānavas, as well as the multitudes of Māra and the stars moving through the sky— this too is a marvel.
Furthermore, O Teacher of the assembly of beings, although we do not desire separation from you,
nevertheless, O lotus-eyed one, you shall become the refuge for men and gods.
Then, at the time of his passing away, the host of gods, filled with joy, proclaimed throughout all directions to him whose eyes were like pure hundred-petaled lotuses:
While this conversation was taking place in the city of Tuṣita, that peerless and most radiant Sudīpā,
the chief queen of King Arcimat, approached the king and said this:
That youthful woman, with eyes like those of a young fawn, resembling a pure Gandharva maiden,
spoke these very sweet words to Arcimat while holding the lamp.
O bull among kings, her arms adorned with ornaments and wearing exquisite garments, she desires to pass the night together with her friends, yet without you.
The best of men, Śataraśmi, ascended to the highest floor of his excellent palace,
where there was a supreme couch, stainless and resembling a garment of white water-lilies.
Pleased by those agreeable words of the goddess Arcimat,
the excellent among men, his resolve exalted, addressed his retinue.
Let them quickly announce to me that Śataraśmi is covered with excellent flowers;
strew it with loose blossoms and make it like the divine realm in heaven.
Adorned with hanging silk streamers, the hundred-rayed chariot shone with great agility;
covered with a net of excellent gold, it resembled the peak of the noble Mount Sumeru.
And let the fourfold army, variegated with spears, iron arrows, and javelins,
swiftly surround the delightful host of Śataraśmi.
The command having been issued by the king, and everything being prepared,
they brought their own family there, approached the king, and said this:
May the protector of the earth preserve his full lifespan of no less than a thousand years;
for this excellent celestial palace stands ready, inspiring joy in you.
Then that queen, resembling a celestial consort, rising from her excellent seat just as the sun had set, spoke to the best of kings.
I undertake this: non-violence toward living beings and the holy life;
I also abstain from what is not given, from intoxicants, and from idle chatter.
O best of men, I shall likewise desist from all slanderous speech;
O lord of men, I shall refrain from harsh words—this is my resolve.
I shall not give rise to envy toward the desires of others, nor shall I harbor malice; I shall cultivate a friendly disposition toward all beings and abandon distorted views.
"O Protector of the Earth, I practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night;
such is the aspiration that arises within me."
Furthermore, O protector of the earth, let there be no thought of sensual desire toward me;
do not expect me, lest demerit accrue to you on account of me, a woman living the holy life.
"I shall fulfill all your desires," the king said. "Take your pleasure within this excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your disposal."
Taking with her a thousand foremost women who were devoted to her, she ascended that excellent celestial palace and sat down there, her every wish fulfilled and pleasing.
For some time, she spent that period in silence upon that couch which resembled snow, a white lotus, or a water-lily, delighting in tranquility and self-restraint.
Then, she laid down her noble body on its right side.
Like a flowering creeper clinging to a noble tree, she lay embracing her bed.
Then, beholding that queen lying upon her bed, resembling a celestial maiden in form,
the hosts of gods descended from the Tuṣita abode and took their positions upon the roof of the palace.
All those immortals, with their heads bowed and hands joined in reverent salutation,
joyfully paid homage at the bedside to that goddess, the mother of the Jina, who possessed vast merit.
Then, filled with great curiosity, many daughters of the gods, wearing pure garlands and desiring to see the Mother of the Jina, approached and took their places upon the roof of the palace.
Having approached and beheld the queen reclining on her bed, who resembled a flash of excellent lightning,
he experienced vast joy and bliss, and then rained down celestial flowers.
Even among humans, such a form as this is truly well-born and a marvel;
were it to remain for some time, it would not be equaled even by the wives of the gods.
O friends, behold his playful charm, which is so appropriate for this woman;
reclining on the bed, he captivates the mind and shines like a golden ray of light.
He will support this Great Man, who is utterly devoted to generosity, self-control, and virtue;
he is stainless and brings an end to all outflows. O Queen, what is lacking for you?
In this beautiful belly, curved like a bow, resembling the palm of a hand, and adorned with a wonderful line of hair,
that one of infinite intelligence shall dwell— ever unstained by the impure and pure.

For one who shall uphold this [sūtra] of infinite qualities, which possesses vast and supreme merit accumulated over a long period of time, the wholesome roots gathered by him over many long nights will be immense.
You are a worthy woman, most excellent; he is a mother, and this son is the foremost of men, free from desire and stainless. O queen of kings, what is lacking for you?
Then the Rākṣasas, assuming various forms and commanded, swiftly took their positions all around in the sky:
"O you who bear excellent weapons, remain here; make all directions unobstructed!"
Immediately following them, hosts of double-tongued serpents stand in all directions for the sake of protection;
even upon hearing the mere movement of their wind, their anger arises like fire.
Immediately following them stood stationed the yakṣas, with blazing crests and deformed shapes; those of evil intent were commanded: "Now turn back, and do not kill anyone at all!"
Standing in their midst were powerful hosts of Gandharvas, possessing beautiful forms;
for the sake of protection, they bore splendid bows, were endowed with excellent marks, and possessed vast intelligence.
The four Lords of the World, together with their own retinues, have stationed themselves in the sky;
today, it is said, the Blessed One will descend, he who increases the welfare and happiness of the world.
Together with the thirty-three gods, the foremost of the thirty-three, the bearer of the excellent wheel, stands in the intermediate space;
he will before long undergo his final passing away, desiring incomparable bliss.
At the foot of the Goddess, many hosts of deities, having joined their ten fingers and bowing toward her,
uttered sweet words while gazing upon the Jina in the Tuṣita heaven.
O you whose power of merit is accumulated through purification, the time has indeed come for you to reach the end of existence;
wait now, for your mother is ready, so have compassion now for the suffering people.
"I am passing away"—thus he uttered auspicious words, and proclaimed this beautiful speech.
Then, at that very moment, the Mother of the Victor beheld a dream, the fruit of excellent maturation.
Resembling snow and silver, with six tusks, beautiful feet and lovely arms, and a deep red head;
that preeminent elephant has entered her womb, possessing a graceful gait and flawless joints of the limbs.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas do not descend into their mother’s womb during the dark fortnight;
rather, Bodhisattvas descend into their mother’s womb on the full moon of the month of Pūrṇa, when it is conjoined with the Puṣya constellation.

When a woman has observed the fast, is endowed with physical height, is endowed with girth, is well-formed, has reached the full bloom of prime youth, is disciplined, learned, mindful, clearly conscious, possesses a mind that is skillful in every respect, is suitable in every way, and is the most excellent among women— it is at such a time that Bodhisattvas descend into their mother’s womb.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva had gone to the Tuṣita heaven, at the time of his passing away, he emitted a radiance by which the entire Buddha-field was illuminated.
A son of the gods asks another son of the gods.
For what reason has the foremost of gods emitted this radiance, cooler than the rays of the moon and as pure as gold,
by which the hosts of the lords of asuras and the lords of men have been gladdened, and even the hells, which were like flames of fire, have been cooled?
Then he said:

For the sake of summoning those of great renown and stainless virtue who protect the people here and there— those trapped in the cage of saṃsāra and overcome by passion— he emitted a radiance that brings about their liberation.
The Bodhisattva said:
O immortals, do not abandon your cities; this is surely no time for rejoicing.
This is the time to shatter the city of old age and death with the blow of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva, mindful, clearly comprehending, and with a mind directed toward the right, descended into his mother’s womb.
Then that lion among men, having uttered a lion’s roar by the river at the time of his passing away,
vanished in an instant and was reborn in the palace of the king of men.
He who illuminates the Tuṣita realm with his beautiful complexion,
that unsurpassed light of the world, is now descending from the city of the gods.
Together with Brahmā, the world, and all generations including recluses and brahmins, he—
the unsurpassed illuminator of the world— shines with his radiance.
Behold this wonder, this marvel: how the Teacher, possessed of great supernormal power, mindful and clearly comprehending, descended into his mother’s womb.
And as long as that most excellent of men, endowed with the supreme marks,
remained in his mother’s womb, he was mindful, wise, and fully conscious.

And immediately after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had entered his mother’s womb, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways; it shook in a manner that was thrilling, beautiful, gladdening, delightful, lovely, refreshing, worthy of praise, worthy of being gazed upon, enchanting, not repulsive, serene, pleasing, free from agitation, and free from terror.
And yet, even while trembling, it does not harm any living being, whether moving or stationary.
Then this earth, together with its oceans and Mount Meru, shook in six ways;
and the world was made stainless and delightful by the splendor of him who dispels the great darkness.
Thus, he who was of great majesty and possessed of mindfulness, having passed away from the Tuṣita heaven,
assumed the form of an elephant with six tusks, resembling a white boar.
While she was lying on her heroic bed, having observed the *poṣadha* vow and being clothed in pure garments,
he— mindful, clearly conscious, and skillful— descended into his mother’s womb.
And at the break of that night, she spoke to her beloved husband:
"O best of kings, a white lordly elephant has entered my womb."
The King, having assembled the five classes of diviners, heard them and said:
"Tell me the true result and maturation of all these dreams she had."
Thereupon, when the soothsayers were questioned by the king himself, they said:
"One who bears the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
You are joyful, O best of men, because one such as you has appeared in your family—
one who supports the earth, a noble embryo, an incomparable being, a great being.
O tiger among the heroes of men, as I have personally received from the ancient teachers, there are only two other destinies for him. (p. 208)
If he shall dwell at home, he will become a lord of the earth, possessing the seven treasures and great supernatural power,
ever victorious and surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of kings.
Then indeed, having renounced the earth consisting of the four continents, he will go forth;
he will become a Buddha, an unsurpassed leader of men and gods.
All the dragon kings and lords of dragons, as many as there were, applied themselves with zeal to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, all the kings of the Suvarṇas and lords of the Suvarṇas applied themselves with zeal for the protection, defense, and guardianship of the Bodhisattva; even the four Great Kings applied themselves with zeal for the protection, defense, and guardianship of the Bodhisattva.
The four world-protectors also provided protection for the Lord of the World,
lest anyone seeking his harm should injure him, the dispeller of Namuci’s power.

Śakra, the lord of the gods; Suyāma, the son of the gods; Saṃtuṣita, the son of the gods; Sunirmita, the son of the gods; Vaśavartin, the son of the gods; Mahābrahmā; and Śuddhāvāsa, the son of the gods—all of them applied themselves with zeal to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb.
Thousands of satisfied gods,
possessing excellent wisdom, have arrived at Arcimapura for the sake of protection, as if it were the city of the immortals.
Entering the delightful and supreme city of Dīpavatī, which had been prepared for them,
it shone brilliantly with hosts of immortals who moved with mind-made strides.
Surrounding the Goddess, it is said, eight thousand hosts of Maheśvara’s attendants, situated in the expanse of the sky, remained seated in mid-air.
Now, behind them, many thousands of Indras with stainless crests sat down for the sake of guarding the one of manifold virtues.
Now, behind those lords of the gods,
thousands of myriads of gods belonging to the realm of desire were seated in the sky, without support.
Behind those hosts of gods were the asuras; behind the asuras were the hosts of double-tongued serpents, along with yakṣas of deformed appearance and throngs of rākṣasas, all seated together.
By this method, the glorious sky was filled with hundreds of thousands of immortals;
it was exceedingly pure, for it was indeed accumulated by men of wholesome merit and was free from passion.
Mahābrahmā said:
The woman who, in her dream, saw the sun entering her womb from the sky, shall give birth to one whose limbs possess excellent marks; he becomes a king, a powerful universal monarch.
The woman who, in her dream, beheld the moon entering her womb from the sky, shall give birth to a son who is the essence of a lord of men; he will become a king, a supreme universal monarch.

The woman who, in her dream, saw a white elephant enter her womb shall give birth to one possessing the essence of the nature of an elephant; he will become a Buddha who has awakened to the meaning of the Dharma.
He asks the goddess:
What do you carry?
She said:
A universal monarch.
I bear within my womb a universal monarch, a supreme man, a tiger among kings, whose golden body illuminates the belly and who is endowed with the most excellent marks.
The gods raised their voices in the sky, proclaiming the word of the Blessed One.
He will become a Buddha, not a king who is a wheel-turning monarch of power.
Mahābrahmā spoke this verse:
You uphold the royal sage, an elephant of supreme jewels who removes the force of passion and power, a lamp for the world that dispels the darkness of ignorance and delusion,
a treasury of virtues, a bearer of an immeasurable mine of gems, possessing an unassailable wheel and the splendor of the immortals.
The goddess said:
Just as passion and hatred do not arise in me upon perceiving the womb of the Lord of Men,
he will undoubtedly become one of equal taste, just as these words issue forth.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother moves, stands, sits, and lies down in comfort solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
No weapon can penetrate her body; neither poison, nor fire, nor lightning can prevail against her, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, divine maidens attend upon the Bodhisattva’s mother with celestial requisites for anointing, massaging, and grooming.
Her body becomes clothed in divine garments and she wears divine ornaments, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
By the very power of the Bodhisattva, she becomes a recipient of divine scents, divine garlands, divine ointments, and divine essences.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, whoever constitutes his inner retinue thinks that he must serve him exceedingly, must listen to him, and must consider it his duty to listen—
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, those who see the Bodhisattva’s mother approach her and invite her with various offerings, all through the very power of the Bodhisattva.
Nothing whatsoever goes above it, not even a bird, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother is free from illness and free from affliction. She is endowed with a well-functioning digestive system that ripens food properly—neither too cold nor too hot—solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother is free from illness and free from affliction. She possesses a digestive system that is balanced and well-functioning, neither too cold nor too hot, due to the very power of the Bodhisattva himself. It is through the Bodhisattva’s power alone that her digestion is properly transformed.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother enjoys exquisite solid and soft foods, the finest and most fresh flavors,
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother is free from passion;
she practices the holy life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, completely pure, and perfectly fulfilled.
Not even in her mind did passion arise for that most excellent woman, toward any man whatsoever, including even King Arcimat himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother observes the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), though she has not previously undertaken them. Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, as many Naga kings as there are— whether lords of Naga kings, or born from eggs, or born from a womb, or born from moisture, or of miraculous birth— [all protect him].
Or, having approached your dwelling, they scatter divine sandalwood powders.
In this way, they scattered powders of agallochum and loose flowers; they honored it for its completion, they honored it for its perfection, and they honored it for its total purity.

Having scattered divine sandalwood powders, they scattered saffron powders, tamāla leaf powders, and loose flowers. They honored him with this complete worship; they honored him with this perfect worship; and they honored him with this pure worship.

Having performed worship with complete offerings and having performed worship with pure offerings, having scattered divine sandalwood powder, divine aloe-wood powder, saffron powder, and tamāla-leaf powder,

and having strewn, overspread, and profusely covered [the ground] with loose flowers, they circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times to the right and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, all the golden kings and golden lords— whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth— enter his dwelling and scatter divine sandalwood powder, scatter many kinds of divine powders, scatter divine saffron powder, scatter divine tamāla-leaf powder,
and scatter divine flower powder.
And they honored him with complete honor; they honored him with perfect honor; and they honored him with utterly pure honor.

Having scattered divine powders— powders of agallochum, powders of kesara, and powders of tamāla leaves— and having scattered divine loose flowers, they circumambulated the mother of the Bodhisattva three times and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika,
and Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods entered her dwelling and scattered divine sandalwood powder, divine aloe-wood powder, saffron powder, and tamāla-leaf powder.
They scattered divine loose flowers over it; they honored it with complete honor, they honored it with perfectly fulfilled honor, and they honored it with utterly pure honor.

Having sprinkled her with divine sandalwood powder, having scattered divine aloe-wood powder, divine saffron powder, divine *tamāla* leaves, and divine loose flowers; and having honored her with complete worship, having honored her with perfect worship, and having honored her with utterly pure worship, they circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times and departed as they pleased,
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when a Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain too low, nor does he remain too high; he does not remain face down, nor on his back, nor on his left side, nor in a squatting position.
Then, indeed, he remained standing on his mother’s right side, having folded his legs crosswise.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain there defiled by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other impurity;
rather, with his limbs cleansed, bathed, and pure, the Bodhisattva dwells within his mother’s womb.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling in his mother’s womb, beholds his mother.

The Bodhisattva’s mother also sees the Bodhisattva within her womb like a form of pure gold; having seen him illuminating her womb like a form of pure gold, she becomes joyful—just as a beryl gem placed inside a crystal casket, even so does the mother see the Bodhisattva illuminating her womb like a form of pure gold.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, hosts of gods come to inquire after her well-being during the nights and days;
and the Bodhisattva welcomes them by raising his right hand, without causing any discomfort to his mother.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, dānavas, rākṣasas, and piśācas do not leave him by day or by night. Nor is any talk of attachment spoken there—neither talk connected with sensual desires nor any other untruthful speech.
On the contrary, they speak only of the excellence of the Bodhisattva: in terms of his form, his being, his splendor, his complexion, his fame, and his roots of merit.
The worship of the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb did not cease.
Divine musical instruments are played; divine aloe-wood incense is burned; a rain of divine flowers falls; a rain of divine powder falls.
And thousands of apsarases sing to him and dance before him as well.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother engages in laughter and conversation with thousands of celestial maidens.
And while the Bodhisattva’s mother was asleep, celestial maidens fanned her with garlands of māndārava flowers by the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this unsurpassed perfection of entering the womb exists within this triple-thousand great-thousand world system.
And behold now another marvel of that divine assembly:
how vast was the discourse that arose, generating supreme joy.
For them there was no talk of sensual pleasures, nor talk of celestial nymphs, nor talk of singing;
there was no talk of instrumental music, nor talk of food, nor talk of drinks.
No talk of ornaments arises among them, nor does talk of clothing ever occur; even the thought of vehicles or pleasure gardens does not arise in their minds.
Excellent! The splendors of one possessed of the power of merit are incomparable throughout the world, including the gods.
This story of the Leader blossoms forth there.
"Excellent is the peerless descent into the womb of him who has reached the perfection of form"—
thus did various discourses blossom forth in the midst of this assembly.
The virtuous, free from worldly motives, pass that time through words of instruction;
this discourse of the one with supreme intelligence also blossoms in the midst of the assembly.
And thus the hosts of gods delight in telling many kinds of stories,
speaking of the form, complexion, splendor, and strength of the Stainless One.
The mothers of all bodhisattvas give birth when the tenth month is complete.
When the tenth month was complete, the queen named Sudīpā said to King Arcimat:
"Your Majesty, it is my desire to go out to the Padmavana park."
