Having heard this from Queen Sudīpā, the king said to his ministers:
"I shall go out to the Padmavana park with my harem for the sake of recreation."
Make the lotus grove very swift [in its growth], free from weeds, grass, leaves, and debris;
create a heap of excellent fragrant flowers, scented with perfumed water.
And in the lotus grove, let the breezes— whose bodies are perfumed with the scent of *tāla* leaves—
sprinkle her with nectar-scented breezes that generate intoxication, and let them blow away [all other scents].
May clouds from the sky, filled with the finest incense of agallochum,
quickly descend upon him, covering the lotus grove thick with the essence of excellent powders.
And fashion each excellent tree from *dukūla* cloth, silk, wool,
and *kośikāra* fibers, like the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of the preeminent gods in heaven.
The gods and goddesses, taking perfumes and garlands, came to the Padminī grove garden of Arcimat.

Wearing earrings of crystal jewels, their garments slipping away, with long necklaces of gems hanging down, they take up perfumes and garlands and, moving along the path of the sky, they gather together.
Some, having filled baskets with māndārava flowers,
and some with yellow sandalwood, while others again with celestial garments (kalpaduṣya).
Taking garlands grown on land and in water, as well as jewels and ornaments, the Apsarases, their hearts filled with joy, headed toward Jambudvīpa.
No fewer than eighty-four thousand celestial maidens,
carrying vessels made of gold and jewels, dissolve into the sky.
The atmosphere was filled with hundreds of gabled pavilions, variegated with crystal and jewels and smeared with plaster,
and with hundreds of banners raised aloft upon silken cloths.
Resembling the breath of an elephant, they shine forth like autumn clouds,
fragrant with the scent of excellent, sweet-smelling flowers, interspersed with lotuses, water-lilies, and campakas.
Even the lords of the serpents, filled with joy, showered the sky with clouds laden with fragrant water; and there were hundreds of other wonders as well.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Arcimat, accompanied by his harem, set out for the Lotus Grove park with great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor.
Having entered that excellent forest, the Goddess, the mother of the Jina, surrounded by her companions,
wanders about like a celestial wife skilled in the arts of love, O Devī who possesses a chariot free from fear.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Queen Sudīpā, surrounded by her female companions, sported upon boats that were equipped with eastern and western railings, covered with canopies spread over them, draped with variegated cloths,

hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, plastered with ointments, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, enclosed with lattice-work railings, and adorned with raised parasols, banners, and flags.
Then, as Queen Sudīpā was being pulled along by the boat, it is said that a thought arose in her:
"I shall disembark from the boat."

And through the power of the Bodhisattva, an island appeared in the middle of the lake—level and not uneven, strewn with golden sand, and covered with soft, blue grasses that were like cotton to the touch and resembled the necks of peacocks; when one’s foot was set down four finger-breadths into the earth, it sank, and trees appeared there, laden with fruit and most delightful.
The goddess was established on that island.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the mother of a Bodhisattva does not give birth to the Bodhisattva while lying down or sitting;

nor, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, does the mother of a Bodhisattva give birth to a Bodhisattva who is defiled by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other impurity. Rather, she gives birth to the Bodhisattva with his limbs already cleansed, bathed, and pure.
With her body exhausted, she supported herself with her arm upon a branch of a tree;
she stretched out gracefully at the time of giving birth to that illustrious one.
Then twenty thousand daughters of the gods quickly assembled;
with their hands joined in reverent salutation and their intentions purified, they spoke thus to the goddess.
Today you shall give birth to one who will destroy old age and disease— one as delicate as the offspring of the immortals,
honored in heaven and on earth, a benefactor who brings welfare to both humans and gods.
Do not give way to despondency; we shall perform your service. Tell us what must be done, and see how all that is accomplished.
Then the four world-protectors, together with their retinues, quickly assembled;
with divine fly-whisks in their hands, they approached the Queen from the right side.
All the hosts of gods, having surrounded the goddess in the sky,
stood there, adorned with garlands and perfumes in their hands, together with their own retinues.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, the Bodhisattva appears from the mother’s right side without causing her any pain.
For the best of men are born from the right side;
all these tigers among men become dwellers here.
Yet her side was not pierced,
nor did any pain arise in that mother of the Conqueror as she gave birth to the Best of Men.
The Tathāgatas appear in a mind-made form;
thus their flanks are not broken, and no pain arises.
Exhausted from dwelling in the womb, he takes seven strides upon the earth;
he gazes at the directions and lets out a great laugh.
What is the reason stated here that one traverses seven steps in succession, neither eight nor six? Listen now to the traditional teaching on this matter.
Exhausted by the confinement of the womb, the Sage, who brings benefit to all the world,
then proceeded with speed toward his final dwelling in a womb.
When his feet were placed on the ground for the seventh time, the hosts of gods prostrated themselves;
suddenly, the Sage was supported by the laps of the world-protectors.
Then a rain arose, a shower of divine flowers,
strewn with the finest māndārava blossoms and thick with divine sandalwood.
For a long time, the foremost of the gods released exalted and supreme incense for the sake of adorning that one of supreme intelligence.
For whatever purpose the Peerless One surveys the directions,
I shall now declare the traditional teaching and the delightful instruction regarding that.
Among beings, whether among gods or humans,
there exists no one for whom such a birth and even an entry into a womb could occur.
When the mother of the Victor gives birth to him in his final existence, her side becomes radiant like a firefly or gold as he is being born, O Omniscient One.
As soon as he was born, that mind of the Preeminent Speaker arose:
"Is there anyone who possesses an intellect equal to mine?"—this was his thought for the purpose of turning back [any such person].
Some are tormented by the noose of saṃsāra just as I am;
for this purpose, the Sun of Men gazes upon all directions.
Then, surveying the directions, the best of speakers beheld thousands of millions of deities; therefore, he let out a laugh.
As soon as he was born, the deities belonging to Māra’s host said:
"You shall become a universal monarch with a great treasury over the four continents."
Then a smile arose upon his face: "O beings, you do not recognize me;
I shall become the Supreme Person, omniscient and all-seeing."
Thus do these distinguished teachers praise this;
for in such a way has the teaching of the Lions among Men been proclaimed.
I pay homage to that most excellent Conqueror, whom she gave birth to while standing amidst the blossoming *śāla* trees, supporting her body as she did so.
Immediately upon being born, the Sugata stood upon level ground;
he took seven steps and gazed toward all directions.
He followed behind him as he walked in meditation, carrying a fan and a parasol,
so that gadflies and mosquitoes might not fall upon the body of that knower of the supreme goal.
The gods first received the Sugata, the Jina, as soon as he was born; afterwards, humans held that most excellent one in their arms.
The gods received the Sugata, who displayed the thirty-two marks;
afterwards, humans carried him, who was unsurpassed, upon their laps.
The lamps of men were extinguished, though the world was illuminated;
when the Sugata was born, his kinsmen ran about seeking water.
Then, the wells in front of them overflowed from their mouths.
Two streams of water rose up— one cold, one warm—
whereby they bathed the Sugata as if he were an image of gold.
Immediately after the Sugata was born, the Bodhisattva’s mother remained both unhurt and unscarred, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, the Bodhisattva’s mother’s womb remained completely full, yet it was not constricted, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, a sandalwood forest appeared on the intermediate island, which came to serve as the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment and use through the very power of the Bodhisattva himself.
There, hundreds of thousands of sons of gods went along together, holding perfumes and garlands in their hands for the sake of worshipping the Bodhisattva.
A son of the gods asks another son of the gods: "Where will you go?"
He said to them:
This supreme consort of the lord of men shall give birth to that noble son, fair as the interior of a fully blossomed, excellent lotus;
he who, having struck down Māra together with his host, shall attain the highest goal upon the circle of the earth—I approach that hero.
His limbs are unstained by the impurities of the womb, like a supreme lotus born in the water;
with a body radiant as the young sun, he surpasses even the gods, including Brahmā.
Then, immediately upon being born into the family of Arcimat, the steadfast one took seven steps here;
having surveyed the directions, he laughed and said: "Now this is my final existence."

Then, many sons of the gods held aloft in the sky a single, brilliantly shining parasol, adorned with the finest jewels and pearls, outshining all others in splendor, while it was fanned by a handle made of *mandārava* flowers.
They held aloft in the sky an excellent golden parasol, its color resembling the sun, a conch shell, and the moon.
Then, having been released, the fans moved about; grasping them with their hands, they fanned the Jina.
Then two streams of water, fragrant with merit, pleasantly warm, abundant, light, lovely, beneficial to humans, auspicious, delightful, and accompanied by coolness, rose up into the sky.
Then, from the peak of Mount Meru, various kinds of upper garments were released, arising as waves on all sides;
strongly scented with universal perfumes and carried by the wind, they caused the earth to tremble violently in six ways.

In celestial palaces made of gold, silver, and beautiful jewels, the gods, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments, proclaimed the well-born Conqueror who was born after his predecessors; gazing upon him, they caused the sky—filled with the moon, the sun, and the stars—to shine brilliantly.

“This great seer, having crossed over the great flood—the world including its gods, nāgas, and yakṣas—will thereafter reach the secure state of the one direction. Thus did the gods, filled with joy, proclaim this to him from the sky.
King Arcimat gave the command.
"Lead the prince here to pay homage at the feet of this queen."
"In what kind of vehicle does the prince sit?"
The gods fashioned a palanquin made of jewels.
"Who will carry this palanquin?"
The four great kings stood in attendance.
"We shall carry the Bodhisattva, the essence of beings, as well as Queen Sudīpā and the Bodhisattva’s nurse."
Seated upon a palanquin, Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā performed the clearing of the way.

Thus, with great splendor, great prosperity, great divine power, and great royal majesty, the Bodhisattva was led from the lotus grove garden into the capital city of Dīpavatī and brought before the queen.
When the Great Lord of the World, the Teacher of the lords of men, entered the shrines without desire,
and they caused him to be saluted with their heads, then his feet would manifest.
Then a deity said to another deity: "It is not fitting that he should pay homage to me;
if he were to offer salutation to anyone else, his head would surely shatter into seven pieces."
As soon as he was born, all beings as far as the Avīci hell became happy through the accomplishment of their aims;
and the gods paid him homage,
for they were all filled with joy.
When the prince had entered the royal palace, the king said to the domestic priest:
"Quickly seek out brahmins who are skilled in the qualities and rules for discerning physical marks."
And having understood this, the gods named Maheśvaras, who have mastery over their own minds, [will protect you];
let not the assemblies of twice-born ones, being unskilled in the true characteristics, engage in conceptualization.
Eight thousand of the most excellent Maheśvaras, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance,
approached him who had been honored by the hosts of gods as soon as he was born.
Standing at the gate of the royal palace, clad in pure and excellent garments and maintaining absolute silence,
they addressed the doorkeeper with voices as sweet as the song of the karaviṅka bird.
"Approach the excellent king and say: 'These eight thousand men, who are experts in the rules for interpreting marks and qualities, are standing here; they would enter if you grant them permission.'"
Having promised "So be it," the gatekeeper entered the royal palace and,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the protector of the earth with a joyful mind.
O you of incomparable strength and radiant fame, rule the kingdom for a long time with your enemies destroyed;
at your gate stand those like the immortals, desiring to enter.
With perfectly full and stainless eyes, moving with the sweet voice of an elephant in rut—of them I have no suspicion, for they are not humans; they are sons of gods.
As they walk back and forth, the dust of the earth does not cling to their excellent feet;
nor do I see any footprints of theirs upon the ground—this too is a marvel.
With profound and steady gestures, noble appearance, and a gaze that is utterly tranquil,
they generate vast joy in the person who gazes upon them.
And another marvel occurred: no shadow of their bodies was seen, nor was any sound of their joints heard as they walked.
Without doubt, O lord of the best of men, they have come to see your excellent son;
having greeted him and paid him homage, behold the gods who were not born from a womb.
With hands holding choice garlands and perfumes, their graceful gestures and bodies enchanting, those excellent Maruts shine like glories; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words of Arcimat, his body trembling with joy, he spoke very hurriedly:
"O friend, let us enter the magnificent residence!"
For what reason? Because such characteristics do not belong to ordinary men, nor does such supernatural power as you describe exist among humans.
Then that doorkeeper, having approached Maheśvara, spoke thus to him—
bowed low with palms joined in reverence, prostrating himself, joyful and delighted in heart.
The king rejoices: "May you enter, sirs, the palace of the bull among kings, which is like a city of the gods, with the permission of the lord of men."
Having heard these words, the eight thousand foremost Maheśvaras entered the royal family of that chief of an unconquered lineage.
Then King Arcimat, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose with his retinue, his body suffused by the power of reverence.
And the bull among kings said to them: "A welcome to all of you, full of affection!
I am delighted by the sight of you and by your power of tranquility and self-restraint."
"We have these excellent seats available; please remain here for our sake, out of favor toward us."
Then, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, those whose actions were irreproachable sat down upon those seats, which had variegated feet made of many pure jewels.
After waiting for some time, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty hear the purpose for our coming here."
O Lord of Men, a son has indeed been born to you, whose limbs are entirely faultless, who is the beauty of the world, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks.
We too are skilled in marks and capable of discerning the characteristics of virtues and faults;
yet we would not have seen this form of a Great Man had we not perceived your greatness.
He said: "Come, behold my son, whose renown brings security, who brings joy to gods and men, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks."
Then, taking the moon of speakers, who possessed virtuous qualities, in his arms, he presented him to the best of the gods with a soft kācilindika garment.
Having beheld from afar the One of Great Power and the Ten Powers,
those lords with sublime gait fell upon the earth with joy, their crowns slipping from their heads.
Then they informed the king.
It is a gain for you, Great King, well-obtained by you, that such a Great Man has been born in your family, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
It is as follows:
Even, broad, long, and extended, with the fifth being the high-shouldered;
the thighs like those of an antelope, large, and standing erect—the [genitals] are enclosed in a sheath, and the body is like a banyan tree: these are the ten.
The hands and feet are soft and webbed; the fingers and toes are full and each has a single hair rising upward from the tip;
the skin is smooth; the space between the shoulders is like that of a swan; and there are seven protuberances—these are the ten.
The tongue is flavorful, the hair is golden, and the lion-like torso is even; the fifth is even and white.
The forehead is broad, the hair is dark blue, and the eyelashes are like those of a cow—these are ten.
With the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, the *uṣṇīṣa*, and the head, the Protector possesses the thirty-two marks.
Then those brahmins were addressed by King Arcimat.
Give the prince a name that is appropriate for him.
Those brahmins said:
"Great King, when the prince was born, a great island and a vast radiance appeared; therefore, let the prince be named Dīpaṅkara."
Thus, after the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven had fashioned the appearance of a brahmin for the prince, they gave him the name Dīpaṃkara.
Suitable nurses attended upon the prince and raised him.
And when the Bodhisattva had reached his youth, the king had three palaces built for the prince’s play and enjoyment, and he established an extensive harem for his service.

The Bodhisattva, accompanied by his harem, went out to the lotus grove in the pleasure garden for the sake of diversion, with great royal majesty, great royal supernatural power, and great royal splendor.
King Arcimat commanded the women of the inner apartments:
"Play with the prince well."

The Bodhisattva descends to the shoreless bank by means of boat-vehicles—boats provided with front and rear decks, surrounded by railings and lattices, covered with canopies, draped with variegated cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and streamers, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, beautifully adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, and moon-shaped ornaments, and with parasols, banners, and flags raised aloft. He descends by these boat-vehicles to the shore where no men dwell.

The harem, exhausted and fast asleep, was such that one woman was clutching her jaw, another was embracing a paṇava drum, another a flute, another a vīṇā lute, another a vallakī lute, another a sughoṣakī lute,
another an anklet, another a mṛdaṅga drum, and another was drooling.
Upon seeing that, the perception of it as a cemetery arose in the Bodhisattva.
In the middle of the lotus pond, a lotus appeared with a pericarp as large as a chariot wheel, surrounded by thousands of other lotuses.
The Bodhisattva sat cross-legged upon that lotus, and that lotus, having closed up, remained situated within the gabled chamber.
All the marks of a householder disappeared from the Bodhisattva, and saffron robes appeared.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal serenity and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. Thus, he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, which is devoid of rapture.

And with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directed and inclined his mind toward the attainment of the divine eye during the first watch of the night.

With the divine eye, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— fair and foul, in happy states and miserable states— and he understands how beings fare according to their karma. With his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, in the middle watch of the night, he recollects his manifold past abodes.

That is to say: one birth, or two births, or three births, or four births, or five births, or ten, or twenty, or thirty, or forty, or fifty, or a hundred births, or a thousand births, or many hundreds of births, or many thousands of births, or even many hundreds of thousands of births; or a *saṃvarta* aeon, or a *vivarta* aeon, or a *saṃvarta-vivarta* aeon;
or many *saṃvarta* aeons, or many *vivarta* aeons, or many *saṃvarta-vivarta* aeons.

"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a limit to my lifespan, and such an experience of pleasure and pain"— thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
With his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, firm, and attained to imperturbability, during the last watch of the night,

at the time of dawn when the night was fading away, whatever [is to be known] by a man-an-elephant, a man-lion, a bull among men, a lotus among men, a white lotus among men, a leader of men, a man— [that he fully realized].

By that true person, that thoroughbred among men, that unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed— one who possesses movement, mindfulness, steadfastness, and intelligence— he has fully known, attained, awakened to,
and perfectly realized supreme perfect enlightenment through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind for the sake of universal and all-encompassing knowledge.
And this great earth shook and trembled in six ways; and from the ground the gods raised a cry, making their sound heard in the sky:

"O worthy ones, this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara will attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."

Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods who move in the intermediate space— the Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins— at that very instant, in that very moment,
the cry rose up as far as the Brahma-world.

"O worthy one, this Blessed One will become the Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara; he will exist for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
An immeasurable, sublime, and great radiance appeared in the world.

To whatever extent there were in the world the intermediate spaces between worlds— regions of darkness plunged in darkness, of gloom plunged in gloom, wretched and born of wretchedness— where even these suns and moons, so possessed of great supernormal power and such great majesty, could not reach with their radiance nor pervade with their light, even those places were suffused by that illumination.

And those beings who were reborn there also recognized one another, thinking: "Indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here."
And at that moment, for that brief instant, all sentient beings became endowed with exclusive, supreme happiness.
Even those who have been reborn in the great Avīci hell transcend the divine power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, and the power of the yakṣas.
The palaces of Māra became darkened, lusterless, devoid of splendor, and unpleasant;
even fragments a *krośa* long fell there, fragments two *krośas* long fell there, and even the tops of the banners fell down.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of remorse, and consumed by the burning sting within him.
And there, Maudgalyāyana, in that very Lotus-Pavilion, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara was surrounded by the four Great Kings, Śakra the lord of the gods, the divine son Suyāma, the divine son Saṃtuṣita,
the divine son Vaśavartin, and Mahābrahmā, together with a retinue of many hosts of gods.
A magnificent worship was performed for the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.

Having scattered, strewn, and profusely showered divine *mandārava* flowers, *mahāmandārava* flowers, *karṇikāra*, *rocamāna*, *bhīṣma*, *mahābhīṣma*, *samantagandha*, and *mahāsamantagandha* blossoms, as well as sandalwood powder, *aguru* powder, *kesara* powder, and *tamāla-leaf* powder over the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, and having honored him with thousands of divine musical instruments,
he then entreated the Great Brahmā right there to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara consented to the Great Brahmā by remaining silent.

The gods, perceiving his acceptance, were thrilled, satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, circumambulated him three times, and vanished right there.
At the end of that very night, the Blessed One arose from his seclusion and set out on a wandering tour through the countryside.
The sun-like one of excellent complexion, like a youth arisen in the sky,
stood filling a hundred yojanas with his radiance as Dīpaṃkara.

The Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, while wandering on his journey and performing deeds for the benefit of a great multitude of gods and humans, arrived at the royal capital of Dīpavatī together with eighty thousand bhikṣus,
out of compassion for his father Arcimat and his kinsmen.
King Arcimat heard it.
The Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, together with eighty thousand bhikṣus, came to the royal capital of Dīpavatī out of compassion for his kinsmen.
And they prepared the road for ten *krośas*, from the city of Dīpavatī as far as the Padminīvana park; it was made level like a chessboard, even as the palm of a hand, sprinkled and swept,

with canopies spread above, draped with various fine cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, and adorned on all ten sides by actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, and musicians, resembling the city of a universal monarch and further embellished with hundreds of lotuses.
King Arcimat took up abundant perfumes and garlands; likewise, a great multitude of people from all around within twelve yojanas gathered perfumes and garlands.
The king, together with eighty thousand vassal kings and the rest of the people, went out to meet the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.

There was another learned man, a master of the six Vedāṅgas, one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas—including their phonetic refinements, the Itihāsas as the fifth, along with the Nighaṇṭus and Kaiṭabhas—who was a skilled teacher of young students among the Brahmin gods;
he taught the Vedic mantras to five hundred young students.
There were two young brahmins there who were friendly and affectionate with one another: the young brahmin named Megha and Meghadatta.
The young brahmin Megha was wise, steadfast, intelligent, and possessed of sharp intellect.
Not long after that, he had mastered all the mantras.
Having now completed his studies of the Vedas, he descended from the Himalayas into the countryside, thinking, "I shall seek the teacher’s fee for my preceptor."

Taking his staff, water-pot, parasol, sandals, and bathing-cloth, whichever village, city, or town boundary he enters becomes free from calamity and free from affliction through the power of the young Māṇavaka Megha’s fire-element.
The traveler informed the man.
Thus, five hundred purāṇas were given by him.
Then this thought occurred to him.
"What if I were now to go to the royal capital Dīpavatī, the city of the universal monarch, which is composed of the seven precious gems and is delightful, so that I may behold it?"
Having now entered the royal capital Dīpavatī, he beheld the royal capital Dīpavatī adorned.
This thought occurred to him:
What is this today in the capital city of Dīpavatī—is it a festival, a religious observance, or a celebration?
Then King Arcimat heard that the young brahmin Metha, having completed his studies of the Vedas, was departing from the Himalayas for the country and would arrive at the royal capital of Dīpanatī;
he thought, "Therefore, let this excellent city be adorned."
Traveling toward that city for a league, he enters it and asks someone there.
There, another young woman—gracious, beautiful to behold, steady, composed, and modest—was walking along carrying a water-jar and seven blue lotuses.
She becomes one who is questioned by him.
Today there is a festival in the city.
Then, indeed, the young woman Prakṛti addressed the young man Megha with verses.
But you are not a mere youth, O young man; you have come here from another city, you who do not realize that the Benefactor of the World, the Light-maker, has arrived at Dīpavatī.
The world-leader Dīpaṃkara, the son of Arcimat, of great renown—the Buddha will enter the city; for his sake, the city has been adorned.
She was questioned by him.
"How did you come by these blue lotuses? Were they purchased?"
She said to him:
For five hundred purāṇas, five lotuses were purchased; two of them were obtained by me for Maitra.
The young brahmin Megha said:
"I will give you five hundred purāṇas; give me those five blue lotuses. With these five blue lotuses, I shall worship the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara;
as for you, worship with two."
She said:
"On this condition, I shall give you the five lotuses:
if you take me as your wife, wherever you may be reborn, I shall be your wife and you shall be my husband."
The young brahmin Megha said:
"I shall generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; how shall I generate the mind toward union?"
She said:
Arise! I shall not create any obstacle for you.
It was accepted by that young brahmin, Megha.
I take your wife for the sake of those lotuses.
I shall worship the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and I shall generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having given five hundred purāṇas, he took five lotuses, and a sublime joy and gladness arose in his body upon hearing the word "Buddha" from the young woman Prakṛti.
If you wish to worship the Leader of the World with delightful lotus garlands, then take me as your wife today; through my love, I shall be ever devoted to you.
Just as the flower of the udumbara tree is difficult to find and only rarely appears in the world, O young man, even so is the appearance of the Buddhas, the great-minded Tathāgatas.
Worship the Buddha, the charioteer of men to be tamed, with delightful lotus garlands;
this shall become the cause for your awakening, and I shall be your wife in every place.
Megha said:
Today I take your wife, who is as beautiful as a water-born lotus, for the sake of the [lotus-born] deities;
I shall worship the Buddha, the charioteer of men to be tamed, and this act will become the cause for my awakening.
She became joyful and gave him lotuses, having recognized his state of affectionate love;
she followed him as he went on his journey to the crossroads where the young man stood.

The Blessed One, surrounded by eighty thousand bhikṣus, set out for the royal capital of Dīpavatī together with King Arcimat, eighty thousand minor kings, many thousands of great kṣatriya householders, and numerous ascetics, brahmins, and followers of other sects.
At the time of the Blessed One’s departure, thousands of deities assembled,
bringing with them thousands of parasols made of the seven precious gems.
Then he, the possessor of great virtues, set out at the head of the excellent assembly;
moving with the playful gait of an elephant in rut, his body was overspread with a network of rays of light.
The sons of the gods hold up parasols made of beryl, crystal, gold, and refined gold, with well-fashioned handles, for the Pure God.
Created by the gods in the sky, resembling the orb of the young sun,
they were beautiful with golden tinkling bells and produced excellent, joyful sounds.
And the King of the Thirty-three held over the umbrella-bearer in this world a divine umbrella made of the seven precious gems and adorned with celestial flowers.

And following after the Lord of Men, they fanned him with spotless, excellent whisks that had handles well-fashioned from solid gold, as bright as refined gold, over the sovereign of the three thousandfold world-system.

The ground that was exceedingly high sinks down, and that which was low becomes exceedingly high, as the Blessed Ones, endowed with the ten powers, enter it; all becomes level through the majesty of the Ten-Powered One.
Immediately thereafter, the Blessed One placed his right foot, which was like a golden lotus, upon the threshold;
there, a wondrous sound arose.
Kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors resounded without being struck;
conchs, small drums, and flutes entered into the presence of the Best of Men.
Whatever jewels were stored in the city, contained within chests and caskets,
those too they struck together as the Knower of the Best Jewels entered.
Then they spread out pairs of soft, costly garments along the path for the Blessed One—
various kinds of Kāśī silk and dukūla cloth dyed with many colors.

The Leader of the World was adorned with silk from Kośikāra, fine linen, cotton, Kācilindika cloth, antelope skins, and woven rugs; as well as those from Vanarusta, Tamakūṭa, Ātapakoṭṭavaka, Subhūmi, Toṣala, Kolama, and Cirāvoka—whether raw, dyed, or of the five kinds of woolen fabric.
From the eastern garden as far as the inner apartments of the lord of the earth,
the royal road shone, strewn with hundreds of thousands of fine cloths.
Then the women, having entered the grove, showered the Lion among Men;
taking handfuls of flowers, they scattered them over him who resembled a mountain of gold.
In proportion as the Greatly Powerful One, the Compassionate One, approaches Dīpavatī,
so do your glorious ones release a shower of flowers.
And those fragrant flowers of five colors, released from his hand,
formed a floral mantle for the Blessed One, the Protector of the World.
In the path of the sky, which is without support, there are fragrant inner thorns;
stand in circumambulation and scatter these flowers to the right.
When the Light of the World walks, they walk; when he stands, they stand;
they do not abandon the deportment of the one possessed of supernormal power who overcomes all.
Even if the winds of universal destruction were to blow across this triple-thousandfold world system, they could not disturb it; how much less could they carry away that flower-garment?
Having seen the Blessed One, who resembles gold and possesses a complexion like the finest, most excellent gold, the hosts of gods in heaven then exclaimed: "Aho! The Dharma!"
The sky and the earth were strewn with scattered flowers; heaps of blossoms reached up to the knees, and a canopy of flowers adorned the atmosphere.
The sounds of "Hikka," mingled with the music of instruments, resounded on all sides, crying out "Ah, the Dharma!
as the Bull among Men entered that preeminent city.
In Dīpavatī, the sweet voices of swans, kalaviṅkas, peacocks, and cuckoos, along with the humming of bees,
are heard mingled with the sounds of lutes and flutes.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the young brahmin Megha saw the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara approaching from afar, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,

his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, strong with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence.

Like a well-trained elephant, with his senses turned inward and his mind not wandering outward, he stood having attained the state of the Dharma; his faculties were tranquil, his mind was peaceful, and he had reached the supreme perfection of self-mastery and calm.

Guarded like an elephant, with his senses conquered, he was as clear, unclouded, serene, gracious, beautiful to behold, and lovely as a lake; he was pleasing and not disagreeable to look upon, illuminating for a league around with a radiance that shone forth.
And upon seeing him, the perception of non-duality arose within him.
I too shall become a Buddha in the world.
Then, Maudgalyāyana, at that time the young brahmin Megha spoke this verse:
After a long time, the eye has arisen in the world; after a long time, there is the appearance of the Tathāgatas.
After a long time, my vow has been fulfilled: "I shall become a Buddha"—of this I have no doubt.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the young brahmin Megha, having generated a sublime sense of rapture and agitation, as well as sublime joy and gladness, threw those five blue lotuses toward the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.
They remained there, surrounding the orb of his face with a network of light.
Prakṛti Māṇavikā also threw those two blue lotuses,
and they too remained suspended in the air.
The Buddha Bhagavats discipline sentient beings by means of three miracles: the miracle of supernatural power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.

The canopy of flowers over the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara—those five lotuses thrown by the young brahmin Megha, those thrown by the young woman Prakṛti, and those thrown by other people—was supernaturally empowered for the sake of training sentient beings and to generate joy and gladness in the young brahmin Megha; it was beautiful, lovely to behold, with four pillars, four doors, and bundles of hanging silk ribbons and garlands.

When Megha saw those lotuses standing all around above the halo of light of the Blessed One— gracious and inspiring confidence— a sense of joy and rapture arose in his body, and a noble intention manifested within him.

Having set aside his water-pot to one side and spread out his antelope skin, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara; while rubbing the soles of the Blessed One’s feet with his hair, he formed this thought:

"O, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara is now."

May I likewise be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, my body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and perfectly confident with the four grounds of self-confidence— just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara is now.
And may I thus set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara does now.
In this way I would maintain a harmonious community of disciples;
and in this way gods and humans would consider me one who should be heard and one who should be trusted.
Thus, having crossed over myself, I would help others cross; being liberated, I would liberate others; being comforted, I would comfort others—just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara does now.

May I be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, having known through his unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge the great attainment of the young brahmin Megha, and having known his accumulation of roots of merit and his mental aspiration, bestowed upon him the prophecy of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— [a prophecy] that was unbroken, unblemished, stainless, and flawless.
"Young man, in a future time, after immeasurable and incalculable eons, you will become in the city of Kapilavastu among the Śākyas a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni—

worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans— just as I am now, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."

He was endowed with the eighty minor marks that adorned his body; he was possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he was powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and perfectly confident through the four grounds of self-confidence.

Thus, having crossed over, you will cause others to cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvana, you will lead others to final nirvana, just as I do now.
And in this way, you will set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; and in this way, you will guide a harmonious community of disciples.
And thus gods and humans will think that what is to be heard must be believed:

"Just as I am now, so you shall become one for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of people, both gods and humans."
And immediately after being prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, Māṇava Megha rose into the air to the height of a palm tree,
draped his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and paid homage to the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara together with his community of disciples.
And at that very moment, at that very instant, this great earth shook and trembled violently in six ways;
and from the earth, the gods let out a cry so that it was heard.

Thus was the young brahmin Megha prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; this will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.

Having heard the sound of the gods of the earth, the gods who move in the intermediate space— the Cāturmahārājika gods, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods— at that very instant, at that very moment, the sound rose up as far as the Brahma-realm.

"In this way, friends, the young brahmin Megha has been prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; it will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
And there was the manifestation in the world of an immeasurable, vast, and great radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— regions of darkness plunged into darkness, of gloom plunged into gloom, wretched and born of wretchedness, where even these suns and moons, so powerful and so majestic, do not reach with their radiance nor pervade with their light— even they were suffused by that illumination. And those beings who had been reborn there recognized one another.
"Indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here.
At that very moment, at that very instant, all beings became endowed with absolute happiness."
Even those who have been reborn in the great Avīci hell transcend the divine power of the gods, the serpent power of the nāgas, and the yakṣa power of the yakṣas.
The palaces of Māra became darkened, lusterless, devoid of brilliance, and unpleasant;
fragments of them a *krośa* in size fell down,
and fragments of them two *krośas* in size also fell down.
Fragments of it three *krośas* long fell down;
fragments of it one *yojana* long fell down;
even the tips of its banners fell down.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of regret, and consumed by the burning sting within him.
Having spread out his antelope skin and set down his water-pot, he cast aside his blue-lotus hand to one side and prostrated with his excellent feet at the eyes of the Visionary One.
And those fragrant flowers of five colors, released from his hand,
formed a floral mantle for the Blessed One, the Lord of the World.

In the path of the sky, which is without support, fragrant flowers with inward-pointing thorns remained; as he performed the circumambulation, they turned to face him from the right as he moved clockwise.
When the Light of the World walks, they walk; when he stands, they stand;
they do not abandon the deportment of the one possessed of supernormal power who overcomes all.
Even if the winds of universal destruction were to carry away this triple-thousandfold world system, they could not disturb it; how much less could they carry away that flower-robe?
Having seen the Blessed One, who resembles gold and possesses a complexion like the finest, most excellent gold, the hosts of gods in heaven then exclaimed: "O, the Dharma!"
Then, when the prophecy had been delivered, the earth with its oceans and boundaries trembled, and in the heavens among the hosts of gods, a wondrous sound arose.
This Megha was prophesied by the Sage Dīpaṃkara— who raised the banner of exclusively well-spoken words— to become a Jina.
You will act for the welfare and happiness of the world including its Brahmās, gods, and asuras;
the lower realms and hells will diminish, while the heavens will increase.
A teacher named Dīpaṃkara appeared as an island, a shelter, and a refuge;
in a kalpa even more incalculable than this, he was the Blessed One, the Lord of Men, whose Dharma was well-proclaimed.
Having realized the supreme goal, the wise one turned the wheel of Dharma with confidence;
mindful and established in truth and Dharma, he delivered beings from great fear and the perilous path.

Megha, having inspired confidence in his mind toward the Victor Dīpaṃkara—the leader of the host of śramaṇas, endowed with most wonderful marks—he paid homage to him; while paying homage, he made this aspiration:
Thus may I wander through this world with a mind free from attachment, just as he wanders;
may I set in motion the wheel that is peerless, well-prepared, and honored by gods and humans.
I shall act for the benefit of the world; I shall teach the Dharma to gods and humans.
Thus may I discipline sentient beings, just like this Light of the World.

Having understood his vow— which is free from attachment yet joined with all causes— the Victorious One, the wise seer of the truth, made a prediction for him whose conduct was unbroken, flawless, stainless, and without blemish.
“O Megha, young brahmin, you shall become a Buddha in the future, after immeasurable eons.
Then, in the abode of the seers at Kapila, you, a Śākyan, shall attain the fruition of your vow.”
He sent another five hundred purāṇas to the teacher.
Having delivered all such things, he informed Meghadatta.
In this way, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara was honored by me and was prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"Let us go there; in the presence of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, we shall lead the holy life and experience that assembly."
He said:
"As for me, since I have not yet completed my Vedic studies, I am unable to go there."
Just as a piece of wood is carried away in the great ocean and perishes upon colliding with another, so too is the meeting with those who are dear.
Megha went into the presence of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and went forth as a monk.

Having relied upon such spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they have propitiated and made offerings to immeasurable and incalculable thousands of millions of Buddhas together with their assemblies of disciples (śrāvakasaṃgha), and having made offerings to immeasurable billions of Pratyekabuddhas,
they experience divine and human prosperity until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi).
He who, having heard that form is the charioteer of men to be tamed, would not go toward form, nor toward grasping, nor toward the state of being grasped.
He said to you:
This cloud is exceedingly inclined toward bowing its head.
Having heard the word "Buddha" from the young brahmin Megha, he was not gladdened;
due to his association with evil friends, he committed the five deeds of immediate retribution.
One who is attached to another's wife goes there, whether at the proper time or at an improper time.
His mother, out of affection for her son, prevents him, thinking: "Lest they kill him there, taking him for an adulterer."
One who is impassioned does not know the goal; one who is impassioned does not see the Dharma.
When passion overcomes a person, he then exists in darkness.
Having caused his mother to be killed, he went to the presence of that woman with whom he was infatuated, and there he confessed his true nature to her.
Thus you are dear to me, since for your sake I have deprived my mother of life and other [possessions].
That woman became anxious.
She said to him:
Do not come to me again.
One who is attached to another's mother.
Then that stepmother said to him:
"Come, deprive my father of life, and you shall be my master."
By him, his father was now deprived of life.
Thus, he was loathed and reviled in that place.
Friends and kinsmen avoid them.
Then, having moved from that dwelling to another dwelling, he thought: "No one here will know of me."
A monk who was a family attendant to his parents, an Arhat of great spiritual power, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that very residence.
Then, that son of a donor was seen by the monk in that very place.
Seeing that monk, he also became suspicious, thinking: "Lest this monk defile this place of mine."
By him, that Arhat monk was now deprived of life.
He then went forth as a monk in the teaching of that one who was at that time the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having now gone forth in that teaching, he caused a schism in the Saṃgha and drew the blood of the Buddha.
Having committed these five actions of immediate retribution, he was reborn in the great hells.

Having run and wandered for a very long time through the eight great hells and their sixteen secondary hells, when the Blessed One Śākyamuni had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and his teaching had begun,
he was born in the great ocean as a species of fish named Timitimiṅgila, with a body many hundreds of *yojanas* in length.

When the householder Sthapakarṇi, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred and traveling on a ship, had entered the great ocean, then that [being] who had become a makara, being hungry and seeking food, opened its mouth wide; thereupon the ships belonging to the householder Sthapakarṇi rushed toward where that makara’s mouth was.
Niryātamukha said:
"Householder, these ships have fallen into the mouth of the submarine fire; whatever must now be done, do it, for there is no more life for you."
Then they paid homage to their respective deities:
some to Śiva, some to Vaiśravaṇa, some to Skanda, some to Varuṇa, some to Yama, some to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, some to Virūḍhaka, some to Virūpākṣa, some to Indra, some to Brahmā,
and some to the deity of the ocean.
When the Venerable Pūrṇaka reflected, he saw that the householder Sthaparakarṇika, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, had fallen into doubt.
Then, having risen into the air from Mount Tuṇḍaturika, he stood suspended in the sky above the ship of Thapakarṇika upon the great ocean.
All those five hundred merchants, having joined their palms in reverence, stood up and said, "O Blessed One, O Blessed One, we have come to you for refuge."
The Elder said:
"I am not the Blessed One; I am his disciple.
All of you, with one voice, utter: 'Homage to the Buddha!'"
All those five hundred merchants cried out, "Homage to the Buddha!"
The sound of the word "Buddha" reached the range of that Timitimiṅgila’s ears.

Upon hearing that sound, the word "Dīpaṃkara Buddha" which he had heard from the young brahmin Megha during an immeasurable and incalculable eon became manifest to him as he was in the form of a *timitimiṅgila* fish in the great ocean.
"The word 'Buddha' is not in vain."
Then, this thought occurred to that being Timitimiṅgila:
The Buddha has appeared in the world, yet we have fallen into the states of woe.
Then, being deeply moved, he closed his mouth once again.

Having died without food while recollecting that sound of the Buddha, immediately upon his death he was reborn in a brahmin family in the great city of Śrāvastī; at that time and on that occasion, a boy was born.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I do not speak of anything other than karma."
Then, the name Dharmaruci was given to that boy.
When he had grown up, he then went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he realized the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and mastery over the powers.
Three times a day he approaches to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One;
whenever he approaches, the Blessed One exhorts and reminds him: "After a long time, Dharmaruci! After a very long time, Dharmaruci!"
He also said:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
It has been long, Blessed One; it has been very long, Sugata."
The monks, with doubt, questioned the Blessed One.
Three times a day Dharmaruci approached the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said to him: "After a long time, Dharmaruci! After a very long time, Dharmaruci! He replied to the Blessed One:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. After a long time, Blessed One; after a very long time, Sugata. Yet, Blessed One, we do not understand the meaning of this speech."
The Blessed One related this matter in detail to those monks, beginning from the time of Dīpaṃkara.
I was the young brahmin named Megha, and this one was Dharmaruci, [known as] Meghadatta.
Thus, monks, the sound of "Buddha" is not in vain; it leads even to the destruction of suffering.
At that time, the Elder Dharmaruci approached the Teacher;
he bowed at the feet of the Jina and said, "It has been a very long time, Dharmaruci."
After a very long time, Dharmaruci addresses the Teacher, the Leader of the World:
"O Jina, you who know all, why do you ask what the reason is for this very long time?"
He spoke again: "Formerly, I was a *timitimingila* in the salt ocean; overcome by hunger and weakness, I was searching everywhere for food."
At that time, many millions of living beings entered my body;
likewise, five hundred merchants entered by means of their vehicle.
And as the bowl was being brought in, those afflicted by the fear of being unprotected and fallen into calamity all spoke with one voice: "Homage to the Buddha, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers!"
Hearing the sound "Buddha," never heard before, I became joyful;
thrilled and with a heart full of rapture, I quickly closed my eyes.
Tens of millions of beings born as animals and hundreds of merchants were awakened by the voice of the One Possessing Ten Powers; at that time, I too emerged from the states of woe.
"By that merit, O Blessed One, this human state has been attained by me;
through the fruit of that well-conducted life, my name is Dharmaruci."
For that very reason, O Self-Existent One, I went forth into homelessness in your teaching;
not long after going forth, I became an Arhat who had shaken off all defilements.
Having wandered through endless saṃsāra for many millions of billions of eons,
I now call to mind the Sugata, who long ago brought benefit to the world.
After a very long time, the eye of Dharma has been purified; my doubt regarding the Dharma has been severed.
Having been shrouded by the darkness of delusion, I have dwelt for a long time in the states of woe.
By that merit, darkness has been abandoned and passion and hatred have been removed;
the rivers of the stream of existence have been dried up without remainder—this is my final birth here.
Even for this Timitimiṅgila, hearing the Buddha brought about a great fruit;
how much more so now, Blessed One, would this hearing not bring about the deathless?
Therefore, having abandoned the five hindrances that obstruct the mind,
one should listen to the word of the Buddha, cultivating the perception that it is difficult to encounter.

Difficult is the attainment of human birth, and difficult is the avoidance of the forest of insubstantial forms; rare is the arising of Buddhas, and rare is the presence of faith and the state of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the Dīpaṃkara-vastu in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite eons ago from this present Bhadrakalpa, immediately after the time of Dīpaṃkara, there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Maṅgala.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the lifespan of human beings during the time of the Samyaksaṃbuddha Maṅgala was one hundred thousand times ten million years.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the perfectly enlightened Buddha Maṅgala had three assemblies of disciples.

In the first assembly of disciples, there were one hundred thousand times ten million [arhats]— all of them whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed, and who had attained their own goal. In the second assembly of disciples, there were ninety times ten million [arhats]— all of them whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed, and who had attained their own goal.

The third assembly of disciples consisted of eighty koṭis, all of whom were arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed,
and who had attained their own goal.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala had a pair of disciples named Sudeva and Dharmadeva;
they were a supreme pair, an auspicious pair—one was foremost in wisdom, and the other was foremost in supernormal power.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, for the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala, there were two foremost female disciples: a nun named Śīvālī and Aśokā;
one was foremost in wisdom, and the other in supernormal powers.
Now, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Perfectly Awakened One Maṅgala had a monk named Pālita who served as his attendant.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhi tree of the Perfectly Awakened One Maṅgala was the Nāga tree.
Indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the city of the Perfectly Awakened One Maṅgala was named Uttara.
It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north.
It was surrounded by seven walls made of gold, with golden roofs.
It was surrounded by seven long ponds that were variegated and beautiful to behold, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those long ponds had stairs made of two materials—gold and silver—and their stair-rungs were made of four materials:
gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
Those long ponds were covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, white lotuses, nalini lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika lotuses.
Those long ponds were covered by such trees as these, namely:
covered with mango, rose-apple, breadfruit, *lakucha*, *bhavya*, and *pālevata* trees.
Furthermore, on the banks of those lotus ponds, there were such terrestrial and aquatic garlands as these:
namely, *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *vārṣika*, *vātuṣka*, blue water-lilies (*indīvara*), *damanaka*, and those brought from the gods.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the city of Uttara was indeed surrounded by seven rows of palm trees.
The royal capital Dīpavatī should be described in detail as follows.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the father of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was a Kṣatriya named Sundara, a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the mother of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was a queen named Śrī.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I was a dragon king named Atula, one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, and had accumulated an abundance of wholesome roots.

Then I honored, revered, respected, and worshipped that Blessed One Maṅgala together with his community of disciples... having offered him a pair of cotton cloths as a covering, I made a vow for enlightenment;
and by him I was prophesied: "In a future time, after immeasurable and incalculable eons, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha."
To the north of Dīpaṃkara, there was a leader named Maṅgala;
having destroyed the darkness in the world, he kindled the torch of the Dharma.
His splendor was incomparable, surpassing that of all other Jinas;
eclipsing the radiance of ten million suns, he shone with his thousand rays.
And that Buddha proclaims the four supreme truths;
having drunk the essence of those truths, they dispelled the great darkness.
Having awakened to incomparable enlightenment, at the first teaching of the Dharma,
there was the initial realization of hundreds of thousands of millions of gods.
When...
then the Fully Awakened One struck the supreme, most excellent drum of the Dharma.
Again, at the time of the gods, when he proclaimed the Truths,
there was a second realization involving ninety crores.
When Sunanda became a universal monarch and approached the Buddha’s Dharma,
then the Perfectly Awakened One beat the supreme and most excellent drum of the Dharma.
The multitude of followers of Sunanda numbered ninety koṭis;
all of them, without exception, became disciples of the Buddha.
Furthermore, at the time of the gods, when he revealed the Truths,
there was a third realization of eighty million [beings] during the third [turning].
When the householder Uttara approached to behold the Buddha,
then the Perfectly Awakened One struck the supreme, most excellent drum of the Dharma.
The people who followed him in the north numbered eighty koṭis;
they were all, without exception, disciples of the Buddha.
There were three assemblies of the great seer Maṅgala—
those whose taints were exhausted, who were free from passion, whose minds were peaceful, and who were reflective.
The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand times ten million;
the second was ninety crores, and the third was eighty.
At that time, I was a dragon king of great supernatural power,
named Atula by name, who had accumulated a vast store of merit.
With divine musical instruments, the Nāgas honored the great seer Maṅgala;
having offered him garments, they went to him for refuge.
Thus did the Buddha Maṅgala, the leader of the world, prophesy for me:
"After immeasurable eons from now, you shall become a Buddha in the world,
in the delightful and prosperous city of the Śākyas called Kapila."
Your mother shall be named Māyā;
your father, Gautama, shall be named Śuddhodana.
Kolita and Upatiṣya shall be the foremost among the disciples; Kṣemā and Utpalavarṇā shall be the foremost among the female disciples;
and he who is named Ānanda shall be his attendant.
The Aśvattha, the most excellent tree, shall become your Bodhi tree.
Having heard that prophecy from the great seer Maṅgala,
and having exerted my vigor and made my mind firm,
I shall practice the conduct of awakening and never abandon anyone.
The city was named Uttara; the Kṣatriya father was named Sundara;
and the mother of the great seer Maṅgala was named Śirikā.
Sudeva and Dharmadeva were the foremost male disciples;
Śīvālī and Aśokā were the foremost female disciples.
The attendant of the great seer Maṅgala was named Pālita;
his Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree, and that Bodhi tree was in full bloom.
The assembly of that great seer consisted of hundreds of thousands of millions;
while remaining in this world, the Great Hero delivered many people.
Having caused the teaching to spread widely, he shall deliver the great multitude of people,
like a blazing mass of fire or like the risen sun.
Just as the waves of the ocean cannot be counted,
even so the sons of the Blessed One cannot be counted.
And that Buddha is of great fortune, as is the True Dharma and the supreme assembly.
All conditioned phenomena that have just passed away are indeed devoid [of self].
Thus ends the story of Maṅgala in the glorious Mahāvastu Avadāna.
p.253 Now begins the section on the umbrella-base (chatravastuka), etc.
On the slopes of the Himalayas, there dwells a yakṣiṇī named Kuṇḍalā.
Then she gave birth to five hundred sons at equal intervals;
having given birth to a thousand sons, she passed away.
They too were dispatched to Vaiśālī as vitality-seizers.
Having gone to Vaiśālī, they steal the vitality of human beings.
There are two kinds of disease-epidemics: the circular one (*maṇḍalaka*) and the localized one (*adhivāsa*).
The circular disease-epidemic, wherever it falls upon a family, leaves nothing remaining; it carries everything away.
The localized disease-epidemic, on the other hand, carries off only a specific region.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī, afflicted by a prevailing outbreak of disease, were dying.
They pay homage to the gods of gods.
This thought occurred to them:
Upon whose arrival, indeed, would the affliction of the people of Vaiśālī be pacified?
Then they sent word to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
"Come! A non-human affliction has arisen among the people of Vaiśālī; upon your arrival, it will be pacified."
Kāśyapa Pūraṇa came to Vaiśālī, yet he did not alleviate that illness.
This thought occurred to them:
Kāśyapa has indeed arrived, yet the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī does not subside.
Then they sent [this] to Maskari Gośāliputra.
He too arrived, yet the non-human plague among the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent a message to Kakuda Kātyāyana.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then, at that time, a message was sent to Ajita Keśakambala.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent word to Sañjayin Veraṭṭiputra;
he too arrived, yet the non-human plague among the people of Vaiśālī was not appeased.
Then they sent [this] to the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Among those kinsmen and blood relations of the people of Vaiśālī, some have passed away and been reborn among the gods.
One of those deities announced it to the people of Vaiśālī.
"These who have been brought by you are not teachers, nor do they profess to be teachers; they are indeed not capable of quelling the non-human plague among the people of Vaiśālī."

This Buddha, the Blessed One, has fully awakened through incalculable eons; he is an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened one, possessing complete knowledge and vision, endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty, omniscient and all-seeing.
In whatever village, field, or boundary he dwells, there all pestilence, strife, clamor, calamities, and misfortunes are pacified.
"Invite him;
for when he has arrived, the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī will be pacified."
He dwells in Rājagṛha, the city of the palace, as delicate as the interior of a choice lotus;
by him, who has conquered the afflictions, all strife and quarrels have been stilled.
Like a golden-colored cloud that arrives at a village, town, or city beset by calamities,
he pacifies the plagues there, just as a powerful rain showers down dust.
Bring him who is pale-complexioned, resembling gold, with a beautiful face like the full sun, and who possesses the fragrance of excellent and sweet conduct; then the disease will be pacified.
In Vaiśālī, there was a Licchavi chief named Tomara, who had a great faction, a large retinue, and was wise.
Thus, having been requested by the community, he was sent forth.
Go to Rājagṛha; there the Buddha, the Blessed One, resides.
He dwells having been invited to stay by Śreṇiya Bimbisāra.

Having gone there, convey our greetings in the name of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī to him and his retinue; inquire after his freedom from illness, his freedom from affliction, and his dwelling in physical well-being, and speak thus:
“Blessed One, a non-human plague has arisen among the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, and many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin.
It would be well, O Blessed One, who desires their welfare—if you would come to Vaiśālī during the month of Taiṣya, out of compassion.”
Then Tomara, having given his word to the Licchavi assembly, mounted fine carriages together with a suitable retinue and, departing from the city of Vaiśālī, set out for the city of Rājagṛha.

Then Tomara the Licchavi, having gone to the city of Rājagṛha and entered it, proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in order to see, approach, and attend upon the Blessed One.

Now at that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, the Uposatha day, when the full moon was complete, the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma to an assembly of five hundred monks and many thousands of other people; he proclaimed the holy life (brahmacarya) which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, both in meaning and in letter, entirely perfect, pure, and radiant.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would permit for a vehicle, alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot.
Now, being unable to force his way through the great assembly that had gathered, he could not approach the Blessed One by force.
Then, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
On the fifteenth day of the Uposatha for the sake of purification, those seers have gathered to observe it;
and Śakra, the lord of the thirty-three gods, who is invincible among them, has come forward to attend upon you.
Shining brightly, you proclaim the supreme state; through the Dharma, you satisfy these many beings.
Like a great cloud with its water, you refresh the earth; having heard these sweet words of yours, [we are refreshed].

Having paid homage to the Great Sage who wears the snake-skin, and saluting him with palms joined in reverence, we go to you for refuge; for those who endure what is unbearable, it is well-gained and a true welcome.
Those who, being full of faith, go for refuge to the one who stands near the edge of the tomara-spears,
and who are then heedful in the teaching of the Sugata, will bring an end to birth and death.
At the conclusion of the verse, a great multitude of people made way for him.
Then Tomara the Licchavi approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and addressed the Blessed One as follows.

"O Blessed One, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, including the elders and the youths— both those from within Vaiśālī and those from outside— bow their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and his community of disciples, inquiring after his well-being and his state of comfort, and they speak thus:"

"Lord, in Vaiśālī a non-human plague has arisen, and many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin; yet the Blessed One is compassionate and merciful toward the world including its devas."
"It would be well if the Blessed One would come to Vaiśālī, out of compassion for the people of Vaiśālī."
The Blessed One said:
The Tathāgata is staying at the residence requested by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra; please grant him permission to depart.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and having circumambulated the Blessed One and the community of monks three times, departed for Rājagṛha.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, approaching King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, greeted King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra with great kindness and courtesy, and said this to him:
"Great King, a non-human plague has arisen in Vaiśālī; many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin."

There, the six teachers who were highly esteemed were brought together: Kāśyapa, Pūraṇa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Saṃjayin Vairaṭṭikaputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
Even with these having arrived, the non-human plague among the people of Vaiśālī does not subside.
Then, O Great King, the deities informed the Licchavis.

This Blessed One is indeed exalted; for through the power of his immeasurable qualities, he has fully arisen as the shelter, the protection, the refuge, and the final resort for the world including its gods—the god beyond gods, the teacher of gods and humans, and of the nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas.
Whoever enters the boundary of a village or field, there all calamities, strife, and misfortunes are pacified through the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Saṅgha.
Indeed, when he has arrived, the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī will be pacified.
"Excellent, Great King! Out of compassion, please grant the Blessed One permission to go to Vaiśālī."
Thus addressed, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra spoke this to the Licchavi Tomara:
"Vāsiṣṭha, if the Licchavis of Vaiśālī should come out to meet the Blessed One as he travels from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī as far as their own territory,
just as I have followed him as far as my own territory, then I shall permit the Blessed One to proceed from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī."
Then Tomara, the Licchavi, having received word from King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, dispatched messengers to the Vaiśālī assembly.
"Thus, O Vāsiṣṭhas, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra speaks."
Then those messengers, having given their word to the Licchavi Tomara, went to Vaiśālī and announced it to the Licchavi assembly.
In this way, O Vāsiṣṭhas, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra spoke to Tomara the Licchavi:
"If the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were to come out to meet the Blessed One as he travels from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī as far as their own territory, just as I provide an escort as far as my own territory,
then I would grant the Blessed One permission to go from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī."
When this had been said, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī [spoke] to their messengers...
O Vāsiṣṭha, this should be said to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra by the word of the Licchavi assembly: [as follows].
"O Great King, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will go out to meet the Blessed One as far as the territory of the Licchavis."
Then those messengers, having given their word to the Licchavi assembly, went to Rājagṛha and informed Tomara.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having assented to the words of the messengers, approached King Śreṇika Bimbisāra and said this to King Śreṇika Bimbisāra:
"Great King, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will perform a reception for the Blessed One."
It would be well if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would grant permission to go to Vaiśālī.

Now the Blessed One was permitted by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra to go to Vaiśālī. He then commanded his ministers: "From Rājagṛha as far as the ford on the Gaṅgā, prepare the road so that it is level like a chessboard, free from unevenness, smooth as the palm of a hand, with canopies spread above, draped with variegated cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, sprinkled and swept clean, and strewn with loose flowers. Have a bridge of boats constructed so that the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, may cross the Gaṅgā on his way to Vaiśālī."

"And at intervals of half a yojana, have pavilions prepared; have provisions of food and drink prepared; and have lodgings and seats prepared for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples.
Provide every kind of comfort so that the Blessed One, along with the community of disciples and the community of monks, may travel easily from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī."
"By means of the mind for the gods, by speech for kings,
not long [in time] for the wealthy, and by action for the poor."
The king gave the command, and the ministers attended to everything exactly as commanded.
The Blessed One set out together with the community of monks.

King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, accompanied by his chariots, cavalry, and infantry, together with his queens, princes, ministers, and retinue, followed the Blessed One as he was traveling toward Vaiśālī. With five hundred royal parasols being held aloft— adorned with hanging clusters of silk streamers and tassels, and featuring flags and banners— he proceeded with great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor, making a stop every half-yojana until he reached his own territory on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The Licchavis of Vaiśālī heard that King Śreṇika Bimbisāra was following the Blessed One with such a retinue as he was coming from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī.

And having heard this, they prepared the road from Vaiśālī as far as the Ganges Ferry— throughout this entire distance belonging to the Licchavis of Vaiśālī— making it level like a chessboard, free from unevenness, smooth as the palm of a hand,
sprinkled and swept, strewn with loose flowers, covered with canopies, encircled by variegated cloths, draped with bundles of hanging silk ribbons, and perfumed with incense.
In various places, they stationed actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, and musicians;

and at intervals of half a yojana, they had pavilions constructed, as well as arrangements for beds and seats, arrangements for drinking water, and arrangements for food, for the Blessed One and his community of disciples.

Having caused eighty-four thousand chariots to be harnessed from within Vaiśālī, and having caused another eighty-four thousand chariots to be harnessed, they were adorned with victory banners, accompanied by joyful sounds, and decorated with flower garlands.

Taking with them parasols, banners, and flags, as well as abundant perfumes and garlands, they mounted their respective auspicious vehicles and set out from the city of Vaiśālī with great royal majesty and great royal power.
