Amidst the clamor of a vast multitude of people and the sounding of *hakkāra* and *hikkāra* shouts, drums, kettledrums, cymbals, flutes, and conchs, they departed from the city of Vaiśālī and proceeded toward the bank of the Ganges to meet the Blessed One in order to pay him honor.
For them also, that very same kind of arrangement occurred.

There are Licchavis here with blue horses, blue chariots, blue reins and whips, blue staves, blue garments, blue ornaments, blue turbans, and blue parasols; they possess blue swords, jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans.
Regarding this, it is said as follows:
The horses are blue, the chariot is blue, and blue are the reins, the whip, and the turban;
the five crests are blue, as are the garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here with yellow horses, yellow chariots, yellow reins, whips, and staves; they wear yellow garments, yellow ornaments, yellow turbans, and yellow parasols, and possess yellow swords, jewels, and sandals.
In this regard, the following is said:
Her horses are yellow, her chariot is yellow, and yellow are her reins, whip, and turban;
her five humps are yellow, as are her garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here with crimson horses, crimson chariots, crimson whips and staves, crimson garments, crimson ornaments, crimson turbans, and crimson parasols; they have crimson jewel-encrusted sandals and fly-whisks.
Regarding this, it is said:
Mañjiṣṭhā, horses, chariots, Mañjiṣṭha, reins, whips, and staffs; Mañjiṣṭha, the five humps, Mañjiṣṭha, garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here with red horses, red chariots, red whips and staves, red garments, red ornaments, red turbans, and red parasols; they have red swords, red jewels, red sandals, and red yak-tail fans.
Regarding this, it is said:
The horses are red, and the chariots are red; the reins, the goads, and the staffs are red;
the five crests are red, as are the garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here with white horses, white chariots, and white whips and staves; they wear white garments, white ornaments, white turbans, white parasols, and white swords; their jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans are all white.
Regarding this, it is said:
They have white horses, a white chariot, and white reins, whips, and staffs;
their five humps are white, as are their garments and ornaments.
There are Licchavis here with green horses, green chariots, and green reins, whips, and staves; they wear green garments, green ornaments, green turbans, green parasols, and green swords;
they possess green jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans.
In this regard, the following is said:
The horses are green, the chariot is green, and the reins, whips, and staffs are green;
the five crests are green, as are the garments and ornaments.

There were Licchavis there with disheveled horses, disheveled chariots, disheveled reins, whips, and staves; with disheveled garments, disheveled ornaments, disheveled turbans, disheveled parasols, and disheveled swords;
and with disheveled jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans.
In this regard, the following is said:
The horses and chariots were separated; the reins, whips, and staves were separated;
the five humps were separated; and the garments and ornaments were separated.
There are Licchavis here with golden parasols and elephants adorned with various ornaments.
There are Licchavis here with golden palanquins adorned with every kind of jewel.
There are Licchavis here in golden chariots, equipped with victory banners, making joyful sounds, with hooves adorned with tinkling ornaments, and with umbrellas, flags, and pennants raised high.
With such power, by such means, with such an assembly, with such royal majesty, with such prosperity, and with such an array of ornaments,
the Licchavis of Vaiśālī— along with Gośṛṅgī and Āmrapālikā, as well as that great multitude of people— went out to meet the Blessed One as far as the Ganges ferry.

The Blessed One, on the further bank of the Gaṅgā, having instructed, inspired, and gladdened King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra and the Magadhan brahmins with a discourse on the Dharma, established eighty-four thousand of those Magadhan brahmins in the realization of the Dharma. Then, looking toward where the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were, he addressed the monks: "Monks, you have never before seen the Trāyastriṃśa gods as they depart from the city of Sudarśana for the pleasure gardens."
Behold now these Licchavis of Vaiśālī!
For what reason?
By such supernatural powers as these, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven depart from the city of Sudarśana to the pleasure gardens.
When flourishing kingdoms are being pacified, kinsmen govern them properly;
likewise, while he dwelt among these Licchavis, the Teacher made the gods his metaphor.
Those Trāyastriṃśa gods who had never before seen a procession going out to the pleasure groves—
such was their assembly as they witnessed this prosperity of the Licchavis.
Some Licchavis went out to meet him with golden parasols and elephants, others with palanquins made of gold,
and still others with chariots made of gold.
All of them, having gathered together with their kinsmen and relatives— young, middle-aged, and elderly—
adorned and wearing garments dyed with lac, went forth to meet him with various graceful movements.
Now, on that Gaṅgā, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra had a boat-bridge [constructed], as did the Vaiśālakas from within and the Vaiśālakas from without;
and a boat-bridge was also constructed by the Gāṅgeya nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara.
"The Blessed One will cross over by means of our [raft]."
At the word of Gośṛṅgī, Śuka invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal on the following day; and the Blessed One accepted this by remaining silent.
By means of his silence, the Blessed One signaled his acceptance; this was understood by that parrot through the power of the Buddha.
He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One and the community of monks, and returned.
Having approached the Blessed Lady Gośṛṅgī, he said:

The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, together with the community of disciples, was invited for a meal on the following day at your word; the Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One ascended the boat-bridge.
King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra saw the Blessed One on his own bridge of boats; the Vaiśālīans from within the city saw the Blessed One together with the community of disciples on their own bridge of boats;
and the Vaiśālīans from outside the city saw the Blessed One together with the community of disciples on their own bridge of boats.
The great nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, sons of Gaṅgā, also saw the Blessed One crossing over with the community of disciples upon their own bridge of boats.

When those Kambalāśvatara Gāṅgeyakas saw the five hundred parasols of King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, and also saw the five hundred parasols of the people of Vaiśālī, they held up five hundred parasols for the Blessed One as he was crossing.
The yakṣas also held up five hundred parasols.
The Four Great Kings also held up five hundred parasols;
the divine son Sunirmita likewise held up a parasol even more distinguished than those;
and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as well as the Four Great Kings, also held up five hundred parasols each.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven also held up five hundred parasols; Śakra, the lord of the gods, held up a parasol;
and the divine son Suyāma also held up a parasol.
Five hundred parasols were held aloft by the Tuṣita gods;
the divine son Saṃtuṣita held up a parasol even more distinguished than those.
Five hundred parasols were held aloft by the Brahmakāyika gods.
Mahābrahmā also held up a parasol even more distinguished than that.
By the Śuddhāvāsa deities, five hundred parasols were held up for the Blessed One as he was crossing the Gaṅgā.
By the divine son Maheśvara as well, a parasol was held up for the Blessed One as he was crossing the Gaṅgā.
By whom have all those thousands of parasols belonging to gods and humans been eclipsed?
These kings, born of royal lineages who perform their daily duties, are worthy [of this];
and this illustrious bull among men is indeed worthy of the parasol.
Those outsiders who, having conquered the hosts of enemies, enjoy an unconquered kingdom— even though they are not perfected— they too, O men, deserve the parasol.
How much more so for him who has completely conquered all afflictions without exception;
indeed, even Namuci with his host could not [overcome] the Blessed One, who is worthy of hundreds of parasols.
Taking five hundred parasols with handles of vaidūrya gem, whose radiance flickers like stars and whose forms do not appear within the sky;
King Bimbisāra followed behind the One Possessing the Ten Powers;
and the Blessed One set out toward the Vajjis together with his retinue.
The Blessed One, having boarded the boat, has crossed over the flood of existence;
and on the further shore, the Licchavi hosts held up five hundred parasols.

Then the Nāgas, dwellers of the great earth and possessors of great strength like the great mountains, as well as those whose abode is the sky, held up five hundred parasols over the Lord of the Earth.
Possessed of supernatural powers and radiance, dwelling upon the paths of the earth and abiding in great strength,
even the Yakṣas and Asuras there, filled with joy, held up five hundred parasols.
With flower garlands and pearls falling away, their faces as beautiful as the full moon of the lord of stars,
even the gods there, filled with joy, held up five hundred parasols.
The four world-protectors also, with joyful minds and free from intoxication and pride,
acting as sweepers of the dust of the stage, bore [the feet] of him who is equal to the upholder of the earth.
Then that lord of the thirty-three gods held over the head of the Conqueror a parasol made of a well-fashioned, excellent net of gold, gems, and jewels, and a well-fashioned garland of red flowers.
Having approached Yama, the lord of the Yāmas, who is worshipped by Yama, Varuṇa, and the Nāgas,
Vasuyāmā held the one as white as an autumnal water-cloud, who possesses the speed of wealth, wind, and thought.
Furthermore, the one dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven approached the Blessed One;
with a clear mind, he held a parasol, his body possessing a firm and even form.
Sunirmita held the parasol, its handle well-fashioned of beryl, variegated with a thousand ribs of coral,
and its surface strewn with blossoming flowers.

The Paranirmitavaśavartin [deity] fashioned a parasol for him whose fame pervades the three worlds— a parasol covered with a burden of excellent gold and adorned with hanging strings of jewel necklaces.
Brahmā, with a serene mind and a heart as pure as the wind-path,
held the moon-like parasol for him who crushes the arguments of opponents.
Furthermore, Maheśvara, the Lord of the Secret of the Parasol, held the parasol— a parasol made of the seven precious gems, adorned with garlands of divine flowers.
Thus this assembly of the realm of desire was convened by the Lord of the Gods;
it was vast, gathered by Maheśvara for the sake of honoring the one who possesses incomparable power.
As many as those parasols were, so many Buddhas were emanated by the Blessed One.
They do not see one another.
To each of them, this thought occurred individually:
Under my very parasol stands the Protector; the Sugata stands; the Banner stands.
By the power of the Buddha, both gods and humans see as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Then the Blessed One, the moon among men, manifested those perfectly awakened ones through his supernormal power;
the Blessed One displayed them, yet they did not see one another.
But the Buddhas endowed with the ten powers, having gone to the Akaniṣṭha realm,
beautify the clear sky as they dwell in the expanse of the heavens, like a sacrificial pillar adorned with jewels.
All are golden-colored; all are endowed with the thirty-two marks.
All resemble mountains of gold; for all, a web of light shines forth. All possess pleasing forms; for all, a web of light shines forth.
All possess immeasurable virtues; all produce supreme joy.
Having seen the surface of the sky adorned by those possessed of the ten powers, the gods and humans, their joy exceedingly great, raised a cry of "Ha! Ha! in exultation.
Filled with the sounds of clapping hands, shouts, and clamor, they approach;
from the sky, they release a fragrant cloud of excellent powdered incense.

Having seen such a miraculous display of the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) by the Blessed One, the gods paid great honor to the Blessed One with *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *karkārava* flowers, *mahākarkārava* flowers, *rocamāna* flowers, *mahārocamāna* flowers, *bhīṣma* flowers, *mahābhīṣma* flowers, *samantagandha* flowers, *mahāsamantagandha* flowers, *pāriyātraka* flowers, golden flowers, and silver flowers.

They scattered and strewed the Blessed One with silver flowers, sandalwood powder, aloeswood powder, and saffron powder; and with divine fragrant powders for sixty yojanas all around, a flood [of these] arose knee-deep.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, what is this? Is it the power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, or the power of the yakṣas, by which these thousands of parasols are now being held aloft by the gods, the nāgas, and the kings?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, this is the power of the Tathāgata’s former wholesome qualities.

If the Tathāgata had not awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then while wandering through saṃsāra, the Blessed One would have exercised as many universal monarchies as there are these parasols. Nevertheless, through the exhaustion of all merit and demerit, the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata will occur.
The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Vāgīśa:
"May it be inspired in you, Vāgīśa, to speak of the Tathāgata’s former connection.
"Very well, Blessed One," the venerable Vāgīśa replied to the Blessed One, and at that moment he spoke this verse:
In the past, there was a teacher, a brahmin free from fear from any quarter;
having abandoned birth, that brahmin was perfected in the holy life.
Having seen sentient beings suffering, afflicted by the nature of suffering,
you turned the wheel of Dharma and cast forth unsurpassed light.

Having set in motion the wheel of Dharma and having produced unsurpassed radiance, the perfectly awakened Great Seer, whose rebirth is exhausted, passed into final nirvana; his disciples, free from fear from any quarter, erected a stupa for him.
The supreme trainees, being well-disciplined, performed these acts for the sake of their renown.
The Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and Vaiśyas performed worship for the great Ṛṣi with dance,
instrumental music, and song, gathered together with various garlands.
The brahmin also reflected: "My father was a wise man;
what if I were now to have a parasol made, fashioned with jewels, beautiful and white?"
Having placed a stainless parasol upon the accumulated stūpa,
the father, shedding tears, paid homage to his son.
Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha, the brahmin passed away; such indeed is the natural law for all who are born.
Through that karma, for eighty cycles of dissolution and evolution, he does not encounter an unfortunate rebirth; this is the fruit of that parasol.
Then, among humans, ruling the kingdom according to Dharma,
you were a world-conqueror (cakravartin) on earth, victorious and possessed of great strength;
O Kṣatriya, the various provinces were your retinue.
He honored him alone, providing comfort by offering a white parasol.
Then, having passed away from there as well, you were reborn among the gods;
you became the foremost of the Maruts, honored by the hosts of deities.
Honored by the hosts of gods and established in the mantle of sovereignty, you dwell even now;
this is the fruit of that white parasol.
He was the supreme among the gods, and he was also the supreme among human beings;
everywhere he was the supreme among both gods and men.
Having been the most excellent among the gods and the most excellent among humans,
and having abandoned even that state upon arriving at your final existence,
you have become a perfectly awakened Buddha, O Seer, whose rebirth has been exhausted.
Thus, having directly known that path leading to the pacification of suffering—
the attainment of which brings an end to suffering— [he proceeds].
And regarding this, the Buddhas of the past and that heroic, majestic one—all were equal in virtue and wisdom; there is no difference between the Buddhas.
And those who are indeed the perfectly awakened ones from time to time— of this there is no doubt—
they all go to a happy destination, reaping the fruits of their own actions.
The Brahmin was possessed of vision, and I was his pupil;
urged by you, O Hero, I have called to mind my former birth.
It was exactly so, as you have spoken, O Lord of Speech:
I was indeed a brahmin at that time, and you were my pupil.
Being thus exhorted by me, you shall remember your former birth;
therefore, you should cause a banner, a flag, and a white parasol to be made.
One should also construct a railing around the stupas to the extent of five finger-breadths;
thus, the donor attains excellent, abundant, and virtuous merit.
And whatever other worship is performed for these [beings] with the Buddha in mind,
all of it becomes fruitful and productive, leading to the attainment of the deathless.
Indeed, I do not see any worship in this world equal to this, much less one superior to it;
for by worshipping another, you attain even greater merit.
Even if all the deities in this world were always to honor him with every kind of jewel, they could never repay him in such a way.

Thus, those of great fame and great compassion, who are compassionate and intent on the welfare of others, are indeed not easily seen; for the Perfectly Awakened Ones are as rare as the flower of the Udumbara tree.

Furthermore, those who speak my praise on account of my concentration, ethical discipline, wisdom, realization, renunciation, application, birth, and lineage— being of great renown and having performed meritorious deeds throughout various births— they become persons whose words are authoritative and who are worthy of being celebrated by many people.
By that very root of merit having been planted,
their physical covering becomes furthermore light and free from affliction.
Therefore, one should perform meritorious deeds as an accumulation for the future life;
for merit is the ultimate support for living beings in the world beyond.
The Blessed One, having crossed the Ganges, entered the boundary of Vaiśālī.
Those non-human beings have fled by the power of the Blessed One.

As the Blessed One was proceeding, Māra the Evil One caused the wandering mendicant named Kuṇḍala to manifest himself, covering with living creatures that entire road which had been prepared by the Licchavis— sprinkled, swept, and strewn with loose flowers.
As the Blessed One was traveling along that path, he said to him:
Turn back!
"The earth is covered with many living beings—small, large, and medium-sized.
When the Buddha walks upon this ground strewn with creatures, distress arises from his treading.
The Blessed One said: [271]...
The touch of the Tathāgatas is as gentle as the breeze that has just begun to blow;
for no harm can ever arise from the bodies of the supreme Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Without fear or malice toward living beings, the Blessed One proceeds without obstruction;
for all creatures, the Blessed One has created a sacrificial grove of lush green grass.
The Blessed One and the community of monks were seated;
those Licchavis questioned the Blessed One.
For whom did the Blessed One consent to stay at home tomorrow—the residents of Vaiśālī from within the city or those from outside?
The Blessed One said:
For indeed, Vāsiṣṭhas, the Tathāgata has not accepted [the invitation] of the inner Vaiśālakas, nor that of the outer Vaiśālakas.
A parrot named Gośṛṅgī, capable of human speech, was sent to the far bank of the Gaṅgā.
By him, in the name of Gośṛṅgī, the Tathāgata together with the community of disciples was invited for a meal on the following day.
The Tathāgata accepted the invitation.

Then those Licchavis, the inhabitants of Vaiśālī, eighty-four thousand kings, and the rest of the great multitude— powerful kṣatriyas and powerful householders— were filled with wonder, asking, "How does this parrot speak?"
The Blessed One said:
What is the wonder here that a parrot speaks with human speech to a female cow?
For even by other birds, O Vāsiṣṭha, sovereignty has been exercised.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great renown, a vast treasury, and a great army. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, teeming with many inhabitants, filled with happy subjects, free from violence and civil unrest, with thieves well-restrained, and perfected in its administration of justice.
His harem was extensive, yet he was childless.
The thought occurred to that king:
"How might I have a son?"
He hears [the report] from the ministers.

"In a hermitage on the slopes of the Himalayas dwell sages of great power who possess the five superknowledges and have attained the four meditative absorptions; they should be asked how a son might be born.
Those sages of great power will instruct you on how a son shall be born to Your Majesty."
Then the king, together with his harem, his princes, his ministers, and his army and vehicles, set out for the hermitage of those seers.
The king, together with his army, his mounts, and his harem, arrived at a place to stay on the intermediate road.
There he saw three birds emerging from the hollow of an *āmbalī* tree: an owl, a myna bird, and a female parrot.
Then, upon seeing him, curiosity arose in that king.
He commanded a man: "Go and find out what is there in this hollow."
Having climbed up, he gazes intently and sees three eggs.
He said:
"Your Majesty, there are three eggs.
The king said:
Bind them individually in separate containers and bring them down so that they do not spoil.
That man, having tied them separately in a bundle, brought them down unharmed.
The ministers are questioned.
Whose eggs are these?
The ministers said:
Indeed, these fowlers are questioned;
this is their domain.
The fowlers were summoned.
The fowlers were questioned by the king.
The king said:
"O, tell me, do you know whose eggs these are?"

There, those fowlers who roam about are experts in the methods regarding the eggs of all species of birds, and they are also experts in the methods concerning the birds themselves, knowing exactly what kind of bird each one is.
They said:
"Great King, these are three eggs: one belongs to an owl, the second to a myna bird, and the third to a female parrot.
The king said:
Are these eggs capable of hatching?
They said:
O Great King, these auspicious [threads] have been spun out, and they are unspoiled.
The king asks.
"What is the method for treating these eggs so that, when treated in this way, they may develop safely and successfully hatch?"
The fowlers said:
Your Majesty, the cotton that has been beaten out should be spread upon both supports.
In that case, these eggs should be smeared with honey and ghee and placed [there], covered on top with beaten cotton wool; this will nourish them for the sake of their mother.
Those eggs were deposited exactly as those fowlers had instructed.
The king reached that hermitage of the seers in due course.
Having stationed his army and vehicles in a secluded place, he approached the hermitage of the seers together with his harem.
Seeing the king, the sages went out to meet him according to the customary conduct of sages.
Welcome, Great King; you are most welcome, Great King. Please be seated, Great King, on these seats.
The king, together with his harem, having bowed at the feet of the sages, sat down.
The most eminent among the sages, the patriarch.
Having exchanged greetings with that king, he asks him:
"What purpose, Great King, do you have for [seeking] from the presence of the sages?"
The king said:
"My harem is extensive, yet I have no son; I am sonless. Please instruct me on how I might obtain a son."
The most eminent among the seers said:
"Great King, those three eggs which were brought down from that hollow of the *śambalī* tree—have them incubated; then sons will be born to you."

The king was amazed: "Noble indeed are these seers! They know even that which is called 'going'—namely, those three eggs which were caused to be brought down from such-and-such a hollow of the *śāmbalī* tree for them as they were dwelling here in this hermitage.
Noble indeed are these seers!"
Having paid homage at the feet of the seers, he set out once more for Vārāṇasī;
traveling by stages, he entered Vārāṇasī.
In due course of time, all three of those eggs were hatched.
From the first [egg] an owl chick was born, from the second a myna chick was born, and from the third a parrot chick was born.
By the king’s command, they are brought up and reared.
At that time, when they had all grown up, the three wise and intelligent ones engaged in conversation and discourse with one another using human speech and the language of men.
Then King Brahmadatta, having recognized their intellectual power, questioned them individually regarding the duties of a king.
And having known them, they give prophecies.
Having heard the prophecy concerning all three of them, King Brahmadatta became joyful.
In Vārāṇasī there was a powerful king named Brahmadatta.
That king had three sons, all of whom were wise:
the first was Kauśika, and the second was Śārika.
And the third was Śuka; all were of a wise nature.
Having ascertained their intellectual power, the king, the lord of men, was pleased and thought,
"I shall ask each of them individually in private about all the duties of kingship."
First I shall ask Kauśika; may it be well with you, O Śakunta!
Son, what do you consider to be the duty of one who governs a kingdom?
Kauśika said: "Ah, after a long time my father asks me about the duties of kings!
Well then, I shall explain them to you; listen with a one-pointed mind."
One should not fall under the power of anger, but rather one should restrain that anger;
for neither profit nor dharma comes to one who is angry, O King.
For when a king is free from anger, O lord of men, his wealth and his dharma flourish;
wisdom prevails everywhere for him, therefore he should restrain his anger.
275. Then, when a dispute has arisen, he should remain composed toward both parties;
having heard the statements of both, he should act in accordance with the Dharma.
O King, having heard the words of both [parties], you should act according to the Dharma, and not out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion.
That wise man does not suffer loss because he acts for the sake of his purpose;
O King, protecting his fame and renown, he seeks heaven.
Therefore, O King, having avoided unrighteousness, govern according to the duties of kings; O protector of the earth, by doing so you shall go there.
Do not indulge excessively in the pleasures that cause attachment;
for one who is intoxicated by sensual desires, the enemy is exceedingly powerful.
Then he should follow all the customs of the city;
thereafter, he should follow the customs of the countryside in accordance with dharma.
He should sustain the realm of city-dwellers and country-folk with virtues,
by the granting of wealth and goods, and by the performance of their necessary tasks.
Then one should win over the entire retinue with a gift of wealth; by the bestowal of enjoyments and goods, one becomes a person whose followers are indivisible.
O King, you know all— both those who are devoted and those who are disaffected—
among the vanguard of the army, the dependents, and the people of both the city and the countryside.
Having personally inspected the state of affairs, he should bestow rewards with joy;
avoiding violence toward all, he should assign the fruit of action according to the Dharma.
O King, act in such a way that you establish the vast multitude of people who have come from former kings within the realm according to their proper order.
O lord of men, always bestow favor upon the distressed and provide protection for the wealthy who dwell within your conquered realm.
A king who delights in gambling with wealth and is constantly devoted to the wives of others becomes disliked by his kingdom and quickly loses his life.
Furthermore, O dear one, he who is free from greed, wise, and always abstaining from the wives of others,
becomes beloved by the kingdom and lives for a very long time.
O King, do not form bonds of enmity with rival kings;
for when enemies, O protector of the earth, encounter one another, they only deliver their enmity back to each other.
And you, O King, should form alliances with neighboring kings;
for kings who possess firm friends honor their subjects as well.
O lord of men, in every matter, you should not speak in a confused or incoherent manner;
rather, you should utter mantras at the proper time, joined with their underlying reasons and causes.
O King, always maintain the secret meaning and keep it concealed; for when their counsel is leaked, O lord of kings, monarchs suffer great calamity.
By upholding a secret matter, one obtains vast glory;
one does not fall under the power of enemies, nor does one later feel regret.

O Lord of Men, those whose counsel is not confused and who are skilled in speech for the sake of accomplishing their purpose do not provoke anger in their enemies, just as a hundred-killer weapon does not provoke anger in those with jeweled horns.
The man who maintains the connection with the purpose of the Guhyakas remains like a servant to him out of fear of the enemy's dissension. 277.
O King, you should always provide protection for those established in the Dharma;
for it is by relying on the wheel of power that the wheel of Dharma turns.
By the power of those established in the Dharma, all calamities are pacified;
the gods rain according to the proper season, and the crops flourish there.
For the sake of benefit in this present life and for happiness in future lives—
such, O Great King, is the result of what is done for those who possess virtuous qualities.
Therefore, O King, you should protect that [dharma] through righteousness;
for it is beneficial to you as a king and it is also beneficial to the kingdom.
For she is a careful observer of all matters, O lord of men;
therefore, be vigilant in the production of grain in both the granary and the treasury.
This much is my meaningful instruction for you;
having grasped all of it, O King, act accordingly.
For you who practice in this way, fame and renown shall arise;
the kingdom will become secure, prosperous, flourishing, and densely populated.
Having heard Kauśika’s excellent speech, which is consistent with both dharma and artha, Śārika, I ask you likewise: explain the duties of kings to me.
The young sarika bird said:
"Ah, after a long time indeed, my dear son, you ask me about the duties of kings!
Well then, I shall explain them to you; listen with a one-pointed mind."
But by two things, my dear, this world is established:
the acquisition of wealth not yet obtained, and the preservation of what has been acquired.
Therefore, O lord of men, for the sake of acquiring wealth and for the protection of what has been acquired, you should exert firm effort in accordance with righteousness.
O King, that lord of the earth who rules by unrighteousness finds his kingdom weak and riddled with vulnerabilities on all sides.
And that lord of the earth, O King, who rules according to the Dharma—
his kingdom becomes stable, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with people.
Restrain those who deserve restraint; uplift those worthy of being uplifted; gather in those who should be gathered in; and be one who delights in bestowing favor.
That lord of people who does not know how to restrain, nor how to encourage, nor even how to gather and favor his subjects, falls away from his goals.

O King, let not your sons, nor your brothers— though they be brave, daring, and powerful lords in the village or the countryside— be deprived of favor by you for the sake of your mother and father. O Ruler of the Earth, grant them your grace.
For when heirs are treated with contempt, they become enemies who are driven to distraction.
Your kingdom shall consist of five realms served by crooked enemies;
do not place trust in them there, nor follow them onto the wrong path.
A kṣatriya who has set out upon a wrong path and follows his passions falls under the power of his enemies and later regrets it.
O Lord of Men, weigh carefully for the sake of attaining strength yourself, for the suppression of enemies,
and out of compassion for the kingdom;
having reflected, speak whether by night or by day.
For they stand listening nearby; having heard, they will act accordingly.
A hero is quickly turned back; a wealthy man gathers strength. One who controls wealth and possesses the power of counsel does not place his wealth in the hands of one who is angry.

Therefore, one should banish the Brahmin who acts for the sake of wealth, along with his sons and wife; likewise, the wealthy Vaiśya who possesses excellent mantras, even if he be of slender means, provided he is a rogue—banish that rogue.
O King, you should appoint as minister one who is wise, a thinker of state affairs,
free from greed, loyal, and a leader of the realm.
The kingdoms of those who possess ministers lacking in wisdom and devoid of discernment flourish only in suffering, along with their sovereign.
O King, through the brilliance of the wisdom of wise ministers,
the kingdoms flourish in happiness along with their sovereign.
A minister who is greedy and of little intelligence, O lord of men,
is of no benefit to the king, nor is he beneficial to the kingdom.
Therefore, O lord of men, one should appoint as the leader of the kingdom a minister who is free from greed, wise,
and devoted to counsel.
There is no eye equal to a spy, and there is no policy equal to spying;
therefore, a lord of men should employ spies in all his affairs.
O King, having fully encompassed all your attendants, the kingdom, the army, and those who depend upon you, consider what ought and ought not to be done, O Ruler of the Earth.
Therefore, O King, appoint a wise doorkeeper;
he shall exercise vigilance for you, which will bring you happiness.
This instruction of mine is so meaningful;
having grasped all of it, O King, act accordingly. 280.
For you who practice in this way, there will be fame and renown;
the kingdom will be secure, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with people.
Kauśika was also questioned by them, and being asked, they explained to me the duty of kings exactly as it is, just as you now ask me, O parrot.
O wise one who considers what is beneficial, how many kinds of power does a king possess?
Tell me, exactly as they are, the duties of a king that ought to be desired.
The parrot said:
O lord of men, a king should desire five kinds of power;
having focused your mind one-pointedly, listen to my words.
The first power is that which is innate; likewise, the second is the power of sons;
the third, O lord of men, is the power of kinsmen and friends;
and the fourth, O King, is the fourfold army.
And proclaim the fifth power, the unsurpassed power of wisdom. O lord of people, for whomever these five powers exist,
his kingdom becomes stable, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with inhabitants.
Furthermore, among these, the power of wisdom is supreme.
Through the power of wisdom, O lord of men, one discerns what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
one avoids what should not be done and carries out what should be done.
It brings happiness to oneself, to one's kinsmen and friends, and to the kingdom.
For even one of noble birth, O lord of men, if he lacks wisdom regarding the king's affairs, is of no benefit to the king nor is he dear to the realm;
rather, O King, his kingdom is swiftly destroyed by rival monarchs. 281.
And the dispassionate natures seek another master.
The wise man who considers his own welfare is highly honored;
he appoints as his leaders those who are excellent, brave, heroic, and discerning.
Having completely abandoned unrighteousness, he always practices the Dharma, thereby attaining fame in this world, as well as a heavenly rebirth in the world beyond.
Practice the Dharma toward your parents, O Great King, O Ruler;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, toward your children, your wife, and your subjects, O lord of men;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice righteousness, O Great King, toward your friends and ministers, O lord of men;
having practiced righteousness here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, toward recluses and likewise toward brahmins;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice righteousness, O Great King, both in the city and among the provinces;
having practiced righteousness here, the king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, in this world and in the next;
having practiced the Dharma here, the king shall go to heaven.
This instruction of mine is so meaningful;
having grasped all of it, O King, act accordingly.
For you who practice in this way, fame and renown shall arise;
the kingdom will become secure, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with people.
To them, the powerful King Brahmadatta spoke thus:
"O sons, you are all-pervading scholars, skillful and thinkers of statecraft."
I shall carry out the words of instruction for all of you;
I have seen what is for your welfare, both in this life and in the world to come, through the discourse on the Dharma.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One, the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
I was then Śuka and Śāriputra was Sārika;
Ānanda was Kauśika, and Brahmadatta was Śuddhodana.

Thus, free from fever, free from fear, and without sorrow, the Blessed One recounted this ancient account of his own birth— immeasurable, full of much suffering, and consisting of high and low deeds— in the midst of the community of monks.
Thus ends the Jātaka titled "The Three Birds" (*Triśakunīya*) in the glorious *Mahāvastu-avadāna*.
Then, having abandoned that existence as a parrot, the Bodhisattva became a prince and taught the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa kuśalāḥ karmapathāḥ*).
Ten masteries have been proclaimed by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun;
listen to me as I speak of them for the sake of the heroic Bodhisattvas.
The venerable ones are self-controlled and wise; likewise, they have attained mastery over eloquence, rebirth, karma, and the mind.
Mastery over the Dharma, as well as mastery over intention;
mastery over time and place—the steadfast one possesses these ten masteries. (283) Having established themselves in these ten masteries, the wise are fearless.
These bulls among men bring millions of beings to spiritual maturity.
The Bodhisattvas, the leaders, purify the Buddha-fields;
these Bodhisattvas are radiant and have attained great compassion.
At the conclusion of the Jātaka, eighty-four thousand living beings were there brought to maturity and attained realization of the Dharma.
When the Buddha, the Blessed One, stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings fled.
A great multitude of people, filled with joy, questioned the Blessed One.
Behold, Blessed One, how all the non-human beings fled as soon as the Blessed One stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī!
The Blessed One said:
What is so wonderful about this, O Vāsiṣṭhas, that when the Tathāgata, the supreme among gods who has attained perfect enlightenment, merely stepped across the boundary, all non-human beings fled?
On another occasion as well, when I was an ṛṣi entering the boundary of the city of Kampilla, all the non-human beings fled.
The Licchavikas said:
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Or at any other time as well, O Vāsiṣṭhas.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, in the kingdom of Pañcāla, in the city of Kampilla, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He was one who well-supported his retinue and was disposed toward generosity and sharing.

That kingdom of his, Kampilla, was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, and its inhabitants were happy; it was free from violence and civil unrest, thieves were well-restrained, and it was rich in commerce.

Now, King Brahmadatta had a son of the family priest named Rakṣita, who was of great renown, who lived by undertaking the ten paths of wholesome action, who saw the peril in sensual pleasures, who possessed wisdom regarding the means of escape, who was full of spiritual urgency, and whose intention was directed toward renunciation. Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he went to the Himalayas and went forth into the ascetic life of a seer.

Then, having established a hermitage there in the Himalayas and constructed huts of grass and leaves, he lived as an outsider subsisting on roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night; thus, he produced the four meditative absorptions and realized the five supernormal powers.

Now, that prince— who had attained the four dhyānas, possessed the five superknowledges, lived in accordance with the undertaking of the ten paths of wholesome action, and was a celibate practitioner— sat cross-legged in his own hermitage and touched both the lunar and solar disks with his hand; indeed,
that rishi of fierce austerity and great fortune held even the hosts of the Brahma-world under his command.
Once, in the great city of Kampilla and its surrounding countryside, a terrible non-human plague broke out.
Touched by that non-human affliction, many thousands of living beings met with misfortune and calamity.
Having seen that great danger in Kampilla, King Brahmadatta dispatched a messenger to the one protected in the Himalayas.
In Kampilla, such a non-human affliction has arisen that many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin.
"It would be well, Blessed One, if you would come to Kampilla out of compassion."
Having heard the swift message, the seer came from the Himalayas to Kampilla.
As that seer was crossing the boundary of Kampilla, all those non-human beings fled.
There in Kampilla, the seer performed a rite for well-being and taught the ten paths of wholesome action to eighty-four thousand living beings.
What kind of talk does that man engage in for an inconceivable length of time?
What is his wisdom, and what is his generosity?
How does he travel the path of happiness in this world and in the next? How is he protected? This, they say, is the way to well-being.

He who at all times disregards perfected deities, men, all kinsmen, and living beings, yet remains compassionate toward creatures and protected by a fierce, blazing [power]— him they call one who has attained well-being.
Or whoever should endure ill-spoken words, accepting them through the power of patience;
having heard harsh and unpleasant speech, being protected by forbearance—this they call a blessing.

He who endures ill-spoken words, those who are born as constant and affectionate friends— confident and non-deceptive— one who shares equally with such friends and always compassionately supports them with wealth, is protected among friends; that, they say, is true well-being.

He who, in the midst of kinsmen and in the midst of companions, always shines forth through virtue, wisdom, and self-mastery—he indeed is protected in the midst of kinsmen; that, they say, is true well-being.

In whom the king, the lord of the earth, has confidence, and who knows both truth and valor—he is incapable of harm here or in the past; he is protected in the midst of kings, and they call that his well-being.
That which is due to a state of moisture.

A mother is compassionate toward her offspring; she gives birth to one who is beautiful and virtuous, protected by the life of a householder. They say that this is a blessing. (286) Those who praise the Buddha with noble Dharma, remaining steadfast and providing him service—these are the virtuous ones.
Those who are learned, who have crossed over doubt, and who are liberated among the Arhats—of them they say that it is a blessing.

Those with serene minds who at the proper time give food, drink, Kāśī-silk, sandalwood, perfumes, and garlands to śramaṇas and brahmins, say that this is a blessing protected in the midst of the village. [They avoid] backbiting, lying, the wives of others, the taking of life, and likewise intoxicants.
"Abandoning this, you shall go to the heavenly realm; they say that being protected in the midst of the village is a blessing.

Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion the seer named Rakṣita was someone else. But you should not view it in this way. For what reason? [Because I myself was that seer named Rakṣita at that time and on that occasion.]"
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, I was the seer named Rakṣita.
And he who at that time and on that occasion was the king named Brahmadatta in the city of Kampilla—
verily, it should not be viewed in this way.
This King Śreṇika Bimbisāra was, at that time, a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Kalpilla.
Even then, when I had become a seer and was merely stepping upon the boundary of Kampilla, all the non-human beings fled;
and now too, as I am merely stepping upon the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings have fled.
Moreover, it was not only now that all the non-human beings fled as soon as I stepped across the boundary; on another occasion as well, they fled as soon as I stepped across the boundary.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king who ruled his realm—one who had performed meritorious deeds, who was illustrious, possessed of great strength, a great treasury, and many mounts, and who maintained a well-gathered retinue.
287. One whose nature is generosity and sharing.
For him, that city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with people and inhabitants.

Now that king had an elephant named Kṛtapuṇya, who was of great renown, great majesty, and great power; by the majesty and power of this elephant, Vārāṇasī and the kingdom of Kāśi became free from pestilence and free from calamity, such that even other villages and districts, whenever its boundary was entered, likewise became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
Once, in Mithilā, the city of Videha, a non-human plague broke out, and many thousands of living beings met with calamitous ruin.
They heard that the elephant-king of the King of Kāśi was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great renown, great majesty, and great power;
and that whichever village or city his boundary entered became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
Then that king of the Vaidehakas spoke to another brahmin.
Go to Vārāṇasī; that King of Kāśi is one who gives everything away and is by nature disposed toward generosity and sharing.
Inform him of this disposition of yours and request that noble elephant from him.
By that nāga having come here, every non-human affliction will be pacified.
Having heard the king's words, that brahmin reached Vārāṇasī by following the route in due order.
And a brahmin was entering Vārāṇasī.

And this King of Kāśi was departing from the city of Vārāṇasī toward the outskirts with great royal majesty and great royal splendor; and that noble elephant, adorned with all ornaments, covered with a golden net, and blazing with glory, went before him.
That brahmin, standing before the King of Kāśi, greeted him with cries of victory.
The king related to that brahmin all the non-human affliction that had occurred in Mithilā, as it had been reported by him to the King of Kāśi.
"Great King, out of compassion for Mithilā, please give this noble elephant."
The king was compassionate and devoted to the welfare of others.
He gave that noble elephant to the brahmin, adorned exactly as it was.
"I give this elephant to you, O brahmin—adorned, covered with a net of gold, noble, fit for a king, and a royal luxury—along with its charioteer.
Go wherever you wish."

Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that he who was the king in Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed thus. Why is that? It was indeed I myself who was the king in Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion.
This should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, this King Śreṇika Bimbisāra was the King of Kāśī.
Now, O Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that the king who was ruling in Mithilā at that time and on that occasion was someone else. [But he was not.]
This should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
This General Siṃha was, at that time and on that occasion, the king.
That other one is a brahmin; this Tomara is a Licchavi.
That elephant is something else entirely.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the king's elephant.
Even then, when I was a noble elephant, all the non-human beings fled from Mithilā;
and now too, as soon as I have stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings have fled.
Moreover, O Vāsiṣṭhas, it was not only now that all non-human beings fled when I stepped across the boundary;
on another occasion as well, when I was in the form of a bull, all non-human beings fled as soon as I stepped across the boundary.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, there was a king ruling in the city of Rājagṛha who was meritorious, illustrious, well-supported by his retinue, disposed toward giving and sharing, possessed of great strength, a great treasury, and a great army of transport animals. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, teeming with many inhabitants, and filled with happy folk; it was free from violence and civil unrest.
In which thieves are well-restrained and legal proceedings are properly conducted.
There, a non-human plague arose, and many thousands of living beings met with ruin and calamity through that non-human disease.
And among the kings of Aṅga, he was Ṛṣabha—gracious, handsome, meritorious, and of great renown.
By the power of his majesty, the entire region of his domain became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
The brahmins and householders of Rājagṛha heard it.
Such was this bull-like king of Aṅga—gracious, beautiful to behold, meritorious, and of great renown.
By the power and majesty of his splendor, the entire realm of Aṅga became free from calamity and devoid of affliction.
They informed the king.
"Great King, listen: such is this bull of the King of Aṅga—gracious, beautiful to behold, meritorious, renowned, and of great majesty.
Whatever village or city boundary he enters becomes free from calamity and free from affliction."
"Great King, bring forth Ṛṣabha; for by his being brought, the non-human plague in Rājagṛha will be pacified."
King Rājagṛhaka sent a brahmin to the King of Aṅga.
"Go, [and] having made the King of Aṅga aware of this danger in Rājagṛha, beg that bull [for me]."
Then that brahmin, having replied "So be it" to the king, traveled from Rājagṛha by stages until he arrived at the city of the King of Aṅga.
Having approached the King of Aṅga and greeted him with wishes for victory and prosperity, he reported the entire matter of the non-human affliction in Rājagṛha in detail and requested the bull.
And that king was both compassionate and intent upon benefiting others.
Having heard of that great danger facing the people of Rājagṛha, he gave that bull to the brahmin.
Go, brahmin; may all the people of Rājagṛha and all sentient beings be happy.
Taking that bull, the brahmin came from the region of Aṅga to the region of Magadha.

And immediately after, Vāsiṣṭhas, the boundary of Rājagṛha was overrun by Ṛṣabha, and all those non-human beings fled; thus the district of Rājagṛha became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
It may be, Vāsiṣṭhas, that you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the King of Aṅga in the city of Aṅga was someone else. But it should not be so viewed. [He was none other than me.]
Furthermore, it should certainly not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, this King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra was the King of Aṅga.
He who was the king in Rājagṛha at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
This should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
This is General Siṃha.
That brahmin from Rājagṛha who brought that bull at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
This should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason? 290.
Vasiṣṭha, this Licchavi Tomara was, at that time and on that occasion, the brahmin woman in Rājagṛha by whom the bull was brought from the presence of the King of Aṅga to Rājagṛha.
It may be, O Vāsiṣṭhas, that you might think that at that time, on that occasion, that bull was someone else; however, he was indeed King Saṃgara.
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, I was the bull of the King of Aṅga.

Even then, when I had become a bull and was merely treading upon the boundary of Rājagṛha, all the non-human beings fled; and now, as I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment and am merely treading upon the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings have fled.
Thus ends the Jātaka of Ṛṣabha in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
Then the Blessed One, proceeding by stages, arrived at Vaiśālī.
The Blessed One now performed a rite for well-being throughout Vaiśālī, both within and without,
and he recited the verses of well-being.

Homage be to the Buddha; homage be to Awakening; homage to Liberation; homage to Liberation! Homage be to Wisdom; homage be to the Knower; pay homage to the one who is the most excellent and supreme in the world!
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether of the earth or of the atmosphere,
let them all, being well-disposed, listen to this benediction spoken by the Jina.

Whatever exquisite jewel there may be in this world or in the next, or even in the heavens, there is nothing equal to the Tathāgata, the God among gods, the Supreme among men. This too is the exquisite jewel in the Buddha; by this truth, may there be well-being for humans and non-humans alike.
This too is a sublime jewel among the teachings; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
That which the Best of Buddhas has praised as pure, which they call the "uninterrupted" concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*)—there is no concentration equal to it.
This too is a sublime jewel among the teachings; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.

Those individuals who are always praised as the eight, namely these four pairs—they have been declared by the Sugata to be worthy of offerings; what is given to them yields great fruit. This too is a sublime jewel within the Saṅgha. By this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
For whomsoever there is the attainment of vision, three qualities are abandoned:
the view of a self-identity, doubt, and whatever constitutes the attachment to rules and rituals.
This too is a sublime jewel within the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Even if a trainee commits a transgression by body, speech, or even by mind, he is incapable of concealing it; such incapacity is said to exist for those who have seen the paths.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans and non-humans alike.

Just as a central pillar fixed in the earth would remain unshaken by the four winds, even so do I describe the true person who, having understood and seen the well-taught Noble Truths of profound meaning. This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be great well-being from humans or non-humans alike.
Those who analyze the Noble Truths well-taught by one of profound wisdom—even if they are exceedingly heedless—do not cling to the eight states of existence.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be great well-being from humans or from non-humans.

Those practitioners of yoga who, with a well-directed mind, are intent on renunciation within the teaching of Gautama—they have attained what was to be attained, having plunged into the deathless; with minds liberated, they enjoy the bliss of Nirvana.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha. By this truth, may there be great well-being from humans or from non-humans.

The old is exhausted, there is no accumulation of the new; they are liberated from future existence. With their seeds destroyed, subject to the nature of non-rebirth, those wise ones pass away like an oil lamp.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Just as a blazing fire that has arisen with great force subsides upon the exhaustion of its fuel,
so too do the sons of the Buddha who practice meditation, having grasped the latent tendency of passion through wisdom, go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
This, too, is a sublime jewel within the Saṅgha, whether from among humans or non-humans.

In the first month of summer, Caitra, in the forest, the flowering shrubs with their tips in bloom waft a fragrance when stirred by the wind. In this same way, the sons of the Buddha who meditate and are endowed with virtue waft a fragrance.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether of the earth or of the atmosphere, may they always show loving-kindness toward human beings; day and night, they shall bring you offerings.
Therefore, protect him with vigilance, just as a mother protects her son out of compassion.
By this truth, may there be well-being for you from humans or from non-humans.
In Vipaśyin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Bhāmaka, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa of great fame, and Śākyamuni Gautama—
in these Buddhas of great supernatural power, whatever deities there are who have placed their faith,
may they indeed protect that [person] and grant well-being to the human race.
Therefore, protect it with heedfulness, just as a mother protects her son out of compassion.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
I pay homage to the Buddha, the most excellent among gods and humans, who outshines the world by turning the Wheel of Dharma out of compassion for all living beings; may there be well-being.
I pay homage to the Dharma; may there be well-being. I pay homage to the Saṅgha; may there be well-being from both humans and non-humans.
After Gośṛṅgī had provided a meal for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, she offered him the Śāla grove;
this was what occurred regarding the Licchavis.

Each one of us is capable of attending upon the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for as long as life lasts, providing robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Nevertheless, let it be done in such a way that the great multitude may be endowed with merit.
Let the grain of humanity be harvested.
By them, a human-sized grain of rice was carried away, or twenty-five more varieties of rice were [carried away].
In this way, they attended upon the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for seven days.
They attend upon the Blessed One— the illustrious, the great lord, the beautiful, and the renowned— just as hosts of stars surround the moon;
they are adorned with yellow ornaments and garments, like blossoming *karṇikāra* trees.
They attend upon the Perfectly Awakened One, wearing thick armlets,
their limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood, and clad in the finest garments of Kāśī.
The Buddha surpasses with his splendor that entire assembly of gods who have gathered together— pure, well-born, and marked by a hundred merits—
just as the king of stars outshines the constellations.
Just as the moon, the maker of light for the hosts of stars, shines resplendent in a cloudless sky,
so does the Buddha surpass all these snowy kings of the kṣatriya lineage with his supreme glory.
Just as the sun prevails in the atmosphere, shining while stationed upon the path of the sun,
even so does the Buddha surpass all those snowy-clad Kṣatriya rulers with his splendor.
Just as the sun blazes in the atmosphere, shining while stationed upon the path of the sun.
In this way, the Buddha surpasses all these snowy mountain-dwelling Kṣatriya rulers with his splendor.
Just as a well-born *kokanada* lotus, radiant, in full bloom, and endowed with fragrance—

so too does the Buddha surpass all these Kṣatriya rulers of the earth with his splendor. Just as the thousand-eyed Śakra, the crusher of the hosts of Asuras, shines among the Thirty-three gods, so too does the Buddha surpass all these Kṣatriya rulers of the earth with his splendor.
Just as Brahmā, out of compassion for all beings, outshines the radiance of all the gods with his splendor,
so too does the Buddha outshine all these kṣatriya rulers of the earth with his splendor.
Having then realized that pure glory endowed with the ten powers and the grace of the deathless,
I have disciplined these Kṣatriya rulers of the earth and displayed this Dharma as if it were in the palm of my hand.
Thus was the Blessed One praised by the Venerable Ānanda.
The Blessed One, having instructed, inspired, and gladdened the Licchavis of Vaiśālī with a discourse on the Dharma, led many hundreds of thousands of living beings to spiritual maturity.
This is the expression of appreciation for the gift and religious offering given by the Licchavis of Vaiśālī.
Just as those honey-bees, having gathered together and taken various kinds of flower nectar, collect it with their mouths and feet; |||||||||
When the collection of conditions for flavor and fragrance arises, that which is spread out becomes excellent honey;
endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, it enters into medicinal foods.
In the same way, when a great person has arrived in a village or a town,
the men and women, along with their sons and wives, become of one mind regarding virtuous deeds.
Having gathered together, they give drink; they provide meals and rice-gruel for the Saṅgha.
They offer drinks, excellent hard foods, and flavors approved by the Noble Ones.
Having offered for a long time, according to their faith and according to their power,
with a mind full of serene confidence again and again, the heap of merit continues to accumulate.
The great multitude, being joyful, performs merit by greeting with salutation and the gesture of joined palms, rising from their seats for them, attending to their needs, and rejoicing in the Dharma.
Having given gifts and performed meritorious deeds, whether by means of speech or by means of mental resolve,
they all, through that very commonality of karma, go to the heavenly realm.
Endowed with divine forms, they sport together with throngs of apsarases;
consuming abundant food and the finest drinks, they take delight, having ascended to the most excellent celestial palaces.
And when they come to the world of men, all of them are born into wealthy families—
prosperous, flourishing, and very rich, crowded with many women and men.
This honey has been prepared, praised by the virtuous, bringing happiness through all flowers.
Whatever purpose was sought in the mind, may it all be accomplished according to one's wish.
Having attained every goal, may you reach Nirvana, which destroys all conditioned phenomena and afflictions.
The Great Lord, the benefactor of the world, praised him along with his sons, wife, kinsmen, and relatives.
Then those Licchavis said to the Blessed One:
"Lord, this great grove of ours among our gardens— namely, the Mahāvana together with its hall and gabled pavilion—
we give it and offer it to the Blessed One and his community of disciples."
The Blessed One then addressed the monks.
Therefore, monks, I authorize [the use of] it for the sake of a monastery, for the sake of a dwelling, and for the sake of a building.
The Blessed One has now come from the Great Forest to the Cāpāla Shrine.
The Licchavis ask about his age.
Where is the Blessed One?
The monks said.
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, this Blessed One has gone from Mahāvana to the Cāpāla shrine for his midday rest.
Then those Licchavis said:
We offer the Cāpāla shrine of the Blessed One, together with his community of disciples.

At a later time, the Licchavis came to the Great Forest to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One; meanwhile, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, went to the Saptāmra Shrine for his midday rest.
The Licchavis asked the monks.
"Noble lady, where is the Blessed One?"
The monks said.
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, this Blessed One, having finished his meal, has gone toward the Saptāmra-cetiya for his midday rest."
Then those Licchavis, having approached the Saptāmra-cetiya and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows.
"Venerable sir, we offer the Saptāmra-cetiya to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples."
Likewise [are] the Bahuputracetiya, the Gautamaka Cetiya, and the Kapinahya Cetiya.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, departed from the great forest and approached the Markaṭahradatīra Caitya for his midday rest.
The Licchavis have come to the Great Forest to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
They ask the monks.
"Noble lady, where is the Blessed One?"
The monks said.
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, this Blessed One, having finished his meal, has gone to the bank of the Markaṭahrada for his midday rest."
Then, having approached the Markaṭahradatīra Caitya and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they said this to the Blessed One:
We offer this Dema Markaṭahradatīra Caitya to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples.
After Āmrapālī had provided a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, she offered the mango grove to him.
Having prepared a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, Bālikā offered her own skin.
Thus ends the Chapter on the Parasol in the *Śrī-Mahāvastu-Avadāna*.

Now, may the excellent community of the Dharma-king of immeasurable glory— the protector of the ninefold treasury of the teaching— endure for a long time, preeminent in splendor and immovable like Mount Sumeru.
In the absence of the appearance of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world.
Silent and beautiful, of great majesty, wandering alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, they tame themselves alone and attain parinirvāṇa.

Now, another Pratyekabuddha entered a village for alms in the Kāśī lands during the forenoon. He was graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his drawing in and stretching out [his limbs], and in his carrying of the outer robe, bowl, and robes. Like an elephant who has performed its task, with senses withdrawn within and mind not turned outward, established in the attainment of the nature of reality (dharmatā), he gazed only a yoke’s length ahead.
And a village headman, pleasing to look upon and inspiring faith in gods and men, was rushing out from the village toward the forest to inspect his work.
Having walked for alms through that village from end to end, the Pratyekabuddha departed from that village with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
The time for alms is nearly at hand, yet no one has given any alms.
Having inspected the worksites, the village headman re-entered the village and saw that pratyekabuddha departing from the village.
The thought occurs to him:
The time for alms is almost upon us;
I shall see what kind of alms have been obtained by this renunciant.
The village headman approached the Pratyekabuddha and asked:
"Noble sir, alms have been obtained."
The Pratyekabuddha, beautiful in his silence, showed the empty bowl to the village headman.
Seeing the Pratyekabuddha’s empty bowl, the village headman said to him:

"How can people who are so lacking in the habit of sharing eat while inflaming their greed, when such a worthy recipient of offerings is departing from this great village with his bowl as clean as when it was washed?
he said.
"Venerable One, please come; I shall give you food."
Having taken that Pratyekabuddha, he entered that village.
Standing at the crossroads of the four great paths, he cries out, "Help! Help! in distress.
Hearing the sound of "Avidha! Avidhanti! from the village headman who was stationed there, the entire village, including its women and men, assembled.
Having approached the village headman, they ask him.
"What is security? Why do you cry out, 'What is not a calamity, what is not a calamity'?"
The village headman said:

I lament this, because these people do not delight in sharing nor have they the habit of sharing, since from such a large village as this, a single monk departs with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
Then those elders in the village, having heard that from the village headman, thought that they should honor that Pratyekabuddha.
The village headman, having invited the Pratyekabuddha into his home and honored him with food, invited him for as long as he lived.
I invite the Noble One for as long as life lasts, with every provision for comfort.
She was her own daughter, recognized by herself.
In this way, you shall serve that noble one with food for that day.
The girl became joyful and satisfied.
A beautiful and auspicious deed has been performed by me.
Now she attended upon that pratyekabuddha daily with food; she was pleasing to the sight, and gods and humans were full of faith toward her.
The Pratyekabuddha, who has fully understood food and whose impurities have all been exhausted, is one of great fortune.
Then, upon seeing that conduct of the Pratyekabuddha, a noble faith arose in the daughter of that village headman;
likewise, other people also became inspired with faith.
Then that Pratyekabuddha, through his faith in that village headman, attained final nirvana right there in that village field, without further clinging.
Then the village headman, having cremated that pratyekabuddha, constructed a stūpa that was neither too small nor too large, and was coated with plaster and clay.
Then that village headman’s daughter daily worshipped that stūpa with a bronze vessel, using perfumes, garlands, and incense.
Afterwards, from that stūpa, those various kinds of garlands were blown away by the wind.
Then, having compressed that garland, she, together with her maidservants, fashioned a long, thick, and densely packed wreath composed of various flowers.
There, that garland completely encircled the entire stūpa of that pratyekabuddha.

Having seen that garland remaining there upon the stūpa— standing there, outshining all other forms and splendors, beautiful, and having exhausted its divine lifespan among the gods— an exceeding clarity of mind arose in her.
Then, with a serene mind, she made this aspiration:
"May such a garland as this one shines here upon this stūpa appear upon my head in whatever place I may be reborn."

Having performed that wholesome deed, she passed away from there and was reborn among the gods, adorned with a garland of jewels. Once reborn there, she was attended by a retinue of a hundred thousand apsarases.
Passing away from there as well, she was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Kṛkī in Vārāṇasī.
After the lapse of nine or ten months, a daughter was born to the queen; she was gracious and beautiful, adorned with a garland of jewels.
She was given the name Mālinī.
The girl was dear and pleasing to King Kṛkī, as well as esteemed by his entire retinue; she was a maiden of such merit that she was beloved throughout the whole city.
A pratyekabuddha should enter a village for alms;
then, with his bowl as clean as when it was washed, he should depart from that village.
Seeing him, the enlightened one, the village headman said this: "Is the Blessed One free from illness? May he obtain alms for his sustenance?"
Then, O Blessed One, he extended his bowl toward the village headman;
yet, not seeing any almsfood there, the village headman became despondent.
This world is blinded, perpetually struck by wrong views;
they do not honor such a worthy recipient of offerings as is fitting.
Having approached the edge of the village and standing at the crossroads, he cries out, "Avidhāvidha! and then the people gather together.
The great multitude, both women and men, having assembled together, approached the village headman and asked, "What shall we do? What is the proper course of action?"
The village headman said:
Surely it must be that among you there is no person who delights in sharing,
for this one bhikkhu here is being tormented alone in this village.
Having heard the words of the village headman, the entire village, together with the women,
repeatedly performed acts of hospitality toward the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then the village headman, together with his wife and his son, addressed him:
"I invite the Tathāgata to dwell in every comfort."
The village headman’s own daughter, dressed in pure garments and fragrant perfumes,
endowed with proper conduct and virtues, attended upon the Tathāgata.
Through the favor of the village headman, in that very village,
the perfectly awakened one, the sage of noble vows whose rebirth is exhausted, attained final nirvana.
Having meditated upon him as having attained parinirvāṇa, the village headman had a stūpa constructed;
he performed worship for the Great Seer with dance, instrumental music, and song.
Having gathered white flowers blown by the wind,
one should collect them into a single heap and fashion them into a long garland.
Just as that variegated garland was placed upon me right there,
may such a garland as this be upon my head.
Wherever I may be reborn here, may this [vow] be fulfilled there.
Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha,
she was reborn as an apsaras among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Placing a hundred thousand *apsarases* before her, she stood there;
she was the most excellent and supreme among them, a woman beautiful in every limb.

305. Then, having passed away from there, those highly powerful celestial maidens were reborn in the womb of King Kṛkī’s wife. When twelve months had elapsed, the king’s wife gave birth to a woman named Mālinī, beautiful in all her limbs.
She was of surpassing complexion and exceeding beauty;
she was the most excellent among princesses, the daughter of the King of Kāśi.
Endowed with the virtues of proper conduct, wearing clean garments and fragrant perfumes,
she stood before King Kṛkī with her palms joined in reverence.
Then the king spoke to her as she stood with palms joined in reverence:
"O blessed lady, you must diligently cause the brahmins to eat for my sake."
Having heard her father’s words, Mālinī fed twenty thousand Brahmins without omission, providing them with all their desires. When those Brahmins beheld Mālinī, who resembled an Apsaras, they said:
And with their minds swallowed by passion, they prattle on once again.
Seeing her agitated, haughty, fickle, and with unrestrained senses, Mālinī reflected: "These are not worthy of a sacrificial gift."
Having ascended the palace, she looked all around and saw a disciple of the Blessed One, the glorious Fully Awakened One.
Having gone to the excellent palace, anointed with the finest sandalwood from Kāśī,
the daughter of King Kṛkī gazed out toward all directions.
She saw.
Behold the disciples of the Buddha entering with serene composure and self-control— those who have cast out all evil and for whom this is their final body.
She sent a maidservant with these words: "Go and offer salutations to these seers;
having saluted them, say: 'Enter, venerable sirs, and be seated.'"
That female slave, having approached and bowed at the feet of those of cultivated self, spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Enter, O Venerable Ones; please be seated."
Having transcended passion, confident and the foremost sages in the world,
the disciples of the Buddha have cast out evil and possess their final bodies.
They entered the king’s inner apartments— which were white, well-constructed, with beautiful gateways, and guarded by swordsmen and shield-bearers— to see the daughter of their lord.
He sat upon a seat that was spread with a Kāśika cloth, adorned with various colorful bundles, variegated with jewels, and strewn with diverse flowers.
Like a lotus of auspicious luster, like a water-born flower unsullied by water,
so should one sit there with an unsullied mind, free from delusion.
She offers with her own hand the method for preparing rice from fine *śāli* grains, accompanied by various seasonings at the proper time, just as it pleases the Venerable Ones.
Those monks said: "The Teacher is the foremost wise one in the world;
let that great hero eat his first meal."
Having heard the report "Buddha," a sound never before heard in the world, she felt even greater faith, thinking: "He is indeed more distinguished than these."
That Mālinī said: "Having eaten, take the food for the Teacher;
and offer my salutation in my name to the Lord of the World."
The Blessed One consented to the meal together with the community of monks,
in the midst of the inner apartments of the king, for the sake of the king’s daughter, who was pleasing to him.
Then those two foremost disciples of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, Tiṣya and Bhāradvāja, having finished their meal at Mālinī’s house and taken the meal for the Blessed One Kāśyapa, set out for Ṛṣivadana.
Having presented the alms-bowl to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, they paid homage to the Blessed One Kāśyapa on behalf of Mālinī.

“Lord, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, the daughter of the king, pays homage to the Blessed One and inquires after his health, along with the community of disciples. She invites the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, for a meal tomorrow;
may the Blessed One, out of compassion, accept her invitation in the inner apartments of King Kṛkī.”
The Blessed One Kāśyapa consented out of consideration for those who were to be converted.
Those men who had gone with those great disciples, having taken up the instruction of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, went and informed Mālinī.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa accepted the invitation for tomorrow’s meal together with the community of monks.
Having heard this from those men, Mālinī prepared a great quantity of solid and soft food that very night, and announced that the time had come for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
The Blessed One knows the right time, knows the proper occasion, knows the right moment, knows individuals, and knows the superior and inferior qualities of individuals.
