Having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, when the time for wandering had arrived and the morning meal was being consumed in Māgadha, he entered the city of Vārāṇasī together with twenty thousand bhikṣus.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, enter the city like a flight of swans.
On the right side is the great śrāvaka Tiṣya;
on the left side is the great śrāvaka Bhāradvāja.
Behind them were four great śrāvakas; for every four there were eight, for every eight sixteen, for every sixteen thirty-two, and for every thirty-two sixty-four.
Thus, the Blessed One, preceded by twenty thousand bhikṣus, entered the inner apartments of King Kṛkī.
As the Blessed One was entering the city, the sunken ground rose up and the surface of the earth became level and well-settled.
Impurities, stones, pebbles, and gravel sank into the earth, and the ground was strewn with loose flowers.
Trees laden with flowers blossomed, and trees laden with fruit bore fruit.

On that path, to the left and to the right, there will be ponds and lotus-pools filled with cool water, covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lilies, white lotuses, water-lilies, and fragrant flowers;
from the mouths of their wells, water flows forth.
Horses will neigh, bulls will bellow, and noble elephants will let out their trumpeting cries.
Immediately, he stepped over the threshold with his foot, and the entire city trembled.

The blind saw light, the deaf heard sound, the insane regained their mindfulness, the sick were freed from their ailments, pregnant women gave birth without disease, and for those who were naked, garments appeared.
The bonds of those bound in fetters burst asunder; jewels enclosed in boxes and caskets clinked together, and vessels rang out.
Whatever lutes, harps, flutes, vīṇās, mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, and paṇavas there are in the city, even those that are unstruck and unplayed upon resound of their own accord;
and parrots, mainas, cuckoos, swans, and peacocks utter their respective cries.

He walks without touching the ground by a distance of four finger-breadths, and upon the surface of the earth, wheel-marks appear with a thousand spokes, hubs, and all characteristics complete; and in the sky, the gods play thousands of divine musical instruments and rain down showers of celestial flowers.
The Blessed One Kaśyapa, together with his community of disciples, having been honored by gods and humans with such wisdom, such splendor, such a gathering, such supernatural power, and such majesty,
entered the inner apartments of King Kṛkī along with his community of disciples.

The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, was served there in the inner four-hall residence with great honor, provided with abundant solid food and soft food that was straight-tasting,
of excellent taste, of unaltered taste, and of fresh taste.

The Blessed One, having finished his meal together with the community of disciples, having washed his hands and set aside his bowl, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Mālinī with a discourse on the Dharma; then, rising from his seat, he departed.
Those twenty thousand brahmins who were the regular guests of Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, became incensed because the Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with his community of disciples,
had been served in the royal palace with great hospitality and great honor by Mālinī.
By them, the entire assembly of brahmins was convened, consisting of many thousands of brahmins.
At that time, at that period, the earth was overrun by brahmins.
Having assembled, they were desirous of having Mālinī killed.
This very woman has arisen here in the royal household as a thorn to the brahmins.

King Kṛkī is devoted to the brahmins, and twenty thousand brahmins eat his daily meal; she was appointed by her father to serve these brahmins with the instruction: "Feed these brahmins their daily meal."
"Having shown contempt for these brahmins, she has caused these śramaṇas to enter the royal palace and has offered them such honor and hospitality.
She is diverting to the śramaṇas for the sake of honor and hospitality that which was intended as a livelihood for the brahmins from the royal family, thinking, 'I am showing them respect.'"
Those brahmins made this resolution: "Mālinī must be killed," while Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, had gone out to inspect his realm.
Those brahmins sent a messenger to King Kṛkī.
Such a lack of respect for the brahmins has arisen in Mālinī;
although the community of Kāśyapa’s disciples was introduced into the royal palace and such honor and hospitality were shown to them, she does not even grant an audience to the brahmins.
She does not act in accordance with what was commanded by the Great King.
Let twenty thousand Brahmins go daily to the royal palace; yet even that does not suffice, for Mālinī does not grant an audience even to the Brahmins.
As soon as the king heard this, he came from the countryside to Vārāṇasī and saw many thousands of brahmins assembled together.
He went straight to where the brahmins were.
The brahmins also went out to meet the king, and having congratulated him with cries of victory, they reported all this matter concerning Mālinī to King Kṛkī:
"Great King, this Mālinī has arisen as a thorn to the brahmins; it is not possible for the brahmins to accept the king's constant offerings as long as Mālinī is not put to death.
This is the resolution that has arisen among the entire assembly of brahmins."
The king also [spoke] to the brahmin women: "This conduct of the brahmin assembly must be followed.
If you have not abandoned your status as brahmin women, then abandon Mālinī."
If you have not abandoned Mālinī, you possess no brahminhood.
As the king was engaged in the ritual duties of the assembly of brahmins, this thought occurred to him:
"This earth is overrun by brahmins and teeming with many brahmins.
If I do not abandon Mālinī, there will be a riot."
Mālinī shall not be thus, nor shall I be thus.
One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon a family for the sake of the village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of the country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the self.
Then the King of Kāśi abandoned Mālinī,
so that her desire might be fulfilled in the assembly of brahmins.
Then those brahmins said:
If Mālinī has been abandoned, let her be summoned by the king.
Then, while standing outside the city at the residence of the brahmins, he sent a messenger with the message:
"Come, bring Mālinī here!"
By the king's command, the messenger arrived at the royal palace.
"Come, Mālinī! You have been abandoned by your father to the brahmins;
you are to be deprived of life by the brahmins.
When Mālinī heard this, she raised a cry, and the entire harem let out a wail.
Because of that sound of wailing, all the people in the city were filled with longing and became distraught;
there was a great cry of lamentation.
311. Mālinī will be sent by messenger from Vārāṇasī to her father’s presence.
She was then sent away by the messengers and brought to her father;
this, O Great King, is Mālinī.
With a throat choked with tears and a weeping face, the king gave Mālinī to the great multitude of brahmins; she was relinquished by him to his father.
Then, at the time when Mālinī was abandoned by her father, she became an obedient servant to the brahmins.
Then Mālinī, with her hands joined in reverence, prostrated herself before the assembly of brahmins.
I desire one formal proposal, if the assembly of brahmins deems it authoritative.
They said.
Speak whatever petition you have.
He said:
I was abandoned by my father to the brahmins; I have now come under your power.
In the assembly of brahmins, it was likewise resolved that Mālinī must be put to death.
Therefore, I wish to live for seven days right here in the presence of this assembly of brahmins, so that I may give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
I have performed services for the brahmins, and by my father’s command, I have also had the brahmins served.
"Therefore, after the passing of seven days, you must either kill me or do whatever you deem fit.
This thought arose in those leading brahmins.
It is exactly as Mālinī says; for a long time she has served the brahmins at her father’s command and fed them.
But later, an evil thought arose in her, whereby she became devoted to the ascetics.
Therefore, she has not been released to give further gifts to the ascetics; instead, she will give alms to those very brahmins for seven nights.
Let this request be granted to her; let her be released for seven nights, for after the passing of seven days, I shall kill her.
For this reason, that which has been decided upon by the assembly of brahmins must be carried out while Mālinī is still alive.
A request was made to her by those brahmins.
Having been set aside for seven nights by a great multitude of people, one should remain heedful in the presence of the brahmins so that it is not lost even during those seven nights.
Now, although she had been dismissed, she surely entered the royal palace again, surrounded by a great multitude of people, and made her request to her father.
I wish to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds for these seven days, according to my intention.
The king said:
"Let it be so; perform, daughter, the meritorious deed according to your wish."
She said:
I shall provide food for seven days here in the royal palace for the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, together with his community of disciples.
The king said:
Rejoice!
The Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with the community of his disciples, was invited by the royal family for a meal for seven days.
Out of compassion, and out of consideration for those to be trained, the Blessed One Kāśyapa consented, thinking that a great multitude of people would come to be disciplined.
Those brahmins, being greatly incensed, desired to kill her while she was still alive.
Mālinī, with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Forgive me for seven days while I give gifts."
O Brahmins, you may give as you wish.
On that first day, she had the Teacher, together with his assembly, fed in the midst of the inner apartments, while her mother and father were present.
And the Teacher spoke a discourse that inspires confidence.
And the king, together with his harem, realizes the Dharma that is free from hindrances.
On the second day, he disciplined five hundred sons.
And on the third day, there was that which was their retinue.
On the fourth day, the Perfectly Awakened One instructed the king’s ministers.
And in the fifth watch, the Teacher established that foremost assembly in the first fruit.
On the sixth day, the Perfectly Awakened One instructed the royal preceptor.
And in the seventh [year], he established the Nigamas and the fruit of stream-entry within the Vinaya.
The king also, with a joyful heart, having seen the Perfectly Awakened One together with his assembly, invited the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the foremost meal.
On the seventh day, Mālinī, having learned that the Blessed One Kāśyapa had finished his meal and had set aside his bowl, formed a solemn aspiration.
"Without delay I shall bring an end to suffering;
may I have such a son as this Blessed One Kāśyapa, who practices for the welfare of gods and humans."
In this way, may my son, having realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment, practice the conduct that benefits gods and humans.
"Do not be negligent, O brother! There is a youth named Aniyavanta;
by him too a vow has been made."
"May my father be such as this Blessed One Kāśyapa is now;
and there may I bring an end to suffering."

Thus, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, King Kṛkī of Kāśi together with his harem, five hundred princes, the ministers, the chief of the army, and for the most part the entire body of merchants, were all disciplined in the noble dharmas;
and this thought occurred to them:
Our spiritual friend Mālinī, having come to us, has purified our Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
yet the brahmins will deprive her of life.
"Perhaps we might even sacrifice ourselves, but not Mālinī."
They sent a message to those brahmins.
"We have come here together with Mālinī; Mālinī is our spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). You are not capable of depriving Mālinī of life by means of people such as us."
When we are all gone, you will be able to deprive that Mālinī of her life.
Then, together with their retinues and their armies and vehicles, they set Mālinī at their head, departed from Vārāṇasī, and proceeded toward where those thousands of brahmins were.
Seeing that infinite army approaching together with Mālinī, those brahmins were afraid and terrified.
They dispatched a messenger to the king.
Let Mālinī go forth and be released on that very day; let her for whom the punishment has been lifted be granted light by her father, and let her have the punishment removed.
"This Mālinī has not offended us;
it is Kāśyapa together with his retinue who has offended us, and we shall inflict punishment upon him."

Then ten men, equipped with armor and joined in groups of a thousand, were dispatched by them to Ṛṣivadana with the command: "Deprive the ascetic Kāśyapa and his community of disciples of their lives.
They were embraced by the Blessed One Kāśyapa with loving-kindness and established in the noble dharmas.
Those brahmins then dispatched another twenty men, equipped with armor, saying: "Deprive the ascetic Kāśyapa of his life."
Those men, equipped with armor and weapons, went to the hermitage of the sage.
The Blessed One, having suffused them with loving-kindness, established them in the noble Dharma.
In this way, thirty, forty, and fifty—however many were sent—were all expanded by the Blessed One Kāśyapa through loving-kindness and established in the noble dharmas.
This is the summoning of the Buddhas.

In order to attract those beings who were to be disciplined by the Blessed One, as many as there were among those thousands of brahmins who were to be converted by the Buddha, that many were sent forth by them; and they were all disciplined by the Blessed One through the noble dharmas.
The remaining many thousands of living beings have entered upon a wrong path.
For those who have been disciplined by the noble dharmas, it comes to pass.
"These brahmins do not know the greatness of the Buddha.
If they were to approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa, they would be endowed with great benefit."
They sent a messenger to those brahmins.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, is a great soul, possessed of great compassion, and intent upon favoring the world.
Gentlemen, do not provoke or cause offense toward the Blessed One Kāśyapa or the community of monks.
Thus, having abandoned pride and intoxication, all of you come to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa; you shall be endowed with great benefit.
The speech of the Buddha is truthful, free from malice, meaningful, pure, sweet to others, clear, and gentle;
it is satisfying, not empty, and destroys all burning afflictions.
The Buddha’s gentle speech is beautiful in color, beautiful in its expression of happiness;
it is not faltering, not deficient, not false, and not otherwise.
The Buddha’s gentle speech is exactly as it is, free from conceptual construction.
The speech of the one of immeasurable wisdom is unarisen and unceasing regarding the knowable and knowledge; it is peerless, not subject to human control, and perfectly articulated.
He speaks what is true and free from malice, and is further possessed of a mind of loving-kindness toward all;
this is the supreme well-spoken word, which brings benefit and is endowed with the ultimate truth.
Whatever is uttered by one possessed [by a deity], whether high, low, or middling, it is spoken word for word and syllable for syllable with purity; this indeed is the supreme well-spoken word.
He speaks words endowed with supreme compassion and joy, joined with the ten fruits;
possessed of eight qualities and fourfold—this indeed is the supreme well-spoken word.
He speaks words that are fivefold meritorious, well-ascertained, or even those that have severed all doubt;
he performs no evil action whatsoever—such is the state of supreme manhood.
Thus endowed with the excellent marks, as you instruct this multitude of great splendor,
abandon your noble kinsmen and your abundant delight, and go forth!
Having plucked the heartwood of the tree— the supreme, excellent fragrance— born from Nanda and desiring to conquer the state of immortality,
he then prepared a meal of rice with that very substance, having first altered its form.
316. Thus do people of limited wisdom revile the great seer Kāśyapa here, who speaks well-phrased words that are beyond reproach, a noble man whom one cannot surpass.
Having abandoned both merit and evil, delighting in the destruction of the fetters of existence,
peaceful and with a well-disciplined mind— that stainless one people revile. And these monks and lay followers are many who take delight in the teaching of Kāśyapa.
Come, let us go together and pay homage to Kāśyapa, who blazes like a sacrificial fire with its crest of flames.
This supreme among bipeds, this leader who bestows vision—
abandoning pride and intoxication, come together and pay homage to Kāśyapa!

All those brahmins were fixed in the category of the eternalists; even if a thousand Buddhas were to teach the Dharma, they would be incapable of understanding it, nor could they develop faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Now, with sticks and clubs in their hands, they rushed toward where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was.
The Blessed One addressed the Earth Deity.
Then, with a body as tall as a palm tree, she stood before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to that Earth Deity:
And who are those brahmins there?
Then she said:
These are my slaves, produced from the earth.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, exert yourself just as servants exert themselves.
Then, having uprooted a large palm trunk, she went out to meet those brahmins;
she threw that palm trunk onto the ground with a loud crashing sound.
Those brahmins, terrified, were destroyed and perished.
Thus ends the story of Mālinī in the glorious Mahāvastu Avadāna.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was wandering on a tour among the Kośalas together with a great saṅgha of five hundred bhikṣus. He arrived at a market town of the Kośalas called Mārakaraṇḍa and stayed there in a certain grove.

Then, at the time of evening, the Blessed One arose from his seclusion, went out from the monastery, looked upward, surveyed the various directions, and gazed upon the level ground; then, manifesting a smile, he walked a long distance on his walking path.

Then, at the time of evening, the Venerable Ānanda saw the Blessed One emerging from his seclusion; having looked upward, surveyed the quarters of the sky, gazed downward, and observed the level ground, he manifested a smile and was walking a long distance on the walking-path.
Having seen this, he approached where many monks were and said this to the monks:

In the evening, this Buddha, the Blessed One, having arisen from seclusion, looked upward, surveyed the quarters of the horizon, and gazed downward; then, having observed the level ground, he manifested a smile and walked a long distance on his walking-path.
Furthermore, friends, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Why then, friends, should we not approach the Blessed One where he is and ask him about this matter?
We shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One will explain it.
"Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with those monks, approached the Blessed One; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
Here, in the evening time, I saw the Blessed One emerging from his seclusion, coming out from the monastery, looking upward and looking downward, surveying the various quarters of the horizon,
gazing evenly upon the level ground, manifesting a smile, and walking a long course of walking meditation.
Furthermore, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda.
And do you, Ānanda, see this spot of earth?
For it is even so, Blessed One.
Ānanda, on this spot of earth there was the site of the arrival of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see, Ānanda, this spot of earth?"
For it is even so, Blessed One.
Ānanda, on this very spot of earth was the site of the hut of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see, Ānanda, this spot of earth?"
For it is thus, Blessed One: on this very spot of earth, there was a walking-path sixty cubits long belonging to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see, Ānanda, this spot of earth?"
For it is so, Blessed One.

Ānanda, on this very spot of earth there were the seats of three Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas: of the Blessed One Krakucchanda, of the Blessed One Kanakamuni, and of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, struck with wonder and amazement, his hair standing on end with agitation, hurriedly and with great haste approached that spot of earth.
Having spread out his fourfold-layered outer robe upon that spot of earth and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One sit here on this very seat that has been prepared."

This spot of earth will have been frequented by four Tathāgatas, Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones: by the Blessed One Krakucchanda, by the Blessed One Kanakamuni, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and by the Blessed One here [now].
May the Blessed One please sit upon the seat that has been prepared.
The Venerable Ānanda, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Those monks also, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
When the Venerable Ānanda was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
Furthermore, Ānanda, do you wish to hear the Tathāgata speak a discourse on the Dharma concerning his former residences, beginning with this very city of Mārakaraṇḍa?
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in this way:
Now, Blessed One, this is the time; now, Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to speak on this matter to the bhikṣus.
The monks, having heard it directly from the Blessed One and having received it directly, will maintain it as suchness.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
Once upon a time, Ānanda, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, this town of Mārakaraṇḍa was a brahmin village named Veruḍiṅga.
In the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga, Ānanda, there was a potter named Ghaṭīkāra who was an attendant to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

Furthermore, Ānanda, the young brahmin named Jyotipāla, the son of the noble brahmin Ajanya, was a childhood friend of the potter Ghaṭikāra; they were playmates who grew up together in the dust, dear and pleasing to one another.

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on tour among the Kośalas with a great community of monks—seven thousand monks in all—approached the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga in the Kośala country; having arrived there, he stayed right there in this very grove.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said: 'The Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas, arrived at Veruḍiṅga, a brahmin village of the Kośalas, and stayed right there in a certain forest grove.'"
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached the young brahmin Jyotipāla and said this to him:
"I have heard this correctly, Jyotipāla:

it is said that the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on tour among the Kośalas with a great saṃgha of monks—seven thousand monks in all—is heading toward Veruḍiṅga, a brahmin village of the Kośalas."
Having arrived there at that time, he dwelt right there in a certain forest grove.
Why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa where he is, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Kāśyapa?
When this had been said, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Tell me, Ghaṭikāra, what is the use of my approaching those shaven-headed ascetics for a sight of them or for attending upon them?
A second and even a third time, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
"Ghaṭikāra, what need have I for those shaven-headed ascetics coming to see me for the sake of paying their respects?"
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"What indeed might be the means by which the young brahmin Jyotipāla would approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the purpose of seeing him and attending upon him?"
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Indeed, not far from that very grove there is a lotus pond named Sumukā; what if I were to go with the young Brahmin Jyotipāla to the lotus pond named Sumukā to bathe my head?"
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached the young brahmin Jyotipāla and said this to him.
Furthermore, Samyagjyotipāla, why should we not go to the lotus pond named Sumukā in order to bathe our heads?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
"In that case, my dear Ghaṭikāra, be happy; do now as you deem timely."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter took a head-bathing cloth and, together with the young brahmin Jyotipāla, approached that lotus pond in order to bathe.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having bathed his head, stood on the bank of the water arranging his hair.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is in this very grove; why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa to see him and to attend upon him?"
When this had been said, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Ghaṭīkāra, what have I to do with those ascetics coming to see me and to pay their respects?"
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter took the young man Jyotipāla by the neck and said this to him:

"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is right here in this very grove. Why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa, go to see the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and attend upon him?"
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having shaken off Ghaṭikāra the potter, went on his way.
Then Ghaṭikāra the potter ran after him, seized him by his matted hair, and said this:

"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is dwelling right here in this forest grove; why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa in order to see him and to attend upon him?"
Then, indeed, venerable Ānanda, this thought occurred to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:

"It is certainly no small matter that Ghaṭikāra the potter, though being of an inferior birth, should touch me on the head with his hands while I have bathed my head, even as far as the hair at the crown."
"In that case, my dear Ghaṭikāra, be happy; do now as you deem it timely."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter, together with the young brahmin Jyotipāla, approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa; having bowed at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:

“Blessed One, this young brahmin Jyotipāla is my childhood friend, one who played with me in the dust; he is dear and pleasing to me, being the son of the noble brahmin Ajanya. May the Blessed One exhort and instruct him.”
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa caused the young brahmin Jyotipāla to undertake the three refuges and the five precepts.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"O Blessed One, I shall not, for the time being, cause all five precepts to be undertaken."
"I have indeed one man who is a harasser and an irritant, who must be deprived of life."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
Furthermore, Jyotipāla, who is that one man who is a harasser and an angry man, whose life should be taken?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla addressed the Blessed One Kāśyapa in this way.
"Lord, this is Ghaṭikāra the potter, who at that time stroked my head with his hair when I had just bathed my head."
Then I spoke as follows.
Let us approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa to see him and to attend upon him.
Moreover, may you, Ghaṭikāra the potter, be happy; here I undertake all these five precepts.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Ghaṭikāra the potter and the young brahmin Jyotipāla with a discourse on the Dharma, dismissed them.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra and the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, departed.
Then, Ānanda, not long after he had departed, the young brahmin Jyotipāla said this to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Tell me, Ghaṭikāra, do you understand the perfectly taught Dharma of the Blessed One Kāśyapa just as I do?"
When this had been said, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
"So it is, Samyagjyotipāla!
I too understand the perfectly taught Dharma of the Blessed One Kāśyapa exactly as you do."
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter.
"But why, Ghaṭikāra, do you not go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa?"
When this had been said, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
"Jyotipāla, I have parents who are aged, elderly, and weak of sight; they have no other attendant."
Therefore, I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Then indeed, Ānanda, before long, a distaste for the household life arose in the young brahmin Jyotipāla, and his mind was inclined toward going forth.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla approached Ghaṭīkāra the potter and said this to him:
"Come, Ghaṭīkāra, let us properly make a vow in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the sake of going forth; I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state."

Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter, taking the young brahmin Jyotipāla with him, approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"Lord, this young brahmin Jyotipāla is my childhood friend, one who played with me in the dust; he is dear and pleasing to me, the son of the noble brahmin Ajanya.
May the Blessed One let him go forth and grant him full ordination."
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa addressed the monks.
"Monks, let the young man Jyotipāla go forth; let him receive full ordination."
Then indeed, Ānanda, the monks ordained the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
Then, Ānanda, not long after the monk Jyotipāla had received full ordination, the Blessed One Kāśyapa set out on a wandering tour among the Kośalas and the Kāśīs.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kāśīs with a great community of monks—seven thousand monks in all—approached the city of Vārāṇasī in the land of the Kāśīs;
having arrived there, he stayed right there at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana.
Ānanda, King Kṛkī indeed heard that the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on tour among the Kāśīs with a great community of monks, seven thousand in number,
had arrived at Vārāṇasī, the city of the Kāśīs, and was staying right there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi, addressed a certain man.
"Come, my good man, go to where the Blessed One Kāśyapa is, and in my name offer salutations to the Blessed One Kāśyapa."
Kṛkī, the King of Kāśī, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, inquired after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, strength, well-being, and comfortable dwelling.
He then invited the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, for a meal the following day at his residence, and the Blessed One Kāśyapa accepted his invitation.
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to that man.
May Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, together with his son and his retinue, be happy;
now do as you deem it the right time.
Then that man, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, set out for the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, Ānanda, that man went to where Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi, was staying.
He spoke this to Kṛkin, the King of Kāśi.
"O Great King, I have conveyed your salutation to the Blessed One Kāśyapa."
When asked about his freedom from illness, his lack of distress, his well-being, strength, and comfortable state, he was invited for a meal together with the community of monks on the following day.
And the Blessed One Kāśyapa consented, saying, "Do now as you deem it timely."
Then, Ānanda, on that very night, King Kṛkī of Kāśi had an abundance of excellent food, both solid and soft, prepared; and when that night had passed, he said to a certain man:
"Come, my good man, go to where the Blessed One Kāśyapa is, and having approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa, speak to him thus:"
"It is time, Blessed One; it is the mealtime at the residence of Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, at which the Blessed One may deem it the right moment."
"Very well, Great King," that man replied to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, and having departed from the city of Vārāṇasī, he set out for the Ṛṣivadana Deer Park.
Then, Ānanda, that man approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"It is time, Blessed One; it is now the mealtime at the residence of King Kṛkī. May the Blessed One do as he deems appropriate."
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having given his consent to that man, dressed early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded and preceded by the community of monks,

set out for the city of Vārāṇasī. Now at that time, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi, surrounded by his princes and ministers, was standing at the gate of his own palace to meet the Blessed One Kāśyapa together with his community of disciples.
While waiting expectantly.
Indeed, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, saw the Blessed One Kāśyapa approaching from afar together with his community of disciples.

Having seen him, he approached where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was together with his community of disciples; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples, and having placed the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples in front, he led them into his own residence.
Now at that time, in the residence of Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, there was a palace named Kokanada, newly built and recently completed, which had not yet been used by any ascetic or brahmin.
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:

"Lord, in my residence there is a new palace named Kokanada, recently completed and never before used by any ascetic or brahmin; may the Blessed One be the first to enjoy it, and afterwards we shall enjoy it."
When this had been said, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi.
Therefore, O Great King, be happy; do now as you deem it timely.
Then indeed, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, had seats prepared in the Kokanada palace and caused hard and soft food to be served.
Then the Blessed One, having ascended the Kokanada palace, sat down upon the seat that had been prepared, as did the community of monks upon their respective seats.
Then indeed, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, with his own hand, satisfied and served the Blessed One Kāśyapa with various kinds of solid and soft food.
And for each one, seven men [were assigned] with seven types of huts and with rice from the *parṇakulaka* variety.
Then King Kṛkī of Kāśi, knowing that the Blessed One Kāśyapa had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, took a certain low seat and approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
May the Blessed One consent to spend the rains retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī.

“Lord, I shall have a monastery built; and in it, seven thousand gabled halls, seven thousand couches, seven thousand pathways, seven thousand horses, and seven thousand park-keepers shall be established, who will each individually attend upon the community of monks.”
In this manner, they will attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks with such service.
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:
For it is not possible, Great King, that my rainy-season residence will take place among the Vajjis.
A second and a third time, it should be done in exactly the same way.
Then, Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi wept and shed tears, thinking: "The Blessed One Kāśyapa does not consent to spend the rains retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī."
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
Furthermore, does the Blessed One have another attendant such as I am?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to King Kṛkī.
"Indeed, O Great King, you are not yet a complete attendant to me."
When this had been said, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, spoke thus to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
But who, O Blessed One, is my attendant who is more full and completely perfect than Pūrṇa?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi.
"Great King, in your own realm there is a brahmin village named Veruḍiṅga;
Ghaṭīkāra lives there, and he is my attendant."
When this had been said, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, spoke thus to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Of what kind, Blessed One, were Ghaṭīkāra’s riches with which he served the Blessed One and the Saṅgha?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:

Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter has for as long as life lasts abstained from taking life; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from taking what is not given; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from unchaste conduct; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from false speech; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from dancing, singing, and instrumental music; and for as long as life lasts he has abstained from wearing perfumes, garlands, and cosmetics.

For as long as life lasts, he abstains from high and luxurious beds; for as long as life lasts, he abstains from eating at improper times; for as long as life lasts, he abstains from accepting gold and silver.
"Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter does not dig the earth himself.

Rather, he takes clay from those places where it has been thrown up by mice, or where it has been deposited by water, or where it has been cut away by water; having taken that clay and fashioned vessels, he sets them down at the crossroads.
Then those who have need of those vessels fill them with either beans, or peas, or rice, and having filled them, they take the vessels."
They proceed indeed without any dependence.
Such, O Great King, were the enjoyments of Ghaṭīkāra the potter, with which he served both the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha.
And his mother and father were aged, elderly, and weak of sight.
Once, O Great King, on a certain occasion, I was dwelling at Veruḍiṅga, a village of brahmins.
Therefore, Great King, having dressed early in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I went into the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga for alms.
Thus, Great King, while wandering for alms with a regular sequence in the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga, I approached the dwelling of Ghaṭīkāra the potter and stood at the entrance.
Now at that time, Ghaṭīkāra the potter had just come out from his own dwelling.
Then, O Great King, the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to the Tathāgata:
Your attendant has departed, Blessed One.
"Here in the upper storeroom are both soup and rice; may the Blessed One partake from this."
Thus, O Great King, having had the soup and rice from the upper storehouse received by the deities and partaken of it, I departed.
Then, O Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter went to his own dwelling.
Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter saw that the soup and rice from the upper store-room had been consumed, and having seen this, he spoke thus to his parents once more.
"Father, who has eaten the soup and rice from the upper storehouse of Ghaṭikāra?"
When this had been said, O Great King, the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter.
By the Blessed One, the son of Kāśyapa.
Then indeed, O Great King, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
Moreover, it is a great gain for me, a truly well-obtained gain, that the Blessed One Kāśyapa has placed such absolute trust in me, even to this extent.
And while he remained thus, the bliss of joy did not leave his body for half a month, nor for seven days the parents who were aged, elderly, and weak of sight.
"Once, Great King, at a time when a thatched hut for the Tathāgata was being roofed over, the grass could not be found."
Therefore, O Great King, I addressed the bhikṣus.
"Go, monks, to the house of Ghaṭikāra the potter and bring some grass."
Then indeed, O Great King, those monks approached the dwelling of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Furthermore, Great King, at that time Ghaṭīkāra the potter had gone out from his own dwelling.
They did not see any grass there; they saw a newly thatched workshop shed.
Then indeed, O Great King, those monks approached the Tathāgata, bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, and addressed the Tathāgata as follows.
"Your attendant has departed, Blessed One; there are no grasses here, but there is a newly thatched workshop."
When this had been said, O Great King, he spoke thus to that bhikṣu:
"Go, monks, and having stripped off the new roof from Ghaṭikāra the potter’s workshop, bring the grass here."
Then, O Great King, those monks approached the residence of Ghaṭikāra the potter; having arrived, they stripped the grass from Ghaṭikāra the potter’s new roofed workshop.
Then, O Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter’s mother and father said this to those monks:
"Who is this who, having stripped the roof of the new workshop belonging to Ghaṭikāra the potter, carries away the straw?"
When this had been said, O Great King, those monks said this to the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter:
Venerable one, wherever the grass was not sufficient for covering the forest hut of the monks and of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, there these grasses were taken away.
When this had been said, O Great King, the mother and father of Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to those monks.
Take away, take away your own [possessions].
Then, O Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter went to his own dwelling.
Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter saw that the workshop with its new roof had been stripped of its straw; and having seen that the straw had been removed, he spoke thus to his parents.
"Father, who has stripped the new roof of Ghaṭikāra the potter's workshop and taken away the grass?"
When this had been said, Ghaṭikāra’s parents spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
The grass in the forest hut of the Blessed One Kāśyapa’s son is not growing there because these monks have carried the grass away.
Then, indeed, O Great King, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
Well-gained indeed are my gains, since even this Blessed One Kāśyapa has become so exceedingly trusted by me, even to the point of being like one of my own people.
And for one month he did not leave the joy and happiness from his body, and for half a month he remained so for his blind parents.

Furthermore, Great King, I do not recall Ghaṭikāra the potter ever experiencing such dejection as you have, namely that the Blessed One Kāśyapa did not consent to spend the rains retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:
"It is indeed a gain for me, a great gain for me, that such a practitioner of the holy life dwells within my realm—one who is a field of merit consisting of two-legged beings."
Then, Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi sent a hundred wagons of fresh water, oil, salt, and boiling broth to Ghaṭikāra the potter, who lived in a leaf-hut.
Then, Ānanda, after Kāśyapa had instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Kṛkī of Kāśi with a discourse on the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, Ānanda, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he addressed the monks.

"Sit down, monks; assemble, monks! Bind yourselves in the cross-legged posture. For I shall remain bound in this cross-legged posture until the minds of these seven thousand monks, seated upon these very seats, are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging."
"Very well, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and they sat down together, assembled, and took their seats cross-legged.
Therefore, Ānanda, while the monk Jyotipāla was alone in seclusion and in retreat, this very reflection arose in his mind.

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans!"

Having directly realized this world— including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans— I shall set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, may I teach the Dharma endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus gods and humans will think that what is to be heard and believed is just as it was for the Blessed One Kāśyapa in the present.

May I become that for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras diminished, while the divine hosts increased.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having known with his own mind this very reflection that had arisen in the mind of the monk Jyotipāla, addressed a certain monk.
"Come, monk, go to where the monk Jyotipāla is, and having approached him, speak thus to the monk Jyotipāla."
"Venerable one, the Teacher addresses you; go to where the Tathāgata is."
Having received the command from the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he approached the monk Jyotipāla and said this to him:
"Venerable Jyotipāla, the Teacher summons you; come to where the Blessed One is."

"Very well, venerable sir," the venerable Jyotipāla replied to that bhikṣu. Having gone to where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and sat down to one side.
To the venerable monk Jyotipāla, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One Kāśyapa said this:
"Was it not the case, Jyotipāla, that this kind of reflection arose in the mind of the single Jyotipāla while he was alone and in seclusion?"
"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata."

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans!"

Having directly known this world— with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans— I shall set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, may I teach the Dharma endowed with all excellent aspects and complete in all its aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus gods and humans will consider that what is to be heard and believed is just as it was for the Blessed One Kāśyapa at present.

May I become that for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras diminished, while the divine hosts increased.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having known with his own mind this very reflection that had arisen in the mind of the monk Jyotipāla, addressed a certain monk.
Come, monk, go to where the monk Jyotipāla is, and having approached him, speak thus to the monk Jyotipāla:
"Venerable one, the Teacher calls you; go to where the Tathāgata is."
Having received the command from the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he approached the monk Jyotipāla and said this to him:
"Venerable Jyotipāla, the Teacher summons you; come to where the Blessed One is."
"Very well, venerable sir," the venerable Jyotipāla replied to that monk. Having approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he sat down to one side.
To the venerable monk Jyotipāla, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One Kāśyapa said this:
"Indeed, Jyotipāla, while Jyotipāla was alone, in seclusion, and withdrawn in meditation, this kind of reflection arose in his mind."

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans!

Having directly known this world and the world beyond, including the world of gods and Māras, and the generation of recluses and brahmins, gods and humans— right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park..."

In the Deer Park, may I set in motion the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world,
in accordance with the Dharma.
And may I teach the Dharma endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And may I maintain the entire community of monks just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus gods and humans will think that what I say should be heard and believed, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

May that be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras diminished, and the divine hosts increased.
Thus addressed, Ānanda, the monk Jyotipāla said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
So it is, Blessed One.
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One spoke thus to the monk Jyotipāla:

"Therefore, Jyotipāla, give this golden seat and pair of fine cloths to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Having performed this merit, both gods and humans will think that it is worth hearing and worthy of faith."
Indeed, Ānanda, the monk Jyotipāla gave a golden seat and a pair of fine cloth garments to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having manifested a smile, gave a prophecy concerning the monk Jyotipāla.
"Jyotipāla, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed,
teacher of gods and humans."
Having directly known this world and the world beyond, including the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,

its gods and humans, you shall set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which has not been set in motion by any ascetic or brahmin, by any god or Māra, or by anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
And thus you shall teach the Dharma, endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus you will lead the entire community of disciples, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
In this way, you will lead the entire community of disciples, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus those gods and humans will consider what is to be heard and what is to be believed, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

Thus you shall become one for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and [the hosts of devas] will increase.
Then indeed, Ānanda, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa had prophesied concerning Jyotipāla, the gods of the earth raised a cry.

"O worthy sirs, this monk named Jyotipāla has been prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa: 'In a future time, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), endowed with knowledge and conduct (vidyācaraṇasampanna), a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.'"
Having directly known this world, and having directly known the other world— including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, as well as this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,

its gods and humans— he will set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma, which has three revolutions and twelve aspects, and which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, he will teach the Dharma endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does at present.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, as a support for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [gods] [heard it as well].
For as long as a short while, a cry arose from the assembly of gods belonging to the Brahma-realm.

"Friend, this monk named Jyotipāla has been prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa: 'In a future time, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.

Having directly known this world and the other world, having directly known the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, [he will abide here...]"

Thus, in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, he will set in motion the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dharma.
And thus he will teach the Dharma endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does at present.
And thus gods and humans will think that what is to be heard and believed is just as it was for the Blessed One Kāśyapa at present.
That will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Then, Ānanda, when the sound had vanished, the Blessed One Kāśyapa instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
"Monks, reflect in this way; do not reflect in that way. Attend to things in this way; do not attend to them in that way."

Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island, not another as your island; with yourselves as your refuge, not another as your refuge; with the Dharma as your island, not another as your island; with the Dharma as your refuge, not another as your refuge.

Then the Blessed One, his body aflame, blazing, and radiant with light, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the monks with a discourse on the Dharma:

"In this way, O monks, you should reflect; in this way you should not reflect. Attend to this; do not attend to that. Make yourselves your own island, make yourselves your own refuge, and seek no other refuge. Make the Dharma your island, make the Dharma your refuge, and seek no other refuge."

Then the Blessed One, with his body aflame, blazing, and radiant, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the monks with a discourse on the Dharma:

"Monks, reflect thus; do not reflect thus. Attend to this; do not attend to that. Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island and no other island, with yourselves as your refuge and no other refuge; dwell with the Dharma as your island and no other island, with the Dharma as your refuge and no other refuge."

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa rose into the air from one palm-tree height, then two palm-tree heights, three, four, five, six, and seven palm-tree heights; standing at the height of seven palm-trees, he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
"Thus, monks, you should reflect; thus you should not reflect; thus you should attend to the mind; thus you should not attend to the mind.
Monks, dwell with yourself as an island, not another as an island; with yourself as a refuge, not another as a refuge; with the Dharma as a refuge, not another as a refuge."

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa descended from seven palm trees' height to six palm trees' height; from six palm trees' height to five; from five to four; from four to three; from three to two; from two to one palm tree's height; and from one palm tree's height he sat down upon his own seat and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
"Monks, reflect in this way; do not reflect in that way. Attend to the mind in this way; do not attend to the mind in that way."

Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island and no other island; with yourselves as your refuge and no other refuge; with the Dharma as your island and no other island; with the Dharma as your refuge and no other refuge.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, breaking his cross-legged posture, addressed those monks.

“Monks, I break my cross-legged posture while all these seven thousand monks remain seated on these very seats; their minds are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging, with the sole exception of the monk Jyotipāla.”
He too has been prophesied by me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

It might be, Ānanda, that you would think that at that time, on that occasion, the monk named Jyotipāla was someone else. But it should not be viewed thus. Why is that? Because I myself, Ānanda, at that time, on that occasion, was the monk named Jyotipāla.
This should not be viewed in such a way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the monk named Jyotipāla.
The Blessed One spoke thus, and the Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted in mind, along with those seven thousand monks, rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One.
Thus ends the Jyotipālasūtra in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.

The monk Jyotipāla, having prepared a drink of rice-gruel for the Blessed One Kāśyapa together with his community of disciples, purchased saffron for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and sprinkled it over the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples;
he also gave a golden seat and a set of fine garments to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
And he made this aspiration:

"Just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident with the four grounds of self-confidence— oh, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata!"

He is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans— just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa is now.
And may I thus set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, with its three turnings and twelve aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And may I maintain a community of disciples just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus those gods and humans will consider me worthy of being heard and worthy of being trusted, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

"Thus, having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvana, may I lead others to final nirvana, just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa does now."
May I become that for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of people, both gods and humans.
Jyotipāla was prophesied by Kāśyapa for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

"Jyotipāla, in a future time, you shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans; in this very Bhadrakalpa, immediately following [me], you shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, your body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics."
Endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he is powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata and confident through the four grounds of self-confidence.

Thus, having crossed over, you will help others cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvana, you will lead others to final nirvana, just as I do now.

Thus you shall become one for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of people, out of compassion for the world, including both gods and humans.
As soon as the monk Jyotipāla had been thus predicted by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently;
and the gods of the earth raised their voices and made this sound heard.
Just as it should be done in detail in other grammatical treatises, so too is this the Blessed One’s own vow.
Having gone forth as a follower of Kāśyapa, Jyotipāla the Bodhisattva was instructed by the Perfectly Awakened One: "Cleanse the monastery and provide water."
Jyotipāla, the Bodhisattva, desiring the cessation of existence, gave rice gruel to drink, along with a golden seat and a pair of garments.

Having given that gift, he made this aspiration: "May I become a leader of the world, a teacher of gods and humans; having proclaimed the noble Dharma, may I likewise proclaim this Dharma for the sake of others, and may I thus establish many beings in the noble Dharmas."

And thus may gods and humans hear my words; and thus may I set in motion the Wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many; may I kindle the torch of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, raise the banner of Dharma with its pennants, and blow the conch of Dharma. May I establish those fallen into hardship—those oppressed by birth and old age, subject to death, and blinded by existence—in the eye of wisdom, and rescue them from the states of woe.

May I liberate from the cycle of existence those scattered throughout the six realms of rebirth—in the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci hells; those cooked and uncooked in hell, those oppressed by the states of woe, those subject to death, and those who possess little happiness and much suffering—may I liberate them from the cycle of existence.
I would act for the welfare of the world; I would teach the Dharma to gods and humans.
In this way he disciplines sentient beings, just as this Light of the World does.
"In the future, in this Fortunate Aeon, you shall become a Buddha, a leader of the world. At Ṛṣivadana in Kapilavastu, you will then be a Śākyan; such will be the fruition of your vow."

Having practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) that was unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, complete, and utterly pure, he passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm named Tuṣita as a son of the gods named Śvetaketu, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty. He surpasses other gods in ten divine qualities: in divine lifespan, divine complexion, divine happiness, divine sovereignty, divine retinue, divine form, divine sounds, divine fragrances, divine tastes, and divine tangibles.

"Other sons of the gods as well shall ask him whatever is to be asked. This son of the gods named Śvetaketu is wise, discerning, confident, skillful, and intelligent; he has gone forth under forty thousand Buddhas and performed services for eighty-five thousand Buddhas—not to mention for the great and powerful disciples and the sixty million Pratyekabuddhas.
Forty thousand Buddhas, leaders of the world, have entered parinirvāṇa—
the Victors under whom the Conqueror practiced the holy life while seeking the cessation of existence.
Fifty thousand Buddhas, the leaders of the world, have entered parinirvāṇa—
those Victors by whom the Jina brought his time to an end, seeking the cessation of existence.
Sixty million self-arisen Pratyekabuddhas have attained parinirvāṇa—
those in whose presence the Jina passed away, seeking the cessation of existence.
Countless millions of Arhats have attained parinirvāṇa under those great teachers;
the Jina met his end while seeking the cessation of existence.
Among these, the former accounts of the Teacher, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, have been proclaimed.
Few have been spoken of, and fewer still remain unsung, among whom the Jina passed away while seeking the cessation of existence.
Thus ends the prediction concerning Jyotipāla in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
The beginning of the royal lineage.
"There comes a time, monks, there comes an occasion, when after the passing of a long period, this world undergoes dissolution.
And when, monks, the world is dissolving, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods."
Monks, there comes that time, there comes that occasion, when after the passing of a long period, this world evolves.

Furthermore, monks, when the world is evolving and the configuration of the world has become established, certain beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan and the exhaustion of their karma, pass away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come to this state of existence.
Those beings are self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, feeding on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever they desire.

Furthermore, monks, it is the nature of things that for those beings who were self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, sustained by joy, dwelling in bliss, and going wherever they desired, these two— the moon and the sun— were not perceived in the world. When the moon and sun were not perceived in the world, the forms of the stars were not perceived in the world.

When the forms of the stars were no longer discernible in the world, the paths of the constellations were no longer discernible in the world; when the paths of the constellations were no longer discernible in the world, night and day were no longer discernible in the world;
when night and day were no longer discernible in the world, months and fortnights were no longer discernible in the world;
and when months and fortnights were not discernible in the world, the seasons and years were no longer discernible in the world.
It is indeed the natural law, O monks, that those beings were self-luminous, moved through the air, and went wherever they desired.
Even this great earth would rise up like a vessel of water.
And it was endowed with excellent color and endowed with excellent flavor; its taste was just like pure, small-bee honey, and its appearance was just like a stream of milk or a stream of ghee.
Then, monks, a certain being who was fickle and of a greedy nature tasted that essence of the earth with his finger.
It gratifies him by its color, its fragrance, and its flavor as well.
Other beings also, having seen that being, follow his example.
They too tasted the essence of the earth with their fingers.
He causes them to taste it as well, even to the extent of its flavor.
Then, monks, at a later time, that being took that essence of the earth as food in the form of mouthfuls.
Other beings also, having seen that being, follow his example.
They too took that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.
And when, monks, those beings consumed that essence of the earth as food in mouthfuls, then heaviness, coarseness, and hardness came upon their bodies.

Furthermore, that former state of theirs—possessing self-luminosity, moving through the air, having bodies made of mind, subsisting on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever they desired—vanished away.

Due to their self-luminosity, their ability to travel through the atmosphere, their mind-made nature, their feeding on joy, their power to go wherever they wish, and their invisibility, the moon and sun were perceived in the world.

When the moon and sun became manifest in the world, the forms of the stars became manifest in the world. When the forms of the stars became manifest in the world, the paths of the constellations became manifest in the world. When the paths of the constellations became manifest in the world, night and day became manifest in the world.
By means of nights and days being known in the world, months and fortnights are known in the world;
by means of months and fortnights being known, seasons and years are known in the world.
Then, monks, those beings, consuming that essence of the earth as their food, possessing its color, eating it, and subsisting on it, remained for a very long period of time.
Those among them who consumed much food became ill-favored in complexion, while those who consumed little food were possessed of a beautiful complexion.
Those who were handsome despised those beings who were ugly.
We are beings of beautiful complexion, while these others are of ugly complexion.
As they dwelt thus, conditioned by their physical appearance and secondary characteristics, and characterized by pride and arrogance, the essence of the earth disappeared.
A crust of earth would appear, having an appearance and color just like that of a mushroom.
And it was endowed with excellent color and endowed with excellent fragrance; its taste was just like that of pure, small-bee honey.
Then, monks, when that essence of the earth had disappeared, those beings uttered this inspired exclamation:
Oh, how wonderful is the taste! Hara is the taste! Thus [he said].
Just as, monks, people nowadays, having eaten a good meal and being happy after their meal, utter this inspired exclamation.
"Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!"
They approached that very same ancient, imperishable fire-essence, yet they did not discern its purpose.
Then, monks, those beings, consuming that crust of earth as their food—taking on its color, subsisting on it, and making it their nourishment—remained for a long, extended period of time.
Those among them who ate much food became coarse, while those who ate little food became beautiful in complexion.
Those who possessed a beautiful complexion looked down upon sentient beings of an ugly complexion.
"We are beautiful in color, while these beings are ugly."
While they were living there, characterized by pride and arrogance based on their physical appearance and complexion, the forest creepers appeared as a replacement for the ground-moss.
Just as a *kalambuka* plant appears in such a color, so too was it endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor; its taste was just like that of a small drop of honey.
Then, monks, when that crust of earth had disappeared, those beings began to lament.
"O, speak! O, speak! they cried.
"Monks, it was just as if beings at present, when touched by some painful condition, were to groan, 'Alas! Alas!', repeating that same ancient expression without understanding its meaning;
even so, monks, when that crust of earth had disappeared, those beings groaned."
"Oh, he speaks! Oh, he speaks!"

Then indeed, monks, when that crust of earth had disappeared, those beings, subsisting on forest creepers as their food, remained for a long time, for a vast duration, with that as their color, that as their nutriment, and that as their sustenance.
Among them, those who ate much food became ill-favored in appearance, while those who ate little food remained beautiful.
Those [beings] looked down upon the ill-favored beings.
"We are beautiful in color, while these beings are ugly."
When those forest creepers, which were the conditions for the color and appearance of their wounds and were of a nature characterized by pride and arrogance, vanished;

Rice—free from husks and powder, fragrant grain—would appear; reaped in the evening, it would be grown, ripened, and sprouted by the morning, such that no trace of its having been cut away would even be discernible.
That too, being harvested in the morning, becomes grown, ripened, and sprouted by evening, and no trace of its cutting is perceived.
Then, monks, when that forest creeper had disappeared, those beings lamented.
"O Veda! O Veda! he exclaimed.
Just as, monks, at present beings, when touched by some painful condition, might groan;
yet they would fall back upon that very same ancient, unchanging, and primordial expression, and would not discern its meaning.
Then, monks, when that forest creeper had disappeared, those beings lived for a very long time subsisting on that rice which was without powder or husk,

consisting of fragrant grains. And, monks, as those beings continued to consume that rice which was without powder or husk, consisting of fragrant grains, then the female characteristics appeared among the women,
and the male characteristics appeared among the men.
With minds excessively impassioned, they gazed intently at one another.
With hearts full of passion for one another and longing for one another, they became infatuated with each other; being thus infatuated, they violated one another.
Furthermore, monks, those beings who saw others being violated there threw sticks at them, they threw clods of earth, and they threw dust.
"Friends, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; friends, a lack of true Dharma has appeared in the world, in that a being indeed defiles another being."

Just as, monks, nowadays when a girl is being married, they place a staff [on her head] and they even place a firebrand; yet they do not understand the meaning of that ancient verse which has come down to them.
At that time, monks, that was indeed considered contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the sacrifice, and contrary to the Vinaya;
but now, monks, it is indeed considered in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the sacrifice, and in accordance with the Vinaya.

Then, monks, those beings, being distressed and loathing that unrighteousness, would go away for one day, they would go away for two days, they would go away for three days, they would go away for four days, they would go away for five days, and they would go away for a fortnight or even a month; they would even have household chores performed, solely for the purpose of concealing that very unrighteousness.
Then, monks, it occurred to a certain being who had gone to gather rice:
Why do I weary myself for its sake? How was it that in the past I used to weary myself for my evening meal in the evening, and for my morning meal in the morning?
"What if I were now to carry away at once all the rice for both the day and the evening?"
Monks, that being indeed used to gather the śāli rice once a day, both in the evening and in the morning.
Then, monks, a certain being said this to that being:
Come, O being, let us go to fetch rice.
When this had been said, monks, that being spoke thus to that being:
Go, O being; rice for both evening and morning has been brought by me all at once.
Then indeed, monks, this thought occurred to that being as well:
Even doing it this way would be good;
what if I were to carry that rice back all at once—once every two days or once every three days?
Monks, that being indeed harvested the śāli rice for two days or three days at a single time.
Then, monks, a certain being said this to that being:
"Come, O being, let us go to fetch rice."
When this had been said, that being spoke thus to that being:
Go, O being; I have brought for you at once rice that lasts for two days and rice that lasts for three days.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to that being as well:
Even so, it would be excellent if this were done now;
what if I were also to bring back rice for four or five days?
Monks, that being indeed harvested the *śāli* rice once every four days or five days.

And when, monks, those beings began to consume that rice— which was without powder, without husk, fragrant, with grains of pure rice— by means of hoarding, then indeed powder and husks appeared upon that rice.
That too, though harvested in the evening, has not grown, nor ripened, nor sprouted by the morning, yet its cut stump remains visible.
Then, monks, those beings ran together; having run together and assembled, they took counsel with one another.
Sirs, we are self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, feeding on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever we desire.
For us, who were self-luminous, moving through the air, mind-made, feeding on joy, abiding in bliss, and going wherever we wished, the sun and moon were not perceived in the world.

When the moon and sun were not discernible in the world, the forms of the stars were not discernible. When the forms of the stars were not discernible in the world, the paths of the constellations were not discernible in the world. When the paths of the constellations were not discernible in the world, night and day were not discernible.
