When nights and days were not discerned, months and fortnights were not discerned.
When months and half-months were not discerned, the seasons and years were not discerned.
This great earth, too, rises up like a vessel of water.
Just as, for example, a stream of ghee or a stream of milk, so too did it appear in color—perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste;
its flavor was just like that of pure, unadulterated honey.
Then, indeed, O sirs, a certain being who was fickle and of a greedy nature tasted that essence of the earth with his finger.
He relishes it by its color, its fragrance, and its flavor.
Then, indeed, sirs, that being at a later time took that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.
Having seen that being, we too would adopt his imitation and take that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.
But since we, sirs, began to consume solid food consisting of the essence of the earth, heaviness, coarseness, and hardness came upon our bodies.
That former state of self-luminosity, moving through the air, possessing a mind-made body, feeding on joy, dwelling in happiness, and going wherever one desired—that too disappeared.

Because those beings possessed self-luminosity, the ability to travel through the air, bodies made of mind, subsistence on joy, abiding in happiness, and the power to go wherever they desired, the moon and sun became manifest in the world. When the moon and sun were manifest in the world, the forms of the stars became manifest.
When the stars were made known by their star-forms, the paths of the constellations became known;
when the paths of the constellations were made known, night and day became known;
and when night and day were made known, the months and fortnights became known.
When months and half-months were discerned, the seasons and years became discernible.
"Venerable sirs, consuming that essence of the earth as our food, having it as our color, it as our nourishment, and it as our sustenance, we remained for a long time, throughout a vast duration."

And when some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among them, and when, sirs, some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among us, then that essence of the earth disappeared and a crust of earth appeared.
Just as a mushroom, so too was that appearance of color possessed of excellent color and possessed of excellent fragrance.
It is just like pure, honey-like nectar without bees; such is its taste.
Thus, sirs, subsisting on that earth-crust as our food, having that as our color, that as our nourishment, and that as our sustenance, we remained for a long time throughout a vast period.
But when some unwholesome, evil qualities became manifest among them, then that crust of earth disappeared and a forest creeper appeared.
It was just like a *kalambukā* flower in its appearance; it was thus endowed with excellent color, endowed with excellent fragrance, and endowed with excellent flavor.
Just as if it were small, pure honey—such is its taste.
"O sirs, consuming that forest creeper as our food, having its color, eating its substance, and taking it as our nourishment, we shall remain for a long duration."

And as soon as some evil, unwholesome states became manifest among them, and as soon as you, sirs, caused some evil, unwholesome states to become manifest, then that forest creeper disappeared and rice appeared— grainless, huskless, fragrant, with edible kernels.
That which is harvested in the evening becomes grown, ripened, and fully developed by the morning; moreover, no trace of its having been cut away is discerned.

Sirs, while we were consuming that rice—free from red powder and husks, with fragrant grains as its fruit—as our food, we remained for a long time, throughout a vast duration, of that same appearance, subsisting on that, and taking that as our nourishment.
But when certain evil, unwholesome states became manifest among us, then the red powder and husk of that rice began to envelop it.
And that which was harvested in the evening has not withered, nor is it ripened, nor has it sprouted; its excellence is still clearly perceived.
Even that *kāśya* grain which was harvested has not grown, nor ripened, nor sprouted again by evening, yet its husk is still visible.
What if we were now to divide the rice fields and establish boundaries?
"Let us measure out this rice field for you, sirs, and this one for ourselves."
Then, monks, those beings established boundaries for the rice fields, saying:
"This rice field belongs to you; this one belongs to us."
Then, monks, it occurred to a certain being who had gone to fetch rice:
"What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I sustain my life when my own portion of rice has been exhausted?"
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
Then, monks, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, would take a portion of rice belonging to another that had not been given.
Monks, a certain being saw another being taking rice that had not been given and belonged to another; having seen him, he approached that being and said to him:
"Is it true, O being, that you are taking rice that has not been given and belongs to another?"
When this had been said, monks, that being spoke thus to that being:
Therefore, O being, it shall not happen again in this way.
Monks, for a second time, as that being had gone to gather rice, this thought occurred to him:
"What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I maintain my livelihood now that my own portion of rice has been exhausted?"
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
And a second time, monks, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, would take rice belonging to another that had not been given.
Having seen him, he approached that being and said this to him:
"Is it true, O being, that for a second time you are taking another's rice that has not been given?"
A second time, monks, that being said this to that being:
Therefore, O being, it shall not happen again in this way.
Monks, when that being had gone to fetch rice, this thought occurred to him for a third time:
"What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I provide a livelihood when my own portion of rice has been exhausted?"
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
Monks, even for a third time, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, took the rice of another that had not been given.
Monks, that being saw that third being taking the rice belonging to another which had not been given.
And having seen him, he approached that being and, striking him with a staff, said this:
"Is it really true, O being, that you have taken another's rice, even as many as three times?"
Then, monks, that being, raising both his arms, wailed and cried out.
"Friends, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; an untrue dharma has appeared in the world, in that indeed the wielding of the rod is known in the world."
Then, monks, that being, having writhed upon the ground and raised both his arms, wailed and cried out.
"Friends, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; friends, the false dharma has appeared in the world, in that indeed theft and false speech are known in the world."

And furthermore, monks, in this very way there was the first appearance in the world of these three evil, unwholesome states: namely, taking what is not given, false speech, and the wielding of the rod.
Then, monks, those beings ran together, assembled, and having run together and assembled, they took counsel.

"Friends, what if we were to appoint that being among us who is most pleasing to all and most influential, who would restrain those among us deserving of restraint and support those deserving of support,
and who would instruct each of us regarding the portion of rice from our respective rice fields?"
Then indeed, monks, those beings elected that being among them who was the most pleasing to all and the most preeminent in majesty.

"May you, sir, restrain those among us who deserve restraint and favor those who deserve favor; we shall appoint you as the foremost among all sentient beings, and in our respective rice-fields, we shall give you a sixth share of the rice."
Because he was authorized by a great body of people, the designation "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Authorized) arose.
Because he deserved a share of the rice from the rice-fields, the designation "Rājā" (King) arose.
He who protects and guards [the people] rightly is one consecrated upon the head (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*).
The perception arose:
"He is equal toward his mother and father as he is toward the people of the towns and countryside"; thus the perception arose: "He has attained the strength and vigor of the countryside."
Therefore, I am a consecrated Kṣatriya king who has attained the power and heroism of the realm.
The son of King Sammata was Kalyāṇa; the son of Kalyāṇa was Rava; the son of Rava was Upoṣadha; and the son of Upoṣadha was King Māndhātṛ.
King Māndhātṛ had many thousands of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants;
the last of these was the Ikṣvāku king named Sujāta, who ruled in the great city of Śāketa.
King Ikṣvāku Sujāta indeed had five sons: Opura, Nipura, Karakaṇḍaka, Ulkāmukha, and Hastikaśīrṣa;
and he had five daughters, the princesses Śuddhā, Vimalā, Vijitā, Jalā, and Jalī.
The prince named Jenta was the son of a courtesan.
His mother was named Jentī.
King Sujāta was won over by her through the wiles of a woman;
the king became filled with affection for her.
The delighted king invited Jentī to choose a boon.
I invite you with a boon, O Jentī;
whatever boon you ask of me, that boon I grant to you.
Then she said:
"Your Majesty, as soon as I have taken leave of my parents, I shall then request a boon from your Highness."
She informed her mother and father.
"I have been invited by the king to choose a boon; therefore, what boon shall I state for you? What boon from the king shall I request?"
Then, among them, each spoke according to what he thought.
"Ask for an excellent village," he said.
Then there was another female wanderer who was wise, skillful, and intelligent.
She said:
"Who are you? You are the daughter of a courtesan; your son has no authority over even his paternal estate, much less over a kingdom."
These five princes, sons of a Kṣatriya maiden, have authority over their paternal kingdom and wealth.

You have been invited by the king to choose a boon, and King Sujāta is one who does not refuse, who speaks the truth, and who acts exactly as he speaks; therefore, you should request a boon from the king.
"Having banished these five princes from the kingdom, consecrate my son Jenta as the crown prince."
After the passing of this god, he will become king in the great city of Śāketa.
Then all this will come to pass for you.
Thus was King Sujāta entreated for this boon by her.
"Great King, having banished these five princes from the kingdom, consecrate Prince Jenta as the crown prince;
then, upon Your Majesty's passing, he shall become king in the great city of Śāketa."
May the king grant this boon to me.
Having heard this, Sujāta became dejected out of affection for those princes; yet, having granted the boon, it was not possible to make it otherwise.
The king said to Queen Jentī:
"So be it; the prince Dinna, the son of the courtesan, shall be consecrated as the crown prince."
In that assembly of people, there was longing because of the greatness of the princes' virtues: "Whatever is the destiny of the princes, that shall be our destiny."
King Sujāta heard that a great multitude of people from the kingdom of Śāketa would go into exile together with the princes.
Therefore, he caused a proclamation to be made in the great city of Śāketa.
Whoever shall depart from Śāketa with the princes, whatever he may require for that purpose shall be granted from the royal treasury.
For those who have need of elephants, horses, chariots, draft animals, vehicles, carts, oxen, mules, goats, sheep, wealth,
or anything else— whether clothing, ornaments, male slaves, or female slaves— all that shall be supplied from the royal treasury for the sake of the king’s business.

While the princes were living abroad, by the king’s command the ministers released the treasury and granaries so that whatever anyone requested was given to them. Thus those princes, together with many thousands of country-folk and a great military force, and with many thousands of wagons, carriages, and vehicles, departed from the city of Śāketa and set out toward the north.
She was taken up by the King of Kāśi and Kośala.
The princes were virtuous, illustrious, sheltered from harm, pleasant to touch, meritorious, and righteous;
all the people of Kāśi and Kośala were fundamentally devoted to them.
Oh, how truly auspicious and righteous these princes are!
Regarding that king, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Śakrapraśna* [Sūtra]:
Gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and whoever else there may be who possess massive bodies, are all associated with the fetters of envy and avarice.
Envy arose within that King of Kāśi and Kośala.
Just as this assembly of people has come to hold these princes in high esteem for their virtues, it is possible that they might deprive me of my life and consecrate these princes in the kingdom.
Then they were banished by that King of Kāśi and Kosala as well.
On the slopes of the Himalayas there dwelt a seer named Kapila, who possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four meditative absorptions, and was of great psychic power and majesty.

His hermitage was very extensive and delightful, provided with roots, flowers, leaves, fruits, and water, and adorned with thousands of roots; furthermore, there was a great grove of *śākoṭa* trees there, and those princes then took up residence in that *śākoṭa* grove as well.
There, the merchants set out and proceeded toward the districts of Kāśī and Kośala.
Those merchants were asked by the people, "From where have you come?"
They said:
"From such-and-such a grove of *śākoṭa* trees."
The Śāketas and the Kośala merchants also go there to that Śākoṭa forest grove.
They too are questioned.
"Where will you go? he asked.
They also said:
The Śākoṭa forest grove along the Himalayas.
Then those princes, fearing that there might be a blemish upon their lineage, and out of dread of such a blemish, married one another's own maternal sisters.
King Sujāta asked his ministers:
"O ministers, where do the princes dwell?"
The ministers said:
"Your Majesty, in the region beyond the Himalayas there is a great forest tract of Śākoṭaka trees; there the princes dwell."
The king asks his ministers.
From where were the wives brought by the princes?
The ministers said:

"Great King, we have heard that out of fear of the corruption of their lineage, the princes have each married their own maternal sisters as wives to one another, thinking, 'Lest there be a corruption of our lineage.'"
Then King Sujāta questioned the domestic priest and other learned brahmins.
It is possible to act in this very way, just as it was done by those princes.
Those brahmin scholars, headed by the family priest, said:
It is possible, Great King, that the princes are not stained by fault on account of that cause.
Having heard this from the learned brahmins, King Sujāta was thrilled, satisfied, and elated, and he uttered this inspired utterance:
Furthermore, sirs, the princes are capable.
Then, for those Kāmārās, the designation, convention, and conceptualization "Śākyas" arose.
Then this thought occurred to those princes: "How long shall we continue to dwell here in this grove of *śākoṭaka* trees?
This great multitude of people is approaching."
"What if we were now to have a city built?"
Then those princes went into the presence of the seer Kapila.
Having bowed at the feet of the seer, they said:
"If the Blessed One Kapila would grant us permission, we would build this city named Kapilavastu after the name of the Seer."
The seer said:
"If you turn this hermitage of mine into a royal family's residence and construct a city there, then I shall grant my permission."
Those princes said to the seer:
We shall act in accordance with the intention of the seer.
Having made this hermitage a royal palace, we shall build a city.
The seer took that vessel, the water-pot of those youths, and gave it to them filled with water.
The princes also, having made that hermitage of the seer their royal palace, had a city constructed.
Because the site was given by the seer Kapila, the name Kapilavastu arose.

Thus the great city of Kapilavastu became prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, populous, filled with happy inhabitants, and surrounded by a vast retinue of subjects;
it became renowned in every direction and intermediate quarter, abounding in festivals and assemblies, dear to merchants, and perfected in commerce.
Now, among those five princes—Opura, Nipura, Karaṇḍaka, Uklāmukha, and Hastikaśīrṣa—the prince Opura was the eldest.
Thus he was consecrated to the kingdom in Kapilavastu.
Opura had a son named Nipura; Nipura, the king, had a son named Karakaṇḍa; Karakaṇḍa, the king, had a son named Ulkāmukha; Ulkāmukha’s son was Hastikaśīrṣa;
and Hastikaśīrṣa’s son was Siṃhahanu.
King Siṃhahanu had four sons—Śuddhodana, Dhautodana, Śuklodana, and Amṛtodana—and a daughter named Amitā.

Now, at that time, there was the daughter of another prominent Śākyan, who was gracious, beautiful to behold, of noble presence, and endowed with supreme beauty; yet this young woman had contracted the disease of leprosy.
She was then seized by that disease of leprosy.

Physicians apply themselves; all possible treatments are performed, yet there is no improvement. Ointments and counter-ointments are applied, and emetics and purgatives are administered, but the disease of leprosy is not pacified.
All [this] is a single wound caused by a stake.
Upon seeing her, compassion arises in every person.
Then, having been placed in a vehicle by her brothers, she was led away toward the Himalayas.

There, having had a cave excavated on Mount Utsaṅga, they caused that girl to enter it; and having provided an abundance of solid and soft food, water, bedding, and clothing, they firmly closed the door of the cave, piled up a great heap of earth over it, and entered the city of Kapilavastu.
Now, as that girl lived there in the cave, due to that lack of wind, the confinement, and the heat of the cave, her entire leprosy disease was expelled;
her body became clean and free of sores, and she acquired such supreme beauty that it could no longer be known whether she was a human being.
Then, at that very spot, a tiger came wandering about.
Animals see with their noses; Brahmins see with the Vedas;
kings see with their spies; and other subjects see with their eyes.
Then that tiger caught the scent of the human.
Then, having sniffed that human scent, he pushed that great heap of dust away with his feet.
And not far from there lived a royal seer named Kāla, who possessed the five superknowledges and had attained the four meditative absorptions.
His hermitage was provided with roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and water; it was endowed with various kinds of trees and was delightful.
Then that seer, while walking about and wandering through the hermitage grounds, arrived at the place where that Śākya maiden had been placed inside the cave.
That tiger also pushed away the entire heap of dust with its paw, until only the wood remained.
Then that tiger, seeing the seer, retreated as the seer [approached].
Seeing that dust removed by the tiger, curiosity arose in the sage.
Then that seer removed those logs and opened the door of the cave.
By him, with supreme vigor, the Śākya maiden was seen, yet he did not even know her to be human.
This seer asks.
"O auspicious lady, who are you?"
That human woman said:
"I am the daughter of such-and-such a Śākya from Kapilavastu."
Thus, I, Jīvantikā, being afflicted here with the disease of leprosy, have been abandoned in this way.
Upon seeing that Śākya maiden, who possessed supreme beauty, a fierce passion arose within him.
Even if one has long practiced the holy life and has not yet eradicated the underlying tendency toward passion,
that poison of passion will flare up again, just as it remains within the wood when it has not been removed.
Now that royal seer, having entered into union with that Śākyan maiden, fell away from his meditations and his supernormal powers.
Then, taking that Śākya maiden, he went to his hermitage.
Now that Śākya maiden lived there in that hermitage together with the royal seer Kola.
She gave birth to sixteen twin sons.
There were thirty-two young sages, gracious and beautiful to behold, wearing deerskins and matted hair.
Then, when those young seers had grown up, they were sent by their mother to Kapilavastu.

"Go, sons, to the great city of Kapilavastu. A certain Śākyan named so-and-so is your father’s maternal grandfather. His sons, such-and-such, are your maternal uncles; they are for the most part eminent Śākyans and kinsmen, and your family lineage is great."
They will provide for your livelihood.
She was instructed in the customary conduct of the Śākyans.
In this way you should approach the assembly of Śākyas; in this way you should offer salutation; in this way you should sit down.
Having instructed them all in the Śākya customs, they were dismissed.
Having paid homage to their mother and father and circumambulated them, they departed and arrived at Kapilavastu by stages.
All of them, according to their seniority and in order of age, entered Kapilavastu.
Upon seeing those young seers, the great multitude of people took notice.
Oh, how such young sages are pleasing and beautiful to behold, wearing deerskins and matted hair!
Then, surrounded by a great multitude of people, they approached the assembly hall of the Śākyas.
And about five hundred Śākyas were seated together, assembled in the assembly hall for some particular business.
Then, having been instructed by their mother, they approached the assembly of the Śākyas with that same deportment.
The assembly of Śākyas was astonished upon seeing that conduct of the young seers, which was the traditional custom of the Śākyas.
Then the Śākyas questioned the young seers.
"From where have you come?"
They reported all that matter to her exactly as she had been instructed by her mother.
"In the Himalayas, from such-and-such a hermitage, she is the daughter of the royal seer Kāla and the daughter of such-and-such a Śākya; she is my mother."
Just as that Śākya maiden had been sent away to that region, so too, having heard it from their mother, those Śākyas reported everything to him.
The Śākyas, having heard this, were delighted.
Their maternal grandfather, that eminent Śākya, is also still living and possesses a great lineage.
That royal seer Kola, having consecrated his eldest son to the kingship in Vārāṇasī, went forth as a seer; that great-souled royal seer became renowned and fully recognized throughout the quarters.
Then those Śākyas became joyful, thinking, "These have been born from a royal seer, not from an ordinary man."
It occurred to those Śākyas:
"These princes are well-born to us; let these Śākya maidens be given to them, as well as their livelihood."
They gave those princes Śākya maidens in marriage and bestowed upon them agricultural lands together with their surrounding districts—
namely, the villages of Āśrama, Nigama, Sumukta, and Karkarabhadra— as well as other agricultural lands with their districts and abundant private wealth.
Because they were born from the seer Kola, they are known as the Koliyas, and they are also known as the Vyāghrāpadyas.
Thus ends the account of the origin of the Koliyas in the glorious Mahāvastu Avadāna.
Now, there was a town of the Śākyas named Devaḍaha.
There was a prominent Śākyan named Subhūti, who had brought home as his wife a Koliyan maiden from a certain town.
To her were born seven daughters: Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Atimāyā, Anantamāyā, Cūlīyā, Kolīsovā, and Mahāprajāpatī.
The arising of illusion.
King Siṃhahanu, the Śākya king, had four sons and one daughter: Śuddhodana, Śuklodana, Dhutodana, Amṛtodana, and the daughter Amitā.
When King Siṃhahanu had passed away, Śuddhodana obtained the kingdom.
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers: "Bring me a maiden who is suitable—one who is both beautiful and of noble birth."
Those ministers dispatched on all sides brahmins who were wise, highly learned, and experts in the rules concerning the characteristics of women, men, and girls.
Go and find a maiden who would be suitable for King Śuddhodana.
While those brahmins were searching through villages, market towns, cities, and provinces, they saw the seven daughters of Subhūti the Śākya in the Śākya town of Devaḍaha;
among those seven daughters, Māyā was the most excellent, and such a maiden is very difficult to find in all of Jambudvīpa.

They informed the king: "In the town of Subhūti the Śākyan, there are seven daughters who are gracious and beautiful to behold; and among all these seven sisters, one is preeminent in beauty, in splendor, and in wisdom, endowed with every excellence—she is named Māyā."
"However many villages, towns, market towns, and districts we have searched, we have never before seen a maiden like Māyā, the daughter of the Śākyan Subhūti.
Then Śuddhodana sent word to Subhūti.
"Give me your daughter Māyā to be my wife; she shall become my chief queen."
Subhūti said to the messengers:
When Māyā’s six elder daughters had been married off, she would then be given to the Great King;
thus those messengers informed King Śuddhodana.
"Great King, Subhūti the Śākya spoke thus."
"As long as these six elder daughters are being married off, then Māyā shall be given to the Great King.
King Śuddhodana again sent a messenger to the Śākya Subhūti, saying,
"Give me all seven of your daughters."
Those messengers informed Subhūti the Śākyan.
King Śuddhodana said,
"Give all seven of my daughters to me."
Subhūti the Śākya sent a message to King Śuddhodana.
"O Great King, let them be granted to you."
Then all those seven girls were brought from the town of Devadaha to Kapilavastu by King Śuddhodana with great royal majesty, great royal power, and great royal prosperity.
King Śuddhodana caused two daughters, Māyā and Mahāprajāpatī, to enter his own inner apartments;
five other daughters were given to his five brothers.
In twelve years, the Bodhisattva will descend from the Tuṣita heaven.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods announce to the Pratyekabuddhas in Jambudvīpa: "A Bodhisattva is about to descend; leave the Buddha-field!"
From the Tuṣita heaven, the one of exceeding fame, possessing infinite knowledge and vision, will descend;
leave the buddha-field of him who bears the excellent marks.
Having heard that sound of "Buddha," the Pratyekabuddhas— who were like the most excellent Maheśvaras, liberated in mind, self-arisen, and masters over their own thoughts— entered into parinirvāṇa.
Then those Pratyekabuddhas, having each delivered their own prophecies, returned to Pāṭaliputra.
In Vārāṇasī, at a distance of one and a half yojanas, there was a great forest tract where five hundred pratyekabuddhas resided.
Having each given their own individual prophecies, they too have entered final nirvāṇa.
Possessing attained vigor, constantly engaged in practice, with uplifted minds and free from indolence,
firm in their prowess and endowed with the power of energy, they wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having risen into the air and entered the fire-element, they attained final nirvana without further clinging.
The flesh and blood were consumed by the fire-element within his own body;
his physical remains fell away.
Cultivating equanimity and compassion, and practicing sympathetic joy at the proper time,

with a mind of loving-kindness, compassionate for the welfare of others, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. (358) Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings, not harming even the slightest among them, having cast away the rod toward the mobile and the immobile, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the insignia of a householder, like a *pāripātra* tree with its leaves withered,
and having gone forth clad in saffron robes, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast aside the emblems of a householder like a fire in ashes,
clad in saffron robes, one should go forth and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

For one who associates [with others], excessive affection may arise; from this affection, suffering follows. But one who associates while feeling revulsion [for such ties] should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates intimacy, excessive affection may arise; from such affection, this suffering follows.
Seeing the danger in excessive affection for those dear, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who associates with others, excessive affection may arise; from such affection, this suffering comes forth.
Loathing the separation from those dear to him, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who associates closely with others, excessive affection may arise; from this affection, suffering follows.
Reflecting upon the dangers inherent in friendships, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates intimacy, excessive affection may arise; from this affection, suffering follows as its consequence.
Reflecting upon the dangers inherent in children, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Looking toward sons and companions, one whose mind is bound loses his true purpose.
One should not desire sons, much less companions; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One whose mind is bound loses wealth while looking toward kinsmen and companions;
one should not desire kinsmen, much less companions—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The entire Khaḍgaviṣāṇagāthā should be recited in detail.
Each of the five hundred Pratyekabuddhas has one verse.
And because the sages fell there, it is called Ṛṣipatana.
In that forest grove, a king of deer named Rāhaka tended a herd of a thousand deer.
He had two sons named Nyagrodha and Viśākha.
Then that king of deer gave five hundred deer to one son, and he gave five hundred deer to the other son as well.
Brahmadatta, the king of Kāśi, used to go out frequently on hunts throughout that forest grove, and there he would kill the deer.
He does not subsist upon as many deer as those that, having entered into forest thickets, deep woods, reed-beds, cane-beds, and thorn-beds, perish after being struck down.
There they are devoured by crows and spears.
Nyagrodha, the king of deer, said to his brother Viśākha:
Viśākha, let us make this request to the King of Kāśi.
You do not personally subsist on as many deer as those that, having been struck down, enter into dense thickets and die, or are devoured by crows and birds of prey.
"We shall provide the king daily with one deer, which shall enter the kitchen of its own accord."
And this herd of deer will not thus fall into misfortune and ruin.
His brother Viśākha said:
"Let it be so; we shall inform him."
Now the king has gone out for a hunt.
Those leaders of the herds, the kings of deer, saw the king from afar as he approached with his army and mounts, surrounded by those bearing swords, bows, spears, and lances.
Then, seeing the king, they went out to meet him face-to-face—undaunted and unafraid, having surrendered their very selves.
Then the King of Kāśi saw the two kings of deer approaching from afar.
He gave an order to his own vanguard of troops.
"No one should disturb these deer as they approach; who knows what the outcome here may be, that they do not flee upon seeing the tip of my spear, but instead come right toward me?"
The vanguard of those troops was deployed between the deer; that vanguard was positioned on both the left and the right.
Those deer approached the king and prostrated at his knees.
The king questioned those kings of the deer.
What is your request? Make known whatever business you have.
Then they petitioned that king with human speech.
O Great King, we inform you.
We were born and raised here in your kingdom, in this forest grove, as were many hundreds of other deer.
"Among these deer, two brothers who are leaders of the herd dwell here in the great king's realm."

Just as the cities, towns, villages, and districts of the Great King are adorned by people, by cattle and oxen, and by thousands of other living beings, both bipeds and quadrupeds; even so these forest groves, hermitages, rivers, and springs are adorned by these deer and birds.
In this way, Great King, this is the adornment of that empowerment.

"O Great King, all these bipeds and quadrupeds, however many there may be dwelling within Your Majesty’s realm—whether they be in villages, in the forest, or on the mountains—they have gone for refuge to Your Majesty;
all of them, O Great King, must be cared for and protected."
And the Great King has authority over them; no other king does.
At whatever time the Great King goes out for a hunt, many hundreds of deer meet with misfortune and ruin.

Those that are struck by his arrows and enter these forest thickets, reed thickets, *śara* grass beds, and *kāśa* grass beds and die there, being devoured by crows and birds, are not as many as those who become the Great King’s source of livelihood; furthermore, the Great King is tainted by unrighteousness (*adharma*).
"If there is favor from the Great King, we two leaders of the herds will each send one deer daily for the Great King.

From one herd, we shall send one deer on the first day; from the second herd, we shall send one deer on the second day. Thus, the Great King’s consumption of deer meat will not be interrupted, and these deer will likewise not fall into misfortune or ruin."
Then the king granted a request to those leaders of the deer herds.
"Let it be as you intend; go, dwell without fear or trembling, and send one deer to me every day."
Having granted their request, the king spoke to his ministers.
No one at all should harass the deer.
Having thus given his command, he entered the city.
All those deer were gathered together by those herd-leaders and comforted.

"Do not fear; we have petitioned the king in such a way that the king shall no longer go out for the hunt, nor shall he ever again harass the deer. Furthermore, one deer must be released for the king every day—one from one herd on one day, and another from another herd on the following day."
Those deer, having counted all those deer from both herds, made a reduction from each respective herd.
From one herd, a deer goes to the king’s kitchen on one day; from another herd, it goes on the next day.
Once, when Viśākha was away from his herd, it was the turn of a pregnant doe to go to the king’s kitchen.
Then that doe was addressed by the deer who was the messenger:
"It is your turn today; go to the king's kitchen."
She said:
"I am pregnant; there are two fetuses in my womb. For now, appoint another [guardian]; when I have given birth, I shall go. Then we two shall pursue the three goals of life for the sake of one."
It will be your turn again only after a very long time, once these two young ones have been born.
That commanding deer reported this matter to the leader of the herd.
The leader of the herd said:
"Command another deer who is between this doe."
This doe, having given birth, will follow behind.
That deer, acting as a messenger, bypassed that female deer and directed [the other] who was between her to go to the king’s kitchen.
He too said:
"It is not my turn today; it is the turn of such-and-such a doe today. In this way, I shall live for a while longer."
In this way, others and yet others are also addressed, and they do not depart without having made their confession;
everyone speaks.
"It is the turn of such-and-such a doe; let her go."
That doe was addressed thus:
"Lady, no one wishes to go without being on duty.
It is your turn; you yourself must go to the king's kitchen."
Then, at the time when she could not be released, out of affection for her fawns and fearing that they too would be killed due to her capture, she went to that second herd of deer.
And she prostrated herself before that leader of the herd.
Thus, the leader of the herd asks them.
"What is this, noble lady? What do you command? What is to be done?"
She said:
Today, therefore, it was my turn from this herd to go to the king’s kitchen; and since I had two calves in my womb, I made a request to that leader of the herd, Viśākha.
"Today is my turn, and these two young ones are within my womb.
Send another; when I have given birth, I shall go then."
And those others who were commanded by that leader of the herd also did not wish to go, saying, "It is not our turn; it is the turn of such-and-such a doe; let her go."
Thus, I am not released by them; as my turn arrives, I am told, "Go, it is your turn. Therefore, I desire that the king of deer release another deer.
At the time when I have given birth, then I shall depart.
Then the king of deer said to the doe:
"Do not be afraid; I shall send another."
That king of deer commanded a messenger deer: "From this herd, send whichever deer's turn it is; I have granted safety to this doe."
That overseer then orders whichever deer's turn it is.
Go to the king's kitchen.
He also said:
"It is not our turn today in the herd; it is Viśākha’s turn. As for the doe whose turn it is, she is pregnant with two fawns in her womb.
Therefore, you must not be released; it is your turn, so you go."
And while that doe was not yet released from there, she came back to this herd and informed the leader of the herd, Nyagrodha.
The herd-leader Nyagrodha granted safety to that doe.
It was commanded by the leader of the herd.
"Release him who is the one whose turn it is from this herd."
It is your turn; go from this herd.
He said:
Today is the turn of the second; I would not go on my rounds when it is not his turn.
In this way, whoever was commanded also did not wish to go to Anosara.
That messenger deer informed Nyagrodha, the lord of deer.
No one wishes to go without a turn; they say, "It is not our turn today; it is the turn of the second deer herd; today is their turn."
The king of beasts said:
"I have granted this doe immunity from death by the thousands.
It is no longer possible to send her back there to the kitchen;
I shall go there myself."
Then that king of deer, having descended from that forest thicket onto the path, went toward Vārāṇasī.
Whichever man sees that king of deer as it goes, he follows after it.
The deer was beautiful in form, variegated and adorned, with red hooves and eyes as dark as collyrium, radiant and lovely to behold.

Placed at the head of a great multitude of people, he proceeded until he entered the inner city; there he was seen and recognized by the citizens as that king of deer before the great throng of people.
Having seen that king of deer, they were filled with longing; "That entire herd has been destroyed, yet here is the leader of the herd himself who has come! 364.

"Let us go and inform the king so that this king of deer may be released and not killed; for his ornament has become a delight to the eyes of this city as he runs about in the parks and by the ponds."
Having seen that deer, they experience delight for the eyes.
Together with that very same chief minister and a great multitude of people, he entered the royal palace following behind the king of deer.
The king of deer entered the kitchen, while the king was seated in the court of justice with these citizens, and they made a representation to him.
"Great King, that entire herd of deer has been completely exhausted."
Harmless, they feed upon dry and green grass and do no wrong to anyone; yet they have all been destroyed—here is that very leader of the herd who has come in person.
"O Great King, such a king of beasts is difficult to find—one so gracious, beautiful to behold, and pleasing to the eyes of people."
People rush out from the city to the gardens, the ponds, the groves, or the lotus-pools; and upon seeing that king of deer, they become joyful, for he has become an ornament of the city’s parks.
O Great King, if it please you, let this king of deer be released alive.
The king commanded his ministers.
"Go and bring that king of deer, the great monarch, from the kitchen."
So, having gone with those ministers, he was brought from the kitchen into the presence of the king.
The king questioned that king of deer.
"Why have you come yourself? There is no longer any other deer for you to hunt, such that you have come yourself."
Then the king of deer said:
For it is not the case, O Great King, that there are no other deer.
But today is the turn of the second deer herd.
In that regard, whichever doe’s turn it was, she became pregnant and carried two young ones in her womb.
That doe was told: "Go to the kitchen; today it is your turn."
In the second deer herd, Viśākha is the leader of the herd.
She went to him and said:
"Today is my turn to go to the king’s kitchen; however, I am pregnant with two children in my womb, and I wish for another to be sent instead. When I have given birth, I shall go."
Then, whichever other deer was summoned did not wish to go; he spoke, saying, "It is this doe's turn; let her go. Yet, he was not released by those deer.
"Today is your turn; you should go. But she did not release him and came to my presence.

"I have been requested by her [the lioness] for the past 365 days: 'Today my turn has come from that herd; I have two cubs in my womb, and I cannot be released from them. Therefore, I wish for the king of beasts to command another from this herd who might go to the royal kitchen, so that by the time I have given birth, I may depart from there.'"
I granted safety to that doe, Mṛgī; yet whenever a deer was commanded by me [to go], he would not wish to do so.
"It is not our turn; it is the turn of the second herd"—thus, whichever one was commanded, he would not wish to come here while it was not his turn.
"I know that I have granted safety to this doe; I am going myself"—thinking thus, I have come here in person.
When the king heard that deer, he and the entire multitude of people were struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh, how youthful this king of deer appears!"
It occurred to that king of Kāśī:

"This is no mere beast that, for the sake of another, sacrifices its own life and knows the Dharma. We are the beasts who do not know the Dharma—those who would bring harm to such jewels among beings who are themselves free from malice."
He said this to that king of deer:
I am pleased with you; you are compassionate and noble-minded, since, even while in the form of a deer, you granted safety to that female deer who was your own servant.
I too, having come to you and by your word, grant safety from fear to all deer.
"From this day forward, I grant safety to all those deer who are in that region; go and dwell there, free from fear and without anxiety."
The king had a proclamation made by the sounding of bells throughout the city.
"By no one in my realm are the deer to be harmed," [the king declared], because that king had granted them the gift of fearlessness.
This report reached as far as the gods.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, in order to test the king, manifested many hundreds and thousands of deer.
The entire Kāśi country was overrun with deer; there was no field where there were not deer.
The king was petitioned by the people of the countryside.
Then that female deer was addressed by Nyagrodha, the king of deer:
"O auspicious lady, go to the herd of Viśākha."
She said:
O King of Beasts, I shall not go; it is better to die at your feet than to live at the feet of Viśākha.
Then that doe spoke this verse:
One should resort only to the *nyagrodha* tree and not long for the *viśākha*;
death under the *nyagrodha* is better than life under the *viśākha*.
The people of the countryside petitioned the king.
The countryside is being ravaged and the prosperous kingdom is perishing;
deer are devouring the grain—restrain them, O lord of men!
Let the countryside be ruined and the flourishing kingdom perish;
yet, having granted a boon to the king of beasts, I would never speak a falsehood.
A gift of deer was given; thus it is called Ṛṣipattana, "the Deer Park."

Twelve years before the Bodhisattva was to descend from the Tuṣita heaven, the Śuddhāvāsa deities, having assumed the guise of brahmins, taught the Vedas, the mantras, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man to those brahmins, so that they might prophesy when the Bodhisattva had arrived here.
